meaning: flirt; flirtatious woman; woman who tries to attract the admiration of men without sincere feelings; V.
etymology: Borrowed from French coquette.

meaning: behave in a way that attracts (sexual) attention; deal triflingly with; N: one (or woman) given to flirting; ADJ. flirtatious
etymology: 1553, from the merger of Early Modern English flirt (“to flick”), flurt (“to mock, jibe, scorn”), and flirt, flurt (“a giddy girl”). Of obscure origin and relation. Apparently related to similar words in Germanic, all of apparently onomatopoeic origin, compare Low German flirt (“a flick of the fingers, a light blow”), Low German flirtje (“a giddy girl”), Low German flirtje (“a flirt”), German Flittchen (“a flirt; tart; hussy”), Norwegian flira (“to giggle, titter”). Compare also Early Modern English jillflirt, gillian flirt, and flirt-gill (“a flirt”), and Scots flird (“a trifling", also, "to jibe, jeer at, talk idly, flirt, flaunt”), which is perhaps from Middle English flerd (“mockery, fraud, deception”), from Old English fleard (“nonsense, vanity, folly, deception”); potentially related to Icelandic flærð (“trickiness, deceit”), Swedish flärd (“vanity, frivolity, flamboyance”), Dutch flard (“tatter, shred”). See flird.

meaning: warmly friendly; gracious; heartfelt; Ex. cordial welcome
etymology: Inherited from Middle English cordial, from Old French cordial, from Medieval Latin cordiālis (“of the heart”), from cor (“heart”).

meaning: extended line of men or fortifications to prevent access or egress; (¾î±ú¿¡¼­ °Üµå¶û ¹ØÀ¸·Î °ÉÄ¡´Â) Àå½Ä ¸®º»; V.
etymology: From Middle English cordon, from Middle French cordon, from Old French cordon, diminutive of corde. More at cord.

meaning: projecting molding on building (usually above columns or pillars); Ã³¸¶ Àå½Ä
etymology: From Middle French corniche or Italian cornice, possibly from either (1) Latin cornīx (“crow”) or (2) Latin coronis (“curved line, flourish in writing”), from Ancient Greek κορωνίς (korōnís). See also corniche.

meaning: horn (or horn-shaped container) overflowing with fruit and grain; symbol of abundance; horn of plenty
etymology: Borrowed from Latin cornūcōpia.

meaning: natural consequence (which naturally follows from something else)
etymology: From Middle English, from Late Latin corōllārium (“money paid for a garland; gift, gratuity, corollary; consequence, deduction”), from corōlla (“small garland”), diminutive of corōna (“crown”).

meaning: bodily (rather than spiritual); of a bodily form; material; tangible
etymology: From Middle English corporealle, equivalent to Latin corporeus + -al, from corpus (“body”); compare corporal.

meaning: very fat; N. corpulence
etymology: From Middle English corpulent, from Old French corpulent, from Latin corpulentus.

meaning: collection (of writings or information); Ex. the corpus of Shakespear'works; Cf. corpse
etymology: Borrowed from Latin corpus (“body”). Doublet of corpse, corps, and riff.

meaning: red or white cell in the blood
etymology: From Latin corpusculum, diminutive of corpus (“body”).

meaning: mutual relationship
etymology: From Middle French corrélation. Morphologically correlate + -ion.

meaning: either of the correlated things; V.
etymology: From cor- + relate.

meaning: confirm; support; strengthen
etymology: First attested in the 1530s; borrowed from Latin corrōborātus (“strengthened”), perfect passive participle of corrōborō (“to support, corroborate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from con- (“together”) + rōborō (“to strengthen”), from rōbur, rōboris (“strength”). Regular participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English, otherwise archaic.

meaning: destroy or wear away gradually by chemical action (over a long period)
etymology: From Middle English corrōden, that borrowed from Old French corroder or directly from Latin corrōdere (“to gnaw”), from con- (“completely”) + rōdere (“to gnaw”).

meaning: eating away by chemicals or disease; (of language) fierce
etymology: From Old French corrosif.

meaning: wrinkled; ridged
small ridge on a smooth surface (face or cloth); V.
etymology: From Middle English wrinkle, wrynkel (“crease, fold, wrinkle”), from the verb (see below). Cognate with Dutch wrinkel (“wrinkle, crease”). Compare also Middle English runkel (“wrinkle”), from Old Norse hrukka (“wrinkle”), from Proto-Germanic *hrunkwǭ (“wrinkle, crease”), whence also French fronce (“crooked smile, scowl, frown”), German Runzel (“wrinkle”), Danish rynke (“wrinkle”), Swedish rynka and rynkla (“wrinkle”).

meaning: wrinkle
etymology: From Middle English crenclen (“to bend, buckle”), from Old English *crinclian, frequentative form of Old English crincan (“to yield”), from Proto-Germanic *kringaną (“to turn, to fall, to yield”), from Proto-Indo-European *ger- (“to turn, wind”). Cognate with North Frisian krenge, krönge (“to obtain, reach, attain”), Dutch krinkelen (“to turn, wind”). Related to cringe.

meaning: pertaining to the universe; vast
etymology: Borrowed from Ancient Greek κοσμικός (kosmikós).

meaning: group that meets socially; select circle; close group of people with shared interests
etymology: Borrowed from French coterie.

meaning: approve; support; tolerate; Ex. countenance his rude behavior; N: face; appearance
etymology: From Middle English contenaunce, countenaunce, from Anglo-Norman countenance and Old French contenance, from the present participle of contenir, or from Late Latin continentia, and therefore a doublet of continence.

meaning: cancel; revoke (an order)
etymology: From Old French contremander, from Medieval Latin contramandō, from contra + mandō (“to order; to command”).

meaning: thing that completes another; things very much alike; thing that has the same purpose in a different system
etymology: From Middle English conterpart, countre parte (“duplicate of a legal document”), equivalent to counter- + part. Compare Old French contrepartie, itself from contre (“facing, opposite”) (from Latin contra (“against”)) + partie (“copy of a person or thing”) (originally past participle of partīre (“to divide”)).

meaning: highly successful action or sudden attack; coup (s) d'\'etat; CF. coup de gr\^ace: deathblow or shot which kills
etymology: Reborrowed in modern times from modern French coup (“blow, strike”), from Old French coup, colp, from Late Latin colpus, from Latin colaphus. Doublet of cope and colpus. The same Old French word had been borrowed into Middle English as coupe, caupe (with different pronunciation).

meaning: join; unite; OP. uncouple
etymology: From Middle English couple, from Old French couple, from Latin cōpula. Doublet of copula.

meaning: messenger
etymology: From a convergence of Middle English corour, currour, from Old French coreor, agent noun of corir (“to run”), and Middle English courier, a borrowing of Middle French courrier, from Italian corriere.

meaning: binding agreement between two groups or people; compact; V: enter into a covenant; promise
etymology: From Middle English covenaunt, borrowed from Old French covenant (“agreement”), from Latin conveniēns, convenientem (“agreeing, agreeable, suitable, convenient”), present participle of conveniō (“to agree”). Cognate with convenient and convene.

meaning: agreement between two groups or people; something for sale at a price advantageous to the buyer; V: negotiate; trade; Ex. bargaining power
etymology: Compare French barguigner and Portuguese barganhar.

meaning: secret; hidden; implied; OP. overt
etymology: From Middle English covert, from Old French covert, past participle of covrir (“to cover”) (corresponding to Latin coopertus); cognate to cover. Not closely related to overt, despite what the most common pronunciation would suggest.

meaning: avaricious; desirous of (someone else'possessions); V. covet: desire eagerly (someone else'possessions)
etymology: From Middle English coveitous, from Anglo-Norman *cuveitus, from Medieval Latin as if *cupiditosus, from Latin cupiditas (“desire”); see covet.

meaning: terrorize; intimidate
etymology: The plural kine is from Middle English kyne, kyn, kuin, kiin, kien (“cows”), either a double plural of Middle English ky, kye (“cows”), equivalent to modern kye + -en, or inherited from Old English cūna (“cows', of cows”), genitive plural of cū (“cow”).

meaning: shrink quivering as from fear; cringe
etymology: Cognate with German kauern (“to squat”), Dutch koeren (“to keep watch (in a cowered position)”), Serbo-Croatian kutriti (“to lie in a bent position”), Swedish kura (“huddle, cower”). Unrelated to coward, which is of Latin origin.

meaning: shy (flirtatiously); showing a (pretended) lack of self-confidence; modest; coquettish; CF. job offer¸¦ ¹Þ¾ÒÀ» ¶§
etymology: From Middle English coy, from Old French coi, earlier quei (“quiet, still”), from Latin qu(i)ētus (“resting, at rest”). Doublet of quit, quiet, quite, and quietus.

meaning: cheat; hoodwink; swindle
etymology: From coz(y) + -en.

meaning: sour; bad-tempered; peevish; difficult to read as handwriting
etymology: From Middle English crabbed; equivalent to crab + -ed.

meaning: bad-tempered; irritable; V. peeve: make angry
etymology: The adverb is derived from the adjective.

meaning: very unrefined; grossly insensible; crude and undiscriminating; Ex. crass behavior
etymology: From Middle English cras, craas, from Old French cras, from Latin crassus (“dense, thick, gross, fat, heavy”). Doublet of grease.

meaning: cowardly
etymology: From Middle English cravant, either borrowed from Old French cravanté (“defeated”), past participle of cravanter (ultimately from Latin crepare), or a modification of creaunt (“defeated”) after craven (“to crave”).

meaning: belief
etymology: From Middle English credence, from Old French credence, from Medieval Latin crēdentia (“belief, faith”), from Latin crēdēns, present active participle of crēdō (“loan, confide in, trust, believe”). Compare French croyance, French créance, Italian credenza, Portuguese crença, Romanian credință, Spanish creencia. Doublet of credenza.

meaning: creed
etymology: Inherited from Middle English credo, from Old French credo, from Latin crēdō (“to believe”); doublet of creed.

meaning: belief on slight evidence; gullibility; naivet\'e; ADJ. credulous
etymology: Inherited from Middle English credulite (“faith, belief”), borrowed from Middle French credulité (French crédulité), from Latin crēdulitās. Corresponding to credulous + -ity (compare credulosity).

meaning: system of religious or ethical belief
etymology: From Middle English crede, from Old English crēda, crēdo, from Latin crēdō (“to believe”), from Proto-Italic *krezdō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱréd-dʰeh₁-ti (“to trust, believe”, literally “to place one's heart”), a compound phrase of the oblique case form of *ḱḗr (“heart”). Creed is cognate with Old Irish creitid (“to believe”), Sanskrit श्रद्दधाति (śráddadhāti, “to have faith or faithfulness, to have belief or confidence, believe”).

meaning: increase in the volume or intensity as in a musical passage; climax; CF. crescent
etymology: Borrowed from Italian crescendo, gerund of crescere (“to grow, to increase”).

meaning: too improbable to be believed; implausible; Ex. far-fetched story
musical introduction to a long musical piece; first offer or proposal (to begin talks in the hope of reaching an agreement); Ex. overtures for peace
etymology: From Middle English overture, from Anglo-Norman, Middle French overture, from Old French overture, from Latin apertūra. Doublet of aperture.

meaning: dejected; dispirited
etymology: From crest + fallen, from the appearance of a horse with its crest (head) on its chest after defeat in a battle.

meaning: top (as of a hill or wave); showy feathers on the head of a bird
etymology: The informal meaning “design, logo” (noun sense 11) stems from a misinterpretation of the heraldic noun sense 4, which specifically refers to the object placed on top of the helm.

meaning: crack; fissure
etymology: From Middle English crevice, from Old French crevace, from crever (“to break, burst”), from Latin crepō (“to break, burst, crack”). Doublet of crevasse.

meaning: shrink back as if in fear; cower
etymology: The noun and adjective are derived from the verb via zero derivation.

meaning: standards used in judging; CF. criterion
etymology: The plural form of criterion, formed according to the Ancient Greek -ον (-on) → -α (-a) pluralisation pattern.

meaning: hag; ugly old woman
etymology: From Middle English crone, from Anglo-Norman carogne (compare central Old French charogne (a term of abuse, literally “carrion, carcass, old sheep, hag”), whence modern French charogne). Doublet of carrion.

meaning: (of someone old) eccentric; odd; whimsical; bad-tempered; N. crotchet: odd or whimsical notion
etymology: From crotchet + -y, using crotchet in the 16th-century sense of a whim or fancy.

meaning: essential or main point; Ex. the crux of the problem; ADJ. crucial: of deciding importance
etymology: Borrowed from Latin crux (“cross, wooden frame for execution”), possibly from the Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn, to bend”). Doublet of cross and crouch (“cross”).

meaning: secret recess or vault usually used for burial; underground room (under a church)
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin crypta (“vault”), from Ancient Greek κρυπτός (kruptós, “hidden”). Doublet of grotto.

meaning: mysterious; hidden; secret
etymology: From Late Latin crypticus, from Ancient Greek κρυπτικός (kruptikós), from κρυπτός (kruptós, “hidden”), from κρύπτω (krúptō, “to hide”). Doublet of kryptic.

meaning: small chamber used for sleeping or work
etymology: From Late Middle English cubicle, from Latin cubiculum (“bedroom”). Doublet of cubiculum.

meaning: one of the parts into which an enclosed space is divided
etymology: First attested 1564, from Middle French compartiment, from Italian compartimento, from Late Latin compartiri (“to divide with, to share with”), from com- + partiri (“to apportion, to divide, to share”).

meaning: style of cooking; Ex. French cuisine
etymology: Borrowed from French cuisine (“cooking, culinary art, kitchen”), from Late Latin cocīna, from earlier coquīna (“kitchen”). Doublet of kitchen.

meaning: relating to cooking or kitchen
etymology: Borrowed from French culinaire, itself a borrowing from Latin culīnārius, from culīna (“kitchen”).

meaning: pick out from others (to kill the weakest members); reject; select; collect (information); N.
etymology: From Middle English cullen, cuilen, coilen, from Old French cuillir (“collect, gather, select”), from Latin colligō (“gather together”). Doublet of coil.

meaning: highest point; climax; V. culminate in: reach the highest point in; end in; Ex. a series of minor clashes culminating in war
etymology: Borrowed from French culmination, from culminer, or from Medieval Latin culminatus + -tion. Morphologically culminate + -ion.

meaning: deserving blame; blameworthy
etymology: From Middle English culpable, from Old French culpable, from Latin culpābilis (“blameworthy”), from culpō (“to blame, condemn”), from culpa (“a fault, crime, mistake”). Compare also culprit.

meaning: one guilty of a crime
etymology: From Anglo-Norman cul. prit, contraction of culpable: prest (d'averrer nostre bille) 'guilty: ready (to prove our case)', words used by prosecutor in opening a trial, mistaken in English for an address to the defendant. See culpable. It may have been influenced by Latin culpa (“blame, fault”).

meaning: artificial channel for water; drain crossing under a road
etymology: * a derivation from an unrecorded Dutch word, possibly *coul-vaart, a combination of Dutch coul-, from French couler (“to flow”), and Dutch vaart (“a trip by boat, a canal”).

meaning: heavy and awkward to carry or wear; burdensome; Ex. cumbersome parcel/uniform
etymology: From Middle English cumbyrsum, cummyrsum; equivalent to cumber (“hindrance”) + -some. Compare encumber and incumbent.

meaning: growing by addition; accumulative
etymology: From cumulate + -ive. Compare also French cumulatif, Italian cumulativo and Spanish cumulativo.

meaning: greed (for wealth); CF. cupid; CF. Cupid
etymology: From French cupidité, from Latin cupiditās (“strong desire”), from cupidus (“keen, desirous”). Compare Cupid.

meaning: superintendent; manager (in charge of a museum or a library)
etymology: From Latin cūrātor (“one who has care of a thing, a manager, guardian, trustee”), from cūrāre (“to take care of”), from cūra (“care, heed, attention, anxiety, grief”).

meaning: churlish, miserly individual; bad-tempered old person
etymology: The word is attested from the late 1500s in the forms curmudgeon and curmudgen, and during the 17th century in numerous spelling variants, including cormogeon, cormogion, cormoggian, cormudgeon, curmudgion, curmuggion, curmudgin, curr-mudgin, curre-megient.

meaning: (of writing) flowing; running; having the successive letters joined
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French cursif, from Medieval Latin cursīvus, from Latin cursus.

meaning: casual; hastily done with little attention to detail
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French cursoire (“rapid”), from Latin cursorius (“hasty, of a race or running”).

meaning: shorten; reduce
etymology: Alteration of curtal, from Old French courtault (“which has been shortened”), itself from court (“short”) (from Latin curtus) + -ault

meaning: skeptical or distrustful of human motives; N. cynicism; CF. cynic: person who believes all people are motivated by selfishness
etymology: Originated 1542, from Classical Latin cynicus (“Cynic/cynic”, adjective) + -al. By surface analysis, cynic + -al. In reference to dogs, with allusion to the ultimate etymology (Ancient Greek κυνικός (kunikós, “doglike”)).

meaning: object of general attention; person or thing that is a center of attention; CF. Ursa Minor
etymology: From Middle French Cynosure (“Ursa Minor; Polaris”), from Latin Cynosūra (“Ursa Minor”), from Ancient Greek Κυνόσουρα (Kunósoura, “Ursa Minor”, literally “dog’s tail”), from κυνός (kunós, “dog's”) + οὐρά (ourá, “tail”).

meaning: work at in a nonserious fashion; splash around; move noisily in a liquid
etymology: From earlier dable, equivalent to dab + -le (frequentative suffix), possibly from Middle Dutch dabbelen (“to pinch; knead; to fumble; to dabble”); cognate with Icelandic dafla (“to dabble”).

meaning: raised platform for speakers or other important people
etymology: From Middle English deis, from Anglo-Norman deis, from Old French deis, dois (modern French dais), from Latin discum, accusative singular of discus (“discus, disc, quoit; dish”) (Late Latin discum (“table”)), from Ancient Greek δίσκος (dískos, “discus, disc; tray”), from δικεῖν (dikeîn, “to cast, to throw; to strike”). Cognate with Italian desco, Occitan des. Doublet of desk, disc, discus, dish, disk, and diskos.

meaning: trifle with; toy with; treat without the necessary seriousness; procrastinate; waste time
etymology: From Middle English dalien, from Anglo-Norman delaier. Doublet of delay.

meaning: damp; unpleasantly wet
etymology: Modern slang senses derived from the drug sense; compare based (“awesome, especially in a right-wing context online”) from drug terminology freebased.

meaning: neat and trim (in appearance); (of small men) neat in appearance and quick in movements; neat; spry
etymology: From Middle English daper (“pretty, neat”), from Middle Dutch dapper (“stalwart, nimble”), Old Dutch *dapar, from Proto-Germanic *dapraz (“stout; solid; heavy; bold”) (compare German tapfer "bold", Norwegian daper "saddened, dreary"), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeb- ‘thick, heavy’ (compare Tocharian A tpär ‘high’, Latvian dàbls ‘strong’, Serbo-Croatian дебео (dèbeo) ‘fat’).

meaning: spotted
smear (as with paint); cover with something sticky; Ex. daub one'clothes with mud/paint; N: small bit of sticky substance; Ex. a daub of paint
etymology: From Middle English daub (noun), from Middle English dauben (“to plaster or whitewash; cover with clay; bespatter”, verb), from Old Northern French dauber (“to whitewash; plaster”), of uncertain origin. Probably from Latin dealbāre (“to whiten thoroughly”), which would make it a doublet of dealbate.

meaning: spread or cover with a sticky substance; N: mark made by smearing
etymology: Cognate with Saterland Frisian smeere, Dutch smeren (“to smear, lubricate”), Low German smeren, German schmieren (“to smear, lubricate”), Danish and Norwegian Bokmål smøre (“to lubricate”), Norwegian Nynorsk smørja (“to lubricate”), Swedish smörja (“to grease”), Faroese and Icelandic smyrja.

meaning: dirty mark with unclear edges made by rubbing; V.
etymology: Derived from the verb (see below). Doublet of smutch.

meaning: intimidate; frighten; discourage; dishearten
etymology: From Middle English daunten, from Old French danter, donter (“to tame”), from Latin domitō (“tame”, verb), frequentative of Latin domō (“tame, conquer”, verb), from Proto-Italic *domaō, from Proto-Indo-European *demh₂- (“to domesticate, tame”). Doublet of dompt.

meaning: bold; fearless
etymology: From daunt + -less.

meaning: loiter; hang around; waste time doing nothing
etymology: The noun is derived from the verb.

meaning: standstill resulting from the opposition of two unrelenting forces; stalemate
etymology: From dead + lock.

meaning: condition of no movement or activity; stop
etymology: From stand + still, a deverbal from stand still. Compare Dutch stilstand (“a standstill”), German Stillstand (“a standstill”), Danish stilstand (“a standstill”).

meaning: wooden; impassive; with no show of feeling; with an expressionless face
etymology: From dead + pan (“face”).

meaning: scarcity
etymology: First attested at least as early as the late 1300s, and appearing in Tyndale’s Pentateuch (1530) as well as the Coverdale Bible (1535). From Middle English derth, derthe, derþe, probably from Old English *dīerþ, *dīerþu, from Proto-West Germanic *diuriþu, from Proto-Germanic *diuriþō (“costliness, preciousness, honour”); corresponding to dear + -th (abstract nominal suffix). Cognate with Old Saxon diuriða (“glory, honour; preciousness”), West Frisian djoerte (“love, dearness, value, worth”), Dutch duurte (“dearness; scarcity, dearth”), Icelandic dýrð (“honour, glory”).

meaning: sudden disastrous downfall or defeat; complete disaster
etymology: The hypothesised derivation from Middle Dutch *bakkelen (“to freeze artificially, lock in place”), a frequentative of bakken (“to stick, stick hard, glue together”) no longer seems likely due to the lack of attestation of *bakkelen in Middle Dutch and by it having the limited meaning of "freeze superficially" in Dutch.

meaning: degrade; reduce in quality or value; degenerate; lower in esteem; disgrace; N. debasement
etymology: From de- + base, from Old French bas, from Latin bassus. Cognate with Spanish debajo (“under, beneath, below”). Compare abase.

meaning: go down on one'knee (s)
etymology: From Middle English knelen, from Old English cnēowlian (“to kneel”), equivalent to knee + -le. Cognate with Dutch knielen, Low German knelen, dialectal German knielen, Alemannic German chnüle, Danish knæle, all meaning “to kneel”.

meaning: corrupt morally; seduce from virtue; N. debauchery: wild behavior (with sex and alcohol)
etymology: Possible corruption by way of Anglicised French term bord (“edge, curb”): curb crawling as a synonym for prostitution. Parallels in modern German: Bordsteinschwalbe (“prostitute”, literally “Curb-stone-swallow”). English words bawd, bawdiness may be similarly connected.

meaning: lead away from proper conduct; entice; ADJ. seductive
etymology: Borrowed from Latin sēdūcō (“to lead apart or astray”), from sē- (“aside, away, astray”) + dūcō (“to lead”); see duct. Compare adduce, conduce, deduce, etc. and Middle English seduct.

meaning: weaken (esp. through heat, hunger, illness); enfeeble
etymology: From debilitatus, the past passive participle of Latin dēbilitō (“to weaken, debilitate”), from the adjective dēbilis (“weak”), itself from de- + habilis (“able”). Equivalent to Latin dēbilitō + -ate (verb-forming suffix; adjective-forming suffix).

meaning: match; short period of great activity; Ex. wrestling bout; bout of drinking/flu
etymology: For the sense development compare bender.

meaning: (of men) friendly, charming, and fashionably dressed; aiming to please; CF. of good disposition
etymology: Via Middle English debonaire from Old French de bon aire (“of good stock; noble”).

meaning: rubble; wreckage; scattered remains of something broken or destroyed
etymology: Borrowed from French débris, itself from dé- (“de-”) + bris (“broken, crumbled”), or from Middle French debriser (“to break apart”), from Old French debrisier, itself from de- + brisier (“to break apart, shatter, bust”), from Frankish *bristijan, *bristan, *brestan (“to break violently, shatter, bust”), from Proto-Germanic *brestaną (“to break, burst”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrest- (“to separate, burst”). Cognate with Old High German bristan (“to break asunder, burst”), Old English berstan (“to break, shatter, burst”), German bersten (“to burst”). More at burst.

meaning: expose as false, exaggerated, worthless, etc.; ridicule
etymology: From de- (“away”) + bunk (“nonsense”) (from bunkum, from Buncombe County) 1923.

meaning: young woman making formal entrance into society
etymology: From French débutante. By surface analysis, debut + French -ante.

meaning: debut; first public appearance; formal presentation of a young woman to society
etymology: Borrowed from French début, from Middle French, derivative of débuter (“to move, begin”), from dé- + but (“mark, goal”), from Old French but (“aim, goal, end, target”), from Old French butte (“mound, knoll, target”), from Frankish *but (“stump, log”), or from Old Norse bútr (“log, stump, butt”); both from Proto-Germanic *butą (“end, piece”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewd- (“to beat, push”). Cognate with Old English butt (“tree stump”). More at butt. The Philippine sense is influenced by Spanish debut.

meaning: decay; fall to a lower level (of morality, civilization, or art); ADJ. decadent
etymology: From French décadence, from Medieval Latin decadentia (“decay”), from *decadens (“decaying”), present participle of *decadere (“to decay”); see decay.

meaning: pour off gently (wine or liquid)
etymology: From French décanter, from Medieval Latin dēcanthāre, from dē- + canthus (“beak of a cup or jug”).

meaning: behead
etymology: From French décapiter, from Late Latin dēcapitāre, literally, “to de-head”.

meaning: slow down
etymology: Late 19th c., from de- + (ac)celerate. Compare deaccelerate.

meaning: falling off at a specific season or stage of growth as of leaves; Ex. deciduous tree/teeth
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dēciduus (“falling down or off”), from dēcidō (“to fall down or off”) + -uus.

meaning: kill (usually one out of ten or every tenth man); destroy or kill a large part of
etymology: The verb is first attested in 1591, the noun in 1641; borrowed from Latin decimātus, perfect passive participle of decimō (“to kill one tenth; to tithe”) (see, from -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix)), from decimus (“tenth”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). As a noun, via Latin decimatus (“tithing area; tithing rights”).

meaning: decode; CF. indecipherable
etymology: As decypher, but not retaining the y from the Old French etyma of cipher (cyfre, cyffre); the i spelling tends to be preferred etymologically, being consistent with its cognates, the French déchiffrer and the Italian decifrare, and with their common ancestor, the Medieval Latin cifra, cifera, ciphra. By surface analysis, de- + cipher.

meaning: downward slope
etymology: from dēclivis (“a sloping downward”), from de (“down”) + clīvus (“a slope”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱleywo-, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley- (“to lean”) (English lean).

meaning: (of a dress) having a low-cut neckline; CF. d\'ecolletage: low neckline (on a dress)
etymology: French décolleté, from the verb décolleter.

meaning: authoritative order; edict; judgment of a court of law; V: order or judge by decree
etymology: From Middle English decre, decree, from Old French decré (French décret), from Latin dēcrētum.

meaning: decay; V. decompose: decay; break and separate into simple parts
etymology: From de- + composition.

meaning: propriety; orderliness and good taste in manners; appropriateness of behavior or conduct
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin decōrum, neuter form of decōrus (“proper, decent”).

meaning: proper (in behavior, conduct, or appearance)
etymology: * Possibly also influenced by Late Latin decorōsus (“beautiful; elegant”), from decoris + -ōsus (suffix meaning ‘full of’ forming adjectives from nouns). Decoris is the genitive singular of decus (“beauty, grace, ornament, splendour; distinction, glory, honour”), from Proto-Indo-European *déḱos (“that which is proper”), from *deḱ- (see above).

meaning: lure or bait; V.
etymology: From Dutch de + kooi, literally "the cage". Possibly related to verb coy (which itself may have been influenced by decoy).

meaning: state of collapse or weakness caused by illness or old age
etymology: From Middle French décrépitude, from Old French, from Latin dēcrepitūdō (“decrepitude”).

meaning: weak and in bad condition from old age or hard use; Ex. decrepit old chair/man
etymology: From Middle English decrepyt (ante 1439), from Middle French décrépit, from Latin dēcrepitus (“very old”), from crepō (“to creak”).

meaning: express strong disapproval of; condemn openly (something dangerous to the public); disparage; Ex. decry the violence of modern films
etymology: C. 1600, from Middle French decrier (“to denigrate; depreciate”), from Old French descrier (“to shout”) (modern décrier). Doublet of descry. The pejorative meaning had not been present in the Middle English loan, but it was present in the French word from at least the 13th century, with a meaning of "to denigrate; depreciate; to announce the depreciation or suppression of a currency", presumably from the interpretation of de- as meaning "down, inferior".

meaning: derived by reasoning; V. deduce: infer; derive by reasoning
etymology: From deduce + -ible.

meaning: mar; disfigure
etymology: From Middle English defacen, from Old French defacier, desfacier (“to mutilate, destroy, disfigure”), from des- (“away from”) (see dis-) + Late Latin facia.

meaning: spoil the appearance of
etymology: Inherited from Middle English merren, from Old English mierran (“to mar, disturb, confuse; scatter, squander, waste; upset, hinder, obstruct; err”), from Proto-Germanic *marzijaną (“to disturb, hinder”), from Proto-Indo-European *mers- (“to annoy, disturb, neglect, forget, ignore”). Cognate with Scots mer, mar (“to obstruct, impede, spoil, ruin”), Dutch marren (“to push along, delay, hinder”), dialectal German merren (“to entangle”), Icelandic merja (“to bruise, crush”), Gothic 𐌼𐌰𐍂𐌶𐌾𐌰𐌽 (marzjan, “to annoy, bother, disturb, offend”), Lithuanian miršti (“to forget, lose, become oblivious, die”), Armenian մոռանալ (moṙanal, “to forget, fail”), Sanskrit मृष् (mṛṣ, “forget, neglect”).

meaning: harm someone'reputation; malign; speak evil of; slander; N. defamation; ADJ. defamatory
etymology: From Middle English defamen, from Anglo-Norman defamer (verb), defame (noun), and its source, Latin diffāmō, from fāma (“fame; rumour; reputation”).

meaning: failure to act; failure to perform a task or be present; V.
etymology: From Middle English defaut, defaute, from Old French defaute (“fault, defect, failure, culpability, lack”), ultimately from Latin de- (“away”) + fallo (“deceive, cheat, escape notice of”).

meaning: resigned to defeat or failure; accepting defeat or failure as a natural outcome; N. CF. defeatism
etymology: From defeat + -ist, after French défaitiste.

meaning: desertion
etymology: From Latin dēfectiō (stem dēfectiōn-).

meaning: shortcoming; V: desert (in order to join the opposite one)
etymology: Borrowed from Latin defectus (“a failure, lack”), from deficere (“to fail, lack, literally 'undo'”), from past participle defectus, from de- (“of, from”) + facere (“to do”).

meaning: give in respectfully; submit; delay till later; exempt temporarily; N. deferment; CF. show respect, comply with, courteous
etymology: Originally a variant of (and hence a doublet of) differ; from Middle English differren (“to postpone”), from Old French differer, from Latin differō. Doublet of differ and dilate. See also infer, collate and confer, delate and defer, relate and refer as well as prelate and prefer among others.

meaning: courteous regard for another'wish; courteous yielding to another'wish or opinion (showing respect); ADJ. deferential; OP. effrontery
etymology: From French déférence. Morphologically defer + -ence.

meaning: refusal to yield; resistance; V. defy; ADJ. defiant
etymology: From Middle English defiaunce, from Old French desfiance, from desfier. By surface analysis, defy + -ance.

meaning: pollute; make filthy or dirty; corrupt morally; profane; desecrate; N: narrow passage or gorge through mountains
etymology: * West Frisian befûjle (“to soil”)

meaning: most reliable; authorative and complete; that cannot be improved; conclusive; decisive; definite; Ex. definitive decision by the supreme court
etymology: From Middle French définitif.

meaning: turn aside; turn away from a straight course
etymology: From Latin deflecto, from de- (“away”) + flecto (“to bend”).

meaning: destroy leaves; deprive of leaves (by the use of chemicals); N. defoliant
etymology: From de- + foliate.

meaning: provide for the payment of; undertake the payment of; pay
etymology: From Middle French desfrayer, French défrayer, from dé- + Old French fraier (“to spend”).

meaning: strip a priest or minister of church authority; unfrock
etymology: From French défroquer, from dé- + froc. By surface analysis, de- + frock.

meaning: long loose garment (worn by monks)
etymology: Cognate with Old High German hroch, roch (“skirt, dress, cowl”) – whence German Rock (“skirt, coat”) –, Saterland Frisian Rok (“skirt”), Dutch rok (“skirt, petticoat”), Old English rocc (“an overgarment, tunic, rochet”), Old Norse rokkr (“skirt, jacket”), whence Danish rok (“garment”).

meaning: neat; skillful
etymology: From Middle English defte, daft (“gentle”), from Old English dæfte (“mild, gentle, meek”), from Proto-West Germanic *daftī (“fitting, suitable”), derived from *dabaną (“to be suitable”). Near cognates include Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌳𐍉𐍆𐍃 (gadōfs, “suitable”), West Frisian deftich (“distinguished”), Dutch deftig (“distinguished”), German deftig (“coarse”). Further cognates include Russian добро (dobro, “wealth, good”) and Latin faber (“craftsman; skillful”). Doublet of daft.

meaning: dead; no longer in use or existence
etymology: Borrowed from Latin dēfunctus, past participle of dēfungor (“to finish, discharge”).

meaning: become worse in quality; deteriorate; ADJ: having become worse; Ex. a degenerate species; N: depraved or corrupt person
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dēgenerātus. See -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.

meaning: humiliation; debasement; degeneration; V. degrade: debase; disgrace; degenerate; reduce (something) in worth; demote (someone); reduce in rank
etymology: From French dégradation. Morphologically degrade + -ation.

meaning: disgrace; N. ADJ. dishonorable
etymology: From Old French deshonor, equivalent to dis- + honor.

meaning: remove water from; dry out
etymology: From de- + hydrate.

meaning: turn into a god; make a god of; idolize; Ex. Kings were deified; CF. deity
etymology: From French déifier, from Latin deificāre, from deus (“god”). By surface analysis, deity + -ify.

meaning: condescend; stoop
etymology: * Occitan deinar, denhar

meaning: bend forward and down; lower or debase oneself; fall to a lower standard of behavior by doing something; condescend; Ex. stoop to lying
etymology: From Middle English stoupen, from Old English stūpian (“to bow, bend”), from Proto-West Germanic *stūpōn, from Proto-Germanic *stūpōną, *stūpijaną (“to stand out”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewb- (“to push, butt, knock”). Compare steep. Cognate with Dutch stuipen (“to bend the upper part of the body forward and downward”), Old Norse stúpa (“to stoop”). Related also to Old Frisian stēpa (“to help”), Old Norse steypa (“to cause to stoop, cast down, overthrow”).

meaning: erase; strike out
etymology: Doublet of delible and deleble.

meaning: harmful
etymology: Adapted borrowing (1640s; 1582 as deletorious) of New Latin dēlētērius, dēlētōrius + -ous, from Ancient Greek δηλητήριος (dēlētḗrios, “noxious, deleterious”), from δηλητήρ (dēlētḗr, “a destroyer”), from δηλέομαι (dēléomai, “I hurt, damage, spoil, waste”). Not related to delete or deleble. Doublet of deletery.

meaning: consider; ponder; ADJ: done on purpose; slow
etymology: Inherited from Middle English deliberat(e), borrowed from Latin dēlīberātus, perfect passive participle of dēlīberō (“to consider, weigh well”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dē- + *līberō / lībrō (“to weigh”)), from *libera / libra (“a balance”); see librate. Doublet of deliber.

meaning: portray; depict; sketch; describe; N. delineation
etymology: First attested in 1559; borrowed from Latin dēlīneātus, perfect passive participle of dēlīneo (“to sketch out, to delineate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from dē- + līnea (“line”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). Regular participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.

meaning: mental disorder marked by confusion; uncontrolled excitement; ADJ. delirious
etymology: Borrowed from Latin dēlīrium (“derangement, madness”).

meaning: flat plain of mud or sand between branches of a river
etymology: * (USSF): from the delta wing, symbol of the USSF, a triangular wing, shaped like the majuscule Greek letter delta Δ

meaning: deceive
etymology: From Middle English deluden, borrowed from Latin dēlūdō (“mock, deceive”), from de + lūdō (“to make sport of, to mock”). See ludicrous.

meaning: flood; rush; V.
etymology: From Middle English deluge, from Old French deluge, alteration of earlier deluvie, from Latin dīluvium, from dīluō (“wash away”). Doublet of diluvium.

meaning: false belief; hallucination; deluding; Ex. delusions of grandeur; Ex. under the delusion that
etymology: From Latin dēlūsiō.

meaning: deceptive; likely to delude; misleading; raising vain hopes; Ex. delusive promises
etymology: From delude + -ive.

meaning: dig; search deeply; investigate
etymology: From Middle English delven, from Old English delfan (“to dig, dig out, burrow, bury”), from Proto-Germanic *delbaną (“to dig”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰelbʰ- (“to dig”). Cognate with West Frisian dolle (“to dig, delve”), Dutch delven (“to dig, delve”), Low German dölven (“to dig, delve”), dialectal German delben, telben (“to dig, delve”).

meaning: person who appeals to people'prejudice; false leader of people; CF. demagoguery
etymology: From Middle French démagogue, from Ancient Greek δημαγωγός (dēmagōgós, “popular leader, mob leader”), from δῆμος (dêmos, “people”) + ἀγωγός (agōgós, “guide”). By surface analysis, dem- + -agogue.

meaning: disgrace; humiliate; debase in dignity; behave
etymology: (1595) From de- + mean (“lowly, base, common”), from Middle English mene, aphetic variation of imene (“mean, base, common”), from Old English ġemǣne (“mean, common”). Compare English bemean.

meaning: behavior; bearing
etymology: From Middle English demenure, from the verb Middle English demenen, demeinen (“to handle, manage”), from Old French demener (“to guide, conduct”), from de- + mener (“to conduct, lead”), from Latin *mināre (“to drive”) and minor (“to project or jut forth”).

meaning: insane
etymology: Past participle of dement + -ed, from Latin dēmentāre.

meaning: death
etymology: The verb is from Middle English dimisen, from the noun.

meaning: related to population balance; N. demography: statistical study of human population
etymology: From demography + -ic.

meaning: destruction; V. demolish
etymology: From Old French demolition, from Latin dēmōlītiō (“a tearing down”). Equivalent to demolish + -ion.

meaning: fiendish; cruel; N. demon: evil supernatural being; devil
evil spirit; devil
etymology: Cognate with Scots fient (“fiend”), Saterland Frisian Fäind (“enemy, fiend, foe”), Cimbrian faint (“enemy, fiend”), Dutch vijand (“enemy”), German Feind (“enemy, fiend, foe”), Vilamovian faeind, fajnd (“enemy”), Yiddish פֿײַנד (faynd), פֿײַנט (faynt, “enemy”), Danish fjende (“adversary, enemy, foe”), Icelandic fjandi (“enemy; fiend, demon, devil”), Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk and Swedish fiende (“enemy”), Old Norse fjándi (“enemy; devil”), Gothic 𐍆𐌹𐌰𐌽𐌳𐍃 (fiands), 𐍆𐌹𐌾𐌰𐌽𐌳𐍃 (fijands, “enemy, foe”). The Old Norse and Gothic terms are present participles of the corresponding verbs fjá/𐍆𐌹𐌾𐌰𐌽 (fijan, “to hate”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₁- (“to hate”) (compare Sanskrit पीयति (pī́yati, “(he) reviles”)).

meaning: of or pertaining to the people
etymology: First attested in 1822, from Ancient Greek δημοτικός (dēmotikós, “common”), from δημότης (dēmótēs, “commoner”), from δῆμος (dêmos, “the common people”).

meaning: object (because of doubts, scruples); raise an objection (showing qualms); hesitate; Ex. demur at the idea of working on Sunday
etymology: From Middle English demuren (“to delay; to linger; to remain (in office); to keep, retain (?)”), from Anglo-Norman demorer and Old French demorer, demourer (“to remain, stay”) (modern French demeurer), from Vulgar Latin dēmorāre, from Latin dēmorārī, the present active infinitive of Latin dēmoror (“to delay, detain; to linger, tarry”), from de- (intensifying prefix) + moror (“to delay, detain; to hinder, impede; to linger, loiter”) (from mora (“a delay; hindrance, obstacle”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)mer- (“to fall into thinking; to remember”), probably referring to a time for thinking) + -or (variant of -ō (suffix forming regular first-conjugation verbs)).

meaning: (of a woman or child) grave; quiet and serious; coy; pretending to be demure
etymology: * (Monastic rule): de aunciene dame de meure porture ke pusse les plus ieuenes rieueler e endoctriner (“an old lady with a mature demeanor able to rule and educate the young girls”).

meaning: blacken; defame
etymology: Derived from Latin dēnigrātus, the perfect passive participle of dēnigrō (“to blacken”) [see -ate (verb-forming suffix)], from dē- (“of; from”) + nigrō (“to blacken”) [from niger (“black”)]. Cognate with Middle English denigart(e) (“darkened, discolored”).

meaning: (animal, person, or plant) inhabitant or resident of a particular place; regular visitor
etymology: From Middle English denisein, from Old French denzein, from deinz (“within”) + -ein, from Late Latin dē intus (“from within”), whence French dans.

meaning: meaning; distinguishing by name; V. denote: indicate; refer to directly; mean; CF. connotation
etymology: From Late Latin dēnotātiō, from Latin dēnotāre (“to denote, mark out”) + -tiō (suffix forming nouns of action), from dē- (“completely”) + notāre (“to mark”); equivalent to denote + -ation.

meaning: final outcome; final development of the plot of a play or other literary work; the end of a story when everything is explained
condemn; criticize; N. denunciation
etymology: From Old French denuncier, from Latin dēnūntiō (“to announce, to denounce, to threaten”), from de + nūntiō (“to announce, to report, to denounce”), from nūntius (“messenger, message”). Doublet of denunciate.

meaning: portray
etymology: From Middle English depicten, from Latin dēpictus, from dēpingō.

meaning: public revelation of something discreditable
reduce; exhaust
etymology: Borrowed from Latin dēplētus (“empty”), from depleō. First attested in 1716; originally a medical term.

meaning: regret; express sorrow and severe disapproval for something bad; Ex. deplore their violent behavior; ADJ. deplorable: very bad; deserving severe disapproval; Ex. deplorable living condition
etymology: From Middle French déplorer, from Old French deplorer, from Latin dēplōrāre (“to lament over, bewail”), from dē- + plōrāre (“to wail, weep aloud”); origin uncertain.

meaning: spread out (troops) in an extended though shallow battle line; distribute (persons or forces) systematically or strategically
etymology: Borrowed from French déployer (“to unroll, unfold”), from Old French desploiier, itself from des- + ploiier, or possibly from Late Latin displicāre (“to unfold, display”), from Latin dis- (“apart”) + plicare (“to fold”). Compare Middle English desployen, dysployen (“to unfold, display”). Doublet of display.

meaning: army unit made up of four or more companies
etymology: From Middle French battaillon (modern French bataillon).

meaning: dethrone; remove from office; give a deposition; testify
etymology: Recorded since c.1300, from Middle English, from Old French deposer, from de- (“down”) + poser (“to put, place”). Deposition (1494 in the legal sense) belongs to deposit, but that related word and depose became thoroughly confused.

meaning: testimony under oath; deposing; dethroning
etymology: From Middle English deposicion, from Old French deposicion (French déposition), from Latin depositio.

meaning: extreme corruption; wickedness; V. deprave
express disapproval of; deplore; protest against; belittle; ADJ. deprecatory
etymology: Borrowed from Latin dēprecātus, perfect active participle of dēprecor (“to pray against (a present or impending evil) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), pray for, intercede for (that which is in danger), rarely imprecate”), from dē- (“off”) + precor (“to pray”).

meaning: lessen in value; belittle; represent as of little value
etymology: Inherited from Middle English depreciaten, borrowed from Late Latin dēpretiātus / dēpreciātus, perfect passive participle of dēpretiō / dēpreciō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dē- + pretium (“price”) + -ō.

meaning: plundering; destruction
etymology: From Middle French déprédation, from Latin depraedatio.

meaning: insane
etymology: Borrowed from French dérangé.

meaning: organization for a special purpose; V: establish
etymology: From French institut, from Middle French, from Latin īnstitūtum.

meaning: instituting; (building for the) organization; established custom, practice, or relationship in a society; mental hospital; Ex. institution of marriage
etymology: From Middle English institucioun, from Old French institution, from Latin institūtiō, from instituō (“to set up”), from in- (“in, on”) + statuō (“to set up, establish”). Equivalent to institute + -ion.

meaning: make into an institution; put or confine in an institution
etymology: From institutional + -ize.

meaning: negligent; (of someone) neglectful of duty; (of something) deserted by an owner; abandoned; N: abandoned property; homeless or vagrant person
etymology: The noun is derived from the adjective.

meaning: neglect of duty; abandonment
etymology: From Latin dērelictiō (“neglect, abandonment”), from dērelinquō (“to neglect, abandon”), from dē- + re- + linquō (“to leave”).

meaning: ridicule; treat with contempt; make fun of; OP. respect
etymology: * Old French dérider (rare), derire

meaning: ridicule; ADJ. derisive; CF. derisory
etymology: From Old French derision, from Latin dērīsiōnem, accusative of dērīsiō, from dērīdēre ("to mock, to laugh at, to deride").

meaning: unoriginal; obtained from another source; Ex. derivative prose style; N.
etymology: From Middle French dérivatif, from Latin dērīvātus, perfect passive participle of dērīvō (“to derive”). Related to derive; by surface analysis, derive + -ative.

meaning: deriving; origin or source of something; Ex. the derivation of the word
etymology: From Middle English derivacioun, borrowed from Middle French dérivation, from Latin dērīvātiō, dērīvātiōnem. Morphologically derive + -ation.

meaning: one who studies the skin and its diseases
etymology: From dermatology + -ist or dermato- + -logist.

meaning: skin disease (on the face)
etymology: From New Latin acnē, probably a corruption of Ancient Greek ἀκμή (akmḗ, “point, top”).

meaning: expressing a low opinion; disparaging; V. derogate: detract; disparage
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin dērogātōrius, from Latin dērogō; corresponding to derogate + -ory.

meaning: catch sight of (something distant)
etymology: Palmer (1890) compares the etymology of Latin explorare "to search a wood &c. with cries".

meaning: profane; violate the sanctity of
etymology: From de- + stem of consecrate.

meaning: break (a law); defile; desecrate; assault sexually; Ex. violate graves
etymology: From Middle English violaten (“to defile, render impure”), from violat(e) (“defiled, desecrated”, also used as the past participle of violaten) + -en, borrowed from Latin violātus, perfect passive participle of violō (“to treat with violence (whether bodily or mental)”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Ultimately from vīs (“strength, power, force, violence”).

meaning: dry up
etymology: From Latin dēsiccō (“to dry completely, dry up”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix), from dē- (“completely, to exhaustion”, a prefix) + siccō (“to dry; to drain, exhaust”), from siccus (“dry”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, de- + siccate.

meaning: (of a place) deserted; unpopulated; (of a person) lonely; forlorn; joyless
etymology: From Middle English desolat(e). See Etymology 2 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.

meaning: reckless, desperate outlaw
etymology: From obsolete Spanish desperado, past participle of desperar, archaic form of desesperar (“to despair”), from Latin disperare (“to despair, to lose hope”), from prefix dis- + sperare (“to hope”). Doublet of desperate.

meaning: having lost all hope; despairing; reckless and violent because of loss of hope or despair; undertaken as a last resort
etymology: From Middle English desperat(e) (“desperate”), borrowed from Latin dēspērātus, perfect passive participle of dēspērō (“to be without hope”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix). The noun is derived from the adjective or from the Latin source through substantivization, see -ate (noun-forming suffix).

meaning: look on with scorn; regard as worthless or distasteful; ADJ. despicable: contemptible
etymology: From Middle English despisen, from Old French despis-, stem of despire, from Latin dēspicere (“to look down upon, despise, scorn”), from dē (“down”) + speciō (“to look at”). Displaced native Old English forsēon.

meaning: plunder; sack; Ex. despoil the village
etymology: From Middle English despoylen, dispoylen, from Old French despoillier ( > French dépouiller), from Latin dēspoliō, dēspoliāre.

meaning: without hope and courage; depressed; gloomy; N. despondency: loss of hope with gloom; dejection
etymology: From Latin dēspondēns, from the verb despondere (“to give up, to abandon”).

meaning: tyrant; harsh, authoritarian ruler; CF. despotism
etymology: From Middle French despote, from Old French despote, from Medieval Latin despota, from Ancient Greek δεσπότης (despótēs, “lord, master, owner”). Cognate with Sanskrit दम्पति (dámpati).

meaning: extremely poor; lacking means of subsistence; utterly lacking; devoid; Ex. destitute of any experience
etymology: From Middle English destitute, destitut, from Latin dēstitūtus.

meaning: make poor; deprive of natural strength or something important; Ex. impoverished soil
etymology: From Middle English empoverishen, impoverishen, empoverischen, enpoverisshen, Anglo-Norman empoveriss-, from Old French empoverir, from em- + povre, from Latin pauper (“poor”) (English poor).

meaning: aimless; haphazard; digressing at random
etymology: From Latin dēsultōrius (“hasty, casual, superficial”), from dēsultor (“a circus rider who jumped from one galloping horse to another”), from dēsiliō (“jump down”), from dē (“down”) + saliō (“jump, leap”).

meaning: emotionally removed; free from emotional involvement; calm and objective; physically separate; N. detachment; CF. attachment
keep waiting; prevent from leaving or going; N. detention
etymology: From Old French detenir. Doublet of détente. Cognate with Italian detenere, Portuguese deter, Romanian deține, and Spanish detener.

meaning: having a fixed order of procedure; precisely defined; invariable; fixed; conclusive; final
etymology: From Middle English determinate, determynat, determinat, from Latin dēterminātus, perfect passive participle of dēterminō (“to limit, set bounds”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.

meaning: resolve; firmness of purpose; measurement or calculation; decision
etymology: From Middle English determinacion, determynacioun, from Old French determinacion, from Latin dēterminātiō. Morphologically determine + -ation.

meaning: something that discourages or deters
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dēterrēns, dēterrentem.

meaning: explosion
etymology: From French détonation; equivalent to detonate + -ion.

meaning: slandering; aspersion; detracting; CF. detractor
etymology: From Middle English detraction, detraccion, detraccioun, from Old French detraccion, from Latin dētractiō.

meaning: harmful; damaging; N. detriment
etymology: From Medieval Latin *dētrīmentālis, from Latin dētrīmentum (“harm”), from dēterō (“to rub off, wear”), from dē- (“down, away”) + terō (“to rub or grab”).

meaning: turn away from (a principle, norm); move away from an accepted standard; swerve; depart; diverge; N. deviation; Ex. deviation of the path of light by a prism
etymology: From Late Latin dēviātus, perfect passive participle of dēviō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more. Compare French dévier.

meaning: roundabout; erratic; deviating from the straight course; not straightforward; not completely honest; Ex. devious route
etymology: 1590s, "out of the common or direct way," from Latin devius (“out of the way, remote, off the main road”), from de via, from de (“off”) (see de-) + via (“way, road”). Compare deviate. Originally in the Latin literal sense; the figurative sense of "deceitful" is first recorded 1630s. Related to deviously, deviousness. Figurative senses of the Latin word were "retired, sequestered, wandering in the byways, foolish, inconsistent."

meaning: think up; invent; plan; bequeath; N: bequest
etymology: From Middle English devisen, devysen, from Old French deviser, from Vulgar Latin devisō, from Latin dīvisō, frequentative of dīvidō.

meaning: empty; lacking
etymology: From obsolete Middle English verb devoiden, from Old French desvuidier (“to empty out”) (compare French dévider).

meaning: deputize; pass or be passed to others (power, work, or property); Ex. devolve on/upon/to
etymology: Borrowed from Latin dēvolvō (“roll or tumble off or down”), from dē- + volvō (“roll”).

meaning: work or appoint as a deputy; N. deputy: person who has the power to take charge when the leading person is away
etymology: From deputy + -ize.

meaning: enthusiastic follower; enthusiast; Ex. devotee of Bach
etymology: From devote + -ee. The narrowed meaning in sense 3 arises from the sound similarity with amputee.

meaning: pious; deeply religious; sincere; earnest; Ex. my devout hope
etymology: From Middle English devout, devot, from Old French devot (French dévot), from Latin dēvōtus, perfect passive participle of dēvōveō. Doublet of devote.

meaning: of religion; (of a person) pious; having reverence for a deity
etymology: From Middle English religiouse, religious, religius, religeous, from Anglo-Norman religieus, religius, from Old French religious, religieux, and their source, Latin religiōsus (“religious, superstitious, conscientious”), from religiō. Doublet of religieux.

meaning: skillful; skill in using hands or mind; N. dexterity
etymology: From Latin dexter (“right, ready”) + -ous. Displaced native Old English handcræftiġ.

meaning: diabolic; devilish; fiendish
etymology: From diabolic + -al.

meaning: crown
etymology: From Middle English diademe, dyademe, from Old French diademe, from Latin diadēma, from Ancient Greek διάδημα (diádēma, “band, especially worn around a tiara”), from διαδέω (diadéō, “bind around”).

meaning: relating to the art of debate; mutual or reciprocal; Ex. dialectical situation; N. dialectic: art of arriving at the truth by the exchange of logical arguments
etymology: From Latin dialecticus + -al. By surface analysis, dialectic + -al or dialect + -ical.

meaning: sheer; transparent
etymology: From Medieval Latin diaphanus, from Ancient Greek διαφανής (diaphanḗs), from δια- (dia-, “through”) + φαίνω (phaínō, “to shine, appear”).

meaning: bitter scolding or denunciation; invective; abuse
etymology: First attested 1581, borrowed from French diatribe, from Latin diatriba (“learned discussion or discourse”), from Ancient Greek διατριβή (diatribḗ, “way of spending time, lecture”), from διά (diá, “through”) + τρίβω (tríbō, “to waste, wear out”)

meaning: division into two opposite parts; split; branching into two parts (especially contradictory ones)
etymology: From Ancient Greek διχοτομία (dikhotomía, “dichotomy”).

meaning: authoritative and weighty statement (made by a judge in court); saying; maxim; CF. obiter dictum: incidental, nonbinding remark (something said in passing)
etymology: From Latin dictum (“proverb, maxim”), from dictus (“having been said”), perfect passive participle of dico (“to say”). Compare Spanish dicho (“saying”). Doublet of dict.

meaning: (of speech or writing) intended to teach a moral lesson; teaching; instructional; N. didacticism
etymology: From French didactique, from Ancient Greek διδακτικός (didaktikós, “skilled in teaching”), from διδακτός (didaktós, “taught, learnt”), from διδάσκω (didáskō, “to teach, educate”). By surface analysis, didact + -ic.

meaning: metal block used for shaping metal or plastic; device for stamping or impressing; mold; CF. dice
etymology: From Middle English deyen, probably from Old Norse deyja, from Proto-Germanic *dawjaną (“to die”). Displaced native Old English sweltan, whence Modern English swelt, and Old English steorfan, whence modern starve.

meaning: shyness; lack of self-confidence; timidity; ADJ. diffident
etymology: From Latin diffīdentiam (“distrust”), from diffīdere (“to mistrust”), from dis- and fīdere (“to trust”). Attested since ∼1400. The original sense was antonymous with confidence, and the modern sense of ‘distrusting oneself’ dates from the 1650s.

meaning: wordy; verbose; rambling; spread out (like a gas); V: spread out in all directions; disperse; N. diffusion; CF. suffuse
etymology: From Middle French diffuser, from Latin diffūsus, past participle of diffundere, from dis- + fundere.

meaning: wandering away from the subject; V. digress
etymology: From Old French digressiun or disgressiun, from Latin dīgressiōnem, from dīgressus + -iō (suffix forming abstract nouns from verbs), the past passive participle of dīgredior (“to step away, to digress”), from dis- + gradior (“to step, walk, go”).

meaning: falling to pieces; in a bad condition; ruined because of neglect; Ex. dilapidated old car/castle; N. dilapidation
expand; dilate on/upon: speak or write at length on (a subject)
etymology: First attested in 1393, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English dilaten, from Old French dilater, from Latin dīlātō (“to spread out”), from dī- + lātus (“wide”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of dilatate.

meaning: delaying; tending to delay
etymology: From Middle English dilatorie, from Old French dilatoire, from Latin dīlātōrius (“extending or putting off (time)”), from dīlātor, from differō. Not etymologically related to delay.

meaning: situation that requires a choice between equally unfavorable options; problem; choice of two unsatisfactory alternatives
etymology: First attested 1523, from Late Latin dilemma, from Ancient Greek δίλημμα (dílēmma, “ambiguous proposition”), from δι- (di-, “having two of”) + λῆμμα (lêmma, “premise, proposition”), equivalent to di- + lemma.

meaning: aimless follower of an art or a field of knowledge (not taking it seriously); amateur; dabbler; CF. delight
etymology: From Italian dilettante, present participle of dilettare (“to delight”), from Latin dēlectāre (“to delight”).

meaning: steadiness of effort; persistent hard work
etymology: Borrowed from French diligence, from Latin diligentia.

meaning: make (a liquid) less concentrated; reduce in strength; Ex. dilute the influence of the president
etymology: From Latin dīlūtus, from dīluere (“to wash away, dissolve, cause to melt, dilute”), from dī-, dis- (“away, apart”) + luere (“to wash”). See lave, and compare deluge.

meaning: lessening; reduction in size; V. diminish
etymology: From Middle English diminucioun, from Anglo-Norman diminuciun, Old French diminucion, from Latin dīminūtiō.

meaning: continued loud noise; V: make a din; instill by wearying repetition
etymology: Borrowed from German DIN.

meaning: tired after long work; V.
etymology: From Middle English wery, weri, from Old English wēriġ (“weary”), from Proto-West Germanic *wōrīg, *wōrag (“weary”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian wuurich (“weary, tired”), West Frisian wurch (“tired”), Dutch dialectal wurrig (“exhausted”), Old Saxon wōrig (“weary”), Old High German wōrag, wuarag (“drunken”), Latvian vārgs (“weak”), Lithuanian vergas (“slave”), Latvian vergs (“slave”).

meaning: small boat (often ship'boat)
etymology: From Bengali ডিঙি (ḍiṅi), perhaps from Sanskrit द्रोण (droṇa, “wooden trough”).

meaning: leave helpless on a deserted island or coast; ADJ. red brown
etymology: From French marron (“feral; fugitive”, adjective), from Spanish cimarrón (“fugitive, wild, feral”); see that entry for more.

meaning: (of things and place) dirty and dull; Ex. dingy street/curtain
etymology: From English dialectal (Kentish) dingy (“dirty”), of unknown origin, though probably from Middle English *dingy, dungy, from Old English *dyncgiġ (“covered with dung, dirty”), an umlaut form of duncge, dung (“dung”), equivalent to dung + -y, hence a doublet of dungy.

meaning: (of colors or surfaces) not bright; cloudy; overcast; boring; (of edge or sound) not sharp; not rapid; sluggish; slow in thinking and understanding; stupid; V.
etymology: Cognate with Scots dull, doll (“slow to understand or hear, deaf, dull”), North Frisian dol (“rash, unthinking, giddy, flippant”), Dutch dol (“crazy, mad, insane”), Low German dul, dol (“mad, silly, stupid, fatuous”), German toll (“crazy, mad, wild, fantastic”), Danish dval (“foolish, absurd”), Icelandic dulur (“secretive, silent”), West-Flemish dul (angry, furious).

meaning: means; effort; Ex. by dint of hard work
etymology: From Middle English dint, dent, dünt, from Old English dynt (“dint, blow, strike, stroke, bruise, stripe; the mark left by a blow; the sound or noise made by a blow, thud”), from Proto-Germanic *duntiz (“a blow”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰen- (“to strike, hit”). Cognate with Swedish dialectal dunt, Icelandic dyntr (“a dint”). Doublet of dent.

meaning: life-size, three-dimensional scene from nature or history; three-dimensional scene with modeled figures against a painted background
etymology: Borrowed from French diorama.

meaning: warning of disaster; disastrous; (of needs and dangers) very great; urgent; Ex. dire prediction/need of food
etymology: Borrowed from Latin dīrus (“fearful, ominous”).

meaning: funeral song; slow mournful piece of music (sung over a dead person)
etymology: From Middle English dirige, from Latin dirige (“steer, direct”), from the beginning of the first antiphon in matins for the dead, Dirige, Domine, deus meus, in conspectu tuo viam meam. Doublet of dirige.

meaning: correct a false impression; undeceive; free from a wrong belief
etymology: From dis- + abuse. Compare French désabuser.

meaning: disloyal; lacking loyality; V. disaffect: cause to lose affection or loyalty
etymology: From disaffect + -ed.

meaning: disapproval; condemnation
etymology: From dis- + approbation.

meaning: state of disorder; a disorderly or untidy state; Ex. with her clothes in disarray
etymology: From Middle English disareyen (“to disarray”), from Middle French desarroyer, from Old French desareer, from des- (“dis-”) + areer (“to array”).

meaning: denial; disclaiming; repudiating; disowning; V. disavow; CF. disclaim
etymology: From disavow + -al.

meaning: dissolve; disperse; (of a group) break up and separate; Ex. The club has disbanded.
etymology: Attested since the 1590s, from Middle French desbander (Modern French débander), from des- (English dis-) + bande (English band), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ- (“to tie”). By surface analysis, dis- + band.

meaning: pay out (as from a fund); N. disbursement; CF. purse
etymology: From Old French desbourser (Modern French débourser). By surface analysis, dis- + burse (“purse”).

meaning: distinguishable; perceivable; Ex. discernible improvement
etymology: From Middle French discernable; spelling changed from -a- to -i- in the 17th century to conform to Latin discernibilis. By surface analysis, discern + -ible.

meaning: mentally quick and observant; having insight; perceptive; able to make good judgments; V. discern: perceive
disown; renounce claim to; deny; CF. disclaimer
etymology: From Middle English disclaimen, from Anglo-Norman disclaimer, from Old French desclamer (French déclamer), des- + clamer.

meaning: reveal; N. disclosure
etymology: From Middle English disclosen, from Middle French desclos, from Old French desclore, itself from Vulgar Latin disclaudere, from Latin dis- + claudere (“to close, shut”) or as a variant of discludo, discludere (cf. disclude). By surface analysis, dis- + close.

meaning: discomposed; confused
disturb the composure of; confuse
etymology: From dis- + compose.

meaning: frustrate; put to rout; defeat; disconcert; embarrass; perturb
etymology: Later sense of “to embarrass, to disconcert” due to confusion with unrelated discomfort.

meaning: confuse; upset; embarrass; perturb
etymology: From Middle French desconcerter, from des- (“dis-”) + concerter (“to bring into agreement, organize”).

meaning: hopelessly sad (at the loss of something)
etymology: From Medieval Latin discōnsōlātus (“comfortless”), from dis- (“away”) + cōnsōlātus (“consoled”).

meaning: conflict; lack of harmony; dissonance (when musical notes are played)
etymology: Verb derives from Middle English discorden, from Anglo-Norman, Old French descorder, from Latin discordāre, from discord-, as above.

meaning: not harmonious; conflicting
etymology: From Late Middle English discordaunt (“(adjective) not in accord or harmony; dissonant; (noun) element not in accord or harmony”), from Anglo-Norman descorda(u)nt, discorda(u)nt, Middle French descordant, discordant, and Old French descordant, discordant (“of people: quarrelsome; of things: in disagreement, at variance”) (modern French discordant), an adjective use of the present participle of descorder, discorder (“to fail to agree or harmonize, clash, disagree, discord”), from Latin discordāre, the present active infinitive of discordō (“to disagree, quarrel with”), from discors (“discordant, different, inharmonious”) + -ō (suffix forming regular first-conjugation verbs). Discors is derived from dis- (“prefix meaning ‘apart, in two’”) + cor (“heart; (figurative) mind; soul”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱḗr (“heart”)). By surface analysis, discord (noun) + -ant (suffix forming adjectives from nouns with the sense ‘exhibiting [the condition or process described by the noun]’).

meaning: disregard; regard (a story or news) as unimportant; deduct from a cost
etymology: Alteration of French descompte, décompte, from Old French disconter, desconter (“reckon off, account back, discount”), from Medieval Latin discomputō (“to deduct, discount”), from Latin dis- (“away”) + computō (“to reckon, count”). By surface analysis, dis- + count.

meaning: serious speech, writing, or conversation; formal discussion (either written or spoken); conversation; V.
etymology: From Middle English discours, borrowed from Middle French discours (“conversation, speech”), from Latin discursus (“the act of running about”), from Latin discurrō (“run about”), from dis- (“apart”) + currō (“run”). Spelling modified by influence of Middle French cours (“course”). Doublet of discursus.

meaning: defame; disgrace; destroy confidence in; disbelieve; N. CF. discreditable: causing discredit; shameful
etymology: From dis- + credit.

meaning: lack of consistency or agreement as between facts; difference; Ex. discrepancy between two descriptions
etymology: Borrowed from Latin discrepantia, from discrepans, from discrepō, from crepō. By surface analysis, discrepant + -cy. See also discrepant.

meaning: separate; unconnected
etymology: From Old French discret, from Latin discrētus, past participle of discernō (“divide”), from dis- + cernō (“sift”). Doublet of discreet.

meaning: prudence; ability to adjust actions to circumstances; freedom of action or judgment; ADJ. discreet; CF. discretionary
etymology: From Middle English discrecioun, from Old French discretion, from Late Latin discrētiō, from Latin discerno. Equivalent to discreet + -ion.

meaning: able to see differences; discerning; prejudiced; N. discrimination
distinguish; make distinctions on the basis of preference
etymology: First attested in 1615; borrowed from Latin discrīminātus, perfect passive participle of discrīminō (“to divide, separate, distinguish”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from discrīmen (“a space between, division, separation, distinction”), from discernō (“to divide, separate, distinguish, discern”). By surface analysis, dis- + criminate.

meaning: quick and active; marked by liveliness and vigor
etymology: Uncertain; probably a collateral form of brusque, but compare Irish briosc, Scottish Gaelic brisg, Welsh brys.

meaning: (of a person or writing) digressing; rambling (without any clear plan)
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French discursif, formed from the stem of Latin discursus and the suffix -if, and in part borrowed from Medieval Latin discursivus. By surface analysis, discourse + -ive.

meaning: treat with scorn or contempt
etymology: From Middle English disdeynen, from Old French desdeignier (modern French dédaigner).

meaning: debark; go ashore (from a ship); unload cargo from a ship; CF. embark
etymology: From dis- + embark.

meaning: disfranchise; deprive of a civil right; OP. enfranchise
etymology: From dis- + enfranchise.

meaning: uncouple; separate; disconnect; stop fighting; OP. engage
etymology: From Middle French désengager ; dis- + engage.

meaning: mar the appearance of; spoil
etymology: From Middle English disfiguren, from Anglo-Norman desfigurer.

meaning: surrender something (stolen); eject; vomit; OP. gorge
etymology: From Middle French desgorger.

meaning: make discontented
etymology: From dis- (intensifier) + gruntle (“grumble, grunt”).

meaning: discourage
etymology: From dis- + hearten.

meaning: untidy (of hair or clothing); V. dishevel
unwillingness
etymology: From dis- + inclination.

meaning: not naive; not candid; sophisticated; worldly wise; OP. ingenuous
etymology: From dis- + ingenuous.

meaning: dig up; unearth; OP. inter
etymology: Borrowed from French désenterrer.

meaning: unprejudiced; free from bias and self-interest; objective
etymology: From disinterest (“to cause to be impartial”, verb) + -ed (suffix forming past tense or past participle forms of verbs), or from dis- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + interested (“having a stake in; showing interest”, adjective).

meaning: disconnected; lacking coherence; V. disjoint: disconnect; disjoin
act or state of separation; disunity; CF. disjunctive: expressing a choice between two ideas; CF. conjunction; CF. conjunctive
etymology: From Old French disjunction, from Latin disiunctiō.

meaning: remove (forcibly); force out of a position; Ex. dislodge the food caught in his throat; CF. lodge
etymology: From Middle English disloggen, from Old French deslogier. Compare French déloger. Equivalent to dis- + lodge.

meaning: take apart; disassemble
etymology: Compare typologically uncloak, reveal, unmask.

meaning: loose sleeveless outer garment; cloak; something that covers or envelops; the layer of the earth between the crust and the core
etymology: From Middle English mantel, from Old English mæntel, mentel (“sleeveless cloak”), from Proto-West Germanic *mantel; later reinforced by Anglo-Norman mantel, both from Latin mantellum (“covering, cloak”) (French manteau), diminutive of mantum (Spanish manto), probably from Gaulish *mantos, *mantalos (“trodden road”), from Proto-Celtic *mantos, *mantlos, from Proto-Indo-European *menH- (“tread, press together; crumble”). Compare Icelandic möttull. Doublet of manteau.

meaning: hard outer covering (as of earth or snow)
etymology: From Middle English cruste, from Anglo-Norman and Old French cruste, from Latin crusta (“hard outer covering”), from Proto-Indo-European *krustós (“hardened”), from *krews- (“to form a crust, begin to freeze”), related to Old Norse hroðr (“scurf”), Old English hruse (“earth”), Old High German hrosa (“crust, ice”), Latvian kruvesis (“frozen mud”), Ancient Greek κρύος (krúos, “frost, icy cold”), κρύσταλλος (krústallos, “crystal, ice”), Avestan 𐬑𐬭𐬎𐬰𐬛𐬭𐬀- (xruzdra-, “hard”), Sanskrit क्रूड् (krūḍ, “thicken, make hard”). Doublet of crusta.

meaning: cut into small parts; cut (a body) apart limb from limb
etymology: From Middle English, from Old French desmembrer, from des- (“de-”) + membre (“limb”) + -er (“verbal suffix”).

meaning: eliminate from consideration; no longer consider; put out of court without further hearing; reject; discharge from employment; direct to leave; ADJ. dismissive; N. dismissal
etymology: Middle English, from Latin dimissus (“sent away, dismissed, banished”), perfect passive participle of dīmittō (“send away, dismiss”), from dis- + mittere (“to send”).

meaning: belittle
etymology: From Middle English disparage (noun), disparagen (verb), from Old French desparage (noun), desparagier (verb), from des- (“dis-”) + parage (“equal rank, rank”).

meaning: (manoeuver) strategic military or naval movement (done for training purposes); carefully planned process; stratagem; V: carry out a military maneuver; use maneuvers in gaining an end
etymology: From Middle French manœuvre (“manipulation, maneuver”) and manouvrer (“to maneuver”), from Old French manovre (“handwork, manual labor”), from Medieval Latin manopera, manuopera (“work done by hand, handwork”), from manu (“by hand”) + operari (“to work”). First recorded in the Capitularies of Charlemagne (800 AD) to mean "chore, manual task", probably as a calque of the Frankish *handuwerk (“hand-work”). Compare Old English handweorc, Old English handġeweorc, German Handwerk. The verb is a doublet of the verb manure.

meaning: basically different; impossible to compare; unrelated
etymology: First attested in 1586; either borrowed from Middle French desparat or directly from Latin disparātus, perfect passive participle of disparō (“to divide”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix)), from dis- (“apart”) + parō (“to arrange”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ (“two”) and the root *per- (“carry forth”).

meaning: difference; condition of inequality; OP. parity
etymology: From Middle French disparité, from Latin disparitātem, accusative of disparitās, from dispār + -tās, from dis- + pār. By surface analysis, dis- + parity.

meaning: calm; impartial; not influenced by personal feelings
etymology: From dis- + passionate.

meaning: speediness; prompt execution; message sent with all due speed; V: send to a specified destination; finish promptly; kill
etymology: Compare typologically deliver (for the meaning to bring or transport) (< Latin dē- + līberō).

meaning: scatter; drive away; cause to vanish
etymology: From Middle English dispelen, from Latin dispellere (“to disperse; to dispel”).

meaning: distribute; prepare and give out (medicines); N. dispensation: dispensing; religious system; official exemption from an obligation or a rule
etymology: From Middle English, from Old French dispenser, from Latin dispēnsāre (“to weigh out, pay out, distribute, regulate, manage, control, dispense”), frequentative of dispendere (“to weigh out”), from dis- (“apart”) + pendere (“to weigh”).

meaning: scatter; Ex. disperse the cloud/crowd
etymology: From Middle French disperser, from Latin dispersus, past participle of dispergō (“to scatter abroad, disperse”), from dis- (“apart”) + spargō (“to scatter”); see sparse.

meaning: lacking in spirit
amuse; Ex. disport oneself; CF. divert
etymology: The noun is derived from Middle English disport, desport (“activity providing amusement, pleasure or relaxation; entertainment, recreation; game, pastime, sport; pleasure derived from an activity; source of comfort; consolation, solace; conduct, deportment; customary behaviour, manner; act, activity; departure”), from Anglo-Norman disport, Old French desport, deport (“game, pastime, sport; pleasure, recreation; disport”), from desporter: see further above.

meaning: argumentative; fond of argument
etymology: From disputation, equivalent to disputati(on) + -ous.

meaning: uneasiness; anxiety; V. disquiet: make anxious
etymology: From dis- + quietude.

meaning: formal systematic inquiry; explanation of the results of a formal inquiry; long formal speech or written report
etymology: Borrowed from French disquisition (“disquisition”), from Latin disquīsītiō (“inquiry, investigation”), from disquīrō (“to investigate”) (from dis- (prefix meaning ‘apart, asunder’) + quaerō (“to look for, seek; to inquire, question”)) + -tiō (suffix forming nouns relating to an action or the result of an action).

meaning: analysis; cutting apart in order to examine
etymology: Borrowed from Latin dissectiōnem, perhaps via Middle French dissection. By surface analysis, dissect + -ion.

meaning: disguise; hide the real nature of; pretend
etymology: First attested in the beginning of the 15th century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English dissemblen, dissimblen, dissemelen, borrowed from Old French dessambler, dissembler, disembler, itself borrowed from Latin dissimulō and modified after sembler, semblance, etc. Doublet of dissimulate, dissimilate, and dissimule. Displaced native Old English mīþan.

meaning: distribute; spread; scatter (like seeds)
etymology: Borrowed from Latin dissēminātus, the perfect passive participle of dissēminō (“to broadcast, disseminate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), further from dis- (“asunder, in all directions”) + sēminō (“to plant, sow”), from sēmen (“seed”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). See also Middle English disseminat(e) (“disseminated”).

meaning: disagree
etymology: From Middle English dissenten, from Latin dissentiō, dissentīre (“to differ in sentiments, disagree, be at odds, contradict, quarrel”), from dis- + sentiō, sentīre (see sense).

meaning: formal essay; treatise
etymology: From Latin dissertātiō, from dissertō.

meaning: dissenting (with an opinion, a group, or a government); rebellious; N.
etymology: From Latin dissidēns, present participle of dissideō (“to sit apart; to disagree”), from dis- (“asunder, apart, in two”) + sedeō (“to sit”).

meaning: pretend; conceal by feigning; dissemble
etymology: Inherited from Middle English dissimulaten, dissimilaten, from Latin dissimulātus + -en (“verb-forming suffix”), perfect passive participle of dissimulō (“to conceal, to pretend, to neglect”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dissimilis (“unlike”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).
