Compare the obsolete dissimule (“to conceal, disguise”), from Old French dissimuler (French dissimuler), ultimately from the same Latin root. Doublet of dissemble, dissimilate, and dissimule.

meaning: squander; waste foolishly; scatter
etymology: The verb is first attested in 1425, in Middle English, the adjective from 1606 to 1765; from Middle English dissipaten, from Latin dissipātus, perfect passive participle of dissipō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), also written dissupō (“to scatter, disperse, demolish, destroy, squander, dissipate”), from dis- (“apart”) + supō (“to throw”). Doublet of dissipe (“to dissipate”), now obsolete.

meaning: disintegration; reduction to a liquid form; looseness in morals; sensual indulgence; debauchery; ADJ. dissolute: lacking in moral restraint; leading an immoral life
etymology: From Middle English dissolucioun, from Old French dissolucion, from Latin dissolūtiō (“a dissolving, destroying, breaking up, dissolution”).

meaning: diminish; bring to a weaker or more difficult condition; demote; lower in rank; separate into components by analysis; Ex. reduced to the ranks; Ex. reduce the house to rubble; N. reduction
etymology: From Middle English reducen, from Old French reduire, from Latin redūcō (“reduce”); from re- (“back”) + dūcō (“lead”). See duke, and compare with redoubt.

meaning: persuade not to do; discourage; N. dissuasion
etymology: From Middle French dissuader, from Latin dissuādeō (“to urge differently”, “to advise against”, “to dissuade”), from dis- (“away from”, “asunder”) + suādeō (“to recommend”, “to advise”, “to urge”).

meaning: discord
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French dissonance, from Latin dissonantia; by surface analysis, dis- + son- + -ance.

meaning: reserved or aloof; cold in manner; Ex. distant greeting; ADV. distantly
etymology: Inherited from Middle English distaunt, from Old French distant, from Latin distāns.

meaning: expand; swell out
etymology: Borrowed from Latin distendō.

meaning: refine (a liquid by evaporating and subsequent condensation); concentrate; separate the most important parts from; Ex. distill fresh water from sea water; CF. brew
honor; excellence; difference; contrast; discrimination; Ex. graduated with distinction; Ex. a writer of real distinction
etymology: From Middle English distinccioun, from Old French distinction (attested from the 12th century), borrowed from Latin distinctiōnem, action noun of distinguō (“separate, distinguish”). By surface analysis, distinct (“to distinguish”) + -ion. Attested in English from the late 14th century.

meaning: clearly different; clearly noticed
etymology: From Middle English distincte, past participle of distincten (“to distinguish, discern”), from Old French destincter, from Latin distinctus, past participle of distinguere (“to distinguish”); see distinguish.

meaning: clearly different from others of the same kind
etymology: From Latin distinctus, perfect passive participle of distinguere (to push apart, to divide; see distinct) + -ive (forming adjectives signifying relation or tendency to). Cognate with French distinctif and Medieval Latin distinctivus.

meaning: twist out of shape; give a false account of; misrepresent; N. distortion
etymology: Borrowed from Latin distortum, past participle of distorqueō (“to twist, torture, distort”).

meaning: absentminded; distracted
etymology: Borrowed from French distrait.

meaning: upset; distracted by anxiety; very anxious and troubled almost to the point of madness; Ex. distraught with grief/worry
etymology: From Middle English distraught, blend of distract (“distracted”) and straught (“stretched, distraught”), past participle of strecchen (“to stretch”). Compare also bestraught, extraught, forstraught, etc. More at distract, stretch.

meaning: take (one'attention) off something; upset emotionally; make anxious; ADJ. distracted
etymology: Borrowed from Latin distractus, from distrahō (“to pull apart”), from dis- + trahō (“to pull”).

meaning: daily; occurring during the daytime
etymology: From Latin diurnālis, from diēs (“day”). Doublet of journal.

meaning: operatic singer; prima donna
etymology: From Italian diva (“diva, goddess”), from Latin dīva (“goddess”), female of dīvus (“divine, divine one; notably a deified mortal”), from Old Latin deivā, from Proto-Italic *deiwā (“goddess”), feminine of *deiwos (“god”), from Proto-Indo-European *deywós (“god”).

meaning: vary; go in different directions from the same point; ADJ. divergent: differing; deviating
etymology: From Medieval Latin dīvergō (“bend away from, go in a different direction”), from Latin dī- + vergō (“bend”).

meaning: differing in some characteristics (from each other); various; N. diversity: variety; dissimilitude; lack of resemblance
etymology: The adverb is derived from Middle English diverse (“differently; at various times”), from divers, diverse (adjective) (see above).

meaning: act of turning aside; pastime; V. divert: turn aside from a course; distract; amuse
etymology: From Middle English diversion, dyversioun, from Medieval Latin diversiō, from Latin divertō (“to divert”); see divert.

meaning: strip (as of clothes); deprive (as of rights); dispossess; N. divestiture (divestment)
etymology: Alteration of devest, from Middle French devester (“strip of possessions”), from Old French desvestir, from des- (“dis-”) + vestir (“to clothe”).

meaning: perceive intuitively (by or as if by magic); foresee the future; foretell; dowse; ADJ. N. divination
etymology: From Old French divin, from Latin dīvīnus (“of a god”), from divus (“god”). Displaced native Old English godcund.

meaning: use a divining rod to search for underground water or minerals
etymology: Unknown; originally a dialectal term from southern England.

meaning: reveal
etymology: Inherited from Middle English divulgen, from Latin dīvulgō + -en (verb-forming suffix), from dī- (“widely”) + vulgō (“to make known, announce; to publish”).

meaning: obedient; easily managed; submissive
etymology: Compare Portuguese dócil ("docile").

meaning: fierce; violent; N. ferocity
etymology: Taken from Latin ferōx (“wild, bold, savage, fierce”) + -ous.

meaning: program as for trial; book where such entries are made; list of things to be done; agenda; label fixed to a package listing contents or directions; V: describe in a docket
etymology: Uncertain; perhaps a diminutive of dock.

meaning: unable to compromise about points of doctrine; dogmatic; unyielding; marked by inflexible attachment to a doctrine without regard to its practical difficulties
etymology: Borrowed from French doctrinaire, from doctrine + -aire.

meaning: teachings in general; particular principle (religious, legal, etc.) taught; dogma; tenet; ADJ. doctrinal
etymology: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin doctrina (“teaching, instruction, learning, knowledge”), from doctor (“a teacher”), from docere (“to teach”); see doctor.

meaning: cause to accept a doctrine without questioning it; Ex. indoctrinated with mindless anti-communism
etymology: From in- + doctrine + -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare French endoctriner.

meaning: provide written evidence (for a claim); record with documents; N.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French document, from Latin documentum.

meaning: shaky; infirm from old age; V. dodder
take off; OP. don
etymology: The noun is derived from the verb.

meaning: determined; stubborn; stubbornly persevering; tenacious; Ex. Inspector Javert'dogged pursuit of Jean Valjean
etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

meaning: continue steadily in spite of difficulties
etymology: From Middle English perseveren, from Old French perseverer, from Latin persevērāre (“to continue steadfastly, persist, persevere”), from perseverus (“very strict or earnest”), from per (“through, by the means of”) + severus (“strict, earnest”). Doublet of perseverate.

meaning: poor verse
etymology: Probably from dog + -rel (“pejorative suffix”), akin to Dog Latin, late 14th c.

meaning: opinionated; holding stubbornly to one'opinion; arbitrary; doctrinal
etymology: From Middle French dogmatique and its etymon, Late Latin dogmaticus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek δογματικός (dogmatikós, “didactic”), from δόγμα (dógma, “dogma”).

meaning: blues; listlessness (lack of spirit or energy); slack (inactive) period; period of stagnation; ocean area near the equator where ships cannot move because there is no wind; Ex. in the doldrums
etymology: From obsolete doldrum (“slothful or stupid person”) plus the plural suffix -s. Doldrum is possibly derived from dull or Middle English dold (past participle of dullen, dollen (“to make or become blunt or dull; to make or become dull-witted or stupid; to make or become inactive”), from dul, dol, dolle (“not sharp, blunt, dull; not quick-witted, stupid; lethargic, sluggish”); see further at dull), modelled after tantrum.

meaning: state of depression or melancholy; style of slow, mournful music (evolved from southern Black American songs)
etymology: In reference to the ancient Roman and medieval Byzantine racing faction, a calque of Latin venetī (“Sea-Blues”) or factio veneta (“the sea-blue faction”) and Byzantine Greek Βένετοι (Bénetoi, “Blues”).

meaning: sorrowful; N. dolor
etymology: From Middle English dolorous, from Old French dolerous (modern French douloureux), from Late Latin dolōrōsus (“painful”), from Latin dolor. Doublet of dolorose.

meaning: slow-thinking stupid person; CF. dull
etymology: First used as a noun in Early Modern English, from dialectal English dold (“stupid, confused”), from Middle English dold, a variant of dulled, dult (“dulled”), past participle of dullen, dollen (“to make dull, make stupid”), from dull, dul, dwal (“stupid”). More at dull.

meaning: home; V. ADJ. domiciled: having one'domicile; Ex. He is domiciled in Britain.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English domicelle, domicylie, from Middle French domicile and directly from Latin domicilium.

meaning: rule over tyrannically
etymology: From Dutch domineren, from Middle French dominer.

meaning: control; rule; enjoy a commanding position in; overlook from a height; ³»·Á´Ùº¸´Ù
etymology: Borrowed from Latin dominātus, perfect active participle of dominor (“to rule, have dominion”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dominus (“lord, master”) + -or (verb-forming suffix).

meaning: exercising the most influence; high and easily seen; stronger than the other part of a system; not recessive
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French dominant.

meaning: put on; OP. doff
etymology: From Latin dominus (“lord, head of household”), akin to Italian don, Sicilian don, Spanish don; from domus (“house”). Doublet of dom, domine, dominie, and dominus.

meaning: clothing or equipment for a special purpose; Ex. cowboy outfit
etymology: Variant of earlier out-fit, from fit out. Equivalent to out- + fit.

meaning: sleeping; temporarily inactive; lethargic; latent
etymology: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin dormiēns, present participle of dormiō (“to sleep”).

meaning: window projecting upright from roof; CF. sleeping room
etymology: From Middle French dormoir (“sleeping room”), from dormir (“to sleep”).

meaning: relating to the back of an animal; Ex. dorsal fin
etymology: From Late Middle English dorsal/dorsale, borrowing from Medieval Latin dorsālis (“of or relating to the back”), from dorsum (“the back”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix); equivalent to dorsum + -al.

meaning: file of documents on a subject or person; file; CF. bundle of papers labeled on the back
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French dossier.

meaning: senility; feeblemindedness of old age; Ex. In one'dotage
etymology: From Middle English dotage, from doten (“to dote”) + -age; equivalent to dote + -age.

meaning: be excessively fond of; show signs of mental decline
etymology: The noun in the sense of "imbecile" is derived from Middle English dote (“simpleton”), itself from doten (see above). The noun in the sense of "darling" and "decay" is derived from the modern verb.

meaning: sullen; gloomy; stubborn
etymology: Compare French dur, Catalan dur, Italian duro, Portuguese duro, Romanian dur, Spanish duro. Doublet of dure.

meaning: silently showing ill humor or resentment; dark; gloomy
etymology: From Middle English soleyn, from Anglo-Norman soleyn (“alone”), from Old French sole (“single, sole, alone”), from Latin sōlus (“by oneself alone”). The change in meaning from "single" to morose occurred in Middle English.

meaning: sit on in order to hatch; think deeply or worry anxiously; N: the young of certain animals; group of young birds hatched at one time
etymology: From Middle English brood, brod, from Old English brōd (“brood; foetus; breeding, hatching”), from Proto-Germanic *brōduz (“heat, breeding”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreh₁- (“breath, mist, vapour, steam”).

meaning: plunge into water or liquid; dip; immerse; drench; wet throughly; extinguish; throw water over; dowse
etymology: Probably of North Germanic origin, related to Swedish dunsa (“to plumb down, fall clumsily”), Danish dunse (“to thump”). Compare Old English dwǣsċan (“to extinguish”) and douse below.

meaning: untidy (of a woman or clothes); slovenly; dressed in an unattractive way; shabby; CF. unattractive woman
etymology: First appears c. 1581. Origin uncertain, probably literally "little poorly dressed woman," formed from doue, "poorly dressed woman". Possibly also related to the Scots dow, meaning to "fade".

meaning: disheartened; dejected; sad; directed downward
etymology: The noun is derived from the adjective.

meaning: dull; lacking color; cheerless ; Ex. drab coat/life
etymology: The English word is cognate with Ancient Greek δρέπω (drépō, “to pluck”), Avestan 𐬛𐬭𐬀𐬟𐬱𐬀 (drafša, “banner, flag”), Lithuanian drãpanos (“household linens”), Old Norse trefja (“to rub, wear out”), trof (“fringes”), Sanskrit द्रापि (drāpi, “mantle, gown”), Serbo-Croatian drápati (“to scratch, scrape”)).

meaning: extremely severe; Ex. draconian punishment; CF. Draco: Athenian politician
etymology: From Latin Dracō (stem Dracōn-) + -ian, from Ancient Greek Δράκων (Drákōn), after the Athenian lawmaker Draco, known for making harsh laws. See δράκων (drákōn, “dragon”).

meaning: sediment in a liquid; lees; worthless residue
etymology: See dreg.

meaning: nonsense; foolishness; V: talk nonsense
etymology: From Middle English dravel, dribil, a deverbal from drevelen, drivelen (Etymology 2).

meaning: speech or writing with no meaning; foolish behavior or language; Ex. make (a) nonsense of: spoil; cause to fail
etymology: From non- (“no, none, lack of”) + sense, from c. 1610. Compare the semantically similar West Frisian ûnsin (“nonsense”), Dutch onzin (“nonsense”), German Unsinn (“nonsense”), English unsense (“nonsense”).

meaning: flow or fall in drops; let saliva flow out slowly from the mouth; move a ball; N.
etymology: From drib + -le (frequentative suffix).

meaning: fall or let fall in drops; shed drops; N: action or sound of falling in drops; liquid that falls in drops
etymology: Dutch druipen, druppelen (“to drip”), German Low German drüppen (“to drip”), German tropfen, tröpfeln (“to drip”), Norwegian Bokmål dryppe, Norwegian Nynorsk drypa (“to drip”).

meaning: flow in drops or in a thin stream; N.
etymology: For other similar cases of incorrect division, see also apron, daffodil, newt, nickname, orange, umpire.

meaning: queer and amusing
etymology: From French drôle (“comical, odd, funny”), from drôle (“buffoon”) from Middle French drolle (“a merry fellow, pleasant rascal”) from Old French drolle (“one who lives luxuriously”), from Middle Dutch drol (“fat little man, goblin”), itself from Old Norse troll, from Proto-Germanic *truzlą. Doublet of drôle and troll.

meaning: strange; eccentric; deviating from the normal
etymology: Began to be used to describe gay people in the late 1800s; see usage notes for more.

meaning: idle person who lives on other people'work; male bee
etymology: The etymology of the sense of "remote-controlled aircraft" is disputed; theories include early military UAVs dumbly flying on preset paths.

meaning: low, indistinct, continuous sound; V. CF. mumble
etymology: From Middle English murmur, murmor, murmour, from Old French murmure (modern French murmure), from Latin murmur (“murmur, humming, muttering, roaring, growling, rushing etc.”).

meaning: waste matter; worthless impurities
etymology: Cognate with Scots dros, drose, drosse (“small particles, fragments, dross”), Middle Dutch droes (“dregs”), Dutch droesem (“dregs”), German Drusen (“lees, dregs”), Latin fracēs (“grounds or dregs of oil”). Related also to drast, dregs.

meaning: hard unpleasant work; menial work
etymology: From drudge (“person who works in a low servile job”) + -ery (suffix meaning ‘the art, craft, or practice of’ forming nouns).

meaning: do drudgery; N: person who drudges
etymology: From Middle English druggen, perhaps from Old English *dryċġan, from Proto-West Germanic *druggjan, from Proto-Germanic *drugjaną, a denominative built to a lost noun *drugjaz (preserved in Old English Dryċġhelm), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrewgʰ-; compare Old English drēogan (“to do; to suffer”).

meaning: questionable; (of something) causing doubt; (of someone) filled with doubt; N. dubiety
etymology: From Latin dubius; like doubt, from Latin duo (cognate to English two), implying “two alternatives” (yes or no, true or false, etc.).

meaning: malleable; pliable; (of metals) easily pulled into shape; flexible; (of someone) easily influenced or controlled
etymology: From Old French, from Latin ductilis (“easily led”).

meaning: sweet sounding; pleasing to the ear; melodious
etymology: From Middle English doucet, from Old French doucet, from dulz, dulce (“sweet, pleasant”) + diminutive -et, from Latin dulcis (“sweet, pleasant”). Cognate with Spanish dulce, French doux, Italian dolce, Portuguese doce, and Romanian dulce. Doublet of dolcetto and doucet.

meaning: astonish (making dumb); ADJ. dumbfounded, dumfounded, dumbstruck
someone easily fooled or deceived; V: deceive
etymology: From French duper, from Middle French duppe, alteration of huppe (“hoopoe”), from Latin, onomatopoeic.

meaning: double-dealing; hypocrisy; being dishonest and deceitful; ADJ. duplicitous
etymology: From Latin duplicare (double). Equivalent to duplex + -ity.

meaning: length of time something lasts
etymology: From Middle English duracioun, from late Old French duracion, from Medieval Latin dūrātiō.

meaning: forcible restraint, especially unlawfully; coercion by threat; illegal coercion; Ex. a promise made under duress
etymology: Inherited from Middle English duresse, from Old French duresse, from Latin dūritia (“hardness”), from dūrus (“hard”).

meaning: (of people or their behavior) respectful; obedient (filled with a sense of duty)
shrink; reduce gradually
etymology: Frequentative form of dwine, from Middle English dwynen, from Old English dwīnan (“to waste away”), from Proto-West Germanic *dwīnan, from Proto-Germanic *dwīnaną. It is equivalent to dwine + -le, akin to Old Norse dvena, dvína, Dutch verdwijnen (“to disappear, dwindle”).

meaning: energetic; vigorously active
etymology: From French dynamique, from Ancient Greek δυναμικός (dunamikós, “powerful”), from δύναμις (dúnamis, “power”), from δύναμαι (dúnamai, “I am able”).

meaning: generator for producing electricity; energetic person
etymology: A shortening of dynamo-electric machine. The element dynamo- is ultimately from Ancient Greek δύναμις (dúnamis, “power”).

meaning: suffering from indigestion; N. dyspepsia: indigestion; difficulty in digesting food
etymology: First attested in 1694. From Ancient Greek δύσπεπτος (dúspeptos, “difficult to digest”), from δυσ- (dus-, “bad”) + πέπτω (péptō, “to digest”).

meaning: abnormal; impaired
etymology: Often confused with the separately derived prefix dis-.

meaning: word blindness; learning disorder marked by impairment of the ability to read
etymology: Learned borrowing from French dyslexie and/or German Dyslexie, coined by German ophthalmologist Rudolf Berlin in 1887, from dys- + lexis + -ia, from Ancient Greek δυσ- (dus-) + λέξις (léxis, “diction”, “word”), from Ancient Greek λέγω (légō, “to speak”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *leg- (“to collect, gather; to speak”). The term was coined with λέξις (léxis) being taken to mean "reading," likely due to semantic conflation of Greek λέγω (légō, “to speak”) and Latin legō (“to read”). By surface analysis, dys- + lex(is) + -ia.

meaning: inflammatory disorder of the lower intestinal tract
etymology: From Middle English dissenterie, from Old French dissenterie, from Latin dysenteria, from Ancient Greek δυσεντερία (dusentería), from δυσ- (dus-, “bad”) + ἔντερα (éntera, “bowels”).

meaning: unrefined; coarse; of earth; Ex. earthy remarks; OP. ethereal
etymology: From Middle English erthy, equivalent to earth + -y. Compare German erdig (“earthy”), Swedish jordig (“earthy”).

meaning: of this earth; terrestrial; worldly; not divine; possible; Ex. no earthly reason
etymology: From Middle English erthely, erthlich, ierðlich, from Old English eorþlīċ, corresponding to earth + -ly. Cognate with Old Norse jarðligr (“earthly”).

meaning: (of the tide) recede; lessen; diminish; N. OP. flow: rise of tide
etymology: See also West Frisian ebbe, Dutch eb, German Ebbe, Danish ebbe, Old Norse efja (“countercurrent”), Old English af. More at of, off.

meaning: showing excitement; overflowing with enthusiasm; boiling; N. ebullience; N. ebullition: state of boiling
etymology: Borrowing from Latin ēbulliēns, present participle of ēbulliō (“to boil”), from bulliō (“to bubble up”) (English boil). Compare bubbling, bubbly, and perky, which use a similar metaphor.

meaning: irregular; odd; unconventional; whimsical; bizarre; not concentric
etymology: From Middle French excentrique, from Medieval Latin eccentricus, from Ancient Greek ἔκκεντρος (ékkentros, “not having the earth as the center of an orbit”), from ἐκ (ek, “out”) + κέντρον (kéntron, “point”). Equivalent to ex- + -centric.

meaning: oddity; idiosyncrasy
etymology: Borrowed from Latin eccentricitās. By surface analysis, eccentric + -ity.

meaning: ecclesiastical; pertaining to the church; N: minister; priest; cleric; clergyman
etymology: From Middle English ecclesyastyke, from Late Latin ecclēsiasticus (“of the church”), from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησιαστικός (ekklēsiastikós). By surface analysis, ecclesiast + -ic. Doublet of Ecclesiasticus.

meaning: small church (in a prison, college, or hospital)
etymology: (printing office): Said to be because printing was first carried on in England in a chapel near Westminster Abbey.

meaning: clergyman attached to a chapel
etymology: From Middle English chapeleyn, from Old French chapelain, from Medieval Latin, Late Latin cappellānus, from cappella. Doublet of capelin. Displaced Old English handprēost.

meaning: chaplain (in the armed forces)
etymology: Borrowed from Italian padre, Spanish padre, or Portuguese padre (“priest”), which are from Latin pater (“father”). Doublet of ayr, faeder, father, pater, and père.

meaning: selective; composed of elements drawn from disparate sources; selecting individual elements from a variety of sources; N. eclecticism
etymology: Cognate to elect.

meaning: careful in choosing; having an effect only on certain things; not general; Ex. eclectic weed killer
darken; extinguish; outshine; surpass; cause an eclipse
etymology: From Middle English eclipse, from Old French eclipse, from Latin eclīpsis, from Ancient Greek ἔκλειψις (ékleipsis, “eclipse”), from ἐκλείπω (ekleípō, “to abandon, go missing, vanish”), from ἐκ (ek, “out”) and λείπω (leípō, “to leave behind”). Doublet of eclipsis. See also ellipse, ellipsis.

meaning: path of the sun and the planets
etymology: Borrowed from Latin eclīptica. So named because an eclipse can occur only when the Moon lies on this plane.

meaning: person concerned with the interrelationship between living organisms and their environment; person concerned with the detrimental effects of human civilization on the environment; CF. ecology
etymology: From eco- + -logist. The less common sense “environmentalist” might be from association with deep ecology, or influenced by Romance-language equivalents such as Spanish ecologista (“environmentalist”).

meaning: ecological community together with its environment
etymology: From eco- + system. Coined by English botanist Arthur Tansley in 1935 in a paper titled The Use and Abuse of Vegetational Concepts in the journal Ecology.

meaning: efficiency or conciseness in using something; thrifty management of resources
etymology: From Middle English yconomye, yconomy, borrowed via Old French yconomie or Medieval Latin from Latin oeconomia, from Ancient Greek οἰκονομία (oikonomía, “management of a household, administration”), from οἶκος (oîkos, “house”) + νέμω (némō, “distribute, allocate”). By surface analysis, eco- + -nomy. The first recorded sense of the word economy, found in a work possibly composed in 1440, is “the management of economic affairs”, in this case, of a monastery.

meaning: rapture; very strong feeling of joy and happiness; any overpowering emotion; ADJ. ecstatic: causing or experiencing ecstasy
etymology: From Old French estaise (“ecstasy, rapture”), from Latin ecstasis, from Ancient Greek ἔκστασις (ékstasis), from ἐξίστημι (exístēmi, “to displace”), from ἐκ (ek, “out”) and ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to stand”).

meaning: great joy and delight; ecstasy; ADJ. rapturous
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French rapture, from Latin raptūra, future active participle of rapiō (“snatch, carry off”).

meaning: swirling current of water, air, etc.; V.
etymology: From Middle English eddy, from Old English edēa, from ed- (“turning, back, reverse”) + ēa (“water”), equivalent to ed- + ea. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁é, and, consequently, cognate with Latin et. Related also to Danish ide (“eddy”), Swedish eda (“eddy”), Norwegian ida, ia, ea (“eddy”), Icelandic iða (“eddy”).

meaning: decree (especially one issued by a sovereign); official command
etymology: From Middle English edycte, borrowed from Latin edictum; earlier form edit, from Old French edit, from the same Latin word.

meaning: ruler in a monarchy; ADJ: (of a country) independent and self-governing; having supreme power; supreme; excellent
etymology: From Middle English sovereyn, from Old French soverain (whence also modern French souverain), from Vulgar Latin *superānus (compare Italian sovrano, Spanish soberano) from Latin super (“above”). Spelling influenced by folk-etymology association with reign. Doublet of soprano, from the same Latin root via Italian. Doublet of souverain. See also suzerain, foreign.

meaning: complete independence and self-government (of a country); supremacy of authority; power to govern
etymology: From Late Middle English sovereynte, souvereynte [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman sovereyneté, soverentee, and Old French soveraineté, souveraineté (modern French souveraineté), from soverain + -té (suffix forming nouns, often denoting a property or quality). Soverain is derived from Vulgar Latin *superānus (“chief; sovereign”), from Latin super (“above; on top of”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *upér (“above, over”)) + -ānus (“suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’, usually denoting a relationship of origin, position, or possession”)). The English word is analysable as sovereign + -ty (suffix forming abstract nouns from adjectives).

meaning: instruct; correct morally
etymology: From Old French edifier (“to build, to edify”), from Latin aedificare (“build”).

meaning: building (of imposing size)
etymology: From Middle English edifice, from Old French edifice, a classical borrowing of Latin aedificium (“building”), derived from aedificāre (“to build, establish”) (whence also English edify).

meaning: weird; causing fear because strange
etymology: From Middle English eri (“fearful”), from Old English earg (“cowardly, fearful”), from Proto-West Germanic *arg, from Proto-Germanic *argaz. Akin to Scots ergh, argh from the same Old English source. Doublet of argh.

meaning: rub out; remove the surface of
etymology: From Middle French effacer (“erase”), from Old French esfacier (“remove the face”).

meaning: able to produce a desired effect; valid
etymology: From Middle English effectual, effectuel, from Old French effectuel, from Late Latin effectualis.

meaning: effectual; producing a strong response; striking; in operation; in effect; Ex. effective speech/photograph
etymology: From French effectif, from Latin effectīvus (“productive; effective”), from efficiō (“to make; to bring about”), equivalent to effect + -ive.

meaning: effect; produce; achieve; Ex. effectuate a reconciliation
etymology: From the participle stem of Renaissance Latin effectuare, or its source, Latin effectus (“effect”); probably after Middle French effectuer.

meaning: having womanly traits
etymology: From Middle English effeminat, effemynat, from Latin effēminātus, past participle of effēminō, from fēmina (“woman”).

meaning: weaken; castrate
etymology: From Medieval Latin ēmasculātus, perfect passive participle of ēmasculō (“to emasculate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ē(x)- (“out, from, apart”) + masculus (“male, masculine”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix), further from mās (“a man, a male”) + -culus (diminutive suffix).

meaning: remove the sex organs (of a male animal or person)
etymology: Likely from an unattested sense of Middle English castrat (“(adjective) castrated; (noun) a castrated animal”), substantivized borrowing of Latin castrātus, perfect passive participle of castrō (“to prune, amputate, castrate”), see -ate (noun-forming suffix)).

meaning: inner excitement or exuberance; showing high spirits; emitting bubbles forming inside; bubbling from fermentation or carbonation; ADJ. effervescent; V. effervesce
etymology: Borrowed from French effervescence. By surface analysis, ef- + Latin ferv- + -escence.

meaning: having lost one'original power; barren; worn out; exhausted
etymology: From Latin effētus (“exhausted”, literally “that has given birth”), 1620s.

meaning: power to produce desired effect; ADJ. efficacious: effectual
etymology: From Old French efficace, from Late Latin efficācia (“efficacy”) (whence -acy), from efficāx (“efficacious”); see efficacious.

meaning: dummy; likeness of a person made of wood, paper, or stone; Ex. burn an effigy of the President
etymology: From French effigie, from Latin effigiēs (“likeness, effigy”), from effingō (“represent, portray”).

meaning: imitation of a real object used as a substitute; effigy
etymology: From dumb + -y. Pacifier sense from dummy teat where dummy is in the sense of a nonfunctional replica.

meaning: noxious (harmful) smell
etymology: From Latin effluvium (“an outlet”), from effluō (“flow out or away”), from ex (“out of, from”) + fluō (“flow”).

meaning: rudeness without any sense of shame; shameless boldness; presumptousness; nerve; cheek
etymology: From late 17th century French effronterie, from effronté (“shameless, insolent”), from Old French esfronté, from Vulgar Latin *exfrontātus. Compare Latin effrōns (“barefaced”), from the prefix ex- (“from”) + frōns (“forehead”) (English: front). By surface analysis, ef- + front + -er + -y.

meaning: shining brightly; brilliant
etymology: From Latin effulgēns (“flashing, glittering”), present participle of effulgeō (“to shine or gleam forth, flash, glitter”), from ē- (variant of ex- (prefix meaning ‘out; away’)) + fulgeō (“to flash, gleam, glisten, glitter, shine”) (from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“shiny; white”)). By surface analysis, ef- + Latin fulg(ere) + -ent.

meaning: pouring forth; unrestrained outpouring of feeling; V. effuse: pour out; ADJ. effusive: pouring forth; gushing
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French effusion, from Latin effūsiō (“outpouring”). Displaced native Old English āgotennes.

meaning: (of liquid) pour out in large quantities from a hole; make an excessive display of feeling (without true feeling); Ex. Blood gushed from the wound.
etymology: Compare Old Norse geysa (“to gush”), German gießen (“to pour”), Old English ġēotan ("to pour"; > English yote). Related to gust.

meaning: excessive interest in one'self; belief that one should be interested in one'self rather than in others; selfishness; ADJ. egoistic, egoistical
etymology: From French égoïsme, from New Latin egoismus, from Latin ego. By surface analysis, ego + -ism.

meaning: one'opinion of oneself; self-esteem
etymology: Borrowed from Latin ego (“I”). Chosen by Freud’s translator as a translation of his use of German Ich as a noun for this concept from the pronoun ich (“I”). Doublet of I and Ich.

meaning: egotistic; excessively self-centered (egocentric); self-important; conceited
etymology: From egotistic + -al.

meaning: tendency to speak or write of oneself excessively; conceit; self-importance
etymology: From Latin ego (“I”) + -t- (perhaps modelled on dogmatism, despotism, idiotism) + -ism.

meaning: notorious; conspicuously bad or shocking
etymology: From Latin ēgregius, from e- (“out of”), + grex (“flock”), + English adjective suffix -ous, from Latin suffix -osus (“full of”); reflecting the positive connotations of "standing out from the flock".

meaning: exit; opening for going out; act of going out; OP. ingress
etymology: From Latin ēgressus, from ex- + gressus, literally “out-way”.

meaning: exclamation; abrupt ejection (to discharge sperm); V. ejaculate
etymology: From French éjaculation, borrowed from Latin ēiaculārī.

meaning: addition of details; intricacy
etymology: From Middle French élaboration. Morphologically elaborate + -ion.

meaning: work out carefully; add more detail or information; ADJ.
etymology: 1575, from Late Latin ēlabōrātus (“worked out”), past participle of ēlabōrō (“to work out”), from ē- (“out, forth, fully”) + labor (“work, toil, exertion”). More at e-, labour.

meaning: filled with excited joy and pride; overjoyed; in high spirits; joyful and proud; Ex. elated crowd; V. elate; N. elation
etymology: Latin elatus (“raised”).

meaning: poem or song expressing lamentation (for the dead); ADJ. elegiacal, elegiac
etymology: From Middle French elegie, from Latin elegīa, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐλεγείᾱ (elegeíā), ellipsis of ἐλεγείᾱ ᾠδή (elegeíā ōidḗ, “an elegiac song”).

meaning: draw out fact or information (by discussion or from someone)
etymology: Borrowed from Latin elicitus from eliciō (“draw forth”).

meaning: cure-all; panacea; something invigorating
etymology: From Medieval Latin elixir (“philosopher's stone”), from Arabic اَلْإِكْسِير (al-ʔiksīr, “philosopher's stone”), from Ancient Greek ξηρίον (xēríon, “powder for drying wounds”), from ξηρός (xērós, “dry”).

meaning: omission of words from a text; mark used to indicate an omission (when the meaning can be understood without them); PL. ellipses
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from Latin ellīpsis, from Ancient Greek ἔλλειψις (élleipsis, “omission”). Doublet of ellipse.

meaning: elliptic; oval; of an ellipse; containing an ellipsis; ambiguous either purposely or because key words have been left out
etymology: From elliptic + -al, from Ancient Greek ἐλλειπτικός (elleiptikós), from ἐλλείπω (elleípō, “I leave out, omit”).

meaning: expressiveness; persuasive speech; ADJ. eloquent: movingly expressive; expressing ideas well so that the hearers can be influeneced
etymology: From Middle English eloquence, from Old French eloquence, from Latin ēloquentia. Doublet of eloquency, directly from Latin.

meaning: explain; make clear; clarify; enlighten; CF. lucid
etymology: From Late Latin ēlūcidātus, perfect passive participle of ēlūcidō (“to lighten, enlighten”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ē(x)- (“out, from”) + lūcidus (“bright, clear, understandable”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix), literally “to make light of (something)”, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“bright; to see; to shine”). Compare French élucider.

meaning: evasive; not frank; baffling; hard to grasp, catch, or understand; V. elude: escape from; escape the understanding or grasp of; Ex. elude the hunter; Ex. His name eludes me.
etymology: From Latin elusus, past participle of eludo (“to parry a blow, to deceive”).

meaning: relating to paradise; blissful
etymology: From Latin Elysium (from Ancient Greek Ἠλύσιον (Ēlúsion, “Elysium; one of the Elysian Fields”)) + -an (adjective-forming suffix).

meaning: place or condition of bliss
etymology: From Latin, from Ancient Greek Ἠλῠ́σῐον (Πεδῐ́ον) (Ēlŭ́sĭon (Pedĭ́on)).

meaning: thin and wasted (from hunger or illness)
issue forth; come out
etymology: From Latin ēmānāre (“to flow out, spring out of, arise, proceed from”), from ē (“out”) + mānāre (“to flow”).

meaning: set free; liberate
etymology: The verb emancipate has verb sense 1.1 (“to set free”) and verb sense 1.3 (“(obsolete) to place under one’s control”) which are contradictory. The Latin word ēmancipō had the same senses, and the Oxford English Dictionary notes that according to the Latin grammarian Paulus Festus (fl. 8th century) this is because both actions were effected by the legal process of mancipation.

meaning: ban on commerce or other activity
etymology: From Spanish embargar (“to arrest”), from late Latin *imbarricāre (“to bar”), from Latin in- + Vulgar Latin *barra (“bar, barrier”).

meaning: commence; go on board a boat; begin a journey
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French embarquer, from em- + barque (“small ship”). Compare with Portuguese embarcar, Spanish abarcar.

meaning: (imbed); enclose; place in something; fix firmly in a surrounding mass
etymology: From em- + bed.

meaning: adorn; ornament; enhance as a story (by adding fictitious details)
etymology: From Middle English embelishen, from Old French embellir, from em- + bel.

meaning: taking for one'own use in violation of trust; stealing (of money placed in one'care)
etymology: From embezzle + -ment.

meaning: ornament richly (a shield or flag); N. emblazonment
etymology: From en- + blazon, from Old French blason (“shield”).

meaning: give a bodily form to; incorporate; include
etymology: From em- + body.

meaning: produce a design in raised relief; decorate with a raised design
etymology: The noun is derived from the verb.

meaning: hug; clasp with the arms; adopt or espouse; accept readily; encircle; include; Ex. embrace the cause/socialism; Ex. all-embracing; CF. brace; CF. bracelet
etymology: The verb is derived from Middle English embracen (“to clasp in one's arms, embrace; to reach out eagerly for, welcome; to enfold, entwine; to ensnare, entangle; to twist, wrap around; to gird, put on; to lace; to be in or put into bonds; to put a shield on the arm; to grasp (a shield or spear); to acquire, take hold of; to receive; to undertake; to affect, influence; to incite; to unlawfully influence a jury; to surround; to conceal, cover; to shelter; to protect; to comfort; to comprehend, understand”) [and other forms], from Old French embracer, embracier (“to kiss”) (modern French embrasser (“to kiss; (dated) to embrace, hug”)), from Late Latin *imbracchiāre, from in- (prefix meaning ‘in, inside, within’)) + bracchium (“arm”). The English word is analysable as em- + brace. The noun is derived from the verb.

meaning: surround
etymology: From en- + circle.

meaning: decorate with needlework; ornament (a story) with fancy or fictitious details; embellish
etymology: From Middle English embrouderen, frequentative of embrouden (“to decorate, embroider”), equivalent to embroid + -er. Middle English embrouden itself comes from Anglo-Norman embrouder, from Old French embrosder (“to embroider”), ultimately of Germanic origin, though the exact pathway is uncertain. Possibly an intensive of Old French brosder, brouder (compare Norman broudaïr), from Gothic *𐌱𐍂𐌿𐌶𐌳𐍉𐌽 (*bruzdōn), related to English bristle and brad. Alternatively, perhaps from Frankish *anbroʀdōn (“to embroider, stitch”), related to Old High German anabrortōn (“to embroider”), Old English onbryrdan (“to prick, incite”).

meaning: throw into confusion; involve in strife, dispute, or quarrel; entangle; CF. imbroglio
etymology: * Spanish embrollar

meaning: undeveloped; rudimentary; N. embryo: organism in the early stage of development
etymology: From New Latin embryonicus.

meaning: correct (usually a text); N. emendation: correction of errors; improvement
etymology: From Middle English emenden, from Latin ēmendō (“to free from fault”), from ex- (“out”) + mendum (“fault, blemish”). Doublet of amend.

meaning: substance causing vomiting; ADJ.
etymology: From French émétique, from Vulgar Latin *emeticus, from Ancient Greek ἐμετικός (emetikós), from ἔμετος (émetos, “vomit”); by surface analysis, em(esis) + -etic.

meaning: rising above others; high; lofty; distinguished; Ex. eminent position
etymology: From Middle French éminent, from Latin present participle ēminēns, ēminentis, from verb ēmineō (“to project, protrude”), from ex- (“out of, from”) + mineō, related to mons (English mount). Compare with imminent. Unrelated to emanate, which is instead from mānō (“to flow”). Displaced native Old English deal.

meaning: agent (sent on a mission to represent another); messenger
etymology: From French émissaire, from Latin emissarius (“agent, scout, spy”).

meaning: soothing or softening remedy (for the skin); ADJ.
etymology: From French émollient, from Latin emolliēns, present active participle of ēmolliō (“make soft”), from ex- + molliō, from mollis (“soft”). By surface analysis, e- + Latin moll- + -i- + -ent.

meaning: salary; payment for an office; compensation
etymology: From Middle English emolument, from Old French emolument, from Latin ēmolumentum.

meaning: ability to identify with another'feelings, ideas, etc.; identification with and understanding of another'feelings; V. empathize; CF. sympathy
etymology: A twentieth-century borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐμπάθεια (empátheia, literally “passion”) (formed from ἐν (en, “in, at”) + πάθος (páthos, “feeling”)), equivalent to em- + -pathy, coined by Edward Bradford Titchener in 1909 to translate German Einfühlung. The modern word in Greek εμπάθεια (empátheia) has an opposite meaning denoting strong negative feelings and prejudice against someone.

meaning: sympathy for the suffering of others; ADJ. compassionate
etymology: From Middle English compassioun, compassion, from Old French compassion, from Ecclesiastical Latin compassio (“sympathy”), from Latin compati, past participle compassus (“to suffer together with”), from com- (“together”) + pati (“to suffer”); see passion. By surface analysis, com- + passion.

meaning: based on experience
etymology: From empiric + -al.

meaning: imitate; rival; try to equal or excel (through imitation)
etymology: First attested in 1586; borrowed from Latin aemulātus, perfect active participle of Latin aemulor (“to rival, emulate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

meaning: in love; Ex. enamored of his own beauty; V. enamor: inspire with love
etymology: Inherited from Middle English enamoured, a partial calque of Old French enamore, past participle of enamorer, enamourer; compare amour and enamor, enamour.

meaning: encode; convert a message into code; put into cipher
etymology: From en- + cipher.

meaning: territory enclosed within an alien land
etymology: Borrowed from French enclave, from Middle French enclave (“enclave”), deverbal of enclaver (“to inclose”), from Old French enclaver (“to inclose, lock in”), from Vulgar Latin *inclāvāre (“to lock in”), from in + Latin clavis (“key”) or clavus (“nail, bolt”). Compare inlock.

meaning: praising; eulogistic; N. encomium: very high praise; eulogy
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἐγκωμιαστικός (enkōmiastikós).

meaning: surround; include; Ex. His activities encompass publishing and computers.
etymology: From Middle English encompassen. By surface analysis, en- + compass.

meaning: gradual intrusion; Ex. I resent all these encroachments on my valuable time; V. encroach: take another'possessions or right gradually or stealthily; intrude; Ex. encroach on/upon
etymology: From encroach + -ment.

meaning: burden; N. encumbrance
etymology: From Middle English encombren, from Old French encombrer, from en- + combrer (“to hinder”) (See cumber). By surface analysis, en- + cumber.

meaning: fond word or act; expression of affection
etymology: From endear + -ment.

meaning: make beloved; Ex. endear her to everyone; ADJ. dear: loved; cherished; high-priced
etymology: From en- + dear.

meaning: prevailing among a specific group of people or in a specific area or country; peculiar to a particular region or people; CF. pandemic
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἐν (en, “in”) + δῆμος (dêmos, “people”) + -ic. Possibly via Ancient Greek ἔνδημος (éndēmos, “among one's people, at home, native”) and/or French endémique. By surface analysis, en- + demic.

meaning: approve; support; write one'signature on the back of; N. endorsement; CF. dorsal
etymology: Alteration influenced by Medieval Latin indorsare of Middle English endosse, from Old French endosser (“to put on the back”), from Latin dossum, alternative form of dorsum (“back”), from which also dorsal (“of the back”). That is, the ‘r’ was dropped in Latin dossum, which developed into Old French and then Middle English endosse, and then the ‘r’ was re-introduced into English via the Medieval Latin indorsare, which had retained the ‘r’. Note that the alternative spelling indorse also uses the initial ‘i’ from Latin (in-, rather than en-), but this form is now rare.

meaning: provide with some quality; endow
etymology: Sense 2 is from a combination of the above. Doublet of induce.

meaning: lasting; surviving; V. endure: bear (pain or suffering) for a long time; remain alive (in spite of difficulties); last; survive
invigorate; give energy to; make forceful and active
etymology: From energy + -ize.

meaning: weaken; take away energy from
etymology: From Latin ēnervātus, past participle of ēnervō (“to weaken”).

meaning: admit to the rights of citizenship (especially the right to vote); CF. franchise
etymology: From Old French enfranchir (“to set free, enfranchise”), from en- (“in”) + franchir (“to set free”), equivalent to en- + franchise.

meaning: attract; employ; hire; pledge oneself; confront; fight; enter into confliction; interlock; lock together; participate; N. engagement: agreement to marry; arrangement to meet someone or to do something; battle
etymology: From Middle English engagen, from Old French engagier (“to pledge, engage”), from Old French en- (“in, under”) + gage (“pledge”), from Frankish *wadi (“pledge”), from Proto-Germanic *wadją (“pledge, guarantee”), from Proto-Indo-European *wedʰ- (“to pledge, redeem a pledge; guarantee, bail”), equivalent to en- + gage. Cognate with Old English weddian (“to engage, covenant, undertake”), German wetten (“to bet, wager”), Icelandic veðja (“to wager”). More at wed.

meaning: charming; attractive
employed; busy; betrothed; involved in conflict
cause; produce; give rise to
etymology: From Middle English engendren, from Old French engendrer, from Latin ingenerāre.

meaning: occupy fully; absorb
etymology: From Middle English engrossen, from Anglo-Norman engrosser (“to gather in large quantities, draft something in final form”); partly from the phrase en gros (“in bulk, in quantity, at wholesale”), from en- + gros; and partly from Medieval Latin ingrossō (“thicken, write something large and in bold lettering”, v.), from in- + grossus (“great, big, thick”), from Old High German grōz (“big, thick, coarse”), from Proto-West Germanic *graut, from Proto-Germanic *grautaz (“large, great, thick, coarse grained, unrefined”), from Proto-Indo-European *ghrewə- (“to fell, put down, fall in”). More at in-, gross. By surface analysis, en- + gross.

meaning: increase; make greater (as in value, reputation, or usefulness); improve
etymology: From Middle English enhauncen, anhaunsen, from Anglo-Norman anhauncer (“enhance, raise”), from Vulgar Latin *inaltiāre (“raise”), derived from Latin in + altus (“high”). The /h/ in Old French was taken from haut (“high”), where it resulted from Frankish influence.

meaning: puzzle; mystery; ADJ. enigmatic: obscure; puzzling
etymology: From Latin aenigma (“riddle”), being derived itself from the Ancient Greek verbal noun αἴνιγμα (aínigma, “dark saying, speaking in riddles”).

meaning: baffle or confuse by a difficult problem; ponder over a problem in an effort to solve; clarify or solve by reasoning; Ex. puzzle out the answer; N.
etymology: The noun appears to be derived from the verb.

meaning: command; order; forbid
etymology: From Middle English enjoinen, from Old French enjoindre (“to join with”), from Latin iniungo (“to attach”), a compound of in- (“into” “upon”) and iungo.

meaning: ill will; hatred; hostility
etymology: From Middle English enemyte, from Old French enemisté, ennemistié, from Late Latin, Vulgar Latin *inimīcitās, *inimīcitātem, from Latin inimīcus (“enemy”). Cognate with French inimitié, Portuguese inimizade, Spanish enemistad. By surface analysis, en(e)m(y) + -ity.

meaning: boredom; listlessness and dissatisfaction resulting from lack of interest; CF. annoy
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French ennui, from Old French enui (“annoyance”), from enuier (modern French ennuyer), from Late Latin inodiō, from Latin in odiō (“hated”). Doublet of annoy.

meaning: hugeness (in a bad sense); excessive wickedness; Ex. enormity of the crime; ADJ. enormous
etymology: From Late Middle English ēnorme (“monstrous or unnatural act; enormity”), from Old French énormité (“enormity”), from Latin ēnormitās (“irregularity; enormity”), from ēnōrmis (“irregular, unusual; enormous, immense”) + -itās (suffix forming nouns indicating states of being). Ēnōrmis is derived from e- (a variant of ex- (prefix meaning ‘out; away’) + nōrma (“norm, standard”) + -is (Latin suffix forming adjectives from nouns).

meaning: please intensely; fill with rapture and delight
etymology: From en- + rapture.

meaning: settle comfortably; place comfortably (in a secure place)
etymology: From en- + sconce, “to place in a sconce (“fortification”)”.

meaning: follow (as a result)
etymology: From Old French ensu-, stem of some conjugated forms of ensuivre (“follow close upon, come afterward”) (French ensuivre), from Latin īnsequere, from īnsequi (“to pursue, follow, follow after; come next”), from in- (“upon”) (see in-) + sequi (“follow”) (see sequel).

meaning: make necessary; require; necessitate; involve; limit the inheritance of (property) to a specified succession of heirs; Ex. entail A on/upon B
etymology: From Middle English entaillen, from Old French entaillier, entailler (“to notch”, literally “to cut in”); from prefix en- + tailler (“to cut”), from Late Latin taliare, from Latin talea. Compare late Latin feudum talliatum (“a fee entailed, i.e., curtailed or limited”).

meaning: full of initiative; showing enterprise
willingness to take new ventures; initiative; business organization; plan (that is difficult or daring); Ex. their latest enterprise to sail round the world in a small boat
etymology: From Old French via Middle English and Middle French entreprise, feminine past participle of entreprendre (“to undertake”), from entre (“in between”) + prendre (“to take”), from Latin inter + prehendō, see prehensile.

meaning: capture; enslave; captivate; hold the complete attention of (as if magic); hold spellbound
etymology: From Middle English enthrallen. By surface analysis, en- + thrall.

meaning: lure; persuade to do (something wrong); attract; tempt
etymology: From Middle English enticen, from Old French enticier (“to stir up or excite”), from a Vulgar Latin *intitiāre (“I set on fire”), from in- + titiō (“firebrand (tool)”), from Proto-Italic *tītjō (“heating”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *teih₁- (“to become hot, melt or to end”).

meaning: behavior (of children) causing trouble with no serious harm; damage; harm; Ex. mischief to the crops; ADJ. mischievous: causing mischief; playfully troublesome
etymology: From Middle English myschef, meschef, meschief, mischef, from Old French meschief, from meschever (“to bring to grief”), from mes- (“badly”) + chever (“happen; come to a head”), from Vulgar Latin *capare, from Latin caput (“head”).

meaning: real being
etymology: From the Medieval Latin entitās, from ēns (“being”) (stem: ent-) + -tās (compare essentia), see there for more information.

meaning: study of insects
etymology: From French entomologie, from Ancient Greek ἔντομον (éntomon, “insect”) + -logie (from Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía, “-logy”)), equivalent to entomo- + -logy.

meaning: put under a spell (condition caused by magical power); carry away (fill with strong feeling) with emotion; put into a trance; fill with delight
etymology: From Middle French entrance (“entry”). Replaced native Middle English ingang (“entrance, admission”), from Old English ingang (“ingress, entry, entrance”).

meaning: hypnotic state; ecstatic state; detachment from one'physical surrounding (as in contemplation or daydreaming); CF. transition
etymology: From Middle English traunce, from Anglo-Norman transe (“fear of coming evil; passage from life to death”), from transir (“to be numb with fear; to die, pass on”), from Latin trānseō (“to cross over”).

meaning: induced sleeping state; ADJ. hypnotic; V. hypnotize
etymology: From modern scholarly Ancient Greek ὕπνωσις (húpnōsis), which formation closes the derivational gap between the ancient words ὑπνόω (hupnóō, “I put to sleep”) and ὑπνωτικός (hupnōtikós, “sleep-inducing, soporific”). Ultimately traces back to ὕπνος (húpnos, “sleep”).

meaning: plead; ask earnestly
etymology: The noun is derived from Late Middle English entrete (“agreement; negotiation; treatment of a subject in discourse”), from the verb.

meaning: entrance; a way in; right to enter; main dish of a meal; Ex. entree into the exclusive circle
businessperson (who assumes the risk of a business venture); contractor; ADJ. entrepreneurial
etymology: Borrowed from French entrepreneur (“one who undertakes or manages”), from Middle French entrepreneur, from entreprendre (“to undertake”) + -eur.

meaning: list; mention one by one
etymology: First attested in 1600–1650; borrowed from Latin enumerātus, the perfect passive participle of enumerō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.

meaning: announce; proclaim; utter or speak, especially distinctly; pronounce clearly; articulate; Ex. This theory was first enunciated by him.
etymology: From Latin ēnuntiātus, past participle of ēnuntiō (“to report, declare”), from ē- + nūntiō (“to report”). Doublet of enounce.

meaning: enclose; surround; N. environs: surrounding area (as of a city)
etymology: * Spanish environ (obsolete)

meaning: long period of time; an age; longest division of geologic time containing two or more eras
ornament worn on the shoulder (of a uniform, etc.)
decorative edge of hanging threads; edge
etymology: From Middle English frenge, from Old French frenge, from Vulgar Latin *frimbia, a metathesis of Latin fimbriae (“fibers, threads, fringe”, plural), of uncertain origin. Compare German Franse and Danish frynse. Displaced native Middle English fnæd (“fringe”), Middle English byrd (“fringe”), Middle English fasel (“fringe”) from Old English fæs (“fringe”), and Old English fnæs (“fringe”). Doublet of fimbria.

meaning: short-lived; fleeting
etymology: From New Latin ephemerus, from Ancient Greek ἐφήμερος (ephḗmeros), the more common form of ἐφημέριος (ephēmérios, “of, for, or during the day, living or lasting but for a day, short-lived, temporary”), from ἐπί (epí, “on”) + ἡμέρα (hēméra, “day”).

meaning: fast; rapid; N. ADJ. fleeting: passing quickly; ephemeral
etymology: From Middle English flete, flet (“fleet”), from Old English flēot (“ship”), likely related to Proto-West Germanic *flotōn, from Proto-Germanic *flutōną (“to float”).

meaning: long heroic poem, novel, or similar work of art (celebrating the feats of a hero); ADJ: (of stories or events) resembling an epic; grand
etymology: From Middle French épique, from Latin epicus, from Ancient Greek ἐπικός (epikós), from ἔπος (épos, “word, story”).

meaning: connoisseur of food and drink; gourmet; ADJ. epicurean; CF. Epicurus
etymology: From Epicurus, the name of an Ancient Greek philosopher who advocated such a lifestyle.

meaning: believing that pleasure is good and suffering is bad and should be avoided; N.
etymology: From Epicurean (“follower of Epicureanism”).

meaning: witty thought or saying, usually short
etymology: From Middle French epigramme, from Latin epigramma, from Ancient Greek ἐπίγραμμα (epígramma, “inscription”).

meaning: short speech at conclusion of dramatic work
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French epilogue, from Latin epilogus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίλογος (epílogos, “a conclusion, peroration of a speech, epilogue of a play”), from ἐπιλέγω (epilégō, “to say in addition”). Eclipsed Middle English lenvoie (“epilogue”) borrowed ultimately from Old French. Equivalent to epi- + -logue.

meaning: (of a story or play) loosely connected; made up of separate and loosely connected parts; N. episode: incident in the course of an experience
etymology: From episode + -ic. Compare French épisodique.

meaning: philosopher who studies the nature of knowledge; N. epistemology
etymology: From epistemology + -ist.

meaning: inscription in memory of a dead person (as on a tombstone)
etymology: From Old French epitafe, from Late Latin epitaphium (“eulogy”), from Ancient Greek ἐπιτάφιος (epitáphios, “relating to a funeral”), from ἐπί (epí, “over”) + τάφος (táphos, “tomb”). By surface analysis epi- + -taph.

meaning: word or phrase characteristically used to describe a person or thing; descriptive phrase to characterize a person (often contemptous)
etymology: From Middle French épithète, from Latin epithetum, epitheton, from Ancient Greek ἐπίθετον (epítheton, “epithet, adjective”), the neuter of ἐπίθετος (epíthetos, “additional”), from ἐπιτίθημι (epitíthēmi, “to add on”), from ἐπι- (epi-, “in addition”) + τίθημι (títhēmi, “to put”) (suf. possibly related to title in the sense of "ascribed appellation") (from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to put, to do”)). Doublet of epitheton.

meaning: perfect example or embodiment; brief summary; Ex. epitome of good manners; V. epitomize: make an epitome of; be an epitome of; embody
etymology: From Middle French, from Latin epitomē, from Ancient Greek ἐπιτομή (epitomḗ, “an abridgment, also a surface-incision”), from ἐπιτέμνω (epitémnō, “to cut upon the surface, cut short, abridge”), from ἐπι- (epi-, “up”) + τέμνω (témnō, “to cut”).

meaning: period of time
etymology: From Medieval Latin epocha, from Ancient Greek ἐποχή (epokhḗ, “a check, cessation, stop, pause, epoch of a star, i.e., the point at which it seems to halt after reaching the highest, and generally the place of a star; hence, a historical epoch”), from ἐπέχω (epékhō, “to hold in, check”), from ἐπι- (epi-, “upon”) + ἔχω (ékhō, “to have, hold”). Doublet of epoche.

meaning: tranquil; of even calm temper; (of temperature) steady; uniform
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin aequābilis, from aequō (“make level”), from aequus (“even, level”).

meaning: calmness of temperament; composure
etymology: From French équanimité, from Latin aequanimitās (“calmness, equanimity”), from aequus (“even; calm; fair”) + animus (“mind, soul”) + -itās. By surface analysis, equ- + anim(us) + -ity.

meaning: rider on horseback; ADJ.
etymology: Ultimately from Latin equester (“of or pertaining to equestrians/cavalry”) + -ianus (“-ian, related to”, adjective marker), from equus (“horse”).

meaning: balance of opposing forces; balance of the mind; equanimity
etymology: From Latin aequilībrium, from equal + lībra (“balance”).

meaning: resembling a horse; Ex. equine face
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin equīnus (“of or pertaining to horses”).

meaning: period of equal days and nights; the beginning of spring and autumn; Ex. vernal/autumnal equinox; ADJ. equinoctial
etymology: The rare alternative plural form equinoctes treats equinox as if it were a Latin word; the plural of Latin nox (“night”) is noctēs.

meaning: balance; balancing force; equilibrium
etymology: From equi- + poise.

meaning: fair; impartial; OP. inequitable
etymology: From French équitable, from Old French, from equité (“equity”).

meaning: fairness; justice; OP. inequity
etymology: From Middle English equitee, equytee, from Old French equité, from Latin aequitās (“uniformity; impartiality; fairness”).

meaning: (of words or statements) ambiguous; intentionally misleading; (of behavior) questionable; OP. unequivocal
etymology: From Late Latin aequivocus + -al, from aequus + vocō. By surface analysis, equi- + vocal.

meaning: use equivocal language to deceive people; lie; mislead; attempt to conceal the truth; N. equivocation
etymology: From Late Middle English equivocaten, from Medieval Latin aequivocātus, perfect passive participle of aequivocō (“to be called by the same name”), from Late Latin aequivocus (“ambiguous, equivocal”). Compare French équivoque.

meaning: eat away; wear away gradually by abrasion; Ex. The sea erodes the rocks.
etymology: From French éroder, from Latin ērōdō.

meaning: pertaining to passionate love or sexual love
etymology: From French érotique, from Ancient Greek ἐρωτικός (erōtikós, “related to love”), from ἔρως (érōs, “sexual love”).

meaning: wandering (esp. in search of adventure); straying from proper moral standards; Ex. knight-errant
etymology: Doublet of arrant.

meaning: odd; irregular in movement or behavior; unpredictable
etymology: From Middle English erratik, from Middle French erratique (from Old French erratique) and its etymon Classical Latin errāticus.

meaning: mistaken; wrong; incorrect
etymology: From late Middle English erroneous, from Middle French erroneux, from Latin erroneus.

meaning: (of a person or book) learned; full of learning; scholarly; N. erudition
etymology: From Latin ērudītus, participle of ērudiō (“educate, train”), from e- (“out of”) + rudis (“rude, unskilled”). Doublet of erudit.

meaning: full of learning; erudite; like a scholar; Ex. scholarly journal
etymology: From scholar + -ly.

meaning: prank; flighty conduct; reckless adventure that disobeys rules
etymology: Borrowed from French escapade (“the act of escaping; a trick”), itself borrowed from Old Spanish escapada, from escapar (“to escape”), from Vulgar Latin *excappāre.

meaning: mischievous trick
etymology: Cognate with Middle Low German prunken (“to flaunt”), German prunken (“to flaunt”), Danish prunke (“to make a show, prank”). Sense of "mischievous act" from earlier verbal sense of "to be crafty or subtle, set in order, adjust". See also prink, prance, prong.

meaning: (esp. of a woman'behavior) capricious; often changing, esp. from one lover to another; impulsive
etymology: From flight + -y. Compare Dutch vluchtig (“volatile; fleeting; cursory”), German flüchtig (“volatile; fleeting; momentary; quick”), Danish flygtig (“elusive; evasive”), Swedish flyktig.

meaning: avoid habitually; Ex. eschew alcoholic drinks
etymology: See also French esquiver.

meaning: hard to understand; known only to the chosen few, esp. initiates; N. esoterica
etymology: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐσωτερικός (esōterikós, “belonging to an inner circle”), from ἐσωτέρω (esōtérō, “further inside”), comparative of ἔσω (ésō, “within”), from ἐς (es), εἰς (eis, “into”) (the term esoteric referred originally to the secret teachings of Greek philosophers, versus public or exoteric ones).

meaning: spying
etymology: Recorded since 1793, from French espionnage, from espionner (“to spy”), from Middle French espionner (“to spy”), from espion (“spy”), from Old French espion (“spy”), from Frankish *spehō (“spy”), from Frankish *spehōn (“to spy”), from Proto-Germanic *spehōną (“to spy, peek, peer”). In modern times, the French pronunciation of the s, which had fallen silent since the 13th century, was restored due to the influence of Italian spione (“spy”), and was therefore also adopted by the English. More at spy.

meaning: adopt; support (an idea or aim); marry; N. espousal
etymology: From Middle English espousen, borrowed from Old French espouser, from Latin spōnsāre (frequentative of spondeō), from Proto-Indo-European *spend-.

meaning: respect; value; judge; N.
etymology: See estimate and aim, an older word, partly a doublet.

meaning: (of a person) worthy of esteem; admirable; deserving esteem; possible to estimate
etymology: From Middle English estimable, estymable, from Old French estimable, from Latin aestimābilis. Equivalent to esteem + -able and estimate + -able.

meaning: impossible to estimate; (apprec) invaluable; of immeasurable worth
etymology: From Middle French inestimable, from Latin inaestimābilis, from in (“un-”, “not”) + aestimābilis (“estimable”). Equivalent to in- + estimable.

meaning: separated; alienated; V. estrange: alienate (people in a family); N. estrangement
like a spirit or fairy; unearthly light; heavenly; unusually refined; Ex. She has an ethereal beauty; CF. ether: upper air
etymology: From Latin aetherius (“of or pertaining to the ether, the sky, Heaven or the air or upper air”), from Ancient Greek αἰθέριος (aithérios, “of or pertaining to the upper air”). By surface analysis, ether + -ial.

meaning: of air; high in the air; lofty; immaterial; unreal
etymology: From air + -y.

meaning: relating to races
etymology: From Middle English ethnik, from Latin ethnicus ("pagan", "heathen"), from Ancient Greek ἐθνικός (ethnikós, “of or for a nation, heathen”), from ἔθνος (éthnos, “a company", later "a people or nation, heathens”). By surface analysis, ethno- + -ic.

meaning: study of humankind; study of the different races of human beings; CF. anthropology
etymology: From ethno- + -logy.

meaning: underlying character of a culture, group, etc.; character or ideas peculiar to a specific person, group, or culture; Ex. the company ethos
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἦθος (êthos, “character; custom, habit”). Cognate to Sanskrit स्वधा (svadhā́, “habit, custom”).

meaning: study of word parts; study of the origins of words
etymology: From Middle English ethymologie, from Old French ethimologie, from Latin etymologia, from Ancient Greek ἐτυμολογία (etumología), from ἔτυμον (étumon, “true sense”) and -λογία (-logía, “study or logic of”), from λόγος (lógos, “word; explanation”). By surface analysis, etymo- + -logy.

meaning: pertaining to the improvement of race; N. eugenics: study of hereditary improvement of the human race
etymology: From eu- + -genic.

meaning: praising; full of eulogy
etymology: From eulogy + -istic.

meaning: expression of praise, often on the occasion of someone'death; V. eulogize
etymology: From Latin eulogium, apparently from a confusion between ēlogium (whence English elogium, elogy) and eulogia (from Ancient Greek εὐλογία (eulogía, “praise”), whence English eulogia); equivalent to eu- + logia ("good words"). Doublet of eulogium.

meaning: mild expression in place of an unpleasant one; ADJ. euphemistic
etymology: Recorded since 1656; from Ancient Greek εὐφημισμός (euphēmismós), from εὐφημίζω (euphēmízō), from εὔφημος (eúphēmos, “uttering sound of good omen, abstaining from inauspicious words”), from εὖ (eû, “well”) + φήμη (phḗmē, “a voice, a prophetic voice, rumor, talk”), from φημί (phēmí, “to speak, say”).

meaning: sweet sound; ADJ. euphonious
etymology: From French euphonie, from Ancient Greek εὐφωνία (euphōnía), from εὐ- (eu-, prefix meaning ‘good, well’) + φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound; (human) voice; discourse, speech”) (from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂- (“to say, speak”)) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, suffix forming feminine abstract nouns). The English word is analysable as eu- + -phony.

meaning: feeling of exaggerated or unfounded (ungrounded; baseless) well-being; feeling of great happiness or well-being (when unreasonable); ADJ. euphoriaric
etymology: From New Latin euphoria, from Ancient Greek εὐφορίᾱ (euphoríā), from εὔφορος (eúphoros, “bearing well”), from εὐ- (eu-, “well”) + φέρω (phérō, “to bear”).

meaning: mercy killing
etymology: First attested in 1606, from Ancient Greek εὐθανασία (euthanasía), from εὐ- (eu-, “good”) + θάνατος (thánatos, “death”)

meaning: fleeting; vanishing; soon disappearing; V. evanesce
etymology: Borrowed from French évanescent (“evanescent”), from Latin ēvānēscēns (“disappearing, vanishing”), present participle of ēvānēscō (“to disappear, vanish; to die out, fade away; to lapse”), from ē- (variant of ex- (prefix meaning ‘away, out’)) + vānēscō (“to vanish”) (from vānus (“empty, vacant, void”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁weh₂- (“to abandon, leave”)) + -ēscō (suffix forming verbs with the sense ‘to become’)).

meaning: not frank; trying to hide the truth; eluding; evading; V. evade: avoid (a duty or responsibility) or escape from by deceit
etymology: From French évasif, from Latin ēvādō.

meaning: show clearly
etymology: From Middle French évincer, from Latin ēvincō (“conquer entirely, prevail over; prove exhaustively”), from ē- (short form of ex- (intensive prefix)) + vincō (“conquer”). Doublet of evict.

meaning: impartial; fair
etymology: From even + handed. First attested in c. 1600.

meaning: tending to call up (emotions, memories)
etymology: From Latin ēvocātīvus (“pertaining to summoning”). By surface analysis, evoke + -ative.

meaning: call forth (memory or feeling); Ex. That old film evoked memories of my childhood; N. evocation
etymology: From French évoquer, from Latin ēvocō (“to call out, summon”), from ex (“out”) and vocō (“call”). Akin to voice.

meaning: female sheep
etymology: See also Old English ēow (“sheep”), West Frisian ei, Dutch ooi, German Aue; also Old Irish oí, Latin ovis, Tocharian B ā(ᵤ)w, Lithuanian avi̇̀s (“ewe”), Russian овца́ (ovcá).

meaning: male sheep; V. strike or drive against with a heavy impact
etymology: From Middle English ram, rom, ramme, from Old English ramm (“ram”), from Proto-Germanic *rammaz (“ram”), possibly from *rammaz (“strong”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Rom (“ram”), Dutch ram (“a male sheep”), German Ramm, Ramme (“ram”). Possibly akin also to Danish ram (“sharp; acrid; rank”), Swedish ram (“strong; perfect”), Faroese ramur (“strong; competent”), Icelandic rammur (“strong; sturdy”).

meaning: worsen; aggravate; embitter
etymology: First attested in 1660; borrowed from Latin exacerbātus, perfect passive participle of Latin exacerbō (“to provoke”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ex- (“out of; thoroughly”) + acerbō (“to embitter, harshen or worsen”).

meaning: make bitter; fill with painful or bitter feelings; make sad and angry; Ex. He was embittered by many disappointments.
etymology: From em- (variant of the suffix en- with the sense ‘to become’) + bitter.

meaning: extremely demanding; Ex. exacting standard of safety
etymology: From exact + -ing.

meaning: demand and obtain by force; Ex. exact a promise from him; N. exaction
etymology: From Latin exāctus (the verb via Middle English exact), perfect passive participle of exigō (“demand, claim as due; measure by a standard, weigh, test”), from ex (“out”) + agō (“drive”).

meaning: raise in rank or dignity; praise highly; inspire; Ex. exalt the imagination; ADJ. exalted; N. exaltation
etymology: From Middle English exalten, from Old French exalter, from Latin exaltō.

meaning: vex; annoy or make angry (by testing the patience)
etymology: First attested in 1534; borrowed from Latin exasperātus, the perfect passive participle of Latin exasperō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ex (“out of; thoroughly”) + asperō (“to make rough”), from asper (“rough”). Participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.

meaning: objectionable; likely to cause dislike; offensive; CF. unexceptionable: entirely acceptable
etymology: From exception + -able.

meaning: exclude; N. exception: objection; exclusion; ADJ. exceptional: unusual; of unusually high quality
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French excepter, from Latin exceptus.

meaning: selected passage (written or musical) taken from a longer work; V.
etymology: From Latin excerptus, past participle of excerpere (“to pick out”), from ex (“out”) + carpere (“to pick, pluck”).

meaning: treasury; Ex. Chancellor of the exchequer
etymology: From Middle English escheker, from Anglo-Norman escheker (“chessboard”), from Medieval Latin scaccarium. This is because the cloth on which the treasurer counted money was chequered like a chessboard.

meaning: legal official of high rank; CF. chancellery (chancellory): position of a chancellor
etymology: The word was present as Late Old English canceler, cancheler, from Norman cancheler, but was displaced in the 13th century by the Old French and Anglo-Norman forms mentioned above.

meaning: keep as precious; cherish
etymology: Inherited from Middle English tresour, from Old French tresor (“treasury”), from Latin thēsaurus (“treasure”), from Ancient Greek θησαυρός (thēsaurós, “treasure house”). Mostly displaced native Old English goldhord (See goldhoard) and Old English ġestrēon. Doublet of thesaurus.

meaning: cut away; cut out; N: government tax on good produced and used inside a country; N. excision
etymology: From Middle Dutch excijs, altered under the influence of Latin excisus (“cut out, removed”), from earlier accijs (“tax”), from Old French acceis (“tax, assessment”) (whence modern French accise), from Vulgar Latin *accensum, ultimately from Latin ad + census (“tax, census”).

meaning: cry out suddenly; N. exclamation; ADJ. exclamatory
etymology: From Middle French exclamer, from Latin exclāmō, exclāmāre (“call out”), from ex- + clāmō (“to call”).

meaning: scold with biting harshness; censure strongly; strip the skin off
etymology: First attested in the first part of the 15ᵗʰ century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English *excoriaten (only attested in its past participle), borrowed from Late Latin excoriātus perfect passive participle of excoriō (“to take the skin or hide off, flay, skin”), from ex- (“out off, from”) + corium (“hide, skin”) + -ō. Regular participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English, later archaic.

meaning: clear from blame or guilt
etymology: From Medieval Latin exculpātus, perfect passive participle of exculpō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ex- (“out, from”) + culpa (“fault; blame”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).

meaning: very bad; detestable
etymology: From Old French execrable, from Latin execrabilis.

meaning: curse; express abhorrence for; detest
etymology: From Latin exsecrārī, execrārī, from ex (“out”) + sacrāre (“to consecrate, declare accursed”).

meaning: put into effect; carry out; kill as a lawful punishment; N. execution
etymology: From Old French executer (French exécuter), from Latin exsecutus, past participle of exsequor (“to follow (up/through)”, particularly in the sense “to go through with a deed or punishment”), from ex- (“out”) + sequor (“to follow”).

meaning: person designated to execute the terms of a will; ¿¹¼ú ÀÛÇ°ÀÇ Á¦ÀÛÀÚ
etymology: From Middle English executour, from Anglo-Norman executour, from Latin exsecūtor, agent noun of exsequor.

meaning: person administering capital punishment
etymology: From execution + -er.

meaning: person having administrative authority; one branch of government executing laws; ADJ: relating to executing
etymology: From Middle French executif, from Latin executivus, from Latin exsequi, from ex- ‘out’ + sequi ‘follow’.

meaning: legislating branch of government; CF. legislate: make laws
etymology: 1676, from stem of legislator + -ure, cognate with French législature.

meaning: judicial branch of government
etymology: Borrowed from Latin iudiciarius, judiciarius.

meaning: explanation, especially of biblical (of the bible) passages
etymology: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐξήγησις (exḗgēsis, “interpretation”), from ἐξηγέομαι (exēgéomai, “to explain, interpret”), from ἐξ (ex, “out”) + ἡγέομαι (hēgéomai, “to lead, guide”).

meaning: serving as a model; outstanding; Ex. exemplary punishment/behavior; N. exemplar: typical example; model
etymology: From Middle English exemplarie, from Latin exemplāris (“exemplary; a copy, facsimile”), from exemplum (“an example; a sample; a copy or transcript”). By surface analysis, example + -ary. Doublet of exemplar. First use appears before 1450.

meaning: show by example; furnish an example; serve as an example of; Ex. His pictures exemplify that sort of painting.
etymology: From Middle English exemplifien, from Middle French exemplifier and its etymon Medieval Latin exemplificō, from Latin exemplum (“example”).

meaning: not subject to a duty or obligation; free from a duty; V.
etymology: From Middle French exempt, from Latin exemptus, past participle of eximō.

meaning: effort; expenditure of much physical work; V. exert oneself: make a great effort
breathe out; OP. inhale
etymology: From Middle French exhaler, from Latin exhalare, from ex (“out”) + halare (“to breathe”).

meaning: invigorating and refreshing; cheering; V. exhilarate: make cheerful and excited; Ex. exhilarated by the ride in the sports car
etymology: By surface analysis, exhilarate + -ing.

meaning: urge (by strong argument or advice); Ex. The general exhorted his men to fight bravely; N. exhortation
etymology: From Middle English exorten, from Old French exhorter, from Latin exhortārī (“to encourage”), from ex- (“out of, from”) + hortārī (“to incite, spur”).

meaning: drive or force forward (by causing impulses); drive to take action; impel; entreat earnestly; Ex. urge horses; N: impulse that prompts action
etymology: From Latin urgeō (“urge”).

meaning: compelling immediate action; pressing; persistent; importunate; Ex. urgent in his demands
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French urgent (“pressing, impelling”), from Latin urgēns, from urgēre (“to press”), from Proto-Indo-European *werǵʰ- (“bind, squeeze”). Equivalent to urge + -ent. Related to German würgen (“to strangle”), Lithuanian ver̃žti (“to string, tighten, constrict”), Russian (poetic) отверза́ть (otverzátʹ, “to open”, literally “to untie”), Polish otwierać (“to open”)) and English worry, wring, wreak, wreck.

meaning: dig out of the ground; remove from a grave
etymology: From Medieval Latin exhumō, from Latin ex- + humō (“to bury”).

meaning: public official who investigates any death thought to be of other than natural causes
etymology: From Middle English coroner, from Old French curuner, from Medieval Latin custōs placitōrum corōnae (“guardian of the crown's pleas”). The function was originally to protect royal properties. Compare crowner. Doublet of crown.

meaning: urgent situation; ADJ. exigent
etymology: From Middle French exigence, from Late Latin exigentia (“urgency”) (from exigēns + -ia), from exigere (“to demand”).

meaning: small in amount; minute
etymology: From Latin exiguus (“strict, exact”), from exigere (“to measure against a standard”).

meaning: pertaining to existence; pertaining to the philosophy of existentialism
etymology: The noun is derived from the adjective.

meaning: departure (of a large number of people)
etymology: Borrowed from Latin Exodus, borrowed from Ancient Greek Ἔξοδος (Éxodos), from ἔξοδος (éxodos, “departure”), from ἐξ- (ex-, “out”) + ὁδός (hodós, “path, road”).

meaning: acquit; exculpate; free from blame or guilt
