etymology: From Middle English exoneraten (attested in past participle exonerated), from Latin exonerātus, past perfect participle of exonerō (“to discharge, unload; to exonerate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Exonerō is from ex- (“out, from”) + onerō (“to burden, lade; to load”) further from onus (oner-) (“a burden, load”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃énh₂os (“burden, load”), from *h₃enh₂- (“to charge, onerate”). Compare French exonérer.

meaning: (of costs or demands) excessive; exceeding reasonable bounds
etymology: From Middle English exorbitant, through Old French from Late Latin exorbitāns, present active participle of exorbitō (“to go out of the track”), from ex (“out”) + orbita (“wheel-track”); see orbit. Compare French exorbitant.

meaning: drive out evil spirits
etymology: From Middle English exorcisen, exorzisen, from Medieval Latin exorcizō, from Ancient Greek ἐξορκίζω (exorkízō, “to banish an evil spirit; bind by oath”), from ἐξ (ex) + ὅρκος (hórkos). Compare Old French exorciser.

meaning: not native; from another part of the world; strange; intriguingly unusual; Ex. exotic flower/dress
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French exotique, from Latin exōticus, from Ancient Greek ἐξωτικός (exōtikós, “foreign”, literally “from the outside”), from ἐξω- (exō-, “outside”), from ἐξ (ex, “out of”).

meaning: make secret plans; plot; arouse the curiosity of; N: secret scheme; plot; secret love affair
etymology: Borrowed from French intrigue, from Italian intricare, from Latin intrīcō (“to entangle, perplex, embarrass”). Doublet of intricate.

meaning: (of a person) outgoing and sociable; broad and extensive; able to increase in size
etymology: From Latin expāns-, past-participle stem of expandere (“to spread out”; see expand) + -ive.

meaning: sociable; eager to mix socially with others
etymology: From outgo + -ing, out + going.

meaning: talk at length; speak or write in detail
etymology: From the participle stem of Latin expatior, from ex- + spatior (“walk about”).

meaning: exile; someone who has withdrawn from his native land; V: exile; banish; leave one'country
etymology: The verb is first attested in 1787, the adjective and noun in 1812; borrowed from Medieval Latin expatriātus, perfect passive participle of expatriō (“to banish”) (see -ate (etymology 1,2 and 3)), from Latin ex- (“out of”) + patria (“native land”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix); possibly after French expatrier and expatrié.

meaning: suitable (for a particular purpose although not necessarily morally correct); practical; politic (prudent); N: something expedient
etymology: From Middle English expedient, from Old French expedient, from Latin expediens (stem expedient-), present participle of expedire (“to bring forward, to dispatch, to expedite; impers. to be profitable, serviceable, advantageous, expedient”), from ex (“out”) + pēs (“foot, hoof”).

meaning: hasten; make go faster
etymology: From Latin expedītus (“unimpeded, unfettered”), perfect passive participle of expediō (“bring forward, set right”).

meaning: done with speed; quick; N. expedition
etymology: From Middle English expedycius (“useful, fitting”), from Latin expedītus (“disengaged, ready, convenient, prompt; unfettered, unencumbered”), past participle of expediō.

meaning: payment or expense; expending; something expended; output; Ex. receipt for the expenditure; Ex. expenditure of all the energy
etymology: From stem of Medieval Latin expenditus, irregular perfect passive participle of expendō (“to weigh, to pay out”), + -ure (“process or result”).

meaning: specialized knowledge (in a particular field); expert skill
etymology: Borrowed from French expertise. Compare gourmandise.

meaning: make amends for (a sin)
etymology: From Latin expiātus, past participle of expiō (“atone for”).

meaning: meaningless word; interjection; profane oath; swear-word
etymology: From Late Latin explētīvus (“serving to fill out”), from Latin explētus, the perfect passive participle of expleō (“fill out”), itself from ex (“out, completely”) + *pleō (“fill”).

meaning: exclamation; Ex. ``Ouch''
etymology: From Middle English interjeccioun, from Old French interjection (13th century), from Latin interiectiōnem, accusative singular of interiectiō (“throwing or placing between; interjection”), perfect passive participle of intericiō (“throw or place between”), from inter (“between”) + iaciō (“throw”). Displaced Old English betwēoxāworpennes (literally “between-thrown-out-ness”), a calque of the Latin.

meaning: vow; promise; use profane oaths; use offensive words
etymology: The original sense in all Germanic languages is “to take an oath”. The sense “to use bad language” developed in Middle English and is based on the Christian prohibition against swearing in general (cf. Matthew 5:33-37) and invoking God’s name in particular (i.e. frequent swearing was considered similar to the use of obscene words).

meaning: word considered offensive; Ex. ``bloody''
solemn promise; blasphemous use of sacred words to express strong feelings; swear-word; Ex. ``For Christ'sake''
etymology: Cognate with Scots aith, athe (“oath”), North Frisian ith, iss (“oath”), Saterland Frisian Eed (“oath”), West Frisian eed (“oath”), Dutch eed (“oath”), German Eid (“oath”), Swedish ed (“oath”), Icelandic eið (“oath”), Latin ūtor (“make use of, employ, avail”, verb), Old Irish óeth (“oath”).

meaning: explain in detail; interpret; clarify; CF. explicable
etymology: Borrowed from Latin explicāre (“unfold, explain”).

meaning: totally clear; definite; outspoken
etymology: Borrowed from French explicite, from Latin explicitus (“disentangled, easy”), variant of explicātus.

meaning: brave and successful act; deed or action, particularly a brave deed; CF. crossing the Atlantic ocean
etymology: From Old French esploit (noun), esploitier (verb).

meaning: explanatory; serving to explain; N. exposition: explaining; exhibition
etymology: From exposit(ion) + -ory.

meaning: protest; remonstrance; reasoning with someone to correct or dissuade; V. expostulate
etymology: From Latin expostulātiōnem, accusative singular of expostulātiō (“complaint, expostulation”), from expostulō (“demand, expostulate”), from ex (“out of, from”) + postulō (“demand or claim”). See expostulate.

meaning: risk, particularly of being exposed to disease or to the elements; unmasking; act of laying something open; Ex. exposure of governmental corruption
etymology: From expos(e) + -ure.

meaning: explain
etymology: From Middle English expounden, from Old French espondre, from Latin exponere. Doublet of expone and expose.

meaning: take possession of (often for public use and without payment)
etymology: From Medieval Latin expropriātus.

meaning: cancel; remove a word or name (from a book or list); erase
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin expungere.

meaning: clean; remove offensive parts of a book
etymology: From Latin expurgātus, perfect passive participle of expurgō (“purge, cleanse, purify”).

meaning: (of something written or painted) still in existence
etymology: First attested in 1545, from Latin extantem, extāns, present participle of extō (“to stand out, exist, be extant”), from ex- (“out”) + stō (“stand”).

meaning: not planned; impromptu; extempore
etymology: From Late Latin extemporāneus, from Latin ex tempore (“impromptu”).

meaning: weaken; mitigate; lessen the seriousness of (bad behavior)
etymology: From Middle English extenuat (“(medicine) made thin, emaciated”), from Latin extenuātus (“diminished, reduced, thinned”), perfect passive participle of extenuō (“to diminish, reduce, thin”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ex- (“out-, thoroughly”) + tenuō (“to enfeeble, weaken, wear down; to lessen, reduce; to make thin”), from tenuis (“fine, slender, thin; feeble, weak”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tenh₂- (“to extend, stretch; thin”)) + -ō (first conjugation-verb forming suffix). Compare attenuate.

meaning: root up; uproot; destroy completely
etymology: The verb is first attested in 1538, the adjective in 1541; borrowed from Latin exstirpātus perfect passive participle of exstirpō (“to uproot”), from ex- (“out of”) + stirps (“the lower part of the trunk of a tree, including the roots; the stem, stalk”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)). Doublet of extirp. Common participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.

meaning: praise very highly; glorify
etymology: Borrowed from Latin extollō (“elevate, raise high”).

meaning: wring from; get money by threats, etc.; obtain by force or threats; CF. extortionate: exorbitant
etymology: Borrowed from Latin extortus, past participle of extorquere (“to twist or wrench out, to extort”); from ex (“out”) + -tort, from torqueō (“twist, turn”).

meaning: twist (to extract liquid); extract by twisting; wrench painfully (necks or hands)
etymology: Cognate with Scots wring (“to wring”), Saterland Frisian wringe (“to wring”), Dutch wringen (“to wring; to wrest; to writhe”), German ringen (“to wrestle; to struggle; to wring”), wringen (“to wring”), Luxembourgish réngen (“to grapple, wrestle”); also Ancient Greek ῥίμφα (rhímpha, “fast, nimbly, rapidly”), Lithuanian rangýti (“to roll up; to curl, twist, wave”).

meaning: surrender of prisoner by one state to another; Ex. extradition treaty; V. extradite
etymology: From French extradition, itself from Latin ex- + traditio.

meaning: not essential; irrelevant; superfluous; external; coming from the outside; Ex. extraneous details/noise/to the subject
etymology: From Latin extrāneus (“from without, strange”). Doublet of strange. Cognate with estrange (verb), Spanish extraño.

meaning: projection; conjecture; V. extrapolate: infer (unknown information) from known information
etymology: Morphologically extrapolate + -ion

meaning: free from an entanglement or difficulty; disentangle
etymology: Borrowed from Latin extrīcātus, past participle of extrīcō. Compare intricate.

meaning: from which it is impossible to get free; that cannot be untied; Ex. inextricable troubles; Ex. inextricable two histories
etymology: From Middle French inextricable, from Latin inextricabilis.

meaning: external; not essential or inherent; extraneous; OP. intrinsic
etymology: From French extrinsèque, from Latin extrinsecus (“from without, without, on the outside”), from *extrim, an assumed adverbial form of exter (“outer, outward”) + secus (“by, on the side”).

meaning: person interested mostly in external objects and actions
etymology: Alteration of earlier extravert (by influence of introvert), from German Extravert, popularized in psychology by Phyllis Blanchard's 1918 "Psycho-Analytic Study of August Comte". By surface analysis, extro- + -vert.

meaning: mix together in close association
etymology: From earlier mingil, mengle, from Middle English menglen, equivalent to ming + -le. Cognate with Dutch mengelen (“to mingle, mix”), German mengen (“to mingle, mix”). More at ming.

meaning: force or push out; thrust out; shape (plastic or metal) by forcing through a die
etymology: Borrowed from Latin extrūdere.

meaning: overflowing abundance; joyful enthusiasm; flamboyance; lavishness; ADJ. exuberant: high-spirited and lively; growing abundantly and strongly
etymology: From French exubérance, from Latin exuberantia (“superabundance”), from exuberare (“to grow thickly, to abound”); from ex- (“out”) + uber (“udder”), which would have originally referred to a cow or she-goat which was making so much milk that it naturally dripped or sprayed from the udder.

meaning: shine brightly without a flame (as of eyes or metals); show redness and heat (in the face) after hard work or because of strong feelings; N: light produced by a heated body; brilliance of a color
etymology: * West Frisian gloeie

meaning: flow out slowly; discharge (gradually); give forth; N. exudation
etymology: Latin exudāre, exsudāre (“to sweat out”), from ex- (“out, out of”) + sudāre (“to sweat”), from Proto-Indo-European *sweyd-.

meaning: (of a thick liquid) pass or flow slowly; N: mud or thick liquid as at the bottom of a river
etymology: * (Verb) Middle English wosen, from Old English wōsan; see above. Compare Swedish osa (“ooze”).

meaning: rejoice
etymology: From Middle French exulter, from Latin exsultō, frequentative of exsiliō (“jump up”), from ex- + saliō (“jump, leap”).

meaning: build; lie; make up (a story) in order to deceive; Ex. fabricate the whole story; CF. fabric: underlying structure; Ex. fabric of society
etymology: From Middle English fabricaten (“to fashion, make”), from Latin fabricātus, perfect active participle of fabricor (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from fabrica (“a fabric, building”) + -or (verb-forming suffix); see fabric and forge. Cognate with French fabriquer.

meaning: front or face (of building); superficial or false appearance
small plane surface (of a gem (precious stone)); a side
etymology: Borrowed from French facette.

meaning: joking (often inappropriately); unserious; humorous
etymology: From French facétieux, from Latin facētia (“jest, wit, humor”), from facētus (“witty, jocose, facetious”).

meaning: easily accomplished; ready or fluent; superficial; not deep; Ex. facile solution to a complex problem; Ex. facile speaker; N. facility: ability to do something easily and well; ease in doing resulting from skill or aptitude; something that facilitates an action; amenity; Ex. with great facility
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French facile, from Latin facilis (“easy to do, easy, doable”), from Latin facere (“to do, make”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to do, put”) Compare Spanish and Portuguese fácil (“easy”), Catalan fàcil, Romanian facil. First use appears c. 1484 in a translation by William Caxton.

meaning: help bring about; make less difficult
etymology: Anglicisation of French faciliter (“facilitate”) through -ate (verb-forming suffix), ultimately from Latin facilis.

meaning: copy
etymology: From Latin fac simile (“make like”), from fac (“make”) (imperative of facere (“make”)) + simile (neuter of similis (“like, similar”)).

meaning: party; clique (within a large group); dissension
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French faction, from Latin factiō (“a group of people acting together, a political faction”), noun of process from perfect passive participle factus, from faciō (“do, make”). Doublet of fashion.

meaning: disagreement of opinions causing strife within a group
etymology: Inherited from Middle English dissencioun, from Middle French dissention, discention, from Old French dissension, from Latin dissensio.

meaning: inclined to form factions; causing dissension
etymology: From Latin factiosus (“divisive; inclined to separate”); derivative of factio.

meaning: artificial; produced artificially; sham; false; Ex. factitious tears
etymology: Borrowed from Latin factītius (“artificial”), alternative form of factīcius, from faciō (“to make, do”). Doublet of fetish.

meaning: handyman; person who does all kinds of work; CF. do everything
etymology: Ellipsis of domine fac totum, dominus fac totum /dominus factotum (“absolute ruler; head servant”), from Medieval Latin domine fac tōtum (“O Lord, do everything”), also with substition of nominative dominus for vocative domine.

meaning: mental or bodily powers; teaching staff
etymology: From Middle English faculte (“power, property”), from Old French faculte, from Latin facultas (“capability, ability, skill, abundance, plenty, stock, goods, property; in Medieval Latin also a body of teachers”), another form of facilitas (“easiness, facility, etc.”), from facul, another form of facilis (“easy, facile”); see facile. Doublet of facility.

meaning: false; based on a fallacy; misleading; N. fallacy: false idea or notion; false reasoning; Ex. popular fallacy; Ex. fallacy of the argument
etymology: From Old French fallacieux (whence -acious), from Latin fallācia, from fallāx, from fallere.

meaning: liable to err
etymology: From Middle English fallible, from Medieval Latin fallibilis (“liable to err, also deceitful”), from Latin fallere (“to deceive”).

meaning: make (something written) false by changing
etymology: From French falsifier, from Late Latin falsificāre (“make false, corrupt, counterfeit, falsify”), from Latin falsificus, from falsus (“false”), corresponding to false + -ify.

meaning: (of land) plowed but not sowed (to improve the quality); uncultivated
etymology: From Middle English falwe, from Old English fealh, fealg (“fallow land”), from Proto-West Germanic *falgu (compare Saterland Frisian Falge, West Frisian falig, felling, Dutch valg, German Felge), from Proto-Indo-European *polḱéh₂ (“arable land”) (compare Gaulish olca, Russian полоса́ (polosá)).

meaning: plant or scatter seed
etymology: See also West Frisian sûch, Dutch zeug, Low German Söög, German Sau, Swedish sugga, Norwegian sugge; also Welsh hwch (“pig”), Sanskrit सूकर (sūkará, “swine, boar”); also Danish so, German Sau, Latin sūs, Tocharian B suwo, Ancient Greek ὗς (hûs), Albanian thi, Avestan 𐬵𐬏 (hū, “boar”). See also swine. Doublet of soor.

meaning: hesitate; weaken in purpose or action; walk or move unsteadily through weakness; N.
etymology: From Middle English falteren (“to stagger; be unsteady, tremble, quiver; to stammer; be entangled, get caught”), further origin unknown. Probably from a North Germanic source such as Old Norse faltrask (“to hesitate, be puzzled, be encumbered”). May also be a frequentative of fold, although the change from d to t is unusual.

meaning: trip and almost fall; proceed unsteadily; act falteringly; N.
etymology: Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *stam- (“to trip up; to stammer, stutter”), thereby related to German stumm (“mute”), Dutch stom (“dumb”). Doublet of stammer. Also related to verb in Dutch stommelen (“to walk silently”).

meaning: excessive zeal; extreme devotion to a belief or cause; N. fanatic; ADJ. fanatic
etymology: From fanatic + -ism.

meaning: imagined; unreal
etymology: From fancy (“to have a fancy for, like; to imagine, suppose”) + -ed.

meaning: breeder or dealer of animals; one who has a special interest, as for raising specific plant or animal
etymology: From fancy (verb) + -er.

meaning: whimsical; visionary; imaginary; produced by imagination; Ex. fanciful scheme
etymology: From fancy + -ful.

meaning: imagination (of a whimsical or fantastic nature); capricious liking; V: imagine; be fond of; ADJ. decorative; elaborate
etymology: From Middle English fansy, fantsy, a contraction of fantasy, fantasye, fantasie, from Old French fantasie, from Medieval Latin fantasia, from Late Latin phantasia (“an idea, notion, fancy, phantasm”), from Ancient Greek φαντασία (phantasía), from φαντάζω (phantázō, “to render visible”), from φαντός (phantós, “visible”), from φαίνω (phaínō, “to make visible”); from the same root as φάος (pháos, “light”); ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰh₂nyéti, from the root *bʰeh₂- (“to shine”). Doublet of fantasia, fantasy, phantasia, and phantasy.

meaning: call by bugles or trumpets; showy display; spectacular public display
etymology: Borrowed from French fanfare; some senses apparently influenced by surface analysis, fan + fare.

meaning: broad comedy; mockery; humorous play full of silly things happening; ADJ. farcical
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French farce (“farce (style of humor); stuffing”) (in the latter sense, via Middle English fars, farsse), from Old French farse, from Medieval Latin farsa, from the feminine perfect passive participle of Latin farciō (“to stuff”). The theatre sense alludes to the pleasant and varied character of certain stuffed food items. Doublet of farse.

meaning: difficult to please; squeamish; fussy; finicky
etymology: Borrowed from Latin fastīdiōsus (“passive: that feels disgust, disdainful, scornful, fastidious; active: that causes disgust, disgusting, loathsome”), from fastīdium (“a loathing, aversion, disgust, niceness of taste, daintiness, etc.”), perhaps for *fastutidium, from fastus (“disdain, haughtiness, arrogance, disgust”) + taedium (“disgust”). Cf. French fastidieux.

meaning: easily shocked or sickened by unpleasant things; fastidious; Ex. A nurse should not be squeamish.
etymology: Origin obscure. Likely a merger of earlier squeamous (“squeamish”), from Middle English squaimous, queimous, from Anglo-Norman escoimus, escoymous, of unknown origin; and dialectal English sweamish, sweemish (“faint, squeamish”), from sweam (“dizziness, sudden qualm of sickness”) and dialectal sweem (“to swoon, be faint, be overcome, feel sick”), from Middle English swemen (“to grieve, make suffer, be faint of heart”), from Old English *swǣman (“to grieve, trouble, afflict”). If so, then related to swim (“to be dizzy, swoon”). See also sweam.

meaning: belief that events are determined by forces or fates beyond one'control; ADJ. fatalistic; CF. fatal: causing death
etymology: From fatal + -ism.

meaning: comprehend; investigate; determine the depth of; N. unit of measurement for the depth of water
etymology: * Old Welsh etem (“thread”)

meaning: too deep to be measured or understood; unfathomable
etymology: From fathom + -less.

meaning: smugly and unconsciously foolish; inane; silly; N. fatuity, fatuousness
etymology: From Latin fatuus (“foolish, silly, simple”).

meaning: animals of a period or region; CF. flora
etymology: Borrowed from New Latin fauna, from Latin Fauna, sister of Faunus (“god of forests and herdsmen”); akin to Ancient Greek θαῦνον (thaûnon, “wild animal, beast”), θώς (thṓs, “jackal, wild dog; panther”), Phrygian δάος (dáos, “wolf”).

meaning: courting favor by cringing and flattering; V. fawn: exhibit affection as a dog; seek favor or attention by obsequiousness
attempt to gain; seek; woo; risk; behave so as to invite; attempt to gain the favor of by attention; Ex. court disaster
etymology: Professional tennis players playing on a tennis court (noun sense 5) in New Delhi, India

meaning: disconcert; dismay; embarrass
etymology: Citations for faze in the Oxford English Dictionary start in 1830, and usage was established by 1890.

meaning: practical; able to be carried out; practicable
etymology: From Anglo-Norman fesable, from Latin facere, Old French fesable, faisable (“doable”), from fere, faire (“to do”) + -able.

meaning: feverish
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin febrīlis, from Latin febris (“fever”). By surface analysis, Latin febr- + -ile.

meaning: fertility; fruitfulness; ADJ. fecund: very productive of crops or young
etymology: From Latin fēcunditās (“fruitfulness, fertility”), from fēcundus, equivalent to fecund + -ity.

meaning: producing many young, fruits, or seeds; (of land) producing good crops; V. fertilize
etymology: From Middle English, from Middle French fertile, from Old French fertile, from Latin fertilis (“fruitful, fertile”), from ferō (“to bear, carry”).

meaning: producing results; profitable; prolific; producing in abundance
etymology: From Middle English fruitefull, equivalent to fruit + -ful. Compare Dutch vruchtvol, German fruchtvoll, Swedish fruktfull.

meaning: pretend
etymology: From Middle English feynen, feinen, borrowed from Old French feindre (“to pretend”), from Latin fingere (“to form, shape, invent”). Compare French feignant (present participle of feindre, literally “feigning”). Also compare feint, figment and fiction.

meaning: trick; shift; sham blow; feigned attack to draw away defensive action; V.
etymology: * Old Spanish finta (modern Spanish finta (“dummy, feint”))

meaning: change position or place; exchange (one thing) for another; change in direction or position; Ex. shift the stolen goods; N. group of workers which takes turns with other groups; working period of such a group
etymology: The noun is from Middle English schyft, shyffte. Cognate with Dutch schift (“split, fissure”), German Schicht (“layer, shift”).

meaning: (of a word or remark) apt; suitably expressed; well chosen
etymology: From felicity + -ous.

meaning: happiness; appropriateness (of a remark, choice, etc.); quality of being felicitous
etymology: From Middle English felicite (“bliss, happiness, joy; delight, pleasure; a source of happiness; good fortune; prosperity; well-being; of a planet: in an influential position”) [and other forms], borrowed from Old French felicité (modern French félicité (“bliss, happiness; felicity”)), from Latin fēlīcitātem, the accusative singular of fēlīcitās (“fertility, fruitfulness; happiness, felicity; good fortune; success”), from fēlīx (“happy; blessed, fortunate, lucky; fertile, fruitful; prosperous; auspicious, favourable”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to nurse, suckle”)) + -itās (a variant of -tās (suffix forming nouns indicating a state of being)).

meaning: of a member of the cat family; N.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin fēlīnus, from fēlēs (“wildcat, marten”).

meaning: cruel; (of a disease) deadly
etymology: Cognate with Dutch vellen (“to fell, cut down”), German fällen (“to fell”), Danish fælde (“to fell”), Norwegian felle (“to fell”).

meaning: person convicted of a grave crime; CF. felony: serious crime
etymology: * Spanish felón (adjective, noun)

meaning: (of an animal) not domestic; wild
etymology: From Latin fera (“wild beast”, noun) + -al or Latin ferus (“wild; savage; cruel”, adjective) + -al. Alternatively, borrowed from Middle French féral or Late Latin ferālis.

meaning: agitation; commotion (noisy and excited activity); unrest (of a political kind); V. produce by fermentation; undergo fermentation; cause (a state of trouble)
etymology: From Middle English ferment, from Middle French ferment, from Latin fermentāre (“to leaven, ferment”), from fermentum (“substance causing fermentation”), possibly from contraction of *fervimentum, from fervēre. See also fervent.

meaning: chemical reaction that splits complex organic compounds; unrest; agitation
etymology: From Middle English fermentacioun, from Latin fermentātiō, fermentātiōnem. By surface analysis, ferment + -ation.

meaning: drive or hunt out of hiding; hunt with ferrets; drive out (as from a hiding place); expel; uncover or discover by searching; Ex. ferret out the secret; N. small fierce animal which catches rats and rabbits by going into their holes
etymology: From Middle English furet, ferret, from Old French furet, from Vulgar Latin *furittum (“weasel, ferret”), diminutive of Latin fūr (“thief”).

meaning: ardent; zealous; hot
etymology: From Middle English fervent, from Old French fervent (modern French fervent), from Latin ferventem, the accusative masculine or feminine singular form of fervēns (“burning, fiery; hot; zealous; etc.”), the present active participle of ferveō (“to burn; to be hot; (figurative) to be agitated, fired up, or inflamed; etc.”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrewh₁- (“to boil; to brew”).

meaning: ardent; zealous; hot
etymology: Borrowed from Latin fervidus, from ferveō. By surface analysis, Latin ferv- + id.

meaning: (of speech) filled with passion; fervent
etymology: From impassion + -ed.

meaning: glowing ardor; intensity of feeling; quality of being fervent or fervid; zeal; intense heat
etymology: From Middle English fervour, from Old French, from Latin fervor (“a boiling or raging heat, heat, vehemence, passion”), from fervere (“to boil, be hot”); see fervent. By surface analysis, Latin ferv- + -or (“abstract noun suffix”).

meaning: rankle; produce irritation or resentment; (of a cut or wound) generate pus or rot; Ex. His insult festered in my mind for days.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English festre, festur, borrowed from Old French festre (cognate with Italian fistola, Occitan fistola, Spanish fístula), from Latin fistula. The verb is derived from the noun, while the “condition of something that festers” noun sense is derived from the verb. Doublet of fistula.

meaning: joyous; celebratory; relating to a feast or festival
etymology: From French festif, from Latin festivus (“pertaining to a feast, gay, lively, joyous”). Equivalent to feast + -ive.

meaning: honor at a festival; celebrate or honor with a feast; N. (outdoor) festival or feast; CF. feast
etymology: * The verb derives from French fêter.

meaning: malodorous; foul
very bad or disagreeable; very dirty; Ex. foul smell/flavor/temper/language/air/deed/weather/means; N. act against the rules; V. make or become foul; commit a foul
etymology: Ancient Greek φαῦλος (phaûlos, “bad”) is a false cognate inasmuch as it is not from the same etymon, instead being cognate to few.

meaning: object believed to have spiritual powers; object of excessive attention or reverence; CF. fetishism
shackle; restrict the freedom of; N. chain or shackle for the foot of a prisoner; CF. foot
etymology: Cognate with Dutch veter (“cable, chain, hawser; bond, fetter”), Faroese fjøtur (“fetter”), Icelandic fjötur (“fetter”), Swedish fjätter (“fetter, shackle”); also Irish feadh (“extent, length”), feá (“fathom”), Scottish Gaelic feadh (“extent, length; fathom”), Latgalian pāda (“foot”), Latvian pēda (“foot”), Lithuanian pėda (“foot”), Belarusian па́даць (pádacʹ, “to fall”), Bulgarian па́дам (pádam, “to grop, fall”), Czech padat (“to fall”), Polish padać (“to fall”), Russian па́дать (pádatʹ, “to fall”), Serbo-Croatian padati, падати (“to fall”), Slovene padati (“to fall”), Ukrainian па́дати (pádaty, “to fall”), Latin peior, pejor (“worse”), Ancient Greek πέδη (pédē, “fetter, shackle; anklet, bangle”), Armenian ետ (et, “back, backward”), հետ (het, “back; with”), Ossetian фестӕг (festæg), фистӕг (fistæg, “pedestrian”), Old Persian 𐎱𐎿𐎫𐎡 (p-s-t-i, “foot soldier, infantryman”), Sanskrit पद्यते (padyate, “to fall, topple; to perish”), Hittite 𒁉𒂊𒁕𒀭 (“place; floor, ground”).

meaning: total failure; CF. bottle
etymology: Doublet of flacon, flagon, and flask.

meaning: command; arbitrary order; Ex. presidential fiat; CF. let it be done
etymology: From Latin fīat (“let it be done”).

meaning: changeable (in affections or friendship); faithless
etymology: From Middle English fikil, fikel, from Old English ficol (“fickle, cunning, tricky, deceitful”), equivalent to fike + -le. More at fike.

meaning: imaginary; non-existent; purposely invented to deceive; untrue; Ex. fictitious name/boyfriend; CF. fictional
etymology: Borrowed from Latin fictīcius.

meaning: loyalty; accuracy
etymology: From Late Middle English fidelite (“allegiance, fealty; faithfulness, trust; agreement made in good faith”), from Old French fidélité (“faithfulness, fidelity”) (modern French fidélité), from Latin fidēlitās (“faithfulness, fidelity”), from fidēlis (“dependable, trustworthy; faithful, loyal”) + -tās (suffix forming feminine abstract nouns denoting a state of being). Fidēlis is derived from fidēs (“belief, faith; confidence, trust; loyalty, fidelity; etc.”) (from Proto-Indo-European *bʰidʰ-, the zero-grade of *bʰeydʰ- (“to convince; to trust”) (whence English bide)) + -ēlis (a variant of -ālis (suffix forming adjectives of relationship)). Doublet of fealty.

meaning: invention; something invented; imaginary thing; Ex. figment of your imagination
etymology: From Late Latin figmentum (“anything made, a fiction”), from fingō (“make, form, feign”); see fiction, feign, feint.

meaning: not literal but metaphorical; using a figure (impression) of speech
etymology: From Middle French figuratif.

meaning: written symbols; number; amount represented in numbers; outline or silhouette of a thing or human body; person (well-known); impression; diagram; pattern; group in a dance; Ex. figure of speech; V. calculate with numbers; adorn with figures; appear; consider; Ex. My name did not figure in the list.
etymology: From Middle English figure, borrowed from Old French figure, from Latin figūra (“form, shape, form of a word, a figure of speech, Late Latin a sketch, drawing”), from fingō (“to form, shape, mold, fashion”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeyǵʰ- (“to mold, shape, form, knead”). Cognate with Ancient Greek τεῖχος (teîkhos), Sanskrit देग्धि (dégdhi), Old English dāg (“dough”). More at dough. Doublet of figura.

meaning: small ornamental statuette (very small statue)
etymology: Borrowed from French figurine, equivalent to figure + -ine.

meaning: steal (things of small value)
etymology: From Middle English filchen (“to pilfer, steal”). The further origin of the word is uncertain, but it is likely from or related to Old English fylċian (“to marshal troops”) and Old English ġefylċe (“band of men, army, host”), which would make it also related to folk.

meaning: steal things of small value; filch; snitch
etymology: From earlier pilfre, from Middle English pilfre (“booty”), from Old French pelfre (“plunder, booty, spoils”), of unknown origin. Compare pelf.

meaning: pertaining to or befitting a son or daughter; Ex. filial respect
etymology: From Middle English filial, from Latin fīliālis, from fīlius (“son”) / fīlia (“daughter”) + -al.

meaning: block legislation or prevent action in a lawmaking body by making very slow long speeches; N; freebooter
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish filibustero (“pirate”), from French flibustier, ultimately from Dutch vrijbuiter (“freebooter”), from vrij (“free”) + buit (“booty”) + -er (“agent”). The alteration in the first syllable in French is due to the word's being somewhat conflated with vlieboot (“light, flat-bottomed cargo vessel with two or three masts”) when it was borrowed into French or another language from Dutch. The word is cognate and analogous to English freebooter.

meaning: pirate or plunderer who makes war in order to grow rich
etymology: From free + booty + -er. Calque of Dutch vrijbuiter (literally “free booty-er”), from vrij (“free”) + buit (“booty”) + -er (occupational suffix). Doublet of filibuster.

meaning: piece of sculpture showing a person'head, shoulders, and upper chest; V: break up; arrest; Ex. crimebuster
etymology: From Middle English busten, a variant of bursten, bresten (“to burst”). Compare Low German basten, a variant of barsten (“to burst”). Cognate with burst and bost.

meaning: delicate ornamental lacelike metalwork
etymology: From French filigrane, from Italian filigrana, from Latin fīlum (“thread”) + grānum (“grain”).

meaning: cord used to draw and tie together two opposite edges (as of a shoe); delicate fabric made of fine threads; V: draw together by tying a lace
etymology: From Middle English lace, laace, las, from Old French las, from Vulgar Latin *laceum, based on Latin laqueus. Doublet of lasso.

meaning: particle removed by a file
conclusion; concluding part
etymology: From Italian finale (“ending”), from Late Latin fīnālis, from Latin fīnis (“end; boundary, limit”). Doublet of final.

meaning: delicate skill; V: handle with finesse
etymology: From Middle English finesse (“a degree of excellence; (of metal) fineness, purity”), from Middle French finesse, Old French finesse (“a fineness; a delicacy; slenderness”), from fine, fin (“fine, thin”) (from Latin fīnis (“an end”); compare Middle English fīn (“of superior quality; precious, valuable; admirable, pleasing; pure, refined; fineness, purity; delicate, exquisite, fine; sharp, thin”)) + -esse (suffix forming nouns describing the condition of being something). The verb is derived from the noun.

meaning: too particular; fussy; difficult to please; too concerned with unimportant details or quality; Ex. finicky about her food
etymology: From finick (“to work in a fastidious manner, wasting time over unnecessary details”) + -y. Compare finicking, finical, and dated finikin. Perhaps suggested by obsolete Dutch fijnkens (“accurately, neatly, prettily”) (modern Dutch fijntjes). Compare also Sicilian finicchiu.

meaning: fastidious; finicky; easily upset
etymology: From fuss + -y.

meaning: trouble or worry over trifles; make nervous; pay too much attention to; N: needless concern or worry (about a trivial thing); anxious nervous condition; display of attention; Ex. make a fuss over the baby
limited
etymology: The noun is derived from the adjective.

meaning: piece of burning wood; hothead; troublemaker; person who stirs up trouble
etymology: From Middle English fyr-brand, furbrond, equivalent to fire + brand. Cognate with German Feuerbrand (“firebrand”).

meaning: person who does things too quickly without thinking; ADJ. hotheaded
etymology: From hot + head. Compare English hotbrain (“a hothead”); Middle English hot-heorte, hat-heorte (“anger”), Old English hātheort (“furious, angry, irascible, passionate, ardent”, literally “hot-heart”).

meaning: crevice; crack
etymology: From Middle English fissure, from Old French fissure, from Latin fissūra (“a cleft, chink”), from findō (“to cleave, split, divide”) + -tūra (nominal suffix).

meaning: spasmodic; intermittent; irregular
etymology: From fit (“convulsion, seizure; sudden burst of activity”) + -ful (suffix forming adjectives from nouns, with the sense of being full of, tending to, or thoroughly possessing the quality expressed by the noun).

meaning: sudden outburst of an illness or feeling; convulsion caused by epilepsy
etymology: Possibly from Middle English fit (“an adversary of equal power”), of uncertain further origin. The original sense appears to have been "to marshal or deploy troops", which shifted to "to suit (troops to a certain location" > "suitable", and may be further related to Icelandic fitja (“to web, knit, cast on”).

meaning: flabby; lacking firmness; weak; Ex. flaccid muscles
etymology: Borrowed from Latin flaccid(us).

meaning: walk lamely; ADJ: lacking firmness; weak
etymology: Cognate with Low German lumpen (“to limp”), Middle High German limpfen (“to hobble, limp”), dialectal German lampen (“to hang down loosely”), Icelandic limpa (“limpness, weakness”).

meaning: droop; grow feeble; decline in vigor or strength; ADJ. flagging; CF. unflagging
etymology: Germanic cognates include Saterland Frisian Flaage (“flag”), West Frisian flagge (“flag”), Dutch vlag (“flag”), German Flagge (“flag”), Swedish flagga (“flag”), Danish flag (“flag, ship's flag”). Compare also Middle English flacken (“to flutter, palpitate”), Swedish dialectal flage (“to flutter in the wind”), Old Norse flögra (“to flap about”). Akin to Old High German flogarōn (“to flutter”), Old High German flogezen (“to flutter, flicker”), Middle English flakeren (“to move quickly to and fro”), Old English flacor (“fluttering, flying”). More at flack, flacker.

meaning: bend or hang downward; become weakened; Ex. His shoulders drooped with tiredness; N.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English droupen, from Old Norse drúpa (“to droop”), from Proto-Germanic *drūpaną, *drupōną (“to hang down, drip, drop”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrewb- (“to drip, drop”). Doublet of drip and drop.

meaning: conspicuously wicked, bad, or offensive; blatant; outrageous
etymology: From Middle French flagrant, from Latin flagrantem, present participle of flagrare (“blaze, burn”). More at black.

meaning: act of extreme violence or viciousness; resentful anger; V: commit an outrage on; produce anger in; ADJ. outrageous: offensive
etymology: The verb is from Middle English outragen, from Old French oultragier.

meaning: beat with or as if with a flail; move wildly; thresh grain by hand; strike or slap; toss about; N: threshing tool consisting of a stick swinging from the end of a long handle
etymology: Alternatively, Proto-West Germanic *flagil may be an early borrowing of Latin flagellum (“winnowing tool, thresher”), diminutive of flagrum (“scourge, whip”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰlag-, *bʰlaǵ- (“to beat”); compare Old Norse blekkja (“to beat, mistreat”). Compare also Old French flael (“flail”), Walloon flayea (“flail”) (locally pronounced "flai"), Italian flagello (“scourge, whip, plague”).

meaning: beat (cereal plants) with a machine or flail to separate the grains from the straw
etymology: Cognate with Dutch dorsen (“to thresh; to thrash”), German and Luxembourgish dreschen (“to thresh; to thrash”), Yiddish דרעשן (dreshn, “to thresh”), Danish tærske (“to thresh”), Faroese treskja (“to thresh”), Icelandic þreskja (“to thresh”), Norwegian Nynorsk treska, treske, treskja, treskje (“to thrash”), Swedish tröska (“to thresh”), Gothic 𐌸𐍂𐌹𐍃𐌺𐌰𐌽 (þriskan, “to thresh”), Finnish rehkiä (“to drudge; to toil”); also Welsh taradr (“auger, wimble; awl, borer; drill”), Latin terō (“to rub or triturate; to wear away or wear out, consume; to tread; to press with a mill; to pass, spend”), Greek τρίβω (trívo, “to grate; to rub”), Albanian tjerr (“to spin”), Belarusian це́рці (cjérci, “to rub; to polish; to pinch; to grind”), Bulgarian три́я (tríja, “to rub; to chafe; to grind”), Czech třít (“to rub; to spawn”), Polish tarć, treć, trzeć, trzyć (“to rub; to shred; to cut; to chafe; to crush; to spawn”), Russian тере́ть (terétʹ, “to rub; to polish; to grind”), Serbo-Croatian тр̏ти, tȑti (“to rub; to cause friction; to scour; to break, crush”), Slovak trieť (“to rub”), Slovene treti (“to crack open; to rub”), Ukrainian те́рти (térty, “to rub; to scrub”), Armenian թուր (tʻur, “sword”), Sogdian ܕܣܦܪܛܪ (dsprtr, “hand towel”), Hittite 𒋻𒌑𒍣 (tar-ú-zi, “to perform a round dance, to dance in twisting manner”), Tocharian A and Tocharian B tärk- (“to allow, let; to let go”), Sanskrit तर्कु (tarku, “spindle”).

meaning: throw lightly; move or lift (the head) with a sudden motion; flip (a coin) to decide something
etymology: The Welsh tos (“a quick jerk”) and tosio (“to jerk, toss”) are probably borrowed from the English.

meaning: talent
etymology: From Middle English flayre, from Old French flair (“scent, odour”), from flairier (“to reek, smell”), from Latin flāgrō, dissimilated variation of frāgrō (“emit a sweet smell”, verb). More at fragrant.

meaning: ornate; highly elaborate; richly colored; ostentatious; showy; CF. flame
etymology: Borrowed from French flamboyant (“flaming, wavy”), participle of flamboyer (“to flame”), from Old French flamboier, from flambe (“flame”). The architectural style derives its name from the flame-like shapes in the tracery.

meaning: display ostentatiously; Ex. ``Honey, if you've got it, flaunt it !''
etymology: Alternatively, it could be related to Swedish flankt (“loosely, flutteringly”) (compare English flaunt-a-flaunt), from flanka (“waver, hang and wave about, ramble”), a nasalised variant of flakka (“to waver”), related to Middle English flacken (“to move to and fro, flutter, palpitate”). See flack.

meaning: strip off skin; plunder; remove the skin from; criticize harshly
etymology: From Middle English flayen, flaien, fleien, from Old English flīeġan ("to cause to fly, put to flight, frighten"), from Proto-Germanic *flaugijaną (“to let fly, cause to fly”), causative of Proto-Germanic *fleuganą (“to fly”).

meaning: spot; mark with flecks; N: small mark or spot
etymology: From Middle English *flekk, *flekke (attested in Middle English flekked (“spotted, flecked”)), from Old Norse flekkr (“spot”), from Proto-Germanic *flekka-. Cognate with Dutch vlek, German Fleck, Swedish fläck.

meaning: inexperienced; N: young bird that has acquired wing feathers and is learning to fly; inexperienced person
wool coat of a sheep; V: shear the fleece from; rob by a trick; swindle; plunder
etymology: From Middle English fles, flees, flese, from Old English flēos, flīes, flȳs, from Proto-West Germanic *fleus.

meaning: remove (fleece or hair) by cutting; remove the hair or fleece from; cut with or as if with shears; N: shears; pair of scissors
etymology: Cognate with West Frisian skarre, Low German, Dutch, and German scheren, Danish skære, Norwegian Bokmål skjære, Norwegian Nynorsk skjera, Swedish skära, Faroese and Icelandic skera, (borrowed from Germanic) Finnish keritä; and (from Indo-European) with Kamkata-viri ċarë́- (“to chop”), Ancient Greek κείρω (keírō, “to cut off”), Latin caro (“flesh”), Albanian shqerr (“to tear, cut”), harr (“to cut, to mow”), Lithuanian ski̇̀rti (“separate”), Welsh ysgar (“separate”). See also sharp.

meaning: person who cheats people
etymology: From trick + -ster.

meaning: light stroke as with a whip; V: move with a light quick blow; strike with a light quick blow (as from a whip); Ex. flick the switch
etymology: The use of flick to mean a film or movie derives from the fact that early films had a low frame rate, thus causing the film to "flick" rapidly when projected onto a screen.

meaning: burn unsteadily or fitfully; move waveringly; N: flickering movement or light; brief sensation; Ex. flicker of excitement
etymology: West Frisian flikkerje (“to flicker”), Dutch flikkeren (“to flicker, flutter”), German Low German flickern (“to light up, flash, flicker”). Compare Old English flacor (“flickering, fluttering”), German flackern (“to flicker, flutter”), Old English flēogan (“to fly”).

meaning: (of a bird with large wings) wave (the wings) lightly, rapidly, and irregularly; vibrate rapidly or erratically; fly by waving quickly; flitter; N.
etymology: From Middle English floteren, from Old English floterian, flotorian (“to float about, flutter”), from Proto-Germanic *flutrōną, frequentative of Proto-Germanic *flutōną (“to float”), equivalent to float + -er (frequentative suffix). Cognate with West Frisian flodderje (“to flutter, beat”), Dutch flodderen (“to flutter, wave”), Low German fluttern, fluddern (“to flutter”), German flittern (“to sparkle, glitter”). More at float.

meaning: hesitate; shrink back (in fear of something unpleasant); Ex. She did not flinch in the face of danger.
etymology: From Middle French flenchir (“to bend”), from Old French flenchir, flanchir, from Frankish *hlankijan, from Proto-Germanic *hlankijaną (“to bend, twist, flex”), from Proto-Indo-European *kleng- (“to bend, turn, wind”). Cognate with Old High German hlenken, whence Middle High German lenken (“to bend”), Modern German lenken (“to cause to veer or turn aside, steer”). Attested in English since the 16th century.

meaning: lacking proper seriousness; Ex. flippant remarks about death; N. flippancy
etymology: 1595, from Northern English dialectal flippand (“prattling, babbling, glib”), present participle of flip (“to babble”), of North Germanic origin. Cognate with Icelandic fleipa (“to babble, prattle”), Swedish dialectal flepa (“to talk nonsense”). Alteration of -and suffix (a variant of the participial -ing) to -ant probably due to influence from words in -ant.

meaning: send (something) spinning, often into the air, by striking with a light quick blow; turn over; Ex. flip over
etymology: Alteration of earlier fillip, from Middle English filippen (“to make a signal or sound with thumb and right forefinger, snap the fingers”), an attenuated variation of flappen (“to flap, clap, slap, strike”). Cognate with Dutch flappen (“to flap”), German flappen (“to flap”).

meaning: fly; fly or move lightly or quickly; dart lightly; pass swiftly by; Ex. a bee flitting from flower to flower
etymology: Cognate Icelandic flytja, Swedish flytta, Danish flytte, Norwegian flytte, Faroese flyta. Compare also Saterland Frisian flitskje (“to rush; run quickly”).

meaning: flat mass of floating ice
etymology: Early 19th century. Probably from Norwegian Nynorsk flo (“layer, slab”), from Old Norse fló (“layer”).

meaning: plants of a region or era
etymology: From Latin Flōra (goddess of flowers).

meaning: condition or period of flowering
etymology: From Latin florēscō, from flōreō (“to bloom, flower”) + -ēscō, from flōs (“flower”), from Proto-Italic *flōs, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃- (“flower, blossom”), from *bʰel- (“to bloom”), as if through the form flōrēscentia.

meaning: ruddy; (of a complexion) reddish; flowery; very ornate; CF. rose
etymology: From French floride (“flourishing”), from Latin floridus (“flowery, blooming”). Doublet of Florida.

meaning: redden; blush; flow suddenly and abundantly; wash out by a rapid brief flow of water; N: reddish tinge; blush; brief rush; rush of strong feeling; Ex. flush of pride; ADJ: having surfaces in the same plane; even; blushing
etymology: From Middle English flusshen, fluschen, of uncertain origin. Compare dialectal flusk (“to fly at, startle a bird out of the bush”) and flusker (“to flutter, fly irregularly”). Perhaps related to Middle English flasshen, flasschen, flaschen, see flash; or a Middle English blend of flowen (“to flow”) + guschen (“to gush”). Compare Saterland Frisian flutskje, German Low German flutschen, German flutschen.

meaning: become red in the face (from embarrassment or shame); become red or rosy; N.
etymology: Cognate with Middle Low German blöschen (“to blush”). Compare also Old English blysian (“to burn; blaze”), Dutch blozen (“to blush”), Danish blusse (“to blush”), Old Norse blys (“torch”), Danish blus (“blaze”).

meaning: give a slight degree of a color or quality to; N: slight degree of a color or quality; Ex. tinged with grey/jealousy
etymology: The noun is derived from the verb.

meaning: slight degree of color; V: give a tint to
etymology: Alteration of earlier tinct, influenced by French teinte (“tint”), from Latin tīnctus (“dyed”), past participle of verb tingō (“tinge”). Doublet of tent (“kind of red wine”). Cognate with Dutch tint, Estonian tint, French teinte, German Tinte, Hungarian tinta, Italian tinta, Luxembourgish Tintin, Portuguese tinta, and Spanish tinta.

meaning: full of flowers; full of ornate expressions
etymology: From Middle English floury, equivalent to flower + -y (adjectival suffix). Piecewise doublet of floury.

meaning: drifting wreckage
etymology: From Anglo-Norman floteson, from Old French flotaison (“a floating”), from floter (“to float”), of Germanic origin (See float.), + -aison, from Latin -atio.

meaning: things thrown from a ship (to lighten the ship)
etymology: From Middle English jetteson, from Anglo-Norman getteson. Doublet of jettison.

meaning: struggle and thrash about; proceed clumsily or falter (as in water, mud, snow, etc.); proceed in confusion
etymology: From Middle English flowndre, from Anglo-Norman floundre, from Old Northern French flondre, from Old Norse flyðra, from Proto-Germanic *flunþrijǭ. Cognate with Danish flynder, German Flunder, Swedish flundra.

meaning: beat with a whip or flail; defeat utterly; talk about thoroughly in order to find the answer; move wildly or violently; Ex. The fishes thrashed about in the net.
etymology: Cognate with Dutch dorsen (“to thresh; to thrash”), German and Luxembourgish dreschen (“to thresh; to thrash”), Yiddish דרעשן (dreshn, “to thresh”), Danish tærske (“to thresh”), Faroese treskja (“to thresh”), Icelandic þreskja (“to thresh”), Norwegian Nynorsk treska, treske, treskja, treskje (“to thrash”), Swedish tröska (“to thresh”), Gothic 𐌸𐍂𐌹𐍃𐌺𐌰𐌽 (þriskan, “to thresh”), Finnish rehkiä (“to drudge; to toil”); also Welsh taradr (“auger, wimble; awl, borer; drill”), Latin terō (“to rub or triturate; to wear away or wear out, consume; to tread; to press with a mill; to pass, spend”), Greek τρίβω (trívo, “to grate; to rub”), Albanian tjerr (“to spin”), Belarusian це́рці (cjérci, “to rub; to polish; to pinch; to grind”), Bulgarian три́я (tríja, “to rub; to chafe; to grind”), Czech třít (“to rub; to spawn”), Polish tarć, treć, trzeć, trzyć (“to rub; to shred; to cut; to chafe; to crush; to spawn”), Russian тере́ть (terétʹ, “to rub; to polish; to grind”), Serbo-Croatian тр̏ти, tȑti (“to rub; to cause friction; to scour; to break, crush”), Slovak trieť (“to rub”), Slovene treti (“to crack open; to rub”), Ukrainian те́рти (térty, “to rub; to scrub”), Armenian թուր (tʻur, “sword”), Sogdian ܕܣܦܪܛܪ (dsprtr, “hand towel”), Hittite 𒋻𒌑𒍣 (tar-ú-zi, “to perform a round dance, to dance in twisting manner”), Tocharian A and Tocharian B tärk- (“to allow, let; to let go”), Sanskrit तर्कु (tarku, “spindle”).

meaning: grow well; prosper; make sweeping gestures; wave; brandish; Ex. The trees flourished in the sun. N: showy movement or gesture; embellishment or ornamentation (esp. in handwriting)
etymology: From Middle English floryschen, from Old French florir (via the arrhizotonic stem floriss-), from Late Latin flōrīre, from Latin flōrēre, from Latin flōrem (“flower”, noun). Corresponds to flower + -ish.

meaning: reject; mock; show contempt for; scorn; Ex. flout the rules
etymology: Perhaps from Middle English flouten (“to play the flute”); compare with Dutch fluiten.

meaning: chain or strap used with a bit to restrain a horse; something that checks; V: check; restrain
etymology: From Middle French courbe (“curve, curved object”), from Latin curvus (“bent, crooked, curved”). Doublet of curve.

meaning: waver; shift; rise and fall as if in waves; change or vary irregularly
etymology: First attested in 1630; borrowed from Latin flūctuātus, perfect passive participle of flūctuō (“(of the sea) to surge, swell; (of man) to waver, fluctuate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

meaning: smoothness of speech; ADJ. fluent
etymology: From Late Latin fluentia, equivalent to fluent + -cy. Cognate with French fluence.

meaning: unlikely occurrence; stroke of fortune; accidental stroke of good luck; ADJ. fluky
etymology: Unknown, perhaps dialectal. It seems to have originally referred to a lucky shot at billiards. Possibly connected to sense 3, referring to whales' use of flukes to move rapidly. Possibly derived from German Glück (“luck, good fortune, happiness”).

meaning: confuse; make nervous and confused; N.
etymology: The noun is derived from the verb.

meaning: having vertical parallel grooves (as in a pillar); V. flute: make long parallel inward curves in; N. flute: long rounded groove incised on the shaft of a column
etymology: From flute + -ed.

meaning: long narrow channel made in a surface to guide the movement of something; Ex. groove of the record
etymology: Cognate with Cimbrian gruuba (“gorge, ravine”), Dutch groef, groeve (“groove; pit, grave”), German Grube (“ditch, pit”), Luxembourgish Grouf (“pit, mine”), Mòcheno gruab (“mine”), Icelandic gróf (“pit, hollow”), Gothic 𐌲𐍂𐍉𐌱𐌰 (grōba, “foxhole”), Serbo-Croatian grèbati (“scratch, dig”). Related to Old English grafan (“to dig”). More at grave.

meaning: speak with involuntarily pauses or repetitions
etymology: From Middle English stameren, from Old English stamerian, from Proto-West Germanic *stamrōn, from Proto-Germanic *stamrōną (“to stammer”). Compare German stammeln, Dutch stameren, Old Norse stammr. Doublet of stumble.

meaning: flowing; series of changes; fluctuation; Ex. in a state of flux
etymology: From Old French flux, from Latin fluxus (“flow”).

meaning: coarse food for cattle, horses, etc.; feed for livestock; CF. food
etymology: Compare Saterland Frisian Fodder, West Frisian foer, Dutch voer (“pasture; fodder”), German Futter (“fodder; feed”), Danish foder, Swedish foder. More at food.

meaning: small weakness of character; slight fault; CF. feeble
etymology: 1640–50, from Early Modern French foible (“feeble”) (contemporary French faible). Doublet of feeble.

meaning: contrast; one that by contrast enhances the distinctive characteristics of another
etymology: Acronym of first outer inner last or similar.

meaning: insert improperly; impose upon another by coercion; palm off; pass off as genuine or worthy; CF. fist
etymology: Probably from archaic Dutch vuisten (“to take into one’s hand”), from Middle Dutch vuysten, from vuyst (“fist”); akin to Old English fyst (“fist”).

meaning: conceal in the palm of the hand; palm off: pass off; Ex. palm off some bad oranges onto the lady/the painting as a real Renoir
etymology: From Middle English palme, from Old English palm, palma (“palm-tree, palm-branch”), from Latin palma (“palm-tree, palm-branch, palm of the hand”), from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₂meh₂, *pl̥h₂emeh₂ (“palm of the hand”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat”). Cognate with Dutch palm, German Palme, Danish palme, Icelandic pálmur (“palm”).

meaning: present falsely; represent falsely to be
masses of leaves; CF. defoliate
etymology: From earlier foilage, from Late Middle English ffoylage, from Middle French feuillage. The more recent form is influenced by Latin folium (“leaf”).

meaning: stir up; incite; instigate; promote the growth of (something evil or unpleasant)
etymology: From Middle English fomenten, a borrowing from Old French fomenter, from Late Latin fōmentāre, from Latin fōmentum (“lotion”), from fovēre (“heat, cherish”).

meaning: rash; reckless; foolishly daring
etymology: From Middle English folehardy, foolhardi, folherdi, from Old French fol hardi (“foolishly bold”), from Old French fol (“foolish, silly; insane, mad”) (from Latin follis (“bellows; purse, sack; inflated ball; belly, paunch”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵʰ- (“to swell”)) + Old French hardi (“durable, hardy, tough”) (past tense of hardir (“to harden”), from the unattested Frankish *hartjan, from Proto-Germanic *harduz (“hard; brave”)), equivalent to fool + hardy. Compare fool-bold, fool-large, etc.

meaning: vain about dress and appearance; N. fop: man who takes too much interest in his clothes and appearance
etymology: From fop + -ish.

meaning: raid; sudden raid or military advance; V.
etymology: Cognate with Old High German fuotar (German Futter (“fodder, feed”)), Old English fōdor, fōþer (“food, fodder, covering, case, basket”), Dutch voeder (“forage, food, feed”), Danish foder (“fodder, feed”), Icelandic fóður (“fodder, sheath”). More at fodder, food, forage.

meaning: patience; forgiveness; V. forbear: refrain from (in a generous and forgiving way); be patient; Ex. forbear to send him to prison
etymology: From forbear (“to keep away from, avoid”) + -ance (suffix forming nouns indicating conditions or states).

meaning: place where a river can be crossed on foot; V.
etymology: Doublet of firth, fjord, and fjard, all via Old Norse; and port, distantly via Latin. Cognate with Low German Föörd, Dutch voord, German Furt, Norwegian and Danish fjord. See also forth and Persian پل (pol, “bridge”).

meaning: ancestors
premonition of evil; feeling of coming evil; V. forebode: be a warning of (something unpleasant)
etymology: From Middle English forbodyng, vorboding, equivalent to fore- + bode + -ing. Compare German Vorbote (“harbinger, omen”).

meaning: suitable to debate or courts of law; of or used in legal proceedings and the tracking of criminals; Ex. forensic science/medicine
etymology: From Latin forēnsis (“of the forum, public”) + -ic, from forum (“forum, marketplace”).

meaning: public square of an ancient Roman city; public place for open discussion; court of law
etymology: From Latin forum (“public market place, forum”). Doublet of fuero and door.

meaning: give an indication beforehand; be a sign of (what is coming); portend; prefigure
etymology: The noun is derived from fore- + shadow (“faint and imperfect representation”, noun), probably modelled after the verb which is attested earlier.

meaning: be a sign of; foreshadow
etymology: From Middle English prefiguren, from Latin praefigurare, from figurare (“to shape, picture”).

meaning: predecessor; one that comes before and indicates the approach of another
etymology: From Middle English forrenner, foreriner. Calque of Latin praecursor (“one who runs before, a forerunner”). Equivalent to fore- + runner and/or forerun + -er.

meaning: ability to foresee future happenings; prudence in providing for the future
etymology: From Middle English forsight, forsyght, forsichte (since 14th c.), a calque of Latin providentia. By surface analysis, fore- + sight. Compare Scots foresicht, Saterland Frisian Foarsicht, archaic Dutch voorzicht (now voorzichtigheid), German Vorsicht (all “caution, foresight”).

meaning: prevent by taking action in advance
etymology: From Middle English forestallen (“to forestall, intercept, ambush, way-lay”), from forestalle (“a forestalling, interception”), from Old English foresteall (“intervention, hindrance of justice, ambush”), from fore- (“ahead of, before”) + steall (“position”), equivalent to fore- + stall.

meaning: of marriage or the wedding ceremony; N; nuptials; wedding ceremony
etymology: Borrowed from Latin nūptiālis (“pertaining to marriage”), from nūptiae (“wedding”), from nūbō (“to marry, to take as husband”).

meaning: something surrendered as punishment for a crime or breach of contract; V: lose as a forfeit; N. forfeiture
etymology: From Middle English forfait from ca. 1300, from Old French forfait (“crime”), originally the past participle of forfaire (“to transgress”), and Medieval Latin foris factum. During the 15th century, the sense shifted from the crime to the penalty for the crime.

meaning: counterfeit; reproduce fraudulently; form by heating in a forge and hammering into shape; move with a sudden increase of speed or power; Ex. forged ahead in the last two years; N: furnace where metals are heated
etymology: * Computing sense perhaps derived from the early SourceForge service, launched in 1999.

meaning: give up; do without
sad and lonely; wretched; desolate
etymology: German verloren (“lost”), Swedish förlorad (“lost”). See further at lese/leese, lorn.

meaning: ceremonious quality; ceremonious adherence to rules; something done just for form'sake; Ex. mere formality
etymology: From Middle French formalité. equivalent to formal + -ity.

meaning: menacing; arousing fear; threatening; difficult to defeat; Ex. formidable foe/question
etymology: From Middle English formidable, from Old French formidable, formible, from Latin formīdābilis (“formidable, terrible”) (whence -able), from formīdō (“fear, dread”).

meaning: threat; V: threaten
etymology: From Middle English manace, from Old French manace, menace, &c., from Late Latin minācia (“threat, menace”), from Latin mināx (“threatening”) + -ia (suffix forming abstract nouns).

meaning: desert; abandon; renounce
etymology: Cognates include Saterland Frisian ferseeke (“to deny, refuse”), West Frisian fersaakje, Dutch verzaken (“to renounce, forsake”), Middle High German versachen (“to deny”), Danish forsage (“to give up”), Swedish försaka (“to be without, give up”), Norwegian forsake (“to give up, renounce”), Gothic 𐍃𐌰𐌺𐌰𐌽 (sakan, “to quarrel; to rebuke”), .

meaning: renounce under oath; abandon; make a solemn promise to give up; CF. abjure
etymology: From Middle English forsweren, from Old English forswerian (“to swear falsely”). Cognate with Old Saxon farswerian, Old High German farsweren, German verschwören. More at for- + swear.

meaning: strong point or special talent in a person'character
etymology: Borrowed 1640–50; earlier fort < Middle French; disyllabic pronunciation by association with Italian forte, from Latin fortis (“strong”). Doublet of fort and fortis.

meaning: straightforward; direct; frank
etymology: From Middle English forþright, forþriʒt, forþriht, from Old English forþriht (“direct, plain”). By surface analysis, forth + right.

meaning: happening in the near future; ready; willing to help; Ex. No answer was forthcoming.
etymology: The noun is derived from forth (“forwards”) + coming (“arrival”).

meaning: bravery; courage; strength of mind
etymology: From Middle English fortitude, from Old French, from Latin fortitūdō (“bravery, strength”), from fortis (“brave, strong”).

meaning: accidental; by chance; N. fortuity
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin fortuītus (“happening by chance, accidental, random, fortuitous”), from *fortu- (“chance, fortune, luck”) + -ītus (suffix forming adjectives). *Fortu- is thought to be from *fortus, from fors (“chance, luck”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“to bear, carry”)) + -tus (suffix forming action nouns). Doublet of fortuity.

meaning: rear; bring up (for a certain period only); encourage; promote the development of (feelings or ideas); Ex. help foster friendly relations; ADJ: giving parental care although not related by blood; Ex. foster parents
etymology: Cognate with Middle Dutch voester (“nursemaid”), Middle Low German vôster (“food”), Old Norse fóstr (“nurturing, education, alimony, child support”), Danish foster (“fetus”), Swedish foster (“fetus”).

meaning: fail completely; sink; CF. flounder
etymology: From Old French fondeur, from Latin fundātor, equivalent to found + -er.

meaning: brawl (noisy quarrel or fight) in which a number of people take part; melee
etymology: From French fracas, derived from fracasser, from Italian fracassare, from fra- + cassare, equivalent to Latin infra + quassare.

meaning: unruly; peevish; cranky; bad-tempered; Ex. fractious horse
etymology: From fraction (“discord”) (now obsolete) + -ous.

meaning: weak; N. frailty
etymology: From Middle English frele, fraill, from Old French fraile, from Latin fragilis. Cognate to fraction, fracture, and doublet of fragile.

meaning: right or privilege granted by authority; right to vote; license to sell a product in a particular territory
etymology: From Middle English franchise, fraunchise, from Old French franchise (“freedom”), a derivative of franc (“free”). More at frank.

meaning: wild; distraught as from fear or worry; Ex. frantic with fear
etymology: From Middle English frantike, frentik, variant of frenetik, from Old French frenetique, from Late Latin phreneticus, alteration of phreniticus, from φρενιτικός (phrenitikós, “mad, suffering from inflammation of the brain”), from φρενῖτις (phrenîtis, “inflammation of the brain”), from φρήν (phrḗn, “the brain”). Doublet of frenetic and phrenitic.

meaning: cheating; deceitful; Ex. fraudulent means; N. fraud: deception; swindle
etymology: From Middle English fraudulent, from Old French fraudulent, from Latin fraudulentus, from fraus (“fraud”).

meaning: filled (with something unpleasant); full; Ex. fraught with danger and difficulties; CF. freight
etymology: * Swedish frakt

meaning: brawl; fight; V: wear away or unravel by rubbing; have loose threads developing; cause to become worn out (a person'temper or nerves); CF. rub
etymology: The noun is derived from the verb.

meaning: frenzied; frantic
madly excited; N. frenzy: violent wild excitement
painting on wet plaster (usually fresh)
etymology: From Italian fresco, from Vulgar Latin *friscum, from Proto-Germanic *friskaz. Doublet of fresh and frisk.

meaning: smooth viscous mixture as of flour (powder made by crushing grain) and water (used as an adhesive); V: cause to adhere by applying paste
etymology: From Middle English paste, from Old French paste (modern pâte), from Late Latin pasta, from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá). Doublet of pasta. The verb is from the noun. Middle English had pasten (“to make a paste of; bake in a pastry”), also from the noun; compare Latin pistō and Medieval Latin pastillātus.

meaning: paste of flour and water (eaten when baked)
etymology: From Middle English pastre, pastri, from pastree (variant of pasterie, from Old French pastaierie and Medieval Latin pasteria, from Late Latin pasta, from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá)) or paste + -ri (modern paste + -ry).

meaning: paste that hardens to a smooth solid and is used for coating walls; V.
etymology: The verb is from Middle English plastren, from the noun.

meaning: be annoyed or vexed; Ex. fret over your poor grades; N: irritation of mind; ADJ. fretful
etymology: *Danish fråse (“to gorge”)

meaning: clash or conflict in opinion; rubbing against
etymology: From Middle French friction and directly from Latin frictionem, nom. frictio (“a rubbing, rubbing down”).

meaning: ornamental horizontal band on a wall
etymology: Late Middle English, from French and Middle French frise, probably from Medieval Latin Frisia (“Frisian (wool)”) due to import via Northern ships. Or, from French friser (“to curl”)..

meaning: intensely cold; cold in manner; Ex. frigid zone
etymology: Borrowed from Latin frīgidus (“cold”), from frīgeō (“to be cold”), from frīgus (“cold, coldness”), from Proto-Indo-European *sríHgos.

meaning: waste (time or money on unimportant things)
etymology: For the development of Middle English /iu̯r(ə)/ into /ə(ɹ)/, compare armour, batter, border, solder.

meaning: lacking in seriousness; flippant; self-indulgently carefree; unworthy of serious attention; relatively unimportant; trivial
etymology: From Latin frīvolus (“silly, empty, trifling, frivolous, worthless”), with the ending modified to match -ous.

meaning: excessive indulgence of one'own desire
etymology: From self- + indulgence.

meaning: free from worries; having no problems
etymology: From care + -free.

meaning: prankish; gay; playful; merry; frisky
etymology: From frolic + -some.

meaning: play and jump about happily; frisk; Ex. frolicking young lambs
etymology: The first element, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *frawaz, is cognate with Middle English frow (“hasty”); the latter element, ultimately from *-līkaz, is cognate with -ly, -like.

meaning: fern leaf; palm or banana leaf
etymology: Borrowed from Latin frons, frond- (“leafy branch”).

meaning: waste material thrown away (as bits of paper scattered untidily); V: cover untidily with scattered litter
etymology: Inherited from Middle English litere, borrowed from Anglo-Norman litere, from Old French litiere (“bedding; bed of loose straw; litter”), from Late Latin lectuāria, from Latin lectus + -āria.

meaning: bear fruit; produce fruit
etymology: Borrowed into Middle English from Old French fructefier.

meaning: thrift; economy; ADJ. frugal: practicing economy; costing little; inexpensive
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French frugalité. By surface analysis, frugal + -ity.

meaning: bearing of fruit; fulfillment; realization; Ex. come to/be brought to fruition
etymology: From Latin fruitiō (“enjoyment”). By surface analysis, fruit + -ion.

meaning: thwart; defeat; prevent from accomplishing a purpose
etymology: From Middle English frustraten (“to prevent, disappoint, render useless”), from Latin frūstrātus, perfect passive participle of frūstrō (“to deceive”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare French frustrer.

meaning: fleeting or transitory; lasting only a short time; roving (wandering); running away or fleeing as from the law; N: one who flees; Ex. fugitives at large
etymology: From Middle English fugitive, fugityve, fugityf, fugitife, fugytif, fugitif, from Latin fugitīvus, from fugitō, from fugiō.

meaning: support on which a lever rests or pivots
etymology: Borrowed from Latin fulcrum (“bedpost, foot of a couch”), from fulciō (“prop up, support”).

meaning: thunder; explode; issue a severe denunciation
etymology: Inherited from Middle English fulminaten, borrowed from Latin fulminātus, perfect passive participle of fulminō (“to lighten, hurl or strike with lightning”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from fulmen (“lightning which strikes and sets on fire, thunderbolt”), from earlier *fulgmen, *fulgimen, from fulgeō, fulgō (“flash, lighten”). Doublet of fulmine. More at fulgent.

meaning: disgustingly excessive; offensively flattering; Ex. fulsome praise/expressions of admire
etymology: The negative sense "offensive, gross; disgusting, sickening" developed secondarily after the 13th century and was influenced by Middle English foul (“foul”). In the 18th century, the word was sometimes even spelled foulsome.

meaning: move the fingers and hands awkwardly (in search of something); mishandle or drop a ball that is in play; bungle; botch; spoil by mishandling; N.
etymology: The ultimate origin for either could perhaps be imitative of fumbling. Or, from Proto-Indo-European *pal- (“to shake, swing”), see also Latin palpo (“to pat, touch softly”), and possibly Proto-West Germanic *fōlijan (“to feel”).

meaning: official (who performs a particular function)
etymology: From French fonctionnaire; by surface analysis, function + -ary.

meaning: made for practical use only (without decoration); functioning; Ex. functional modern furniture; CF. functionalism
etymology: From function + -al.

meaning: basic; primary; essential
etymology: From Middle English foundamental, fundamental, from Late Latin fundāmentālis, from Latin fundāmentum (“foundation”), from fundō (“to lay the foundation (of something), to found”), from fundus (“bottom”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰmḗn. By surface analysis, fundament + -al.

meaning: sad; solemn; suitable for a funeral
etymology: From Middle French funerail, from Latin funereus + -al.

meaning: frenzy; great anger and excitement; CF. fury
etymology: From Middle English furour, from Middle French fureur, from Old French furor, from Latin furor, from furō (“To rage, to be out of one's mind”).

meaning: stealthy; quiet and secret (trying to escape notice); sneaky; Ex. furtive glance
etymology: From Middle English *furtyve (implied in furtyvely (adverb)), from Middle French furtif, furtive (“furtive, stealthy”) (modern French furtif), from Latin fūrtīvus (“clandestine, furtive, secret; concealed, hidden; stolen”), from fūrtum (“theft; robbery”) (from fūr (“thief”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“to bear, carry”)) + -īvus (suffix forming adjectives).

meaning: move, give, or take in a quiet, stealthy way; N: one who sneaks; ADJ. sneaky
etymology: Possibly from Middle English sniken (“to creep, crawl”), from Old English snīcan (“to creep, crawl”), from Proto-West Germanic *snīkan, from Proto-Germanic *snīkaną (“to creep, crawl”), of sound-symbolic origin; compare formally unrelated snake, snoop, snook, snoke, and snoot. Cognate with Danish snige (“to sneak”), Swedish snika (“to sneak, hanker after”), Icelandic sníkja (“to sneak, hanker after”). Possibly related to snitch.

meaning: done slyly and secretly (being dishonest)
clever in deceiving; secretive; not telling one'intentions
etymology: Cognate with Icelandic slægur (“crafty, sly”), Norwegian Nynorsk sløg (“sly”). Related to sleight, slay. In all likelihood, however, unrelated with Saterland Frisian slau (“sly, crafty”), Dutch sluw (“sly, cunning”), Low German slu (“sly, cunning”), German schlau (“clever, crafty”). Doublet of sleight and slöjd

meaning: simultaneous firing or outburst (of missiles, questions, etc.)
etymology: From French fusillade, from fusiller (“shoot with a firearm”), from fusil (“rifle, gun”).

meaning: union; coalition; V. fuse
etymology: First appears c. 1555, in a translation by Richard Eden. From Middle French fusion, from Latin fūsiōnem (the accusative of fūsiō), from fusus, past participle of fundō (“to pour; to melt”) (see also found). Doublet of foison.

meaning: useless; hopeless; ineffectual
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French futile, from Latin fūtilis.

meaning: animal-biting fly; irritating person
etymology: Sense 2.1.1 (“person who upsets the status quo”) may allude to the Apology by the Greek philosopher Plato (428/427 or 424/423 – 348/347 B.C.E.), where he describes Socrates (c. 470 – 399 B.C.E.) acting as a goad to the Athenian political scene like a gadfly (Ancient Greek μῠ́ωψ (mŭ́ōps)) arousing a sluggish horse.

meaning: social blunder
etymology: From French gaffe (“blunder”). Doublet of gaff.

meaning: deny
etymology: From Middle English gainsayen, ȝeinseggen (“to say against, say in opposition to”), equivalent to gain- + say. Compare Old Danish gensige (“to speak against; gainsay”), Swedish gensaga (“a speaking against; protest”).

meaning: manner of walking or running; speed
etymology: From a specialised use of gate (“way, manner, behaviour, habit", properly "way, path, street, journey”), from Middle English gate (“way, path, road, street”), from Old Norse gata (“path, lane, alley, road”), from Proto-Germanic *gatwǭ (“passageway, street”). Doublet of gate.

meaning: large isolated system of stars, such as the Milky Way; collection of brilliant personalities
etymology: From Middle English galaxye, galaxie, from Old French galaxie, from Latin galaxias, from Ancient Greek γαλαξίας (galaxías, “Milky Way”), shortening of γαλαξίας κύκλος (galaxías kúklos, “milky circle”), from γάλα (gála, “milk”).

meaning: windstorm; gust of wind; emotional outburst (laughters, tears); Ex. gale of laughter
etymology: From Middle English galen, from Old English galan (“to sing, enchant, call, cry, scream; sing charms, practice incantation”), from Proto-Germanic *galaną (“to roop, sing, charm”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰel- (“to shout, scream, charm away”). Cognate with Danish gale (“to crow”), Swedish gala (“to crow”), Icelandic gala (“to sing, chant, crow”), Dutch galm (“echo, sound, noise”). Related to yell.

meaning: bitterness of feeling; nerve; effrontery; ´ãÁó (bile); CF. gall bladder
etymology: Related to Dutch gal, German Galle, Swedish galle, galla, Ancient Greek χολή (kholḗ). Also remotely related with yellow and gold.

meaning: large three-masted sailing ship
etymology: From Middle French galion or Spanish galeón. Originally an augmentative form of a Romance language cognate of galley, the word spread around the Mediterranean from the 12th century, taking on different meanings depending on place and time.

meaning: low ship with sails (rowed along by slaves)
etymology: From Middle English galeie, from Old French galee, from Latin galea, from Byzantine Greek γάλεα (gálea) of unknown origin, probably from Ancient Greek γαλέη (galéē), a kind of a small fish, from γαλεός (galeós, “dog-fish or small shark”).

meaning: sailing vessel built for great speed
etymology: From Middle English clipper, equivalent to clip (“cut, shorten”) + -er (suffix forming agent nouns). The type of sailing ship is probably also from clip, in the sense of “move or run rapidly”. Perhaps influenced by Middle Dutch klepper (“swift horse”), from kleppen (“to clap”), which is onomatopoeic.

meaning: small boat
etymology: From Middle French pinasse, from Spanish pinaza, from pino (“pine”) + -aza.

meaning: cut off with shears; fasten; N: something clipped off (as a short extract from film); clasp or fastener
etymology: From Middle English clippen, cleppen, clüppen, from Old English clyppan (“to hug, embrace, cherish, clasp”), from Proto-Germanic *klumpijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *glemb-, *glembʰ- (“lump, clump, clod, clamp”). Cognate with Old Frisian kleppa, klippa (“to hug, embrace”), Middle High German klimpen, klimpfen (“to contract tightly, constrict, squeeze”).

meaning: stimulate or shock by an electric current; stimulate by shock; shock into action; stir up; coat with rust-resistant zinc by using electricity
etymology: Learned borrowing from French galvaniser. By surface analysis, galvano- + -ize. Named after Italian physiologist Luigi Aloisio Galvani (1737–1798).

meaning: of the production of electricity by the action of an acid on a metal; having the effect of an electric shock; Ex. galvanic cell; galvanic effect; CF. Luigi Galvani
etymology: From French galvanique, named after Italian physiologist Luigi Aloisio Galvani (1737–1798) + -ique.

meaning: opening in chess in which a piece is sacrificed; action made to produce a future advantage
etymology: Borrowed from Italian gambetto (“act of tripping; gambit”), from gamba (“leg”) + -etto (diminutive suffix). First attested in 1656.

meaning: strategem to gain an advantage; tactic; Ex. management ploy
etymology: Possibly from a shortened form of employ or deploy. Or from earlier ploye, from Middle English, borrowed from Middle French ployer (compare modern plier), from Latin plicāre.

meaning: romp; skip about; leap about playfully; frolic; N.
etymology: From earlier gambolde, from Middle French gambade (modern gambade).

meaning: play or frolic boisterously; gambol; N.
etymology: Probably a variant of ramp.

meaning: outer skin of an orange used for giving a special taste to food; spice; interest; flavor; spirited enjoyment; Ex. add a certain zest to the affair; Ex. zest for life
etymology: Borrowed from French zeste.

meaning: in a spirited manner; with courage; Ex. fight gamely against a superior boxer; ADJ. game
etymology: From game + -ly; compare Old English gamenlīċ (“belonging to games, sportive, theatrical, ridiculous”) and Middle High German gāmelich, gemelich (“joyful”).

meaning: entire range
