meaning: lack of proportion (between the parts); ADJ. disproportionate
etymology: From dis- + proportion.

meaning: weakness of mind; state of being an imbecile; N. imbecile: stupid person; fool
etymology: From Middle English inbecillite, from Middle French imbecilité, imbecillité, and its etymon Classical Latin imbēcillitās. By surface analysis, imbecile + -ity.

meaning: drink in
etymology: From Middle English imbiben, from Latin imbibō, from im- + bibō (“to drink”) (whence also beverage), from Proto-Italic *pibō, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₃-, whence also potable, potion.

meaning: complicated situation (as in a play); painful or complex misunderstanding (as in a play); entanglement; confused mass (as of papers); V. embroil
etymology: Borrowed from Italian imbroglio (“tangle, entanglement, muddle”) (im-, alternative form of in- (prefix forming verbs denoting derivation) + broglio (“confusion; intrigue, fraud, rigging, stuffing”); see also imbrogliare (“to tangle”)), cognate with and probably from an earlier form of French embrouiller (“to embroil, muddle”) (em- (“em-”), a form of en- (“en-”, prefix meaning ‘caused’) + brouiller (“to confuse, mix up”)). Doublet of embroil.

meaning: saturate (soak thoroughly); fill; Ex. imbue someone with feelings
etymology: From Latin imbuō (“wet, moisten”). Compare imbibe.

meaning: spotless; flawless; absolutely clean
etymology: * Spanish inmaculado

meaning: one that pays rent to use property owned by another
etymology: From Middle English tenaunt, from Anglo-Norman tenaunt and Old French tenant, present participle of tenir (“to hold”), from Latin tenēre (“hold, keep”).

meaning: possession of land or building by rent; period of a tenant'occupancy
etymology: From tenant + -cy.

meaning: impending; near at hand
etymology: From the present participle of Latin imminēre (“to overhang”), from mineō ("to project, overhang"), related to minae (English menace) and mons (English mount). Compare with eminent.

meaning: state of being immovable
etymology: From Middle French immobilité, equivalent to immobile + -ity.

meaning: offer or kill as a sacrifice (by fire)
etymology: The adjective is first attested in 1534, the verb in 1548; borrowed from Latin immolātus, perfect passive participle of immolō (“to sacrifice”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

meaning: resistant to; free or exempt from; N. immunity
etymology: From Middle English, from Middle French immun, from Latin immūnis (“exempt from public service”), from in- (“not”) + mūnus (“service”).

meaning: imprison; shut up in confinement; CF. wall
etymology: From Middle English enmuren and Middle French emmurer, both from Old French enmurer, from Latin immūrō, from in- + mūrus (“wall”). Modern spelling is modelled after the Latin.

meaning: unchangeable
etymology: From Middle English immutable, from Latin immūtābilis (“unchangeable”); im- + mutable.

meaning: injure; hurt; damage
etymology: From Middle English impairen, empeiren, from Old French empeirier, from Early Medieval Latin impeiōrāre, from in- + Late Latin peiōrāre (“worsen”), from peiōrem (“worse”), comparative of malus (“bad”).

meaning: pierce (with a sharp point); Ex. impaled by the spear
etymology: From Middle French, from Medieval Latin impālāre, from Latin palus, whence also pale.

meaning: imperceptible (not easily understood); intangible; OP. palpable: tangible; easily perceptible
etymology: From Middle French impalpable, from Medieval Latin impalpabilis. See im- + palpable.

meaning: not biased; fair; N. impartiality
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French impartial. See im- + partial.

meaning: grant a share of; make known; Ex. news to impart
etymology: From Middle English imparten, borrowed from Middle French impartir, empartir, from Late Latin impartiō, impertiō, from im- (“in”) + Latin partiō (“divide”).

meaning: not able to be traveled or crossed
etymology: From im- + pass + -able.

meaning: predicament (dangerous condition) from which there is no escape; situation allowing for no further progress
etymology: Borrowed from French impasse.

meaning: without feeling; expressionless; imperturbable; stoical; Ex. impassive face
etymology: From im- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + passive (“which is, or is capable of being, acted on; (obsolete) which suffers, or may suffer, pain, death, etc.”, adjective).

meaning: charge (a public official) with crime in office; raise doubts about; indict; Ex. impeach a witness'credibility
etymology: From Middle English empechen, borrowed from Anglo-Norman empecher, from Old French empeechier (“to hinder”), from Latin impedicāre (“to fetter”). Cognate with French empêcher (“to prevent”).

meaning: faultless
etymology: From Middle French impeccable, from Latin impeccabilis (“not liable to sin”), from im- (“not”) + peccare (“to err, to sin”).

meaning: evidence concerning one'authority; written proof of a person'position; Ex. The new ambassador presented his credentials to the court.
etymology: From Medieval Latin crēdentiālis (“giving authority”), from Latin crēdentia (“trust”).

meaning: without money
etymology: From im- + pecunious, from Latin pecūniōsus, from pecūnia (“money”) + -ōsus (“full of”).

meaning: hide; retard or obstruct the progress of; block
etymology: Borrowed from Latin impediō (“to shackle”), from pēs (“foot”) (compare pedestrian). First attested use as a verb was in William Shakespeare's Macbeth, see quotations.

meaning: delay (in development); ADJ. retarded: (as of a child) slower in development
etymology: From Middle English retarden, from Anglo-Norman retarder, from Latin retardō (“to retard”, from re- + tardus (“slow”)).

meaning: hindrance; stumbling-block; speech defect preventing clear articulation; Ex. speech impediment
etymology: From Middle English impediment, borrowed from Latin impedimentum.

meaning: drive or force onward; drive to take action; urge to action
etymology: From Middle English impellen, borrowed from Latin impellō.

meaning: nearing; approaching; about to happen
etymology: From impend + -ing.

meaning: not able to be pierced or entered; beyond understanding; impossible to understand; Ex. impenetrable mystery
etymology: From Middle English inpenetrabel, inpenetrabyle, from Middle French impenetrable or directly from its etymon, Latin impenetrābilis. By surface analysis, im- + penetrable.

meaning: not repentant
etymology: The noun is derived from the adjective.

meaning: absolutely necessary; that must be done; critically important; expressing command; Ex. It is imperative that; N: something that must be done
etymology: Borrowed from Latin imperātīvus.

meaning: unnoticeable; impossible to perceive; undetectable
etymology: Inherited from Middle English imperceptible, from Middle French imperceptible and its etymon Medieval Latin imperceptibilis. By surface analysis, im- + perceptible.

meaning: like an emperor; related to an empire; CF. imperialism
etymology: From Middle English imperial, from Old French imperial, from Latin imperiālis (“of the empire or emperor, imperial”), from imperium (“empire, imperial government”) + -ālis, from imperō (“command, order”), from im- (“form of in”) + parō (“prepare, arrange; intend”). Displaced Old English cāserlīċ.

meaning: put in danger
etymology: From im- + peril.

meaning: domineering; too commanding; haughty; CF. imperial/emperor
etymology: From Latin imperiōsus (“mighty, powerful”), from imperium (“command, authority, power”).

meaning: impervious; not permitting passage through its substance; impossible to permeate
etymology: Apparently from im- + permeable. Compare French imperméable, from Latin impermeābilis, from im- + permeābilis (“permeable”).

meaning: insolent; rude; not pertinent; N. impertinence
etymology: Inherited from Middle English impertinent, from Middle French impertinent, from Old French impertinent, from Latin impertinēns; by surface analysis, im- + pertinent.

meaning: unshakably calm; placid
etymology: From Late Middle English imperturbable (“undisturbed; impossible to disturb”), borrowed from Late Latin imperturbābilis, from Latin im- (variant of in- (prefix meaning ‘not’)) + Late Latin perturbabilis (“perturbable”) (from Latin perturbō (“to confuse; to alarm, disturb, trouble, perturb”) + -bilis (suffix forming adjectives denoting a capacity or worth of being acted upon)). Perturbō is derived from per- (intensifying prefix) + turbō (“to agitate, disturb, unsettle, perturb; to upset”) (from turba (“disorder, disturbance, turmoil”) (possibly from Ancient Greek τῠ́ρβη (tŭ́rbē, “confusion, disorder, tumult”), either from Pre-Greek, or Proto-Indo-European *(s)twerH- (“to agitate, stir up; to urge on, propel”)) + -ō (suffix forming infinitives of regular first-conjugation verbs)). By surface analysis, im- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + perturbable.

meaning: composed; calm; self-possessed
etymology: From collect + -ed.

meaning: impenetrable; incapable of being damaged or distressed; incapable of being affected (in one'opinions); Ex. impervious to water/criticism
etymology: From Latin impervius (“that cannot be passed through”), from in- (“not”) + pervius (“letting things through”).

meaning: violent; hasty; rash; impulsive; without careful thought; Ex. impetuous decision
etymology: From Middle English impetuous, from Old French impetueux, from Late Latin impetuōsus (“violent”), from Latin impetus (“attack, violence”).

meaning: moving force; momentum; force of a moving body; incentive; stimulus; impulse
etymology: Borrowed from Latin impetus (“a rushing upon, an attack, assault, onset”), from impetō (“to rush upon, attack”), from in- (“upon”) + petō (“to seek, fall upon”).

meaning: irreverence; lack of respect for God or piety
etymology: From Old French impieté, from Latin impietas, from in- (“not”) + pietas (“piety”), from pius (“pious, devout”) + -tās (“-ty, -dom”). By surface analysis, impious + -ety.

meaning: infringe; encroach; influence; touch; collide with; Ex. The effects are impinging on every aspect of our lives.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin impingō (“dash against, impinge”). Compare impact, derived from the perfect passive participle of impingō.

meaning: irreverent
etymology: From Latin impius.

meaning: incapable of being pacified; impossible to appease; Ex. implacable enemy
etymology: From Middle English implācāble (“immitigable, unappeasable”) from Old French implacable (“harsh, unrelenting; implacable”) (modern French implacable), from Latin implācābilis (“unappeasable, implacable; irreconcilable”), from im- (variant of in- (prefix meaning ‘not’)) + plācābilis (“placable; appeasing, moderating, pacifying, propitiating; acceptable”) (from plācō (“to assuage, pacify, placate; to appease; to reconcile”) + -bilis (suffix forming adjectives indicating a capacity or worth of being acted upon)).

meaning: unlikely (to be true); unbelievable; Ex. implausible alibi
etymology: From im- + plausible.

meaning: put into effect; enforce; carry out; supply with tools; Ex. implement the plan/suggestion; N: tool or instrument
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin implēmentum (“a filling up”), from Latin impleō (“to fill up”).

meaning: incriminate; involve incriminatingly; show to be involved (in a crime); Ex. implicate someone in the crime
etymology: First attested in the 15th century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English implicaten (poorly attested), from implicat(e) (“wrapped, entwined; involved, connected (with)”, possibly also used as the past participle of implicaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), borrowed from Latin implicātus, perfect passive participle of implicō (“to entangle, involve”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from plicō (“to fold”). Doublet of imply and employ.

meaning: something hinted at or suggested; implying; implicating
etymology: From Middle French implication, from Latin implicationem (accusative of implicatio). Equivalent to implicate + -ion.

meaning: understood but not stated; implied; unquestioning and complete; Ex. implicit trust
etymology: From Middle French implicite, from Latin implicitus, past participle of implico (“to infold, involve, entangle”); see implicate.

meaning: burst inward; CF. vaccum tube
etymology: Back-formation from implosion.

meaning: beg
etymology: The noun is derived from the verb.

meaning: suggest a meaning not expressed; signify
etymology: From Middle English implien, emplien, borrowed from Old French emplier, from Latin implicare (“to infold, involve”), from in (“in”) + plicare (“to fold”). Doublet of employ and implicate.

meaning: not wise; not expedient; not politic
etymology: From im- + politic.

meaning: weightless; that cannot undergo precise evaluation; CF. pound
etymology: From im- + ponderable.

meaning: significance; importance; meaning
etymology: From Middle English importen, from Old French emporter, importer, from Latin importō (“bring in from abroad, import”, verb), from in (“in, at, on; into”) + portō (“to carry, bear; convey”).

meaning: expressing a meaning; important; Ex. significant smile; N. significance: importance; meaning; V. signify: denote; mean; signal; make known; matter; be significant
etymology: From Latin significans, present participle of significare, from signum (“sign”) + ficare (“do, make”), variant of facere.

meaning: urging; always demanding; troublesomely urgent or persistent
etymology: First attested in 1477, in Middle english; from Latin importūnus + -ate (adjective-forming suffix), modelled on Middle French importuné. By surface analysis, importune + -ate (compare inopportune). The noun was substantivized from the adjective, see -ate (noun-forming suffix).

meaning: beg persistently; make repeated requests (in an annoying way)
etymology: From Middle French importuner and its etymon Medieval Latin importūnor (“to make oneself troublesome”), from Latin importūnus (“unfit, troublesome”), originally "having no harbor".

meaning: assuming a false identity; masquerade; CF. impostor
etymology: From Middle French imposture, from Late Latin impostura, Latin impostus.

meaning: wear a mask or disguise; pretend; N: costume party or ball at which masks are worn; pretense; disguise
etymology: The verb is derived from the noun.

meaning: weak; ineffective; lacking in physical strength or power
etymology: From Old French impotent, from Latin impotēns, from in- (expresses negation) + potēns (“powerful”).

meaning: desire; want intensely
etymology: From Middle English craven, from Old English crafian (“to crave, ask, implore, demand, summon”), from Proto-West Germanic *krafōn, from Proto-Germanic *krafjaną (“to demand”). Cognate with Danish kræve (“to demand, require”), Swedish kräva (“to crave, demand”), Icelandic krefja (“to demand”), Norwegian kreve (“to demand”).

meaning: curse; swearword
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin imprecātiō (“calling down of curses”), from imprecor (“call down, invoke”).

meaning: invulnerable; impossible to capture or enter by force; Ex. impregnable fort/argument; CF. take
etymology: From Late Middle English imprenable, impregnable (“impossible to capture, impregnable”), from Old French imprenable (modern French imprenable (“impregnable”)), from im- (a variant of in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + prenable (“(military) of a building, position, etc.: takable”) (from prendre (“to take”) + -able (suffix meaning ‘creating an effect or influence’)). Prendre is derived from Latin prēndere, present active infinitive of prēndō, a variant of prehendō (“to catch, lay hold of; to grasp; to grab, snatch; to seize, take”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed- (“to find; to hold; to seize, take”). The intrusive g in the English word was modelled after words like deign and reign.

meaning: make pregnant; fill thoroughly; saturate
etymology: The adjective is first attested in 1540, the verb in 1605; borrowed from Medieval Latin impraegnātus, perfect passive participle of Latin impraegnō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Doublet of impregn; participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.

meaning: without previous preparation; off the cuff (end of a sleeve); on the spur of the moment
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French impromptu.

meaning: improperness; unsuitableness
etymology: From French impropriété, from Latin improprietās. By surface analysis, improper + -iety or im- + propriety.

meaning: thriftless; not providing for the future
etymology: From the Latin improvidens, equivalent to in- + provident.

meaning: compose on the spur of the moment
etymology: From French improviser; ultimately from Latin improvisus.

meaning: lacking caution; not prudent; injudicious
etymology: From Middle French imprudent, from Latin imprūdens (“not foreseeing, ignorant”), prefix im- (“not”) + prūdens (“foreseeing, skilled, judicious”).

meaning: impertinence; insolence
etymology: From Middle French impudence, from Latin impudentia.

meaning: dispute or contradict (often in an insulting way); attack as false or questionable; challenge; gainsay; CF. fight
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French impugner, from Latin impugnō, from im- + pugnō (“fight”), from pugnus (“fist”), as in English pugilism (“fighting with fists, boxing”).

meaning: powerlessness; feebleness
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French impuissance.

meaning: freedom from punishment or harm; CF. punish
etymology: From Middle French impunité, from Latin impunitas, from impunis (“without punishment”).

meaning: attribute; ascribe; charge; N. imputation
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French imputer, from Latin imputō (“to bring into the reckoning, charge, impute”).

meaning: unintentionally; by oversight; carelessly
etymology: From inadvertent + -ly.

meaning: watch over and direct; supervise; N. oversight: unintentional failure to notice or do something; supervision
etymology: From Middle English overseen, ouverseen, from Old English ofersēon (“to observe, oversee; to overlook, neglect”), equivalent to over- + see.

meaning: not to be taken away; nontransferable; Ex. inalienable rights
etymology: Borrowed around 1645 from French inaliénable, from in- + aliénable (“alienable”), equivalent to in- + alienable.

meaning: silly; senseless; Ex. inane remarks; N. inanity
etymology: From Latin inānis (“empty, vain, useless”), of unknown origin.

meaning: lifeless; not animate
etymology: Inherited from Middle English inanimat(e), from Late Latin inanimātus, from Latin in- + animātus (“animated”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix). By surface analysis, in- + animate. The noun was derived by substantivization from the adjective, see -ate (noun-forming suffix).

meaning: speechless; producing indistinct speech; not articulate; not expressing oneself clearly
etymology: From Latin inarticulatus and from in- + articulate. See -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

meaning: unable for the moment to speak (because of strong feeling); Ex. speechless with anger
etymology: From Middle English specheles, from Old English sprǣċlēas (“speechless; without the power of speak”), from Proto-Germanic *sprēkalausaz, equivalent to speech + -less. Cognate with West Frisian sprakeleas (“speechless”), Dutch sprakeloos (“speechless”), German Low German spraaklos (“speechless”), German sprachlos (“speechless”).

meaning: begin formally; install in office; induct into office by a formal ceremony; N. inauguration; ADJ. inaugural
etymology: Further from in- (“against; into; on, upon; to, towards”) + augurō (“to act as an augur, interpret omens, augur; to foretell, predict; to conjecture, guess”), from augur (“soothsayer, augur”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix) (further etymology uncertain; see the entry).

meaning: strikingly bright; shining with intense heat; emitting visible light when heated; Ex. incandescent light bulb; CF. candle
etymology: Borrowed from French incandescent, from Latin incandescens, from incandesco (“be heated, glow”), from in- (intensifying prefix) + candesco (“become white”), from candidus (“white”).

meaning: singing or chanting of magic spells; magical formula; (the saying of) words used in magic; CF. enchant
etymology: From Middle English incantacioun, from Old French incantation, from Latin incantatio. More at enchant.

meaning: tune (melody) in which a number of words are sung on the same note; V: sing (a chant); utter (a slogan) in the manner of a chant
etymology: From Middle English chaunten, from Old French chanter, from Latin cantāre (“sing”). Doublet of cant.

meaning: quality of pleasing; amulet; action or formula thought to have magical power; spell; V: attract; cast a spell on; bewitch
etymology: From Middle English charme, from Old French charme (“chant, magic spell”), from Latin carmen (“song, incantation”). Displaced native Old English lybb (“drug, poison, charm”).

meaning: cast a spell over; captivate completely
etymology: From Middle English bewicchen, bewycchen, biwicchen, equivalent to be- + witch.

meaning: repeat aloud (something learned); describe; Ex. recite his complaints; N. recitation
etymology: From Middle English reciten, from Old French reciter, from Latin recitō.

meaning: act of reciting publicly; detailed account; performance of music or dance (by a solo performer)
etymology: From recite + -al.

meaning: disable; N. incapacity: lack of capacity
etymology: Mid-17th century, from incapacity + -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare French incapaciter.

meaning: imprison
etymology: The adjective is first attested in 1528, the verb in 1575; borrowed from Medieval Latin incarcerātus, perfect passive participle of incarcerō (“to imprison”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from Latin in- (“in”) + carcer (“a prison”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). Common participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.

meaning: endowed with flesh; invested with bodily form; personified; Ex. devil incarnate; V: give bodily form to; embody
etymology: First attested in 1395, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English incarnat(e) (“(of God or Christ) embodied in human form or flesh, incarnate; provided with new tissues, healed; (with devel, in curses) bloody”), borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin incarnātus, perfect passive participle of incarnor (“to be made flesh, become incarnate”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from in- + Latin carō (“flesh”, carn- in its oblique stem) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, in- + Latin carn- + -ate.

meaning: act of assuming a human body and human nature; one who personifies something; personification; Ex. previous incarnation/reincarnation
etymology: From Middle English incarnacion, borrowed from Old French incarnacion, from Medieval Latin, Ecclesiastical Latin incarnatio, from Late Latin incarnari (“to be made flesh”).

meaning: represent (an inanimate object) as a person; be the embodiment or perfect example of; Ex. She is evil/patience personified; N. personification
etymology: From person + -ify, after French personnifier.

meaning: arsonist; ADJ: causing fire; of arson; Ex. incendiary bomb
etymology: From Middle English incendiarie, from Old French incendiaire, from Latin incendiārius (“setting alight”), from incendium (“destructive fire”), from incendō (“to set on fire, kindle”), from in- (“into, in, on, upon”) + candeō (“to be hot”).

meaning: enrage; infuriate (make furious); make extremely angry; outrage; N: aromatic substance burned to produce a pleasant odor
etymology: From Middle English encens, from Old French encens (“sweet-smelling substance”) from Late Latin incensum (“burnt incense”, literally “something burnt”), neuter past participle of incendō (“to set on fire”). Compare incendiary. Doublet of incienso. Displaced native Old English rēcels.

meaning: spur; motive; something which encourages one to greater activity
etymology: From Medieval Latin incentīvus (“that strikes up or sets the tune”), from incinō (“to strike up”), from in- (“in, on”) + canō (“to sing”) + -ive. The formation appears to have been influenced by incendō (“to set on fire”).

meaning: start; beginning
etymology: The layering sense derives from the 2010 science fiction film Inception, in which a team of people infiltrate someone’s subconscious mind, proceeding through several layers of dreams with the goal of causing the target to incept an idea.

meaning: uninterrupted; unceasing
etymology: From Late Middle English incessaunte, from Late Latin incessāns, incessantem, from Latin in- + cessāns.

meaning: (of desire, wish, plan) recently begun; not explicit; at the beginning of development; rudimentary; elementary; Ex. inchoate mass
etymology: The adjective is first attested in 1534, the verb circa 1631; borrowed from Latin incohātus (“begun, unfinished”), perfect passive participle of incohō (“to begin”), see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3). Cognate with Spanish incoar (“to initiate, commence, begin”).

meaning: rate of occurrence; particular occurrence; Ex. high incidence of infant mortality
etymology: From Middle French incidence, from Medieval Latin incidentia (“a falling upon”), from Latin incidens, present participle of incidere (“to fall upon”), from in (“on”) + cadere (“to fall”).

meaning: not essential; minor; N: something incidental
etymology: From incident + -al.

meaning: event; event that causes a crisis
etymology: Recorded since 1412, from Middle French incident, from Latin incidens, the present active participle of incidō (“to happen, befall”), itself from in- (“on”) + -cidō, the combining form of cadō (“to fall”).

meaning: burn to ashes
etymology: From Latin incinerātus, perfect participle of incinerō (“to burn into ashes”), from cinis (“ashes”).

meaning: beginning; in an early stage
etymology: Borrowed from Latin incipiēns, present participle of incipiō (“begin”).

meaning: (appreciatively) cutting; sharp; Ex. incisive remarks; V. incise: make a cut into
etymology: Late Middle English (in the sense “cutting, penetrating”), borrowed from Medieval Latin incīsīvus, from incīdō (“to cut in, cut through”) + -īvus (“-ive”, adjectival suffix). Compare Middle French incisif.

meaning: arouse to action; goad; motivate; induce to exist; Ex. incite a riot/the crowd to rebellion
etymology: From Middle French inciter, from Latin incitō (“to set in motion, hasten, urge, incite”), from in (“in, on”) + citō (“to set in motion, urge”), frequentative of cieō (“to rouse, excite, call”).

meaning: stormy; unkind; unmerciful; CF. clement
etymology: From Latin inclēmēns (“unmerciful, severe”), from in- (“not”) + clēmēns (“mild, placid”).

meaning: slope; slant; Ex. steep incline
etymology: From Middle English enclinen, from Old French encliner (modern incliner), from Latin inclīnō (“incline, tilt”), from in- + clīnō (compare -cline), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley- (English lean).

meaning: tending or leaning toward; bent; V. incline: slant; dispose; be disposed; tend
etymology: From incline + -ed.

meaning: have a tendency; take care of; minister; serve at; apply one'attention; attend
etymology: From Middle English tenden, from Middle French tendre, from Old French tendre (“to stretch, stretch out, hold forth, offer, tender”), from Latin tendere (“to stretch, stretch out, extend, spread out”).

meaning: tending to include all; all-inclusive; Ex. inclusive charge
etymology: Derived from Middle French inclusif, from Medieval Latin inclūsīvus, from Latin inclūsus + -īvus.

meaning: with identity concealed; using an assumed name; ADJ.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian incognito, from Latin incognitus (“unknown”), from in- (“not”) + cognitus (“known”), perfect passive participle of cognoscere.

meaning: unintelligible; muddled; unable to express one'thoughts in an orderly manner; illogical; lacking cohesion; not coherent
etymology: From in- + coherent.

meaning: not spacious; inconvenient
etymology: From in- + commodious. Compare Latin incommodus.

meaning: inharmonious; N. incompatibility
etymology: Borrowed from French incompatible.

meaning: lack of harmony; absurdity; ADJ. incongruous: lacking in harmony; inappropriate
etymology: From Middle French incongruité, from Medieval Latin incongruitās, from Latin incongruus.

meaning: clothe; N: clothing; array; apparel
etymology: The noun is from Middle English atir, from the verb.

meaning: insignificant; unimportant
etymology: From in- + consequential.

meaning: state of being self-contradictory; lack of uniformity or steadiness; ADJ. inconsistent: displaying a lack of consistency; erratic; contradictory; incompatible
lacking self-restraint; not continent; licentious
etymology: From Middle English incontinent, from Old French incontinent, from Latin incontinens, from in + continens.

meaning: indisputable; impossible to dispute; not open to question; unquestionable
etymology: From in- + controvertible.

meaning: introduce something into a larger whole; include; embody; give material form to; ADJ.
etymology: From Middle English, from Late Latin incorporātus, perfect passive participle of incorporō (“to embody, to incorporate”), from in- (“in”) + corpus, corporis (“body”).

meaning: without a material body; insubstantial
etymology: From Latin incorporeus + -al. By surface analysis, in- + corporeal.

meaning: uncorrectable
etymology: From Middle English incorrigible, from Middle French incorrigible (1334), or directly from Latin incorrigibilis (“not to be corrected”), from in- (“not”) + corrigere (“to correct”) + -ibilis (“-able”), equivalent to in- + corrigible. Recorded since 1340.

meaning: tendency to disbelief
etymology: Attested since 1430. From Middle English incredulite, from Old French incredulité, from Late Latin incredulitas, from Latin incredulus (“unbelieving”) + -itas (“-ity”), equivalent to incredulous + -ity.

meaning: withholding belief; skeptical; showing disbelief
etymology: Borrowed from Latin incrēdulus (“unbelieving”).

meaning: increase
etymology: From Middle English encrement, increment, from Latin incrēmentum, from incrēscō (whence increase), from in- + crēscō (“grow”). Equivalent to increase + -ment.

meaning: accuse of or implicate in a crime; serve as evidence against; cause to seem or make guilty of a crime; Ex. incriminating evidence
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin incrīminātus, perfect passive participle of Latin incrīminō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). First attested in 1736. By surface analysis, in- + criminate.

meaning: hard coating or crust; V. incrust: encrust; cover with a crust
etymology: From Latin incrustātiō.

meaning: hatch; warm (eggs) with the body to promote hatching; maintain at optimal environment conditions for development; be holding in one'body an infection which is going to develop into a disease; N. incubation; CF. incubation:disease
etymology: First attested in 1641; borrowed from Latin incubātus, an alternative to incubitus, perfect passive participle of incubō (“to hatch”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from in- (“in”) + cubō (“to lie”).

meaning: since; owing to the fact that
burden; very worriying problem; mental care; nightmare; male devil; CF. succubus
etymology: From Late Latin incubus, from Latin incubō (“nightmare, one who lies down on the sleeper”), from incubō (“to lie upon, to hatch”, from in- (“on”) + cubō (“to lie down”)).

meaning: teach (ideas or principles); instill
etymology: Borrowed from Latin inculcātus, perfect passive participle of inculcō (“impress upon, force upon”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from in- (“in”) + calcō (“tread upon, trample”), from calx (“heel”). Participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.

meaning: obligatory; imposed as an obligation; currently holding an office; N: person who holds an office
etymology: From Latin incumbentem + English -ent (suffix denoting the causing, doing, or promoting of an action). Incumbentem is the accusative singular of incumbēns (“reclining”), the present active participle of incumbō (“to lay upon, to lean or recline on; to fall upon, to press down on”), from in- (prefix meaning ‘against; into; on, upon’) + *cumbō (“to lie down, recline”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱewb-).

meaning: bring upon oneself
etymology: From Middle English incurren, from Anglo-Norman encurir, Middle French encourir, from Old French encorre, from Latin incurrere.

meaning: temporary invasion; CF. excursion: short journey
etymology: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French, from Latin incursiō.

meaning: hostile invasion; advance that lessens the quantity or difficulty of something; Ex. The long illness made serious inroads on his savings; CF. raid
etymology: The verb is derived from the noun.

meaning: tireless; untiring; showing no sign of getting tired
etymology: From Middle French, from Latin indēfatīgābilis (“untiring”), from in- (“not”) + dēfatīgō (“to tire out”).

meaning: not able to be erased
etymology: From Latin indēlēbilis (“indestructible”). By surface analysis, in- + delible.

meaning: make secure against damage or loss; compensate for damage or loss; CF. make uninjured
etymology: From indemn (“unhurt”) + -ify (forming verbs)

meaning: notch; deep recess; V. indent; CF. tooth
etymology: From indent + -ation.

meaning: bind as servant or apprentice to master; bind by indenture; N: contract binding one party into the service of another for a specified time (as between an apprentice and his master)
etymology: From Anglo-Norman endenture, from Old French endenteure, from endenter (“to dent”). The name of the contract derives from the irregular dent-shaped cut (indentation) used to prove the authenticity of the two parts, similar to a chirograph.

meaning: uncertain; not clearly fixed; indefinite
suggestive; implying; serving to indicate
etymology: From Middle French indicatif, from Late Latin indicātīvus. By surface analysis, indicate + -ive.

meaning: signs; indications; Ex. indices of a student'potential; CF. index: something that reveals or indicates; sign; Ex. cost-of-living index
etymology: Borrowed from Latin indicēs.

meaning: charge; N. indictment
etymology: The irregular spelling is due to the word having been borrowed into Middle English from Old French, and not from Latin as was the case with most other descendants of dictāre (but see dight). The borrowed /iː/ regularly shifted to /aɪ/ in the course of the Great Vowel Shift; the ⟨c⟩ represents a later attempt at graphic Latinisation.

meaning: unmoved or unconcerned by; having no interest in; mediocre; neither good nor bad
etymology: From Old French indifferent, from Latin indifferens. By surface analysis, in- + different.

meaning: poverty
etymology: Only relation to antonym affluence is common Latinate suffix + -ence.

meaning: native; Ex. plant indigenous to the New World
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin indigenus (“native, born in a country”), from indi- (indu-), an old derivative of in (“in”), gen- the root of gignō (“give birth to”), and English -ous. Compare indigene, Ancient Greek ἐνδογενής (endogenḗs, “born in the house”), and the separately formed piecewise doublet endogenous. Unrelated to Indian.

meaning: poor; destitute
etymology: From Middle English indigent, from Old French indigent, from Latin indigēns, present participle of indigeō (“to need”), from indu (“in, within”) + egeō (“to be in need, want”).

meaning: anger at an injustice; Ex. righteous indignation; ADJ. indignant
etymology: From Middle English indignacioun, borrowed from Old French indignation, from Latin indignātiō, from indignor (“to scorn, resent”), from indignus (“unworthy, not fitting”), from in- (“not”) + dignus (“worthy, appropriate”). Attested since ca. 1374. Doublet of indignatio.

meaning: morally upright; just
etymology: From earlier rightuous, rightwose, rightwos, rightwise, from Middle English rightwise, rightwis, from Old English rihtwīs (“righteous, just”), corresponding to right + -wise (with assimilation of second element to -ous), or to right + wise (“way, manner”). Cognate with Scots richtwis (“righteous”), Old High German rehtwīsic (“righteous, just”), Icelandic réttvíss (“righteous, just”). Compare also thefteous, mighteous.

meaning: legally correct; Ex. rightful owner
etymology: From Middle English rightful, ryghtfull, riȝtful, from Old English *rihtfull (suggested by derivative unrihtfull (“unrightful”)), equivalent to right + -ful.

meaning: treatment or situation that causes shame or loss of dignity, respect; offensive or insulting treatment; humiliating or degrading treatment; Ex. I suffered the indignity of having to say that in front of them.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin indignitās, indignitātem. Equivalent to indign + -ity.

meaning: choosing at random; confused; not based on careful distinctions
etymology: First attested in 1598; from in- + discriminate.

meaning: too certain to be disputed; beyond doubt
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin indisputābilis. By surface analysis, in- + disputable.

meaning: permanent; impossible to dissolve or disintegrate
etymology: From Middle French indissoluble, from Latin indissolubilis.

meaning: write; compose
etymology: Originally a variant of indict; from Middle English enditen, endyten, from Old French enditer, from Late Latin indictāre, from in- + dictare (“to declare”). Doublet of indict.

meaning: lazy
etymology: From French indolent or directly from Late Latin indolēns, from in- (“not”) + dolēns (“hurting”), from doleo (“to hurt”). The later sense of “living easily, slothful” perhaps developed in French.

meaning: unconquerable; unyielding
etymology: From Late Latin indomitābilis, from in- (“not”) + domitō, frequentative of domō (“to tame”). By surface analysis, in- + domitable.

meaning: unable to be doubted; which cannot be doubted; unquestionable
etymology: Either from French indubitable or Latin indubitābilis. By surface analysis, in- + dubitable.

meaning: persuade; lead to do something; bring about; N. inducement
etymology: From Middle English enducen, borrowed from Latin indūcere (“lead in, bring in, introduce”), from in + dūcō (“lead, conduct”). Compare also abduce, adduce, conduce, deduce, produce, reduce etc. Doublet of endue.

meaning: pertaining to induction or proceeding from the specific to the general
etymology: From Middle French inductif, from Late Latin inductivus.

meaning: place formally in office; install; admit as a member; initiate; N. induction: inducting; process of deriving general principles from particular facts
etymology: Originated 1350–1400 from Middle English induct, borrowed from Latin inductus, perfect passive participle of indūcō, equivalent to induce + -tus (past participle suffix).

meaning: humoring; yielding; lenient; showing indulgence
etymology: From Latin indulgēns, indulgentem, present participle of indulgēre.

meaning: yield to; gratify; allow oneself a special pleasure; Ex. indulge one'every whim/a child/in a big cigarette; N. indulgence
etymology: From Latin indulgeō (“to indulge”).

meaning: indulge; comply with the wishes of; N. quality that makes something amusing; state of mind; mood; Ex. in a bad humor; Ex. out of humor
diligent; hard-working; N. industry
etymology: From Middle French industrieux, from Late Latin industriosus (“diligent, active, industrious”), from Latin industria (“diligence, industry”); see industry.

meaning: habitually intoxicated; drunk; N. inebriety
etymology: From Latin inēbriātus, past participle of inēbriō (“intoxicate”) from in- + ēbrius (“drunk, intoxicated”) from Proto-Italic *ēɣʷrios, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ēgʷʰ-ryo-s from root *h₁egʷʰ- (“drink”); whence also ebrious and inebriate.

meaning: make drunk; intoxicate; N. intoxicated person
etymology: From Latin inēbriō, inēbriāre, from ēbrius (“drunk”).

meaning: make drunk; stimulate or excite; Ex. intoxicated by all the money he might win
etymology: First attested in 1450, in Middle English; from Middle English intoxicaten, from intoxicat(e) (“(of a weapon or drug) smeared, anointed or filled with poison; (of a human being, animal) poisoned, intoxicated”, also used as the past participle of intoxicaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), borrowed from intoxicātus, perfect passive participle of intoxicō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Late Latin toxicō (“to smear, anoint with poison”), from toxicus (“toxic, poisonous”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix), from Ancient Greek τοξικόν (toxikón). By surface analysis, in- + toxic + -ate.

meaning: unutterable; not to be uttered; taboo; that cannot be expressed in speech; indescribable; unspeakable; inexpressible; Ex. ineffable name/joy
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French ineffable, a learned borrowing from Latin ineffābilis, from in- (“not”) + effābilis (“utterable”).

meaning: not effective; not having a desired effect; weak
etymology: From in- + effectual.

meaning: irresistible; not to be escaped; unavoidable
etymology: From Middle French inéluctable (whence in- + e- and -able), from Latin inēlūctābilis, from in- + ēlūctor (“struggle out”) + -bilis.

meaning: unsuited; inappropriate; lacking skill; incompetent; CF. inapt: (of statements or ideas) inappropriate
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French inepte, from Latin ineptus, from in- + aptus (whence English apt).

meaning: unfairness; ADJ. inequitable
etymology: From in- + equity. Piecewise doublet of iniquity.

meaning: infallibility
etymology: From inerrant + -cy.

meaning: inactive; lacking power to move; unable to move or act; Ex. chemically inert; N. inertia: state of being inert; force which keeps a thing in the position or state
etymology: From French inerte, from Latin iners (“inactive, inert”).

meaning: unavoidable
etymology: From Middle French inevitable, from Latin inēvītābilis (“unavoidable”), from in- + ēvītābilis (“avoidable”), from ēvītāre (“to avoid”), from ē- (“out”) + vītāre (“to shun”).

meaning: relentless; unyielding; implacable; not capable of being changed by entreaty or efforts; Ex. inexorable price rises
etymology: From Middle French inexorable, from Latin inexōrābilis (“relentless, inexorable”) (or directly from the Latin word), from in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + exōrābilis (“that may be moved or persuaded by entreaty; exorable”). Exōrābilis is derived from exōrāre (from exōrō (“to persuade, win over; to beg, entreat, plead”), from ex- (prefix meaning ‘out of’) + ōrō (“to beg, entreat, plead, pray; to deliver a speech, orate”), from ōs (“mouth”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃éh₁os (“mouth”)) + -bilis (suffix forming adjectives indicating a capacity or worth of being acted upon). By surface analysis, in- + exorable.

meaning: unerring; never making mistakes
etymology: From Medieval Latin īnfallibilis, from Latin in- + fallibilis. Compare French infaillible. By surface analysis, in- + fallible.

meaning: notoriously bad; notorious; well known for being bad; Ex. infamous behavior; N: infamy: infamous act; evil fame or reputation
etymology: From Middle English enfamouse, in-fames, infamous, from Medieval Latin īnfāmōsus, from Latin īnfāmis; by surface analysis, in- + famous. Displaced native Old English unhlīsful.

meaning: childish; infantlike
etymology: Mid-15th century, "pertaining to infants," from Latin infantilis (“pertaining to an infant”), equivalent to infant + -ile, from īnfāns. Sense of "infant-like" is from 1772.

meaning: deduce; conclude; N. inference
etymology: From Latin inferō, from Latin in- (“in, at, on; into”) + Latin ferō (“bear, carry; suffer”) (cognate to Old English beran, whence English bear), from Proto-Italic *ferō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰéreti (“to bear, carry”), from the root *bʰer-. Literally “carry forward”, equivalent to “bear in”, as in concluding from a premise. Doublet of inbear.

meaning: pertaining to hell; devilish; N. inferno: place of fiery heat or destruction
etymology: From Middle French infernal, from Medieval Latin infernalis, from Latin īnfernus, from īnferum (“netherworld, underworld, hell”), equivalent to inferno + -al.

meaning: unbeliever (with respect to a particular religion)
etymology: First attested 1460, from Middle French infidèle, from Latin īnfidēlis (“unfaithful”), from in- (“not”) + fidēlis (“faithful”). See fidelity.

meaning: pass into or through; penetrate or enter (an organization) sneakily; Ex. infiltrate the troops into enemy territory; CF. infiltrator
etymology: From Middle English infiltrate (adjective), from Medieval Latin infiltrātus, from infiltrō.

meaning: enter into; pierce; permeate; see through; grasp the inner significance of; understand
etymology: From Latin penētrātus, perfect passive participle of penētrō (“to put, set, or place within, enter, pierce, penetrate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from penes (“within, with”) by analogy to intrō (“to go in, enter”). Compare French pénétrer.

meaning: very small
etymology: From New Latin īnfīnītēsimus + -al. Displaced earlier coordinate term fluxion.

meaning: weakness
etymology: From infirm + -ity.

meaning: exaggerated; pompous; enlarged (with air or gas)
flowing into
etymology: From Latin īnflūxus (“inflow; influence”), from īnfluō (“flow or run into”).

meaning: violation (of a rule or regulation); breach
etymology: From Middle French infraction, from Latin infractio, from infractum, past participle of infringere, from in (“in”) + frangere (“to break”).

meaning: violate (a law); encroach (the right of another person)
etymology: Borrowed from Latin īnfringō, īnfringere (“to break off, break, bruise, weaken, destroy”), from in (“in”) + frangere (“to break”).

meaning: marked by inventive skill; clever; resourceful; N. ingenuity
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French ingénieux, from Old French engenious, from Latin ingeniōsus (“endowed with good natural capacity, gifted with genius”), from ingenium (“innate or natural quality, natural capacity, genius”), from in- (“in”) + gignere (“to produce”), Old Latin genere. See also engine.

meaning: clever and imaginative (in dealing with difficult situations); N. resource, resourcefulness
etymology: From resource + -ful.

meaning: naive and trusting; young; unsophisticated; candid
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin ingenuus (“of noble character, frank”). Doublet of ingenu.

meaning: ing\'enue; young innocent girl
etymology: Borrowed from French ingénue, the feminine form of ingénu (“guileless”), originally from the Latin ingenuus (“ingenuous”).

meaning: deeply established; firmly rooted; Ex. ingrained dirt/prejudice
etymology: From ingrain + -ed.

meaning: ungrateful person (not expressing thanks)
etymology: First attested in 1393, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English ingrat, from Latin ingrātus (“disagreeable”), from in- (“not”) + grātus (“pleasing”). Cognate with French ingrat.

meaning: become popular with; bring (oneself) in favor of another; Ex. ingratiate himself with the boss
etymology: First attested in 1622. From Italian ingraziare or Medieval Latin *ingratiatus, from Latin in grātiam (“for the favor of”).

meaning: firmly established by nature or habit; intrinsic
etymology: From Latin inhaerentem, accusative singular of inhaerēns, present active participle of inhaereō (“to be closely connected with; to adhere to”).

meaning: restrain; prohibit; retard or prevent; N. inhibition
etymology: From Latin inhibitus, perfect passive participle of inhibeō (“to hold in, check, restrain”), from in (“in, at, on”), + habeō (“to have, hold, keep”).

meaning: (of a person) unable to express what one really feels
having no inhibitions; free in behavior and feelings
etymology: From un- + inhibited.

meaning: (of someone) unfriendly; hostile; (of something) harmful; detrimental; CF. enemy
etymology: From Late Latin inimīcālis (“hostile”), from inimīcus (“enemy”) (from in- (“not”) + amīcus (“friend”)) + -ālis.

meaning: matchless; not able to be imitated
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French inimitable, from Latin inimitabilis, corresponding to in- + imitable.

meaning: wicked; immoral; unrighteous; N. iniquity; Ex. den of iniquity
etymology: From iniquity + -ous (suffix forming adjectives indicating the presence of a quality in any degree (typically an abundance)).

meaning: begin; originate; receive into a group; introduce to a new field or activity; Ex. initiate someone into the mysteries of a secret religion; N: one who has been initiated
etymology: Borrowed from Latin initiātus, perfect passive participle of initiō (“to begin, originate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from initium (“a beginning”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix), from initus (“an entrance, coming in, approach”) + -ium, from ineō + -tus, from in- + eō (“to go”). Cognate with French initier.

meaning: harmful; causing injury
etymology: From Middle English injurious, from Anglo-Norman enjurius, from Latin iniūriōsus; analysable as injury + -ous.

meaning: hint; slight indication
etymology: Sense 3 (“desire, inclination”) may have been influenced by incline (“to tend to believe or do something”) or French enclin (“inclined, prone”).

meaning: inborn
etymology: The adjective is first attested in the 1420s, the verb in 1602; from Middle English innat(e) (“innate, inborn”), borrowed from Latin innātus (“inborn, innate”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), perfect active participle of innāscor (“to be born in, grow up in”), from in- (“in, at on”) + nāscor (“to be born”); see natal, native. The verb is derived from the adjective, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

meaning: harmless
etymology: From Latin innocuus (“harmless”) (therefore, no gemination in + nocuous).

meaning: change; something newly introduced; introduction of something new; V. innovate: begin or introduce (something new); be creative; ADJ. innovative
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French innovation, from Old French innovacion, from Late Latin innovatio, innovationem, from Latin innovo, innovatus. Morphologically innovate + -ion.

meaning: indirect or subtle (derogatory) hint; insinuation; Ex. sexual innuendo
etymology: From the Latin innuendō (“by nodding”), ablative singular form of innuendum (“a nodding”), gerund of innuō (“to give a nod”).

meaning: untimely; inappropriate or ill-timed; poorly chosen
etymology: From Latin inopportūnus. By surface analysis, in- + opportune.

meaning: beyond reasonable limits; unrestrained; excessive; Ex. inordinate demands
etymology: From Middle English inordinat, from Latin inōrdinātus (“not arranged, disordered, irregular”), from in- + ordinatus, past participle of ōrdināre (“to arrange, order”).

meaning: questioner (especially harsh); investigator; person making an inquisition
etymology: From Old French inquisiteur, from Latin inquīsītor.

meaning: eager for knowledge; unduly curious
etymology: Late 14th century, from Old French inquisitif, from Late Latin inquisitivus, from Latin inquisitus, past participle of inquirere. See also inquire.

meaning: unwholesome; not healthful; Ex. insalubrious place
etymology: From in- + salubrious.

meaning: conducive to good health; Ex. healthful mountain air
etymology: From Middle English helthful, helþful, helþeful, equivalent to health + -ful.

meaning: possessing good health; healthful
etymology: From health + -y.

meaning: conducive to mental or physical health; healthful
etymology: From earlier holesome, from Middle English holsom, holsum, helsum, halsum, from Old English *hālsum, *hǣlsum, from Proto-West Germanic *hailasam, from Proto-Germanic *hailasamaz, equivalent to whole + -some or hale (“healthy”) + -some. Cognate with Saterland Frisian heelsoam, Dutch heilzaam, German Low German heelsaam, German heilsam, Icelandic heilsamur, Norwegian Nynorsk helsesam, Swedish hälsosam (“wholesome”).

meaning: not easily satisfied; unquenchable; Ex. insatiable appetite
etymology: Inherited from Middle English insaciable, from Middle French insatiable, from Old French insaciable, from Late Latin insatiabilis. By surface analysis, in- + satiable.

meaning: difficult to understand; impenetrable; not readily understood; mysterious
etymology: Borrowed into late Middle English from Late Latin īnscrūtābilis, from in- (“not”) + scrūtō (“to examine”), corresponding to in- + scrutable

meaning: without feeling; lacking sense; foolish
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin īnsēnsātus. By surface analysis, in- + sensate.

meaning: unconscious; unresponsive; insensitive; unaware; imperceptible; Ex. insensible of his danger/to pain; Ex. insensible change; CF. not the opposite of sensible
etymology: From Middle English insensible, from Old French insensible, from Late Latin īnsēnsibilis.

meaning: treacherous; stealthy; sly; working or spreading harmfully in a stealthy manner; Ex. insidious spreading of dry rot
etymology: From Middle French insidieux, from Latin īnsidiōsus (“cunning, artful, deceitful”), from īnsidiae (“a lying in wait, an ambush, artifice, stratagem”) + -ōsus, from īnsideō (“to sit in or on”), from in (“in, on”) + sedeō (“to sit”).

meaning: discerning; perceptive
etymology: A recent formation from insight + -ful.

meaning: hint; imply; suggest indirectly; creep in; introduce or insert (oneself) by artful means; Ex. insinuate himself into the boss'favor; CF. ingratiate
etymology: First attested in 1529; Borrowed from Latin īnsinuātus, perfect passive participle of īnsinuō (“to push in, creep in, steal in”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from in- (“in”) + sinus (“a winding, bend, bay, fold, bosom”) -ō (verb-forming suffix). Regular participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.

meaning: move with body close to the ground; move stealthily or slowly; N.
etymology: English creep

meaning: exhibiting art or skill; deceitful; cunning; CF. artifice
etymology: From art (“skill that is attained by study, practice, or observation”) + -ful (suffix forming adjectives from nouns, with the sense of being full of, tending to, or thoroughly possessing the quality expressed by the noun).

meaning: lacking in flavor; lacking interest; dull; Ex. insipid food/character
etymology: From French insipide, from Latin īnsipidus (“tasteless”), from in- (“not”) + sapidus (“savory”). In some senses, perhaps influenced by insipient (“unwise, foolish, stupid”).

meaning: impudent disrespect; haughtiness; ADJ. insolent; CF. haughty + rude
etymology: From Middle French insolence, from Latin īnsolentia.

meaning: bankrupt; lacking money to pay; N. insolvency
etymology: From in- + solvent.

meaning: wakefulness; inability to sleep
etymology: Borrowed from Latin īnsomnia, from Latin in- (“without”) + somnus (“sleep”, noun) + -ia, equivalent to in- + somn- + -ia.

meaning: without concern or care; unconcerned; indifferent
etymology: From French insouciant, from in- (“not”, prefix) + souciant (“worrying”), 1828.

meaning: start; urge; provoke; incite; Ex. instigate a search/quarrel
etymology: Borrowed from Latin īnstīgātus, perfect passive participle of īnstīgō (“to instigate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

meaning: disobedience; rebelliousness; ADJ. insubordinate
etymology: From in- + subordination, on the model of French insubordination.

meaning: lacking substance; insignificant; frail; immaterial
etymology: Probably from Middle French insubstantiel, from Latin insubstantiālis, from in- + substantiālis. By surface analysis, in- + substantial.

meaning: narrow-mindedness; isolation; ADJ. insular: of an island; isolated; narrow-minded; CF. peninsula
etymology: From insular + -ity.

meaning: insurmountable; unbeatable; Ex. insuperable difficulties
etymology: From Latin insuperabilis.

meaning: chances; probability; disagreement; Ex. The odds are that it will rain. Ex. at odds with
etymology: From odd (“uneven, strange”).

meaning: rebellious; N.
etymology: From Latin īnsurgentem, accusative singular of īnsurgēns, present active participle of īnsurgō (“to rise up against, revolt”), from in (“against”) + surgō (“to rise”), itself from sub (“up from below”) + regō (“to guide, direct, rule, govern, administer”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ- (“to move in a straight line, to rule, guide, lead straight, put right”).

meaning: overwhelming; unbeatable; insuperable
etymology: From in- + surmountable.

meaning: rebellion; uprising
etymology: From Late Middle English insurreccion (“uprising against a government, rebellion, revolt; civil disorder, riot; illegal armed assault”) [and other forms], from Middle French insurrection, Old French insurreccïon (modern French insurrection), and from their etymon Latin īnsurrēctiōnem (rare), the accusative singular of īnsurrēctiō (“rising up, insurrection, rebellion”), from īnsurgō (“to rise up”), from in- (prefix meaning ‘in, inside, within’) + surgō (“to arise, get up; to rise”) (from sub- (prefix meaning ‘(from) beneath, under’) + regō (“to direct, govern, rule; to guide, steer; to manage, oversee”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ- (“to right oneself, straighten; just; right”))).

meaning: not able to be perceived by touch; vague
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French intangible, from Medieval Latin intangibilis, from Late Latin tangibilis, from Latin tango.

meaning: complete; necessary for completeness; Ex. integral part
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French integral, from Medieval Latin integrālis, from Latin integer (“entire”); see integer.

meaning: make whole; combine; make into one unit
etymology: First attested in the 1450's as an adjective, first attested in 1638 as a verb; from Middle English integrat(e) (“intact, whole”), borrowed from Latin integrātus, perfect passive participle of integrō (“to make whole, renew, repair, begin again”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from integer (“whole, fresh”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). See integer and integral.

meaning: honesty; uprightness; wholeness; state of being whole and undivided; completeness
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French intégrité, from Latin integritās (“soundness, integrity”), from integer. Doublet of entirety.

meaning: (sitting or standing) straight up; honest; moral
etymology: From Middle English upright, uppryght, upriht, from Old English upriht (“upright; erect”), from Proto-Germanic *upprehtaz, equivalent to up- + right. Cognate with Saterland Frisian apgjucht (“upright”), West Frisian oprjocht (“upright”), Dutch oprecht (“upright”), German Low German uprecht (“upright”), German aufrecht (“upright”), Swedish upprätt (“upright”), Icelandic uppréttur (“upright”).

meaning: higher mental powers; person of great intellectual ability
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin intellēctus (“understanding, intellect”), from Latin intellegō (“understand; reason”), from inter (“between, among”) + legō (“read”), with connotation of bind.

meaning: intellectuals; members of the educated elite (often used derogatorily)
etymology: From Russian интеллиге́нция (intelligéncija) or Polish inteligencja, from Latin intellegentia (“intelligence”). Doublet of intelligence.

meaning: bury; N. interment
etymology: From Middle English enteren, borrowed from Old French enterrer, enterer, from Vulgar Latin *interrāre (“to put in earth”).

meaning: place for burying the dead
etymology: From Middle English cimiterie, from Old French cimitiere, from Medieval Latin cimitērium, from Late Latin coemētērium, from Ancient Greek κοιμητήριον (koimētḗrion), from κοιμάω (koimáō, “I put to sleep”); compare cœmeterium. Displaced Middle English charnel (“mass grave, cemetery”) and Old English līctūn (“cemetery”).

meaning: prohibit; forbid; N.
etymology: From Middle English entrediten, from Old French entredire (“forbid”), from Latin interdīcō (“prohibit, forbid”), from inter- (“between”) + dīcō (“say”), from Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ-.

meaning: meantime; Ex. in the interim; ADJ. taking place during an interim; Ex. interim paper
etymology: Borrowed from Latin interim (“meanwhile”).

meaning: intruder; one who interferes
etymology: From inter- + loper (“runner, rover”), as in landloper (“vagrant”) (from lope (“to leap, to jump”) (originally dialectal)). Originally spelt enterloper and used in specific sense, “unauthorized trader trespassing on privileges of chartered companies”, later general sense of “self-interested intruder” from 1630s.

meaning: endless
etymology: From Middle English interminable, from Middle French interminable and its etymon Late Latin interminābilis. By surface analysis, in- + terminable.

meaning: periodic; on and off; stopping and starting at intervals
etymology: From Middle French intermittent, from Latin intermittens (“sending between”), from prefix inter- (“among, on”) + mittens (“sending”), from mittere (“to send”).

meaning: mutually destructive
etymology: Borrowed from Latin internecīnus (“deadly”), from internecium (“a massacre, bloodbath; an eradication”) + -īnus. In Latin, the sememe 'between' was here not expressed by the prefix, it instead either had a somewhat emphatic meaning or meant "down, under", comparable to its use in other Latin terms related to death: see interficiō and intereō. The English current sense is thus a reanalysis of the Latin through English inter-.

meaning: insert between
etymology: From Latin interpolātus, perfect passive participle of interpolō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare French interpoler.

meaning: period between two successive reigns or governments
etymology: The plural form interregna is a learned borrowing from Latin interrēgna.

meaning: question closely; cross-examine; cross-question
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin interrogātus, the perfect passive participle of Latin interrogō (“to inquire, interrogate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

meaning: come between; interfere; Ex. intervened to prevent a fight; N. intervention
etymology: Back-formation from intervention, and/or from Latin interveniō (“come between”, verb).

meaning: hint; suggest; imply; ADJ: marked by close relationship; familiar; private; personal; Ex. intimate knowledge/thoughts in the diary; N: close friend or confidant; CF. intimacy
etymology: Borrowed from Latin intimātus, the perfect passive participle of intimō (“to put or bring into, to impress, to make familiar”) (see -ate (adjective forming suffix)), from intimus (“inmost, innermost, most intimate”), superlative of intus (“within”), from in (“in”); see interior.

meaning: frighten; N. intimidation
etymology: From Medieval Latin intimidātus, perfect passive participle of Latin intimidō (“to intimidate, terrify”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- (“in”) + timidus (“afraid, timid”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix); see timid.

meaning: unruly; difficult to manage; Ex. intractable problem/child
etymology: From in- + tractable.

meaning: refusal of any compromise; stubbornness; ADJ. intransigent: uncompromising
etymology: From French intransigeance, noun form of intransigeant, borrowed from Spanish intransigente at the end of the nineteenth century. Morphologically, from in- + transiger + -ant, literally "uncompromising".

meaning: fearless
etymology: From French intrépide, from Latin intrepidus, from in- (“not”) + trepidus (“anxious, nervous”).

meaning: essential; inherent; built-in
etymology: From Middle French intrinsèque, from Latin intrīnsecus (“on the inside, inwardly”), from *intrim, an assumed adverbial form of inter (“within”) + secus (“by, on the side”).

meaning: looking within oneself; N. introspection: self-examination
etymology: From Latin intro "inward, within" (see intro-) + Latin specere "look at".

meaning: one who is introspective or inclined to think more about oneself; ADJ. introverted
etymology: From New Latin intrōvertere, from intro- (“within”) and vertere (“to turn”). Popularized as a psychological term by the German works of Carl Jung. By surface analysis, intro- + -vert.

meaning: put or force in without being asked; trespass; enter as an uninvited person; Ex. intrude one'own opinion into the report; CF. thrust in
etymology: From Latin intrudere, from in- + trudere (“to thrust”).

meaning: immediate insight; power of knowing without reasoning; ADJ. intuitive; V. intuit: know by intuition
etymology: From Middle French intuition, from Medieval Latin intuitiō (“a looking at, immediate cognition”), from Latin intueor (“to look at, consider”), from in- (“in, on”) + tueor (“to look, watch, guard, see, observe”). Equivalent to intuit + -ion.

meaning: flood; overflow; submerge; cover completely; Ex. inundated with work
etymology: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin inundātus, the perfect passive participle of inundō (“to flood, overflow”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- + undō (“to overflow, wave”), from unda (“wave”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).

meaning: (of water) cover completely; defeat completely by much greater force; Ex. overwhelmed by grief
etymology: Inherited from Middle English overwhelmen, equivalent to over- + whelm.

meaning: place under water; dip; go under water; cover completely (as with water); Ex. submerged in work
etymology: Borrowed from Latin submergere, from sub (“under”) + mergere (“to plunge”). By surface analysis, sub- + merge.

meaning: surround and swallow up
etymology: From en- + gulf.

meaning: accustomed; hardened; Ex. inured to the Alaskan cold; V. inure: make used to something undesirable; harden; CF. unfeeling
weaken; destroy; make invalid; nullify
etymology: First attested in 1649; borrowed from Middle French invalider, from invalide + -er. By surface analysis, in- + validate or invalid + -ate.

meaning: one incapacitated (disabled) by a chronic illness; ADJ: incapacitated by illness; not valid; null; V: allow to leave (a military force) because of ill-health
etymology: From in- + valid.

meaning: abuse
etymology: From Middle French invective, from Medieval Latin invectiva (“abusive speech”), from Latin invectīvus, from invectus, perfect passive participle of invehō (“bring in”), from in- + vehō (“carry”). See vehicle, and compare with inveigh.

meaning: denounce; utter censure or invective; Ex. inveigh against the evils of drink
etymology: Borrowed from Latin invehō (“bring in, carry in”), from in- + vehō (“carry”). Compare vehicle, invective.

meaning: deceive; lead astray by deception; wheedle (cajole); Ex. inveigle her into joining the club; CF. interest dishonestly
etymology: For the pronunciation with /iː/, compare the development of people; that with /eɪ/ is presumably a spelling pronunciation.

meaning: opposite
etymology: Recorded since 1440, from Latin inversus, the past participle of invertere (“to invert”), itself from in- (“against, in”) + vertere (“to turn”).

meaning: turn upside down or inside out; reverse the position or condition of
etymology: From Middle French invertir.

meaning: deep-rooted; habitual; CF. grow old
etymology: The adjective is first attested in 1528, the verb in 1574; borrowed from Latin inveterātus (“of long standing, chronic”), perfect passive participle of inveterō and participial adjective (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from in- (“in, into”) + veterō (“to age”), from vetus, veteris (“old”). Cognate with Italian inveterato, French invétéré. By surface analysis, in- (“not, opposite”) + veterate.

meaning: designed to create ill will or envy; tending to rouse ill will or envy; Ex. invidious comparison
etymology: Borrowed from Latin invidiōsus, from invidia (“envy, ill will”), from in- (“upon”) + videō (“to see”); the meaning developed from “look back at” to “look askance at” to “envy.” Doublet of envious, from Old French.

meaning: unconquerable
etymology: From Middle French invincible, from Latin invincibilis (“unconquerable”), from in- (“not”) + vincibilis (“conquerable”), from vincere (“to conquer”).

meaning: secure from corruption, attack, or violation (or profanation); unassailable; Ex. inviolable oath/rights; N. inviolability
etymology: From Middle French inviolable, from Latin inviolābilis (“untouchable”), from violō (“violate”). Equivalent to in- + violable. Piecewise doublet of unviolable.

meaning: prayer for help (used in invoking); calling upon as a reference or support; act of invoking
etymology: From Middle English invocacioun, from Old French invocacion, from Latin invocatio, invocationem. Equivalent to invoke + -ation.

meaning: call and bring into use (a right or law); call on/upon (a higher power or god) for help; ask for; beg for; conjure (a spirit); Ex. invoke the veto power; Ex. invoke one'advisor/God
etymology: From Middle English *invoken, envoken, borrowed from Old French envoquer, from Latin invocāre (“to call upon”), itself from in- + vocare (“to call”). Doublet of invocate.

meaning: incapable of injury; impossible to damage or injure
etymology: From Middle French invulnérable, from Latin invulnerābilis, from vulnerābilis, from vulnerō (“to wound”), from vulnus (“wound”), equivalent to in- + vulnerable.

meaning: very small quantity
etymology: Sense “jot, small quantity” in reference to a phrase in the New Testament: ”one iote or one title, shall in no wise passe from the law”, iota being the smallest letter of the Greek alphabet.

meaning: irritable; easily angered
etymology: From Middle English, from Old French irascible, from Late Latin īrāscibilis, from Latin īrāscī (“to be angry, enraged”) + -bilis. See also -ible.

meaning: angry; CF. ire: anger; wrath
etymology: From Latin īrātus (“angered, angry”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from īrāscor (“to be angry”), from īra (“anger, wrath”).

meaning: exhibiting rainbowlike colors; Ex. iridescent oil slick; N. iridescence
etymology: Coined around 1800, from Latin iris, iridis (“rainbow”) + -escent.

meaning: annoying; tedious; V. irk: annoy
etymology: From Middle English irkesome, irksum, equivalent to irk + -some, or perhaps continuing (in altered form) from Old English weorcsum (“painful, hurtful”).

meaning: expressing irony; occurring in an unexpected and contrary manner
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin īrōnicus, from Ancient Greek εἰρωνικός (eirōnikós). Compare Middle French, ironique, equivalent to irony + -ic.

meaning: hidden sarcasm or satire; use of words that seem to mean the opposite of what they actually mean; use of words to convey the opposite of their literal meaning
etymology: First attested in 1502. From Middle French ironie, from Old French, from Latin īrōnīa, from Ancient Greek εἰρωνεία (eirōneía, “irony, pretext”), from εἴρων (eírōn, “one who feigns ignorance”).

meaning: impossible to reconcile; incompatible; not able to be resolved
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French irréconciliable, from Late Latin irreconciliābilis, from in- (“not”) + reconciliō (“to reconcile”) + -ābilis (“-able”). By surface analysis, ir- + reconcilable.

meaning: indisputable; incontrovertible; undeniable
etymology: From Late Latin irrefūtābilis, from ir- (“not”) + refūtābilis (“refutable”), from refūtō (“to refute”) + -bilis (“-able”), equivalent to ir- + refutable.

meaning: not applicable; unrelated
etymology: From ir- + relevant.

meaning: incurable; uncorrectable; impossible to remedy
etymology: Ultimately from Latin irremediābilis. By surface analysis, ir- + remediable.

meaning: not able to be corrected or repaired; impossible to repair
etymology: From Middle French irréparable, from Old French, from Latin irreparabilis, equivalent to ir- + reparable.

meaning: unable to be restrained or held back; impossible to hold back
etymology: From ir- + repressible.

meaning: beyond reproach; blameless; impeccable; Ex. irreproachable conduct
etymology: First attested in 1630. Borrowed from French irréprochable, from Middle French inreprochable. See also ir- + reproachable.

meaning: uncertain how to act; weak; lacking in resolution; indecisive; N. irresolution
etymology: First attested in 1580. Borrowed from French irrésolu or composed from ir- + resolute.

meaning: marked by indecision; inconclusive; Ex. indecisive battle
etymology: From in- + decisive.

meaning: irresolution; inability to make up one'mind
etymology: From French indécision.

meaning: impossible to recover or regain; CF. retrieve
etymology: From ir- + retrievable.

meaning: lack of proper respect or reverence; ADJ. irreverent
etymology: From Middle English irreverence, from Latin irreverentia, from irreverēns (“irreverent”) + -ia (suffix forming abstract nouns). By surface analysis, ir- + reverence.

meaning: unalterable; irreversible; impossible to revoke
etymology: From Middle French irrévocable, from Latin irrevocabilis; equivalent to ir- + revoke + -able.

meaning: varying from of an element
etymology: From iso- (“equal”) + -tope (“place”), because the different isotopes of an element always occupy the same place in the periodic table. The term was coined by Scottish doctor Margaret Todd in 1909 and first used publicly on February 27, 1913 by English chemist Frederick Soddy.

meaning: narrow neck of land connecting two larger bodies of land
etymology: Borrowing from Latin isthmus (“a strip of land between two seas”), from Ancient Greek ῐ̓σθμός (ĭsthmós, “neck, narrow passage”), possibly from εἶμῐ (eîmĭ, “to go”). Cognate to Old Norse eið (“isthmus”).

meaning: traveling from place to place (to perform work); Ex. itinerant preacher
etymology: By surface analysis, Latin itiner- + -ant.

meaning: plan of a trip; record of a trip
etymology: From Middle English itinerarie, from Latin itinerārium (“an account of a journey, a road-book”), from iter (“a way, journey”). By surface analysis, Latin itiner- + -ary.

meaning: chatter rapidly or unintelligibly
etymology: From Middle English jaberen, javeren, chaveren (“to chatter, babble”), dissimilated forms of jablen, chavelen (“to jabber”), from Middle English chavel ("jaw"; > modern English jowl). Equivalent to jowl + -er (iterative suffix).

meaning: poke abruptly with something sharp; punch with short blows
etymology: Originally a Scottish (unclear if Scots or Scottish English) form of English job (“peck, poke, thrust”), from Middle English jobben.

meaning: tired or uninterested by surfeit; fatigued; surfeited; worn out; wearied; Ex. jaded appetite
etymology: From jade (“worn-out horse”), possibly from Old Norse jalda (“mare”). Jade as a term of abuse for a woman dates from 1560.

meaning: language used by special group; technical terminology; gibberish; nonsensical or incoherent talk
etymology: From Middle English jargoun, jargon, from Old French jargon, a variant of gargon, gargun (“chatter; talk; language”).

meaning: yellowed; prejudiced (envious, hostile, or resentful) from long and disappointing experience of human affairs; Ex. with a jaundiced eye
etymology: From jaundice + -ed.

meaning: medical condition in which the skin, the white part of the eyes, etc. turn yellow; V: affect with jaundice; affect with prejudice, envy, or hostility; bias
etymology: From Middle English jaundis, jaunis, from Middle French jaunisse, from jaune (“yellow”) + -isse (“-ness”). Jaune, from Old French jalne, from Latin galbinus (“yellowish”), from galbus (“yellow”).

meaning: trip; short journey
etymology: Origin uncertain. Perhaps a palatalised alteration of daunt (“to discourage”). Compare Scots jaunder (“to ramble, jaunt to taunt, jeer”), dialectal Swedish ganta (“to play the buffoon, romp, jest”); perhaps akin to English jump. Compare jaunce. Modern usage likely influenced by jaunty.

meaning: cheerful and pleased with life; lighthearted; animated; easy and carefree; dapper in appearance; Ex. jaunty person/hat
etymology: Formerly spelt janty, from French gentil. See gentle, and compare genty. Doublet of genteel, gentile, and gentle.

meaning: endanger; imperil; put at risk; N. jeopardy: danger
etymology: From jeopardy + -ize.

meaning: throw overboard (from a ship or plane)
etymology: From Anglo-Norman getteson, from Old French getaison, from geter, jeter (modern French: would be *jetaison like pendaison); possibly from a Vulgar Latin *iectātiō, from *iectātus < iectāre, from Latin iactō. Doublet of jetsam.

meaning: agree; be in harmony with; gibe
etymology: The noun is derived from the verb.

meaning: extremely aggressive and militant patriot; warlike chauvinist; N. jingoism: extreme nationalism
etymology: From jingo + -ist.

meaning: given to (having a tendency of) joking
etymology: From Latin iocōsus (“humorous”), from iocus (“jest, joke”).

meaning: said or done in jest or playfully; marked by joking
etymology: From Latin iocularis, from ioculus (“a little jest”), diminutive of iocus (“a jest”).

meaning: playful remark or act; V. act or speak playfully
etymology: From Middle English geste (“idle tale”), from Old French geste (“acts, exploits”), from Latin gesta (“acts, deeds”). Doublet of gest.

meaning: merry
etymology: From Old French jocond, from Latin iūcundus (“pleasant, agreeable”). Doublet of jucund.

meaning: gaiety; cheerfulness; ADJ. jolly: merry; gay
etymology: From Middle English jolyfte, from Old French joliveté (“gaiety, cheerfulness; amorous passion; life of pleasure”), from jolif. Equivalent to jolly + -ty.

meaning: shove; bump; push against (someone) rather roughly; Ex. jostled by the crowds
etymology: Originally justle (“to have sex with”), formed from Middle English jousten, from the Old French joster (“to joust”), from Latin iuxtā (“next to”), from iungō (“join, connect”), equivalent to joust + -le.

meaning: push forward; push roughly; Ex. pushing and shoving to get on the bus; N.
etymology: See also West Frisian skowe, Low German schuven, Dutch schuiven, German schieben, Danish skubbe, Norwegian Bokmål skyve, Norwegian Nynorsk skuva; also Lithuanian skùbti (“to hurry”), Polish skubać (“to pluck”), Albanian humb (“to lose”).

meaning: hit or knock against with force; N.
etymology: Apparently related to Middle English bumben, bummen (“to make a hollow noise”), Dutch bommen (“to hum, buzz”), German Low German bumsen (“to bump, push”), German bummen (“to hum, buzz”), Icelandic bumba (“drum”). More at bum, bumble. Compare also bomb.

meaning: good-natured; merry; cheerful
etymology: Sense 1 (“cheerful and good-humoured”) refers to the fact that individuals born under the astrological influence of the planet Jupiter were believed to have that disposition.

meaning: rejoicing; great joy
etymology: From Old French jubilacion, from Latin iūbilātiō (“a shouting for joy”). Cognate with Spanish jubilación (“retirement”).

meaning: sound on judgment; wise
etymology: From French judicieux, ultimately derived from Latin iudico. Related to judge, judicial.

meaning: irresistible crushing force; overwhelming advancing force that crushes everything in its path
etymology: Borrowed in the 17th century into British English in India, either through Hindustani جَگَنَّاتھ (jagannāth) / जगन्नाथ (jagannāth) or directly from Odia ଜଗନ୍ନାଥ (jagannātha), ultimately from Sanskrit ज॒ग॒न्ना॒थ (jagannāthá, “lord of universe”) (Jagannatha), a title for the Hindu deity Vishnu's avatar Krishna. The sense comes from witnessing the Rath Yatra (chariot parade) at Puri, Odisha, a huge annual procession which features a wagon of the idol of Jagannath; pulled with ropes by hundreds of devotees, the wagon develops considerable momentum and becomes unstoppable. The r was not originally pronounced: for non-rhotic dialects of British English, the spelling with -er- accurately suggests the Hindi-Urdu pronunciation of the second vowel (a schwa ə); compare e.g. gorm. The spelling of the ending was influenced by the suffix -naut (“traveller, voyager”). Doublet of Jagannath.

meaning: pitcher; container for holding liquids
etymology: From Middle English jugge, of uncertain origin. Possibly a variant of Middle English jubbe, jobbe, iubbe, geobbe, itself of unknown origin; or perhaps continuing (in altered form) Old English ċēac (“pitcher; jug”). Compare also jug (“a low woman, maidservant”), from Jug, familiar form of Joanna. Prison sense attested from at least 1825 in Britain.

meaning: crisis; point in time; joining point; joint; act of joining
