etymology: Inherited from Middle English juncture, from Latin iūnctūra. Doublet of jointure.

meaning: trip especially one taken for pleasure by an official at public expense
etymology: Meaning shifted to “feast or banquet” by 1520s, probably via the notion of a picnic basket. This in turn led to the sense of “pleasure trip” (1814), and then to specifically to “trip made ostensibly for business but which entails merrymaking or entertainment” by 1886 in American English.

meaning: group of persons joined in political intrigue; cabal; group of military officers ruling a country after seizing power (by force)
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish junta (literally "a thing gathered or joined"), feminine form of junto, from Latin iunctus, perfect passive participle of iungō (“join”). Attested from 1623.

meaning: science of law
etymology: Borrowed from Latin iūrisprūdentia (“expertise in the law”).

meaning: right and power to apply the law; authority
etymology: Borrowed from Latin iūrisdictiō.

meaning: of the law and its administration; CF. judicial: of courts of law; CF. judiciary
etymology: From juridic + -al or alternatively borrowed from Latin iuridicalis.

meaning: place side by side; CF. next
etymology: Borrowed from French juxtaposer, corresponding to juxta- + pose, derived from Latin iuxtā (“near, next to”) + pōnō (“place”).

meaning: tube in which patterns made by the reflection in mirrors of colored pieces of glass, etc. produce interesting symmetrical effects; series of changing events; Ex. kaleidoscope of European history; CF. beautiful
etymology: The verb is derived from the noun.

meaning: range of knowledge; Ex. beyond one'ken
etymology: From Middle English kennen (“to give birth, conceive, generate, beget; to develop (as a fetus), hatch out (of eggs); to sustain, nourish, nurture”), from Old English cennan (“to give birth, conceive, generate, beget”), from Proto-West Germanic *kannjan, from Proto-Germanic *kanjaną.

meaning: central or vital part; core; whole seed (as of corn)
etymology: From Middle English kernel, kirnel, kürnel, from Old English cyrnel, from Proto-West Germanic *kurnil, diminutive of Proto-Germanic *kurną (“seed, grain, corn”), equivalent to corn + -le. Cognate with Yiddish קערנדל (kerndl), Middle Dutch kernel, cornel, Middle High German kornel. Related also to Old Norse kjarni (“kernel”).

meaning: grouch; spoilsport; one who intentionally spoils the pleasure of others
etymology: From kill + joy, first attested in 1776.

meaning: bad-tempered complaint; person who keeps complaining; V: complain; grumble
etymology: From Middle English grouchen, variant of grucchen (“to complain, mumble, murmur”). See grutch.

meaning: one who spoils the pleasure of others
etymology: From the verbal expression spoil sport (“ruin the amusement”).

meaning: start a fire; ignite; inspire; arouse
etymology: From Middle English kyndelen, from Old Norse kynda (“to inflame”), from Proto-Germanic *kundijaną.

meaning: related; belonging to the same group; similar in nature or character; Ex. kindred languages; N: relative; kin; kinship
etymology: From Middle English kyndrede, from older kynrede (“kindred”), from Old English *cynrēd, *cynrǣden (“kindred, family, stock”), from cynn (“kind, kin, lineage”) + -rǣden (“condition, state”). Equivalent to kin + -red, see these. The -d- is epenthetic between a nasal and a liquid (as e.g. in spindle).

meaning: producing motion; of motion
etymology: From Ancient Greek κινητικός (kinētikós, “puts in motion”), from κινέω (kinéō, “I move, put in motion”).

meaning: fate; destiny; Ex. Kismet is the Arabic word for fate.
etymology: From Ottoman Turkish قسمت (kısmet, “fate, destiny”) (Turkish kısmet), from Arabic قِسْمَة (qisma, “division, lot, destiny”).

meaning: person who has a compulsive desire to steal
etymology: From Ancient Greek κλέπτω (kléptō, “I steal”) (from Proto-Hellenic *klépt͏̌ō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *klep-) + -maniac.

meaning: untrustworthy person; rogue; scoundrel; jack; N. knavery
etymology: From Middle English knave, knafe, from Old English cnafa (“child, boy, youth; servant”), from Proto-West Germanic *knabō. Cognate to Dutch knaap and German Knabe.

meaning: mix; work dough; mix and work into a uniform mass (with the hands); Ex. knead dough
etymology: From Middle English kneden, from Old English cnedan, from Proto-West Germanic *knedan, from Proto-Germanic *knudaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gnet- (“to press together”).

meaning: tolling of a bell especially to indicate a funeral, disaster, etc.; sound of the funeral bell; V.
etymology: From Middle English knyllen, from Old English cnyllan (“to strike; knock; clap”), from Proto-West Germanic *knuʀlijan, from Proto-Germanic *knuzlijaną (“to beat; push; mash”), from Proto-Indo-European *gen- (“to squeeze, pinch, kink, ball up”).

meaning: sound (a large bell) slowly at regular intervals; N: sound of a bell; fixed tax or charge
etymology: Alternate etymology derives Old English toll from Medieval Latin tolōneum, tolōnium, alteration (due to the Germanic forms above) of Latin telōneum, from Ancient Greek τελώνιον (telṓnion, “toll-house”), from τέλος (télos, “tax”).

meaning: regulation requiring all people to leave the streets at stated times; signal (as a bell) announcing the hour of a curfew
etymology: From Middle English curfu, from Old French cuevre-fu (French couvre-feu), from the imperative of covrir (“to cover”) + fu (“fire”). Compare kerchief.

meaning: contract into wrinkles; grow together; join together closely; make (a fabric or garment) by interwining yarn or thread; Ex. knit the brow; Ex. The bones should knit together in a few weeks.
etymology: Cognate with Low German knütten and Old Norse knýta (whence Danish knytte, Norwegian Nynorsk knyta). More at knot.

meaning: make (a piece of needlework) by looping thread with a hooked needle; N. CF. crotchet
etymology: From French crochet, from Middle French crochet, from Old French crochet, crokét (“curved instrument, hook”), diminutive of Old French croc (“hook”), from Old Frankish *krōk (“hook”) or from Old Norse krókr (“hook, bend, bight”), both from Proto-Germanic *krōkaz (“hook”), from Proto-Indo-European *gerg- (“tracery, basket, twist”). Cognate with Middle English crōc (“crook, hook”), Middle Dutch croec, crōc (“curl”). Doublet of crocket, croquet, and crotchet. More at crook, crooked.

meaning: little round hill; hillock
etymology: Related to Old Norse knollr (found only in names of places), Dutch knol (“tuber”), Swedish knöl (“tuber”), Danish knold (“hillock, clod, tuber”) and German Knolle (“bulb”).

meaning: intricate; difficult; tangled; CF. knot
etymology: * Swedish knotig, knutig (“knotty”)

meaning: honor; glory; acclaim or praise for exceptional achievement
etymology: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek κῦδος (kûdos, “praise, renown”).

meaning: group of attendants; retinue; CF. surround
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French entourage, from entourer (“to surround”).

meaning: likely to change; unstable; Ex. emotionally labile; N. lability
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French labile, borrowed from Latin lābilis (“slipping, transitent”).

meaning: demanding much work or care; tedious
etymology: From Old French laborios, from Latin laboriosus. By surface analysis, labor + -ious

meaning: maze
etymology: From Middle English laberynt, laberynthe, from Latin labyrinthus, from Ancient Greek λᾰβύρῐνθος (lăbúrĭnthos, “a maze”).

meaning: torn ragged wound; V. lacerate: tear (the skin as with broken glass); wound
etymology: From Latin lacerātiō, first attested in 1598. By surface analysis, lacerate + -tion. Compare lacerate.

meaning: tear or be torn quickly and violently; Ex. The sail ripped under the force of the wind; N.
etymology: See also West Frisian rippe, ripje, roppe, ropje (“to rip”), Dutch dialectal rippen, Low German ruppen, German Low German röpen, German rupfen, also Old English rīpan, rīepan (“to plunder”), West Frisian rippe (“to rip, tear”), German raufen (“to rip”); also Albanian rrabe ‘maquis’, possibly Latin rubus (“bramble”). More at reave, rob.

meaning: scrap of cloth; ADJ. ragged: old and torn; seeming unfinished and imperfect; Ex. ragged debut/performance
etymology: From Middle English ragge, from Old English ragg (suggested by derivative raggiġ (“shaggy; bristly; ragged”)), from Old Norse rǫgg (“tuft; shagginess”), from Proto-Germanic *rawwa-, probably related to *rūhaz. Cognate with Swedish ragg. Related to rug.

meaning: producing tears; tearful
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin lachrymōsus, lacrimōsus, from lachryma, lacrima (“tear”) + -osus (“-ful”), from Old Latin dacrima, from Proto-Indo-European *dakru-, cognate with English tear.

meaning: lacking interest or effort; lacking purpose or zest; lazy; halfhearted; languid
etymology: From the archaic expression lackadaisy + -ic + -al.

meaning: exhibiting little interest or enthusiasm
etymology: From half + hearted.

meaning: lacking luster (shine; gloss); dull
etymology: From lack + luster.

meaning: brief and to the point; using few words; terse
etymology: From Latin Lacōnicus (“Spartan”), from Ancient Greek Λακωνικός (Lakōnikós, “Laconian”). Laconia was the region inhabited and ruled by the Spartans, who were known for their brevity in speech.

meaning: slow; sluggish; N: one who lags; straggler
etymology: From lag + -ard.

meaning: move or develop more slowly; straggle; Ex. lag behind the rest; N.
etymology: Of unknown origin. Possibly of North Germanic origin.

meaning: stray or fall behind (a main group); spread out in a scattered group; Ex. straggling marathon racer; Ex. straggling branch
etymology: From Middle English straglen, of uncertain origin, possibly from (or cognate to) dialectal Norwegian stragla (“to walk laboriously”).

meaning: shallow body of water or lake near a sea; lake separated from a sea by sandbars or coral reefs
etymology: Borrowed from French lagune, from Italian laguna, from Latin lacūna. Related to Old English lagu via Proto-Indo-European. Doublet of lacuna and lacune.

meaning: laypersons; laymen; persons not connected with the clergy
etymology: From Anglo-Norman laite, from Latin laitas, from Ancient Greek λαός (laós, “people”).

meaning: man who is not a cleric; man who is nonprofessional
etymology: From Middle English layman, lay man, equivalent to lay (“non-clergy”) + man. Cognate with Old Frisian lēkmann, lēkmonn (“layman”), obsolete Dutch leekeman (“layman”), Old High German leihman (“layman”), Danish lægmand (“layman”), Swedish lekman (“layman”), Norwegian lekmann (“layman”), Icelandic leikmaður (“layman”).

meaning: grieve; express sorrow; N. lamentation
etymology: A back-formation from lamentation or else from Middle French lamenter and its etymon Latin lāmentor (“to wail, weep”), from lāmentum (“wailing, moaning, weeping”); with formative -mentum, from the root *la-, probably ultimately imitative. Also see latrare.

meaning: ridicule; N: written attack ridiculing or satirizing a person, group, or institution
etymology: Lampons ! lampons !

meaning: small surgical tool for making incisions
etymology: From Middle English launcet, from Old French lancete, a diminutive of lance. By surface analysis, lance + -et.

meaning: pierce with a lance; cut into; N: spearlike weapon
etymology: From Middle English launce, from Old French lance, from Latin lancea.

meaning: lacking energy or vitality; weary; sluggish; listless
etymology: * Spanish lánguido (“languid, weak”)

meaning: lose animation or strength
etymology: : Cognate with slack.

meaning: lack of physical or mental energy; lassitude; depression
etymology: The noun is derived from Middle English langore, langour (“disease, illness; misery, sadness; suffering; condition or event causing sadness, suffering, etc.; unwholesomeness; idleness, inertia; depression, self-disgust; expression of grief”) [and other forms], from Middle French languer, langueur, langour, and Anglo-Norman langor, langour, langur, Old French langueur, languour (“disease, illness; suffering; emotional fatigue, sadness; listlessness; stagnation”) (modern French langueur (“languor”)), and from their etymon Latin languor (“faintness, feebleness; languor; apathy”), from languēre, the present active infinitive of langueō (“to feel faint or weak; (figurative) to be idle, inactive; to be listless”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)leg-, *(s)leh₁g-. The English word is cognate with Catalan llangor, Italian languore (“faintness, weakness; languor”), langore (obsolete), Old Occitan langor (modern Occitan langor), Portuguese langor, languor (obsolete), Spanish langor.

meaning: long and thin; Ex. Lank, gaunt, Abraham Lincoln
etymology: From Middle English lank, from Old English hlanc, from Proto-West Germanic *hlank, from Proto-Germanic *hlankaz (“lank, thin”), from Proto-Indo-European *kleng- (“to bend, turn, wind, twist”); compare German lenken (“to turn”), Gelenk (“joint”), Old High German hlanca (“hip, side, flank”), and English link (of a chain).

meaning: take in food or drink with one'tongue; splash gently; Ex. waves lapping the shore; N: front area from the waist to the knees of a seated person
etymology: From Middle English lappe, from Old English læppa (“skirt or flap of a garment”), from Proto-West Germanic *lappō, from Proto-Germanic *lappô (“cloth; rag”), of uncertain origin, possibly Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“to hang loosely”). Cognate with Dutch lap (“cloth; rag”), German Lappen (“cloth; lobe; flap”), Icelandic leppur (“rag; patch”).

meaning: theft; Ex. petit larceny
etymology: Coined in Middle English (as larceni) between 1425 and 1475 from Anglo-Norman larcin (“theft”), from Latin latrocinium (“robbery”), from latro (“robber, mercenary”), from Ancient Greek λάτρον (látron, “pay, hire”). Doublet of latrociny.

meaning: pantry; place where food is kept
etymology: Inherited from Middle English larder, from Anglo-Norman larder and Old French lardier, from Latin lardārium. By surface analysis, lard + -er.

meaning: generous gift (given to people who do not have enough)
lustful
etymology: From Latin lascīviōsus, from lascīvia (“sportiveness, lustfulness”).

meaning: intense sexual desire; intense eagerness; V.
etymology: Akin to Old Saxon, Dutch lust, Old Frisian, Old High German, German Lust, Swedish lust, Danish lyst, Icelandic lyst, Old Norse losti, Gothic 𐌻𐌿𐍃𐍄𐌿𐍃 (lustus), and perhaps to Sanskrit लष् (laṣ), लषति (laṣati, “to desire”) and Albanian lushë (“bitch, savage dog, promiscuous woman”), or to English loose. Compare list (“to please”), listless.

meaning: languor; weariness; listlessness
etymology: Borrowed from French lassitude, from Latin lassitūdō (“faintness, weariness”), from lassus (“faint, weary”), perhaps for *ladtus, and thus akin to English late.

meaning: present but not yet noticeable or active; dormant; hidden; N. latency; CF. potential
etymology: From Middle English latent, latente, from Old French latent, from Latin latēns, present participle of lateō (“lie hidden”).

meaning: of or coming from the side
etymology: Borrowed from Latin laterālis (“belonging to the side”), from latus (“the side or flank”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix).

meaning: freedom from narrow limitations
etymology: Borrowed into Middle English from Old French latitude, from Latin lātitūdō (“breadth, width, latitude”), from lātus (“broad, wide”), from older stlātus. Possibly related with lateral, though this is uncertain.

meaning: praise; N. ADJ. laudable: praiseworthy; ADJ. laudatory: expressing praise
etymology: Inherited from Middle English lauden, from Old French lauder, from Latin laudō, laudāre, from laus (“praise, glory, fame, renown”), from echoic Proto-Indo-European root *leh₁wdʰ- (“song, sound”). Cognate with Old English lēoþ (“song, poem”), German Lied (“song”). Doublet of leed.

meaning: liberal; wasteful; generous or wasteful in giving or using; abundant; profuse; great; Ex. decorated lavishly; V. give in abundance
etymology: From Middle English laves, lavas, lavage (“extravagant, wasteful, prodigal”), from lavas (“excessive abundance”), from Old French lavasse, lavache (“torrent of rain”); possibly later conflated in some senses by Middle English laven (“to pour out”), equivalent to lave + -ish. Compare Scots lawage, lavisch, lavish (“unrestrained, excessively prodigal, extravagant”). Compare also English lavy (“lavish, liberal”), Dutch lafenis (“lavishness”).

meaning: careless; negligent; not paying enough attention; Ex. lax service
etymology: From Middle English lax, from Old English leax (“salmon”), from Proto-West Germanic *lahs (“salmon”), from Proto-Germanic *lahsaz (“salmon”), from Proto-Indo-European *laḱs- (“salmon, trout”). Cognate with Middle Dutch lacks, lachs, lasche (“salmon”), Middle Low German las (“salmon”), German Lachs (“salmon”), Norwegian laks (“salmon”), Danish laks (“salmon”), Swedish lax (“salmon”), Icelandic lax (“salmon”), Lithuanian lašišà (“salmon”), Latvian lasis, Russian лосо́сь (losósʹ, “salmon”), Albanian leshterik (“eel-grass”). Doublet of lox.

meaning: add leaven to; cause to rise or grow lighter; enliven; N: agent, such as yeast, that causes dough to rise (by fermentation); element that lightens or enlivens
etymology: From Middle English levayn, borrowed from Old French levain, from Vulgar Latin *levāmen, a noun based on Latin levō (“raise”).

meaning: make lively or spirited; animate
etymology: From life + en- -en (intensifying verbal circumfix). See liven.

meaning: gross lewdness; lustfulness; ADJ. lecherous; N. lecher: lecherous man
etymology: From Old French and Anglo-Norman lecherie. See lecher.

meaning: reading desk or stand for a public speaker
etymology: 15th century partial re-Latinization of early 14th century Middle English lettorne, lettron, from Old French leitrun, from Medieval Latin lectrinum, from Late Latin lectrum, from lectus (from whence also lecture), form of Latin legō (“to read”).

meaning: (of someone) suspicious; wary; cautious
etymology: First attested in 1718, “untrustful, suspicious”, either from leer (“sideward look”) + -y, lear (“learning, knowledge”) + -y. More at leer, lear.

meaning: room to move; margin; latitude; Ex. leeway for the deadline
etymology: From lee (“side away from the wind”) + way.

meaning: border; room; allowance beyond what is needed; Ex. margin of safety
etymology: From Middle English margyn, from Latin marginem (possibly via Old French margin), accusative of margō (“edge, brink, border, margin”). Doublet of marge and margo.

meaning: of a margin; barely within a limit; Ex. marginal effect/writing ability
etymology: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin marginālis, equivalent to margin + -al.

meaning: gift made by a will; something handed down from an ancestor
etymology: The boardgame sense was coined by game designer Rob Daviau in 2011 with the game Risk Legacy.

meaning: explanatory list of symbols on a map
etymology: From Middle English legende, from Old French legende, from Medieval Latin legenda (“a legend, story, especially the lives of the saints”), from Latin legenda (“things which ought to be read”), from lego (“to read”).

meaning: sleight (dexterity) of hand; CF. light of hand
etymology: From Middle English legerdemeyn, lechardemane, from Old French léger de main (literally “light of hand”), a phrase that meant “dexterous, skillful at fooling others (especially through sleights of hand)”, which was however treated as a noun when it was borrowed by late Middle English. The Modern French descendant léger de main of the Old French phrase is archaic but still sometimes found in older literature and simply means “skillful” without any connotation of sleight of hand.

meaning: mildness; permissiveness; ADJ. lenient: not severe in judgment or punishment
etymology: From lenience + -y, from Latin lēn(iō) (“to soften, soothe”), from lēnis (“soft”).

meaning: allowing much freedom; lenient; Ex. permissive society
etymology: From French permissif.

meaning: like a lion
etymology: From Late Middle English leonin, leonine (“characteristic of a lion, lionlike”), from Old French leonin, and from its etymon Latin leōnīnus (“of or pertaining to a lion”), from leō (“lion”) (from Ancient Greek λέων (léōn, “lion”); further etymology uncertain) + -īnus (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’).

meaning: deadly
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin lētālis (“deadly, mortal, fatal”), improperly written lēthālis, from lētum (“death”), improperly written as lēthum, from a supposed connection with Ancient Greek λήθη (lḗthē, “oblivion, forgetfulness”).

meaning: drowsy; dull; N. lethargy: state of sluggishness and inactivity
etymology: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ληθαργικός (lēthargikós), from λήθαργος (lḗthargos, “forgetful, lethargic”), from λήθη (lḗthē, “a forgetting, forgetfulness”) (from which Lethe (“river in Hades”)) + ἀργός (argós, “not working”). By surface analysis, lethargy + -ic.

meaning: earthen or stone embankment to prevent flooding; CF. raise
etymology: From French levée, from lever (“to raise, rise”).

meaning: rise and float in the air (especially by magical means); CF. light
etymology: First attested in 1673; borrowed from New Latin levitātus, perfect passive participle of levitō (“to levitate; to have one's motion directed upward, as opposed to the downward motion induced by gravity”) (first attested c. 1670), modeled on gravitō (“to gravitate”) (← Latin gravis (“heavy”)), from levis (“light”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

meaning: lack of seriousness or steadiness; frivolity; lightness of manner
etymology: Coined in 1564, from Latin levitās (“lightness, frivolity”), from levis (“lightness (in weight)”). Cognate to lever, and more distantly, light.

meaning: impose (a fine); collect (a payment); impose or collect (a tax); Ex. levy a tax on tobacco
etymology: lever (“to raise”), from Latin lēvāre (“to raise, lift”).

meaning: lustful
etymology: From Middle English lewed, lewd, leued (“unlearned, lay, lascivious”), from Old English lǣwede (“unlearned, ignorant, lay”), of uncertain origin. Formally similar to a derivative of the past participle of Old English lǣwan (“to reveal, betray”) in the sense of "exposed as being unlearned" or "easily betrayed, clueless", from Proto-West Germanic *lāwijan, from Proto-Germanic *lēwijaną (“to betray”), from *lēwą (“an opportunity, cause”), from Proto-Indo-European *lēw- (“to leave”). If so, then cognate with Old High German gilāen, firlāen (“to betray”), Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐌻𐌴𐍅𐌾𐌰𐌽 (galēwjan, “to give over, betray”), Gothic 𐌻𐌴𐍅 (lēw, “an opportunity, cause”). Or, according to the OED, probably from Vulgar Latin *laigo-, from Late Latin lāicus (“of the people”), from Ancient Greek λαϊκός (laïkós).

meaning: compiler of a dictionary; CF. lexicography: work of compiling a dictionary
etymology: From French lexicographe + -er, from Ancient Greek λεξικός (lexikós, “of words”) + γράφω (gráphō, “write”). By surface analysis, lexico- + -grapher.

meaning: dictionary
etymology: Attested at least since 1583 (in William Fulke's A Defense of the Sincere and True Translations of the Holy Scriptures into the English tongue) in the sense 'a dictionary of a classical language'.

meaning: drawback; handicap; debts; obligation; responsibility; condition of being liable; ADJ. liable: likely; responsible (for paying)
etymology: From liable + -ity.

meaning: contact that keeps parties in communication; communication between groups; one that maintains communication; go-between; secret love affair; V. liaise: keep a connection
etymology: Borrowed from French liaison (“binding”), from Latin ligātiō (stem ligātiōn-; whence the English doublet ligation), derived from ligō (“to bind”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵ- (“to bind”).

meaning: defamatory written statement; act of writing something that smears a person'character; V. ADJ. libelous
etymology: From Middle English libel, from Old French libelle, from Latin libellus (“petition”, literally “booklet”). Doublet of libelle.

meaning: debauched person; dissolute or licentious person; rou\'e; CF. free
etymology: From Latin libertinus (“a freedman, prop. adj., of or belonging to the condition of a freedman”), from libertus (“a freedman”), from liber (“free”); see liberal, liberate.

meaning: lecherous man
lustful
etymology: From Middle English libidinous, borrowed from Latin libīdinōsus.

meaning: psychic and emotional energy or urges behind human activity; sexual desire
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin libīdō (“lust, desire”). Used originally in psychoanalytic contexts.

meaning: text of an opera or oratorio; CF. book
etymology: From Italian libretto, diminutive of libro (“book”), from Latin liber (“book”).

meaning: amoral; lewd and lascivious; unrestrained
etymology: From Latin licentiōsus, from licentia (“license, freedom”).

meaning: official or legal permission; latitude of action or speech; excessive freedom that causes harm or damage; V.
etymology: From Middle English licence, licens, lisence, lissens, licance, from Old French licence, from Latin licentia (“license”), from licens, present participle of licere (“to be allowed, be allowable”); compare linquere, Ancient Greek λείπω (leípō, “leave”).

meaning: legal claim or right on a property
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French lien, from Latin ligāmen (“bond”), from ligō (“tie, bind”).

meaning: like wood
etymology: From Latin ligneus; compare Latin lignōsus; equivalent to lign- + -eous.

meaning: extremely small; CF. Lilliput in Gulliver'Travels
etymology: From the name of a fictional island called Lilliput in the novel Gulliver's Travels by Jonathan Swift.

meaning: flexible; supple; pliable; V.
etymology: Unknown; possibly related to limb or limp + -er, as seen in clever, slipper (“slippery”), waker (“alert”), etc.

meaning: region near heaven or hell where certain souls are kept; prison (slang); Ex. Purgatory and Limbo
etymology: The verb is derived from the noun.

meaning: dwelling place; home
etymology: From Middle English abod, abad, from Old English *ābād, related to ābīdan (“to abide”); see abide. Cognate with Scots abade, abaid (“abode”). For the change of nouns, compare abode, preterite of abide.

meaning: dwell; abide by: comply with; put up with; tolerate; Ex. abide by the rules; Ex. I can't abide rude people.
etymology: Cognate with Scots abide (“to abide, remain”), Middle High German erbīten (“to await, expect”), Gothic 𐌿𐍃𐌱𐌴𐌹𐌳𐌰𐌽 (usbeidan, “to expect, await, have patience”). The sense of pay for is due to influence from aby.

meaning: draw; outline; describe; CF. line ?
etymology: From Middle English limnen, limyne, lymm, lymn, lymne (“to illuminate (a manuscript)”), a variant of luminen (“to illuminate (a manuscript)”), short form of enluminen (“to shed light on, illuminate; to enlighten; to make bright or clear; to give colour to; to illuminate (a manuscript); to depict, describe; to adorn or embellish with figures of speech or poetry; to make famous, glorious, or illustrious”), from Old French enluminer (“to brighten, light up; to give colour to; to illuminate (a manuscript)”), from Latin illūminō (“to brighten, light up; to adorn; to make conspicuous”), from il- (a variant of in- (prefix meaning ‘in, inside’)) + lūminō (“to brighten, illuminate; to reveal”) (from lūmen (“light; (poetic) brightness”) (from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“bright; to shine; to see”)) + -ō (suffix forming regular first-conjugation verbs)).

meaning: crystal clear
etymology: From French limpide, from Latin limpidus.

meaning: descent; ancestry
etymology: From Middle English linage, from Old French linage, from ligne, from Latin linea (“line”); equivalent to line + -age.

meaning: features especially of the face; distinctive shape or contour of the face; CF. line
distinctive part of the faces (as the eyes or mouth); features: overall appearance of the face; prominent or distinctive quality; prominent article; film; V: make prominent
etymology: From Middle English feture, from Anglo-Norman feture, from Old French faiture, from Latin factūra, from Latin factus, from Latin faciō (“do, make”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to do, put, place, set”). Doublet of facture.

meaning: loiter or dawdle; be slow in leaving; delay going; continue or persist; be slow to disappear; Ex. The smell lingered for days.
etymology: From Middle English lengeren, frequentative of lengen (“to stay, dwell, tarry”), from Old English lenġan (“to lengthen, delay, extend”), from Proto-West Germanic *langijan, from Proto-Germanic *langijaną (compare West Frisian lingje (“to linger”), Dutch lengen, German längen, Icelandic lengja (“to lengthen”)), related to the root of English long. Equivalent to linge or long + -er (frequentative verb suffix).

meaning: continue in existence; last; continue in a course of action in spite of opposition; Ex. persist in/with something; ADJ. persistent
etymology: From Middle French persister (Modern French persister), from Latin persistere, from per- + sistere (“to stand”).

meaning: pertaining to language
etymology: Borrowed from German linguistisch, equivalent to linguist + -ic. Compare linguistics. Ultimately from Latin lingua (“tongue, language”). Attested in English since 1825.

meaning: treat (a person) as a celebrity
etymology: From lion + -ize.

meaning: settle accounts; pay off (a debt); clear up; eliminate; kill or abolish
etymology: Verb sense 1.2.3 (“to kill; to abolish or eliminate”) is a semantic loan from Russian ликвиди́ровать (likvidírovatʹ); while verb sense 1.2.4 and verb sense 2 (business-related senses) were influenced by French liquider and Italian liquidare, all ultimately from Latin liquidus (see above).

meaning: tilt (as of a ship); lean over (to one side)
etymology: * Finnish lista (“(informal) list; batten”).

meaning: lacking in spirit or energy; languid
etymology: From Middle English lystles, equivalent to list (“desire”) + -less. Compare German lustlos and Dutch lusteloos (“lethargic, listless”). Doublet of lustless.

meaning: supplicatory prayer; prayer in which the priest calls out and the people replies in the same words
etymology: From Middle English, from Old French letanie, from Latin litania, from Ancient Greek λιτανεία (litaneía, “prayer”), from λιτή (litḗ, “prayer, entreaty”).

meaning: flexible; supple; CF. limber
etymology: Akin to Saterland Frisian lied (“thin, skinny, gaunt”), Danish, Dutch, and archaic German lind (“mild”). Some sources also list Latin lenis (“soft”) and/or Latin lentus (“supple”) as possible cognates.

meaning: flexible; pliant; slender; CF. willow
etymology: From willow + -y.

meaning: lawsuit; N. litigant: one party in a lawsuit; V. litigate
etymology: Borrowed from Latin lītigātiō, equivalent to litigate + -ion.

meaning: understatement for emphasis; Ex. ``not bad (=pretty good)''
etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin lītotēs, from Ancient Greek λιτότης (litótēs, literally “plainness”), from λιτός (litós, “simple”).

meaning: state with less truth than seems warranted by the facts; Ex. He understated the seriousness of the crime; N. understatement; OP. overstate
etymology: From under- + state.

meaning: lead-colored; black and blue (as from a bruise); ashen; enraged; extremely angry
etymology: From Middle English livid, livide, from Old French livide, from Latin līvidus (“bluish, livid; envious”), from līveō (“be of a bluish color or livid; envy”), from Proto-Italic *sliwēō, from Proto-Indo-European *sliwo-, suffixed form of *(s)leh₃y- (“bluish”). See also Old English slā (“sloe”), Welsh lliw (“splendor, color”), Old Irish li, Lithuanian slyvas (“plum”), and Russian and Old Church Slavonic слива (sliva, “plum”).

meaning: reluctant; unwilling; disinclined; Ex. Romeo and Juliet were both loath for him to go.
etymology: The word is cognate with Danish led (“disgusting, loathsome; nasty”), Dutch leed (“sad; (Belgium) angry”), French laid (“ugly; morally corrupt”), Catalan lleig (“ugly”), Icelandic leiður (“annoyed, vexed; sad; (archaic or poetic) annoying, wearisome”), Italian laido (“filthy, foul; obscene”), Old Frisian leed, Old High German leid (Middle High German leit, modern German leid (“uncomfortable”), Leid (“grief, sorrow, woe; affliction, suffering; harm, injury; wrong”)), Old Saxon lêð, lēth (“evil person or thing”), Swedish led (“bored; tired; (archaic) disgusting, loathsome; evil”).

meaning: detest; ADJ. loathsome: arousing loathing; offensive; Ex. loathsome smell
etymology: From Middle English lothe, from Old English lāþian, from Proto-West Germanic *laiþēn, from Proto-Germanic *laiþāną. Cognate with Old Norse leiðask ( > Danish ledes, Icelandic leiðast, all reflexive), German Leid.

meaning: metal-bearing vein (long deposit of an ore)
etymology: Doublet of load, which has however become semantically restricted. The now-archaic lode continues the old sense of Old English lād (“way, course, journey”) but by the 19th century survived only dialectally in the sense of “watercourse”, as a technical term in mining, and in the compounds lodestone, lodestar.

meaning: very high
etymology: From Middle English lofty, lofti, lofte (“of high rank; noble; ornate”), equivalent to loft (“sky, firmament; upper room”) + -y.

meaning: room or space under the roof; attic
etymology: Cognate with Scots loft, laft (“loft”), Irish lochta (“loft”).

meaning: record of a voyage or flight; record of day-to-day activities; section of a trunk; V.
etymology: Alternatively, directly from Norwegian låg (“fallen tree”), which could have been borrowed through the Norwegian timber trade. However the Old Norse/Middle Norwegian vowel is long while Middle English vowel is short.

meaning: hang about/around; stand idly about; linger
etymology: From Middle English loitren, from Middle Dutch loteren ("to shake, wag, wobble"; > modern Dutch leuteren (“to dawdle, ramble”)), ultimately connected with a frequentative form of Proto-Germanic *lūtaną (“to bend, stoop, cower, shrink from, decline”), see lout. Cognate with Dutch leuteren (“to dawdle”), Alemannic German lottern (“to wobble”), German lottern (“live a slovenly life”). More at lout, little.

meaning: lounge about
etymology: From Middle English lollen, lullen (“to lounge idly, hang loosely”), of uncertain origin; the Middle English Dictionary suggests a derivation from Middle Dutch lollen, lullen (“to doze; to mumble, talk nonsense”), though the words could merely be cognate. Compare modern Dutch lol (“fun”)), Icelandic lolla (“to act lazily”). See also lull.

meaning: stand, sit, or lie in a lazy, relaxed way
etymology: Origin uncertain. Perhaps borrowed from French s'allonger (“to lie down”). Compare French longer (“to walk along”). Compare also German lungern (“to hang or lounge around, linger”).

meaning: long life; long duration
etymology: Early 17th century, learned borrowing from Latin longaevitās, from longaevus (“ancient, aged”) + -itās. The first part is related to English long and this association led to the alternative pronunciation with /ŋ/.

meaning: appear or take shape (usually in an enlarged, indistinct, or distorted form); Ex. The shadow of the gallows loomed threateningly. N: apparatus for making thread into cloth
etymology: Compare typologically Serbo-Croatian ра́збо̄ј (“loom (weaving frame)”) akin to ра̀збити (“to break, to smash, to crack”).

meaning: framework from which a noose is suspended (used for execution by hanging)
etymology: For the pronunciation /ˈɡæləs/, compare bellows, bodice.

meaning: loop formed in a rope
etymology: Alternatively, and perhaps more likely, borrowed from Middle Low German nȫse (“loop, noose, snare”), itself of obscure origin. Perhaps derived from an incorrect division of ēn' ȫse (literally “a loop”), from Middle Low German ȫse, from Old Saxon *ōsia, from Proto-West Germanic *ansiju (“eyelet, loop”). Compare also Saterland Frisian Noose, Nouze (“loop, eyelet”) and Saterland Frisian Oose (“eyelet, loop”), potentially created via the same process.

meaning: gallop slowly
etymology: From Middle English lopen, from Old Norse hlaupa (“to leap, jump”). See leap. Cognate with German laufen (“walk, run”), Danish løbe (“run”), Dutch lopen (“walk, run”), Norwegian løpe (“run”). Doublet of leap.

meaning: talkative; N. loquacity
etymology: From Latin loquāx, loquācis (“talkative”) + -ous or from loquacity + -ous, ultimately from Latin loquor + -acious.

meaning: clumsy person; ADJ. loutish; CF. from countrysides ?
etymology: Non-Germanic cognates are probably Old Church Slavonic лоудити (luditi, “to deceive”), Serbo-Croatian lud and Albanian lut (“to beg, pray”).

meaning: moo; make the sound of a cow
etymology: Cognate with Scots laich (“low”), Saterland Frisian läich (“low”), West Frisian leech (“low”), Dutch laag (“low”), German Low German leeg, leeg' (“low; inferior”), West Flemish leeg (“lazy”), Danish lav (“low”), Faroese and Icelandic lágur (“low”), Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, and Swedish låg (“low”), Finnish laaka (“flat”), Ingrian laaku (“gentle”); also Irish laigh, luigh (“to lie”), Manx lhie (“lie; lay”), Scottish Gaelic laigh (“lie; lay”), Faliscan 𐌋𐌄𐌂𐌄𐌕 (lecet, “he lies down”), Latin lectus (“bed”), South Picene 𐌅𐌄𐌉𐌀𐌕 (veiat, “to lie”), Ancient Greek λέχομαι (lékhomai, “to lie down”), Albanian lag (“band, encampment, troop”), Belarusian ляжа́ць (ljažácʹ, “to lie”), Bulgarian лежа́ (ležá, “to lie”), Czech ležet (“to lie”), Macedonian лежи (leži, “to lie”), Polish leżeć (“to lie”), Russian лежа́ть (ležátʹ, “to lie”), Serbo-Croatian лѐжати, lèžati (“to lie”), Slovene ležáti (“to lie”), Ukrainian лежа́ти (ležáty, “to lie”), Tocharian B lyäk- (“to lie”). More at lie.

meaning: apply a lubricant to; N. lubricant: substance that reduces friction
etymology: Borrowed from Latin lūbricātus, perfect passive participle of lūbricō (“make slippery”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more), from lūbricus (“slippery”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *slewbʰ- (“slip, slide”).

meaning: easily understood; clear; intelligible; N. lucidity
etymology: Latin lucidus, from lūceō (“shine”) + -idus.

meaning: profitable; producing wealth
etymology: Borrowed from French lucratif, from Latin lucrativus (“profitable”), from lucratus, past participle of lucror (“to gain”), from lucrum (“gain”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂w- (“profit, gain”). Compare Spanish lucrar. By surface analysis, lucre + -ative.

meaning: money; profit; Ex. filthy lucre
etymology: From Middle English lūcre, lucor, lucour, lucur (“gain in money, profit; money; wages; illicit gain; advantage, benefit”), from Old French lucre or Latin lucrum (“advantage, profit; love of gain, avarice”), from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂w- (“gain, profit”) + *-tlom (variant of *-trom (suffix forming nouns denoting tools or instruments)).

meaning: dirty matter; ADJ. filthy
etymology: From Middle English filth, from Old English fȳlþu, from Proto-West Germanic *fūliþu, equivalent to foul + -th (abstract nominal suffix).

meaning: laughable; ridiculous; trifling
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin lūdicrus. First attested in 1619.

meaning: mournful; sorrowful
etymology: Borrowed from Latin lūgubris (“mournful; gloomy”), with the suffix -ious.

meaning: moment of calm; period of reduced activity; Ex. a lull in the rain; V: cause to become less active; cause to sleep or rest; Ex. lull the opponents into a false sense of security; CF. lullaby
etymology: Cognate with Scots lul, lule, loll (“to lull, put to sleep, howl, caterwaul”), Dutch lollen (“to sing badly, caterwaul”), Dutch lullen (“to chatter, prate, cheat, deceive”), Low German lullen (“to lull”), German lullen (“to lull”), Danish lulle (“to lull, sing to sleep”), Swedish lulla (“to lull”), Icelandic lúlla (“to lull”).

meaning: move heavily or clumsily; Ex. The bear lumbered through the woods; N: timber
etymology: Exact origin unknown. The earliest recorded reference for the noun was to heavy, useless objects such as old, discarded furniture. Perhaps from the verb lumber in reference to meaning "awkward to move"; Online Etymological Dictionary thinks this may derive from the same root as lame. Possibly influenced by Lumbar, an obsolete variant of Lombard, the Italian immigrant class known for being pawnbrokers and money-lenders in early England. Compare English lumpish.

meaning: unit of light energy (one candle'worth)
etymology: Borrowed from Latin lūmen (“light, an opening”). Use as a unit was first adopted by French physicist André Blondel in 1894.

meaning: celebrity (in a specific field); dignitary; object that gives light (as a celestial body)
etymology: From Late Middle English lūminārī, lūminārīe (“lamp; source of spiritual light, example of holiness; glory”), borrowed from Old French luminarie (“lamp, lights, lighting; candles; brightness, illumination”), variant of luminaire (“light fixture”) (modern French luminaire), from Medieval Latin lūminārium, from lūmināre (“that which gives light; light; lamp; body giving light, especially a heavenly body”), from lūmen (“light; brightness”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“bright; to shine”)) + -āris (suffix forming adjectives indicating a relationship or a pertaining to). Doublet of luminaire.

meaning: person of high rank or position
etymology: Borrowed from French dignitaire.

meaning: shining (esp. in the dark); issuing light; Ex. luminous paint/road signs
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French lumineus, from Latin lūminōsus.

meaning: pertaining to the moon
etymology: From Middle English lunar (“shaped like the crescent moon”), from Latin lūnāris (“of or pertaining to the moon, lunar”) (possibly through Middle French lunaire (modern French lunaire (“lunar”)), from lūna (“the Moon; crescent shape”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *lewk- (“bright; to shine”)) + -is (suffix forming adjectives).

meaning: insane; Ex. lunatic asylum
etymology: From Middle English lunatik, from Old French lunatique, from Late Latin lunaticus (“moonstruck”), derived from Latin luna (“moon”), the connection stemming from the belief that changes of the moon caused intermittent insanity.

meaning: wild; sensational; graphic; gruesome; horrible; Ex. lurid details of the murder
etymology: Borrowed from Latin lūridus (“pale yellow, wan”).

meaning: stealthily lie in waiting; slink; exist unperceived
etymology: Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk lurka (“to sneak away, go slowly”), dialectal Swedish lurka (“to dawdle, be slow in one's work”), Saterland Frisian lüürkje (“to look secretly, spy”), West Frisian luorkje (“to lurk”), Middle Low German lûrken (“to deceitfully stalk”).

meaning: move furtively; ADJ. slinky: stealthy; furtive; sneaky (as in ambush)
etymology: Cognate with West Frisian slinke, Dutch slinken (“to shrink; shrivel”), Low German slinken, Swedish slinka (“to glide”). Compare also German schleichen (“to slink”). More at sleek.

meaning: pleasing to taste or smell; delicious
etymology: An alternative etymology connects luscious to a Middle English term: lucius, an alteration of licious, believed to be a shortening of delicious.

meaning: shine; gloss (of a polished surface)
etymology: From Middle French lustre, from Old Italian lustro, from Old Italian lustrare (“brighten”), from Latin lūstrō (“to purify, to brighten”), from Latin lūstrum (“purification ritual”).

meaning: shining; brilliant; Ex. lustrous hair
etymology: From lustre + -ous.

meaning: abundant; growing healthily and in large amounts; excessively ornate; rich and splendid; fertile; Ex. luxuriant forests/prose; CF. luxurious, luxuriate
etymology: Borrowed from Latin lūxuriāns, present participle of lūxuriō, itself from lūxuria (“luxury, excess”). Equivalent to luxury + -ant.

meaning: gruesome; grisly; ghastly; CF. of death
etymology: Another theory derives the French term (through Spanish macabro) from Arabic مَقَابِر (maqābir, “cemeteries”), plural of مَقْبَرَة (maqbara) or مَقْبُرَة (maqbura).

meaning: mortuary; place where bodies are kept before burial or cremation
etymology: Borrowed from French morgue. The second sense developed from the first, via "a prison examination room", probably with reference to the haughty attitude of the jailers.

meaning: incinerate (a corpse); N. crematory, crematorium
etymology: First attested in 1889; borrowed from Latin cremātus, perfect passive participle of cremō (“to burn to ashes; to cremate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

meaning: ceremonial staff used as a symbol of authority; clublike medieval weapon
etymology: From Middle English mace, borrowed from Old French mace, mache, from Vulgar Latin *mattia, *mattea, matia, (compare Italian mazza, Spanish maza), probably from Proto-West Germanic *mattjō (“cutting tool, hoe”).

meaning: soften by soaking in liquid; waste away; Ex. macerate powdered wood to make paper
etymology: First attested in 1534; borrowed from Latin mācerātus, perfect passive participle of mācerō (see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3)), from Proto-Indo-European *mag-, *mak- (“to knead”), whence make. Cognate with French macérer.

meaning: crafty; double-dealing; of the political doctrine of Machiavelli, which holds that craft and deceit are justified in pursuing political power
etymology: From Machiavelli + -an, from the name of the Italian statesman and writer Niccolò Machiavelli (1469–1527), whose work The Prince (1532) advises that acquiring and exercising power may require unethical methods.

meaning: evil schemes or plots; schemes or plots to achieve an evil end; V. machinate
spotted; stained; CF. immaculate
pastoral song; song for several singers without instruments
etymology: From Italian madrigale, from Latin mātrīcālis.

meaning: violent whirlpool; violent or tublent situation; CF. stream
etymology: * Swedish malström

meaning: authoritative; imperious; commanding; of a magistrate; Ex. magisterial study of Roman law; Ex. magisterial manner
etymology: From Late Latin magisterialis, from Latin magisterium.

meaning: official with power to administer the law
etymology: From Middle English magistrat, maiestrat (“magistrate; magistracy”), borrowed from Latin magistrātus. See also -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office).

meaning: generosity; ADJ. magnanimous: generous
etymology: From Middle French magnanimité, from Old French [Term?], from Latin magnanimitās.

meaning: person of prominence or influence; powerful or influential person (in business or industry); Ex. oil magnate
etymology: Borrowed into late Middle English from Late Latin magnātēs, plural of magnās, from magnus (“great”), mid 15th c.

meaning: boastful; pompous
etymology: From post-Classical Latin magniloquens (“talkative, verbose”).

meaning: greatness (in size or extent); extent
etymology: From Latin magnitūdō (“greatness, size”), magnus + -tūdō.

meaning: mutilate; injure lastingly; disable; cripple; Ex. maimed for life
etymology: From Middle English maymen, mahaymen, from Anglo-Norman maheimer, mahaigner, of Germanic origin; see mayhem.

meaning: tear or cut to pieces; mutilate or disfigure; Ex. badly mangled bodies
etymology: Alternate etymology derives mangle from Middle English *mankelen, a frequentative form of manken (“to mutilate”), from Old English *mancian, bemancian (“to maim”). More at mank.

meaning: clumsy; not skillful; awkward; bungling
etymology: Borrowed from French maladroit, from mal- (“bad, badly”) + adroit (“skilful”), equivalent to mal- + adroit.

meaning: illness
etymology: From Middle English maladie, from Old French maladie (“sickness, illness, disease”), from malade (“ill, sick”), from Latin male habitus (“ill-kept, not in good condition”), 1st century AD. See also malice and habit.

meaning: uneasiness; vague feeling of ill health (without any particular pain or appearance of disease)
etymology: From French malaise (“ill ease”), from mal- (“bad, badly”) + aise (“ease”). Compare ill at ease.

meaning: comic misuse of a word; CF. Mrs. Malaprop
etymology: From the name of Mrs. Malaprop, a character in the play The Rivals (1775) by Richard Brinsley Sheridan + -ism. As dramatic characters in English comic plays of this time often had allusive names, it is likely that Sheridan fashioned the name from malapropos (“inappropriate; inappropriately”), from French mal à propos. Mrs. Malaprop is a classic example of a familiar comedic character archetype who unintentionally substitutes inappropriate but like-sounding words that take on a ludicrous meaning when used incorrectly.

meaning: inappropriate; ADV.
etymology: From French mal à propos, from mal (“bad, badly”) and à propos (“appropriate, relevant”).

meaning: person dissatisfied with existing state of affairs; discontented person; ADJ: discontented
etymology: From Middle French malcontent, from mal- + content; compare Late Latin malecontentus.

meaning: curse
etymology: From late Middle English malediccion, from Middle French malédiction, from Latin maledictiō (“curse”) from malus (“evil”) + dictiō (“speech”) noun of action from perfect passive participle dictus (“spoken”), from verb dīcō (“speak”).

meaning: evildoer; criminal
etymology: From Middle English malefactour, from Late Latin malefactor, from Latin malefaciō, from male (“evilly”) + factus (“made or done”), past participle of facio (“to make or do”).

meaning: doing evil; N. maleficience
etymology: Modification of maleficent; compare beneficient.

meaning: wishing evil; exhibiting ill will; N. malevolence
etymology: From Middle English *malevolent (suggested by Middle English malevolence), from Old French malivolent and Latin malevolentem, from male (“badly, wrongly”) + volens (“willing, wishing”), from velle (“to wish”).

meaning: wrongdoing; misconduct (by a public official)
etymology: From Old French malfaisance, derived from malfaire, maufaire (“to do evil”), from Latin malefaciō (“to do evil”), from male (“evilly”) + faciō (“to do, make”).

meaning: hateful; spiteful; expressing malice; N. malice: desire to harm others; spite
etymology: From Middle English malicious, from Old French malicios, from Latin malitiōsus, from malitia (“malice”), from malus (“bad”). Displaced native Middle English ivelwilled and ivelwilly (“malicious”), related to Old English yfelwillende (literally “evil-willing”). By surface analysis, malice + -ious.

meaning: speak evil of; bad-mouth (criticize spitefully); defame; ADJ: harmful; Ex. malign influence
etymology: From Middle English maligne, from Old French maligne, from Latin malignus, from malus (“bad”) + genus (“sort, kind”). Compare benign.

meaning: tending to cause death; highly injurious; aggressively malevolent; Ex. malignant tumor
etymology: From Middle French malignant, from Late Latin malignans. See malign.

meaning: one who feigns illness to escape duty; V. malinger: feign illness to avoid work
etymology: From malinger + -er.

meaning: (of a metal) capable of being shaped by pounding (beating); pliable; (of someone) impressionable (easily influenced); easily controlled; tractable
etymology: From Middle French malléable, borrowed from Late Latin malleābilis, derived from Latin malleāre (“to hammer”), from malleus (“hammer”), from Proto-Indo-European *mal-ni- (“crushing”), an extended variant of *melh₂- (“crush, grind”).

meaning: foul-smelling
etymology: From mal- + odorous.

meaning: mixture of decaying organic matter used as fertilizer; V: put or make compost
etymology: From Middle English compost, from Old Northern French compost (“a mixture of leaves, manure, etc., for fertilizing land, also a condiment”), from Latin compositus (“composed”), from componere. Doublet of compote, which was taken from modern French, composite, and kompot.

meaning: vertebrate animal whose female suckles its young
etymology: Borrowed from Latin mammal, coined 1758 by Linnaeus for the class of mammals, from Late Latin mammalis (“of the breast”), from Latin mamma (“breast”), perhaps cognate with mamma (mother).

meaning: having a backbone or spinal column; N: group of animals having a segmented spinal column
etymology: Adapted borrowing of French vertébré, from Latin vertebrātus (“jointed”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more).

meaning: give or take milk at the breast or udder
etymology: From Middle English sukelen; probably a back-formation of Middle English sukeling (“a suckling; infant”), formally equivalent to suck + -le (frequentative suffix). See suckling.

meaning: suckle; take care of (as a nurse); bear in mind; Ex. nursing mother; Ex. nurse a hope/grudge against someone
etymology: From Middle English norice, from Old French norrice, from Late Latin nūtrīcia, noun based on Latin nūtrīcius (“that which nourishes”), from nūtrīx (“wet nurse”), from nūtriō (“to suckle”).

meaning: gigantic; enormous
etymology: Adjectival use was popularized in the early 1800s by references to the Cheshire Mammoth Cheese presented to American paleontologist and president Thomas Jefferson.

meaning: restrain; handcuff; N.
etymology: The verb is probably derived from the noun, although according to the Oxford English Dictionary it is attested slightly earlier.

meaning: order; charge; authoritative command; power to govern another country; power to given to a government; region under administration; V: give a mandate to; place under a mandate; Ex. mandated territory
etymology: Sense 3 in Canadian English is likely a semantic loan from French mandat.

meaning: obligatory; compulsory; of a mandate
etymology: From Late Latin mandatorius (“of or belonging to a mandator”), from mandātor (“one who commands”), equivalent to mandate + -ory; see mandate.

meaning: shabby; wretched; suffering from mange; of bad appearance
etymology: From mange + -y.

meaning: skin disease (esp. of domestic animals) marked by loss of hair
etymology: From Middle English manjewe, manjeue, from Old French manjue, derived from mangier (“to eat”) (modern French manger (“to eat”)), from Latin manducare.

meaning: raging mad; insane; N. maniac: insane person; CF. mania: disorder of the mind; intense enthusiasm
etymology: From maniac + -al.

meaning: evident; visible; obvious; V: show plainly
etymology: From Middle English manifest, manifeste, from Latin manifestus, manufestus (“palpable, manifest”), from Latin manus (“hand”) + an uncertain second element. Doublet of manifesto.

meaning: outward demonstration; manifesting; indication of the presence of something; Ex. manifestation of his pronounced musical bent
etymology: From Middle English manifestacion, manyfestacion, manyfestacioun; from Late Latin manifestātiō. In the political sense, a semantic loan from French manifestation. By surface analysis, manifest + -ation.

meaning: distinct; very noticeable; Ex. pronounced limp
public declaration of principles; statement of policy
etymology: Since the mid 17th century, from Italian manifesto, from manifestare + -o, from Latin manifestō (“to make public”), from Latin manus + an uncertain second element. Doublet of manifest.

meaning: many in number or kind; numerous; varied
etymology: From Middle English manifold, from Old English maniġfeald (“manifold, various, varied, complicated, numerous, abundant, plural”), from Proto-Germanic *managafalþaz, equivalent to many + -fold. Cognate with Middle High German manecvalt (“manifold”), Icelandic margfaldr (“multiple”). Compare also German mannigfaltig (“various”), Dutch menigvoudig (“various”), Danish mangefold (“multiple”), Swedish mångfald (“diversity”).

meaning: operate with one'hands; control or play upon (people, forces, etc.) artfully; maneuver; Ex. how to manipulate publicity and men; ADJ. manipulative
etymology: Back-formation from manipulation.

meaning: affected; not natural; Ex. mannered way of speech
etymology: From Middle English manered; equivalent to manner + -ed.

meaning: distinctive behavioral trait; affected style in art (according to a set of styles)
etymology: From manner + -ism.

meaning: emancipate; free from slavery or bondage
etymology: From Middle English manumitten, from Latin manūmittere, from pre-Classical Latin manū ēmittere (literally “send out from one’s hand”).

meaning: pertaining to marriage
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French marital, and its source, Latin marītālis, from marītus (“husband”).

meaning: bordering on (adjacent to) the sea; nautical; of the ships or the sea; Ex. Maritime Provinces
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French maritime, from Latin maritimus.

meaning: noticeable; targeted for vengeance or attack; Ex. marked improvement/man
etymology: Less common disyllabic pronunciation (/ˈmɑː.kɪd/) is likely an analogy derived from markedness (explaining its restriction to sense 2).

meaning: damaged; disfigured; V. mar: spoil; disfigure
etymology: From Middle English marred, merred (“troubled, distressed, vexed, bewildered”), from Old English *mierred, ġemyrred (“disturbed, troubled”), past participle of Old English mierran, ġemyrran (“to hinder, obstruct, force, trouble, err”), equivalent to mar + -ed.

meaning: put in order; guide ceremoniously to the correct place; Ex. marshal the children into the museum; N: military officer; official
etymology: From marshal.

meaning: (cause to) join the armed forces; obtain (help, sympathy, or support)
etymology: From en- + list.

meaning: one of a family of mammals that nurse their offspring in a pouch (pocket of skin or leather); CF. kangaroo, opossum, wombat
etymology: Borrowed from Latin marsūpial, from marsūpiālis (“of a purse”) and marsūpium (“purse, pouch”), from Ancient Greek μαρσύπιον (marsúpion) or μαρσύππιον (marsúppion), variants of μαρσίππιον (marsíppion), diminutive of μάρσιππος (mársippos, “bag, pouch”).

meaning: warlike; of war; Ex. martial art/law
etymology: From Middle English martial, marcial, mercial, mercialle (“relating to war, warlike; military; for use in fighting or warfare; brave, hardy; combative, fierce; ruthless, vicious; domineering, overbearing”), from Middle French martial (modern French martial (“martial”)), or directly from its etymon Latin mārtiālis (“of or pertaining to Mars, the Roman god of war”), from Mārtius (“of or pertaining to Mars”) + -ālis (suffix forming adjectives of relationship). The English word is cognate with Italian marziale (“martial”), Portuguese marcial (“martial”), Spanish marcial (“martial”).

meaning: student at a military school
etymology: Doublet of caddie, cadeau, cadel, capital, capitellum, and caudillo.

meaning: strict disciplinarian; person who demands total obedience to rules and orders; CF. Jean Martinet
etymology: After the example of 17th-century French army officer Jean Martinet.

meaning: one who voluntarily suffers death for his or her religion or cause; great sufferer; Ex. martyr to his rheumatism
etymology: From Middle English martir, from Old English martyr, itself a borrowing from Ecclesiastical Latin martyr, from Ancient Greek μάρτυρ (mártur), later form of μάρτυς (mártus, “witness”).

meaning: person who enjoys his own pain; CF. masochism
etymology: Leopold von Sacher-Masoch + -ist. Coined by Richard von Krafft-Ebing and popularized by Freud in relation to sadomasochism.

meaning: chew
etymology: From Latin masticātus, perfect passive participle of masticō (“to chew”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Alternatively, back-formation from mastication, either ultimately from Ancient Greek μαστιχάω (mastikháō, “to grind the teeth”). Compare French mastiquer.

meaning: preoccupation with physical comforts and things; excessive regard for worldly concerns (rather than spiritual matters)
etymology: Borrowed from French matérialisme. By surface analysis, material + -ism.

meaning: motherly; N. maternity: motherhood
etymology: The noun is derived from the adjective.

meaning: woman who rules a family or larger social group
etymology: Of Latin origin, via or reinforced by Old French matriarche, from Latin māter (“mother”) + -archa, -arches, from Ancient Greek -άρχης (-árkhēs), from ἀρχός (arkhós, “chief”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ergʰ- (“to begin, rule, command”). By surface analysis, matri- + -arch.

meaning: enroll (in college or graduate school); CF. matrix
etymology: The adjective is first attested in 1487, in Middle English, the verb in 1557; borrowed from Latin mātrīculātus, perfect passive participle of mātrīculō (“to register”) (see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3)), from mātrīcula (“public register”), a diminutive of Latin mātrīx (“list”). By surface analysis, matricul(a) + -ate.

meaning: point of origin; array of numbers or algebraic symbols; mold or die; Ex. the matrix of Western civilization
etymology: Slang usage coined with the 1999 sci-fi action film The Matrix.

meaning: effusively sentimental
etymology: From Middle English Maudelen, a dialectal form of Mary Magdalene (typically depicted weeping), from Old French Madelaine (whence Madeleine), from Late Latin Magdalena (see Magdalena, Magdalene, and Maudlin).

meaning: swayed by sentiment; appealing to the sentiments
etymology: From sentiment + -al.

meaning: handle roughly; batter; injure by beating; Ex. mauled by his overexcited fans; N: heavy long-handled hammer
etymology: From Middle English malle (“mace, maul”), from Anglo-Norman mail, from Old French mail, from Latin malleus (“hammer”). Doublet of malleus.

meaning: monumental tomb; large stately tomb; CF. Mausolos
etymology: By surface analysis, Mausolus + -eum.

meaning: pale purple
etymology: Borrowed from French mauve (“mallow”), from Latin malva, which has a purple colour. Doublet of mallow. Coined in 1856 by the chemist William Henry Perkin, when he accidentally created the first aniline dye.

meaning: rebel; nonconformist (in a group)
etymology: The poker noun sense (“a queen and a jack as a starting hand in Texas hold ’em”) may be from the theme song of the US Western television series Maverick (1957–1962), which says of the eponymous protagonist that “[g]amblin’ is his game” and that he is “livin’ on jacks and queens”.

meaning: mushy (sentimental) and gushy; icky-sticky sentimental; excessively and objectionably sentimental
etymology: From mawk + -ish.

meaning: proverb; truth pithily stated
etymology: From Anglo-Norman maxime and Middle French maxime, from Late Latin maxima (“axiom”), noun use of the feminine singular form of Latin maximus (apparently as used in the phrase prōpositiō maxima (“greatest premise”)). Doublet of maxima.

meaning: injury to body; crime of willfully maiming or crippling a person; violent disorder; Ex. mayhem in the zoo; CF. maim
etymology: The etymology of the Old French words is uncertain; they are possibly from Proto-Germanic *maidijaną (“to damage; to hurt; to change; to exchange”) (compare Gothic 𐌼𐌰𐌹𐌳𐌾𐌰𐌽 (maidjan, “to alter, falsify”); Middle High German meidem, meiden (“gelding”); Old Norse meiða (“to injure”)), from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“to change; to exchange; etc.”), possibly from *mey- (“to change; to exchange”). If so, the English word is a doublet of mad.

meaning: scanty; inadequate
etymology: Norwegian Bokmål mager and Danish mager. Doublet of maigre.

meaning: indirect in speech (when something unpleasant must be said); hypocritical; evasive
wind or turn in its course; follow a winding or turning course; move aimlessly and idly
etymology: From Latin Maeander, from Ancient Greek Μαίανδρος (Maíandros) – a river in Asia Minor (present day Turkey) known for its winding course (modern Turkish Menderes).

meaning: interfering; V. meddle: interfere
etymology: From meddle + -some.

meaning: settle a dispute through the services of an outsider; act as an intermediary; produce by mediating; Ex. mediate a cease-fire
etymology: The adjective is first attested in the 1440s in Middle English, the verb in 1538; from Middle English mediat(e) (“intermediate; intercessory”), borrowed from Late Latin mediātus, perfect passive participle of mediō (“to divide in the middle; (in Medieval Latin) to be in the middle, be or become between, mediate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from medius (“middle”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).

meaning: intermediate; acting as a mediator; N: mediator; go-between
etymology: From French intermédiaire, adjusted to simulate a borrowing from Medieval Latin *intermediārius.

meaning: ordinary; commonplace; neither good nor bad
etymology: From the late Middle English medioker, from the French médiocre, from the Middle French médiocre, from the Classical Latin mediocris (“in a middle state”, “of middle size”, “middling”, “moderate”, “ordinary”, from medius (“middle”) + ocris (“rugged mountain”)); compare mediocrely and mediocrity.

meaning: reflection; thought; V. meditate
etymology: From Old French meditacion, from Latin meditatio, from meditatus, the past participle of meditārī (“to meditate, to think over, consider”), itself from Proto-Indo-European *med- (“to measure, limit, consider, advise”).

meaning: element that is a creature'natural environment; nutrient setting in which microorganisms are cultivated; appropriate occupation or means of expression; channel of communication; compromise; middle position between extremes; intervening substance through which something else is transmitted
etymology: Borrowed from Latin medium, neuter of medius (“middle”), from Proto-Italic *meðjos, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“between”). Compare middle. Doublet of mid, medio, media, and meson.

meaning: mixture
etymology: From Middle English medle, from Anglo-Norman medlee, Old French medlee, from the feminine past participle of early Medieval Latin misculō (“to mix”). Compare meddle. Doublet of melee.

meaning: submissive; patient and long-suffering
etymology: Cognate with Swedish and Norwegian Nynorsk mjuk (“soft”), Norwegian Bokmål myk (“soft”), and Danish myg (“supple”), Dutch muik (“soft, overripe”), dialectal German mauch (“dry and decayed, rotten”), Mauche (“malanders”). Compare as well Welsh mwyth (“soft, weak”), Latin ēmungō (“to blow one's nose”), Tocharian A muk- (“to let go, give up”), Lithuanian mùkti (“to slip away from”), Ancient Greek μύσσομαι (mússomai, “to blow the nose”), Sanskrit मु॒ञ्चति॑ (muñcáti, “to release, let loose”).

meaning: man who is courting a woman
etymology: From Middle English sutour, from Anglo-Norman suytour, seuter, from Late Latin secutor (“follower, pursuer”).

meaning: mania for doing grandiose things; mental disorder characterized by delusions of wealth, power, or importance
etymology: Borrowed from French mégalomanie; equivalent to megalo- + -mania.

meaning: gloomy; morose; blue; N. ADJ. melancholic; CF. melancholia
etymology: From Middle English malencolie, from Old French melancolie, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολία (melankholía, “atrabiliousness”) (from μέλας (mélas), μελαν- (melan-, “black, dark, murky”) + χολή (kholḗ, “bile”)), referring to the humour which ancient Hippocratic and later Galenic medicine associated with sadness and despondency. Compare the Latin ātra bīlis (“black bile”). The adjectival use is a Middle English innovation, perhaps influenced by the suffixes -y, -ly. Doublet of melancholia.

meaning: gloomy; depressed
etymology: (depressed): Compare typologically Russian тоска́ зелёная (toská zeljónaja) (<+ зелёный (zeljónyj)). Also compare фиоле́тово (fiolétovo).

meaning: fight
etymology: Borrowed from French mêlée, from Old French meslee, feminine past participle of mesler (“to mix”), derived from Latin misceō (“mix”). Doublet of medley.

meaning: (of words or a voice) sweetly or smoothly flowing; melodious; having a pleasant tune
etymology: From Middle English mellifluous, mellyfluous, from Latin mellifluus (“flowing like honey”) + -ous, from mel (“honey”) + fluō (“flow”). Compare superfluous and fluid, from same root, and with dulcet (“sweet speech”), alternative Latinate term with a similar meaning.

meaning: token; reminder of the past; keepsake; Ex. memento of your visit
etymology: Borrowed from Latin mementō (“remember”), imperative form of meminī (“to remember”).

meaning: commemorate
etymology: From memorial + -ize.

meaning: something, such as a monument or holiday, intended to honor the memory of a person or event; ADJ: commemorative
etymology: From Late Latin memoriale, neuter of memorialis. By surface analysis, memory + -ial.

meaning: collection of wild animals on exhibition; zoo
etymology: From French ménagerie, derived from ménager (“to keep house”), household. Housekeeping used to include taking care of domestic animals.

meaning: lying; habitually dishonest; N. mendacity
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French mendacieux, from Latin mendācium (“lie, untruth”), from mendāx (“lying”), + -ious.

meaning: beggar; ADJ: living as a beggar
etymology: From Middle English mendicant, from Latin mendīcāns, present participle of mendīcō (“beg”). Compare French mendiant.

meaning: money or goods given to the poor
etymology: From Middle English almes, almesse, ælmesse, from Old English ælmesse, from Proto-West Germanic *alemōsinā, a borrowing from Vulgar Latin *alemosyna, from Late Latin eleēmosyna, from Ancient Greek ἐλεημοσύνη (eleēmosúnē, “alms”), from ἐλεέω (eleéō, “to have mercy”), from ἔλεος (éleos, “mercy”). Compare Saterland Frisian Aalmoose (“alms”), Dutch aalmoes (“alms”), German Almosen (“alms”), Catalan almoina (“alms”), Portuguese esmola (“alms”), Galician esmola (“alms”), Spanish limosna (“alms”), French aumône (“alms”).

meaning: suitable for servants; lowly; mean; N: someone who does menial work (esp. servant in a house)
etymology: From Middle English meyneal, from Anglo-Norman mesnal, from maisnee (“household”), from Vulgar Latin *mānsiōnāta, from Latin mānsiō (“house”).

meaning: counselor; teacher
etymology: From French mentor, from Ancient Greek Μέντωρ (Méntōr, “Mentor”), a mythological character in the Odyssey, whose name, a historical name from Ancient Greece, shares the same root as English mind. Cognate to Sanskrit मन्तृ (mantṛ, “advisor, counselor”) and Latin monitor (“one who admonishes”), and perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *monéyeti (compare Latin moneō (“to warn”), causative form of *men- (“to think”).

meaning: concerning trade or merchants
etymology: Borrowed from French mercantile, from Italian mercantile, from mercante (“merchant”), from Latin mercāns (“trading”).

meaning: motivated solely by money or gain; N.
etymology: From Middle English mercenarye (“someone paid to work, hireling”), from Latin mercēnārius (“hired for money”), from mercēs (“reward, wages, price”).

meaning: capricious; quick and changing; fickle; containing the element mercury; Ex. mercurial temper; CF. mood
etymology: Later adjective and noun uses may have been directly derived from Latin mercuriālis (adjective), whence Middle English mercurial (“under the astrological influence of the planet Mercury”).

meaning: mercury
etymology: From Middle English quyk silver, quyksilver, quikselver, from Old English cwicseolfor (“quicksilver”, literally “living silver”) (see Latin argentum vīvum) from its ability to move. See quick in the sense of "living". Cognate with Dutch kwikzilver, German Low German Quicksülver, German Quecksilber, Danish kviksølv, Norwegian Bokmål kvikksølv, Swedish kvicksilver. By surface analysis, quick (“living”) + silver.

meaning: flashy; tawdry; attractive on the surface but of no real value; Ex. metericious argument/jewel; CF. prostitute
etymology: From Latin meretrīcius, from meretrīx (“harlot, prostitute”), from mereō (“earn, deserve, merit”) (English merit) + -trīx (“(female agent)”) (English -trix).

meaning: of the common people; deficient in refinement; not refined; coarse; Ex. vulgar display of wealth; N. vulgarism: vulgarity; crudely indecent word; CF. vulgarian: vulgar person; boor; lout
etymology: From Middle English vulgare, from Latin vulgāris, from volgus, vulgus (“mob; common folk”), from Proto-Indo-European *welH-. Compare Welsh gwala (“plenty, sufficiency”), Ancient Greek ἁλία (halía, “assembly”), εἰλέω (eiléō, “to compress”), Proto-Slavic *valъ.

meaning: combination (of two business corporations); act of merging
etymology: From merge + -er.

meaning: hypnotize; N. mesmerism; CF. Franz Mesmer
etymology: Back-formation from mesmerism, thus mesmerism + -ize; first attested in 1829.

meaning: pertaining to the art of removing metals from ores; N. metallurgy: science that deals with extracting metals from ores
etymology: From metallurgy + -ical.

meaning: change of form; Ex. metamorphosis of caterpillar to butterfly; V. metamorphose: change by metamorphosis
etymology: First attested in 1533, from Latin metamorphōsis, from Ancient Greek μεταμόρφωσις (metamórphōsis), from μετά (metá, “change”) + μορφή (morphḗ, “form”). Analyzable as meta- + -morph + -osis

meaning: implied comparison; CF. simile
etymology: From Middle French métaphore, from Latin metaphora, from Ancient Greek μεταφορά (metaphorá), from μεταφέρω (metaphérō, “to transfer, apply”), from μετά (metá, “with, across, after”) + φέρω (phérō, “to bear, carry”).

meaning: rise or fly high in the air; Ex. The rocket soared into the sky.
etymology: From Middle English soren, from Old French essorer (“to fly up, soar”), from Vulgar Latin *exaurare (“to rise into the air”), from Latin ex (“out”) + aura (“the air, a breeze”), from Ancient Greek αὔρα (aúra, “breath”). Compare aura, and exhale.

meaning: pertaining to speculative philosophy; of metaphysics; N. metaphysics: branch of philosophy that examines the nature of reality
etymology: From Middle English metaphisicalle, methafisical, from Medieval Latin metaphysicālis. By surface analysis, meta- + physical.

meaning: measure; distribute; administer; Ex. mete out justice/punishment
etymology: Cognate with Scots mete (“to measure”), Saterland Frisian meete (“to measure”), West Frisian mjitte (“to measure”), Dutch meten (“to measure”), German messen (“to measure”), Swedish mäta (“to measure”), Latin modus (“limit, measure, target”), Ancient Greek μεδίμνος (medímnos, “measure, bushel”), Ancient Greek μέδεσθαι (médesthai, “care for”), Old Armenian միտ (mit, “mind”).

meaning: like a meteor; swift; momentarily brilliant; Ex. meteoric rise to fame; N. meteor
etymology: From meteor + -ic.

meaning: systematic; N. method: systematic method of procedure
etymology: From Ancient Greek μεθοδικός (methodikós, “going to work by rule, systematic, crafty”) + -al.

meaning: excessively careful (with great attention to detail); painstaking; scrupulous
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin meticulōsus (“full of fear, timid, fearful, terrible, frightful”), from metus (“fear”) and -culōsus, extracted from perīculōsus (“perilous”). Sense of “characterized by very precise, conscientious attention to details” is a semantic loan from French méticuleux.

meaning: large city
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin mētropolis, from Ancient Greek μητρόπολις (mētrópolis, “mother city”), from μήτηρ (mḗtēr, “mother”) + πόλις (pólis, “city (state)”). By surface analysis, metro- + -polis. Doublet of metropole.

meaning: courage (to continue bravely in spite of difficulties); spirit; ADJ. mettlesome
etymology: From figurative use of metal (since 16th century). The two spellings were originally interchangeable variants, but came to be distinguished by sense in the 18th century.

meaning: swamp gas; heavy vaporous atmosphere often emanating from decaying matter; pervasive corrupting influence; noxious atmosphere or influence
etymology: First attested in 1665. From Ancient Greek μίασμα (míasma, “stain; pollution”).

meaning: wetland; marsh; V: flood; overwhelm; drench in with liquid
etymology: The word has alternatively been suggested to be a borrowing from Dutch zwamp (“swamp, marsh, fen”). Other cognates include Middle Low German swamp (“sponge, mushroom”), Dutch zomp (“swamp, lake, marshy place”), German Low German Sump (“swamp, bog, marsh”), German Sumpf (“swamp”), Swedish sump (“swamp”). Related also to Dutch zwam (“fungus, punk, tinder”), German Schwamm (“mushroom, fungus, sponge”), Swedish svamp (“mushroom, fungus, sponge”), Icelandic svampur, sveppur (“fungus”), Gothic 𐍃𐍅𐌿𐌼𐍃𐌻 (swumsl, “a ditch”). Related to sump, swim.

meaning: small representative world; world in miniature; Ex. microcosm of English society
etymology: From French microcosme, from Latin microcosmus, from Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”) + κόσμος (kósmos, “universe, order”); micro- + -cosm.

meaning: small model; small painting; ADJ: small
etymology: Borrowed from Italian miniatura (“manuscript illumination”), from miniare (“to illuminate”), from Latin miniō (“to colour red”), from minium (“red lead, minium”). Not related to minimum, minor or min (which are all from a different root, *mi-n-), though the sense development may have been influenced by association with them or sound symbolism.

meaning: changing its habitat; wandering; Ex. migrant birds/workers; N: one that migrates
etymology: Borrowed from French migrant.

meaning: wandering; V. migrate: move from one region and settle in another; move periodically from one region to another
etymology: Borrowed from Latin migrātōrius or migrate + -ory.

meaning: social environment; means of expression; Ex. feel out of one'milieu; Ex. His proper milieu is watercolor.
etymology: Borrowed from French milieu (“physical or social environment; group of people with a common point of view”), from Middle French milieu, meilleu, mileu, from Old French milliu, meillieu, mileu (“middle”), from mi- (prefix meaning ‘half’) (from Latin medius (“half; middle”)) + lieu, leu (“place”) (from Latin locus (“place; spot (specific location)”)).

meaning: combative; bellicose; N.
etymology: From Middle French militant, from Latin mīlitāns, present participle of mīlitāre (“to serve as a soldier”).

meaning: work against; Ex. militate against the chances of promotion; CF. serve as a soldier
etymology: First attested in 1598; borrowed from Latin mīlitātus, perfect passive participle from mīlitō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Semantically from its cognate, French militer.

meaning: army composed of ordinary citizens rather than professional soldiers
etymology: The use of "militia" rather than "police" to refer to the police force (of Belarus and some other countries) originated in the USSR.

meaning: thousand-year period (as in the New Testament); hoped-for period of happiness and prosperity
etymology: From Late Latin mīllennium, from Latin mīllennis (“1000-year”) + -ium (forming abstract nouns).

meaning: imitation
etymology: From mimic + -ry.

meaning: pantomime (act without dialogue); mimicry; mimer; V: mimic; pantomime
etymology: Possibly from Middle English mime, from Old English mīma (“a buffoon, jester, mime”), from Latin mimus, from Ancient Greek μῖμος (mîmos, “imitator, actor”), but more likely re-borrowed in modern times from French mime (“mimic actor”), from the same source.

meaning: menacing; threatening
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French minatoire, from Late Latin minātōrius. Compare menace.

meaning: affectedly dainty (delicate); V. mince: cut (esp. meat) into very small pieces; walk with exaggerated primness; walk in an unnatural way, taking little short steps; Ex. The actor minced across the stage; CF. mincemeat; CF. mincer
delicate; delicately beautiful; fastidious; not easy to please; Ex. dainty movement/dress
etymology: From Middle English deynte (as noun), from Old French deintié, from Latin dignitātem. Doublet of dignity.

meaning: delicate; very finely made; extremely beautiful; Ex. exquisite piece of jewelry
etymology: From Latin exquīsītus (“to be outsought”), perfect passive participle of exquīrō (“to outseek”).

meaning: delicate; of very fine quality
etymology: From Middle English chois, from Old French chois (“choice”), from choisir (“to choose, perceive”), possibly via assumed Vulgar Latin *causīre (“to choose”), from Gothic 𐌺𐌰𐌿𐍃𐌾𐌰𐌽 (kausjan, “to make a choice, taste, test, choose”), from Proto-Germanic *kauzijaną, from *keusaną (“to choose”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵews- (“to choose”).
