Akin to Old High German kiosan (“to choose”), Old English ċēosan (“to choose”), Old Norse kjósa (“to choose”). More at choose.

meaning: servile dependent; obsequious follower
etymology: First use appears c. 1490, from Middle French mignon (“lover, royal favourite, darling”), from Old French mignon (“dainty, pleasing, gentle, kind”), from Frankish *minnju (“love, friendship, affection, memory”), from Proto-Germanic *minjō (“affectionate thought, care”), from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to think”). Doublet of mignon.

meaning: extremely small
extremely small; CF. minutes: official record of the proceedings at a meeting
etymology: From Middle English mynute, minute, mynet, from Old French minute, from Medieval Latin minūta (“60th of an hour; note”). Doublet of menu and menudo.

meaning: petty or trivial details; CF. minutia
etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

meaning: unreal reflection; optical illusion
etymology: An unadapted borrowing from French mirage c. 1812.

meaning: entangle; stick in swampy ground; stick or sink in mire; N: bog; deep mud; Ex. sucked deeper into the mire
etymology: From Middle English mire, a borrowing from Old Norse mýrr, from Proto-Germanic *miuzijō, whence also Swedish myr, Norwegian myr, Icelandic mýri, Dutch *mier (in placenames, for example Mierlo). Related to Proto-Germanic *meusą, whence Old English mēos, and Proto-Germanic *musą, whence Old English mos (English moss).

meaning: merriment; laughter
etymology: From Middle English merth, myrthe, murhthe, from Old English myrgþ (“mirth, joy”), from Proto-West Germanic *murgiþu (“briefness, brevity”); equivalent to merry + -th (abstract nominal suffix). Cognate with Middle Dutch merchte (“pleasure, joy, delight”).

meaning: mischance; ill luck; Ex. death by misadventure
etymology: From Middle English misaventure, from Old French mesaventure, from mes- (“mis-”) + aventure (“adventure”). Equivalent to mis- + adventure. Compare disadventure.

meaning: one who hates mankind; misanthropist
etymology: From Ancient Greek from μισέω (miséō, “I hate”) and ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos, “man; human”); compare miser.

meaning: despicable; unpleasant; disgusting; Ex. vile slander
etymology: From Middle English vile, vyle, vyl, from Anglo-Norman ville, Old French vil, vile, from Latin vīlis.

meaning: error; misunderstanding; V. misapprehend
etymology: From mis- + apprehension.

meaning: mixture of writings on various subjects; collection of various items
etymology: Borrowed from French miscellanées, from Latin mīscellānea, from miscellus (“mixed”), from misceō (“to mix”).

meaning: made up of a variety of parts
etymology: Borrowed from Latin miscellāneus, from miscellus (“mixed”), from misceō (“mix”).

meaning: ill luck
etymology: From Anglo-Norman meschance, Old French meschance, meschaunce.

meaning: interpret incorrectly; misinterpret; misjudge
etymology: From Middle English misconstruen, equivalent to mis- + construe.

meaning: wretch; wrongdoer; villain; Ex. kindness to the miscreant; CF. believe
etymology: From Middle English myscreaunt, miscreaunt, from Old French mescreant (1080) "mis-believer", present participle of mescreire "to misbelieve" (modern mécroire). Cognate with French mécréant.

meaning: miserable person; bad or despicable person; ADJ. wretched: miserable; bad; contemptible; vile
etymology: From Middle English wrecche, from Old English wreċċa (“exile, outcast”), from Proto-Germanic *wrakjô (“exile, fugitive, warrior”), from Proto-Indo-European *wreg- (“to track, follow”). Doublet of garçon.

meaning: minor crime; misdeed; wrongdoing
etymology: From mis- + demeanor.

meaning: immoral behavior; bad management; V.
etymology: From mis- + conduct (noun sense).

meaning: stingy; mean
etymology: From miser + -ly, attested from the 1540s.

meaning: doubts
unfortunate accident
etymology: From Middle English mishap, myshappe, myssehappe, equivalent to mis- + hap.

meaning: wrong or improper name; incorrect designation
etymology: The verb is derived from the noun.

meaning: hatred of marriage
etymology: From miso- + -gamy.

meaning: hater of woman; CF. misogyny
etymology: From Ancient Greek μῑσογύνης (mīsogúnēs), from μῑσέω (mīséō, “I hate”) + γυνή (gunḗ, “woman”), equivalent to misogyny + -ist.

meaning: object to be thrown or projected
etymology: From Latin missile (“thrown weapon, projectile”), neuter of missilis (“throwable, capable of being thrown”), from mittere (“to send”). From 1611. Compare Middle French missile (“projectile”), from 1636.

meaning: letter; written statement; CF. sent
etymology: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin missīvus, from mittō (“to send”).

meaning: very small object or insect-like creature; small coin
etymology: From Middle English mite, from Old English mīte (“mite, tiny insect”), from Proto-West Germanic *mītā, from Proto-Germanic *mītǭ (“biting insect”, literally “cutter”), from *maitaną (“to cut”), from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“small”) or *meh₂y- (“to cut”). Akin to Old High German mīza (“mite”), Middle Dutch mīte (“moth, mite”), Dutch mijt (“moth, mite”), Danish mide (“mite”).

meaning: appease; moderate; make or become less in force or intensity
etymology: From Middle English mitigaten (“to relieve pain, soothe; (swelling) to abate; (hemorrhoids) to relieve; (the mind) to placate, appease; to end, check; to stop, cease”), from mitigat(e) (“mitigated, alleviated, relived”, also used as the past participle of mitigaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), borrowed from Latin mītigātus, the perfect passive participle of mītigō (“to make soft, ripe; to tame, pacify”), from mītis (“gentle, mild, ripe”) + -igō (“to do, make”), of uncertain origin, but perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *meh₁y- (“mild, soft”).

meaning: pertaining to memory; assisting the memory; N: device, such as as formula or rhyme, used as a mnemonic aid
etymology: * Portuguese mnemónica

meaning: movable; not fixed; N. mobility
etymology: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin mōbilis (“easy to be moved, moveable”), from moveō (“move”). The video-gaming sense was coined by Richard Bartle to describe NPCs or creatures capable of moving "under their own power" in the 1978 video game Multi-User Dungeon. Bartle retracted an earlier claim of his that it was from the kinetic sculpture sense of mobile (for the "unpredictable but limited" motion of the hanging ornaments).

meaning: ridicule; deride; imitate often in derision
etymology: Cognate with Dutch mokken (“to sulk; pout; mope; grumble”), Old High German firmucken (“to be stupid”), Modern German mucksen (“to utter a word; mumble; grumble”), West Frisian mokke (“to mope; sulk; grumble”), Swedish mucka (“to murmur”), dialectal Dutch mokkel (“kiss”).

meaning: prevailing style; current fashion; manner; way of doing something; Ex. in the latest mode; Ex. simple mode of life
etymology: From Old French mode (masculine), from Latin modus (“measure, due measure, rhythm, melody”). Doublet of modus.

meaning: limited quantity; small amount; Ex. He does not have a modicum of sense; CF. moderate
etymology: The plural form modica is derived from Latin modica.

meaning: fashionable; conforming to the current fashion
etymology: From mode + -ish.

meaning: tone down in intensity; change the intensity or tone of; regulate; change from one musical key to another; Ex. modulate from E to G
etymology: From Latin modulor (“to measure, regulate, modulate”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix), from modulus (“measure”). Compare module, modulus. By surface analysis, modul(e) + -ate.

meaning: powerful person; Ex. oil moguls; CF. Mogol, Moghul; CF. Mongolian
etymology: Figurative use of Moghul, which originally meant Mongol, or person of Mongolian descent. In this context, it refers to the Mughal Empire (Mughal being Persian or Arabic for "Mongol") of the Indian subcontinent that existed between 1526 and 1857: the early Mughal emperors claimed a heritage dating back to the Mongol ruler Genghis Khan. The modern meaning of the word is supposedly derived from the storied riches of the Mughal emperors, which, for example, produced the Taj Mahal.

meaning: the smallest particle (one or more atoms) of a substance that has all the properties of that substance
etymology: Borrowed from French molécule, from New Latin molecula (“a molecule”), diminutive of Latin moles (“a mass”).

meaning: soothe an angry person
etymology: From Middle English mollifien, from Late Latin mollificō, from Latin mollis (“soft”). By surface analysis, Latin moll- + -ify.

meaning: pamper; coddle; baby; indulge excessively
etymology: From molly + coddle.

meaning: periodically shed or cast off hairs or feathers (for replacement by a new growth)
melted; Ex. molten lava
etymology: From Middle English molten, from Old English molten, ġemolten (“melted, molten”), from Proto-Germanic *multanaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *meltaną (“to melt”). Cognate with Scots moltin, Swedish multen.

meaning: very important; N. moment; CF. momentary
etymology: From moment (“weight, importance”) + -ous.

meaning: quantity of motion of a moving body; impetus; moving force
etymology: Borrowed from Latin mōmentum. Doublet of moment and movement.

meaning: government under a single ruler
etymology: From Old French monarchie, from Late Latin monarchia, from Ancient Greek μοναρχία (monarkhía), from μόνος (mónos, “only”) + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “power, authority”). By surface analysis, mon- (“one, single”) + -archy (“rule, command”).

meaning: related to monks or monasteries; removed from worldly concerns
etymology: From Middle French monastique, from Late Latin monasticus.

meaning: pertaining to money
etymology: From Middle French monétaire, from Late Latin monētārius (“pertaining to money”), from Latin monētārius (“of a mint”), from monēta (“mint, coinage”), from the presence—from 273 BC to AD 84—of the chief Roman mint at the Templum Iunonis Monetae (“Temple of Juno Moneta”), q.v. Doublet of minter.

meaning: having only one color
etymology: From mono- + chromatic, mono- from Ancient Greek μόνος (mónos, “alone, only, sole, single”), chromatic from Ancient Greek χρῶμα (khrôma, “color”).

meaning: painting in only one color; ADJ.
etymology: From Ancient Greek μονόχρωμος (monókhrōmos), from μόνος (mónos, “one”) + χρῶμα (khrôma, “color”); mono- + -chrome.

meaning: design composed of one or more initials of a name; V.
etymology: From French monogramme, from the Classical Latin adjective monogrammus, from the conjectured Ancient Greek * μονόγραμμος (monógrammos, “outlined”, “drawn with single lines”).

meaning: scholarly article
etymology: From mono- (“one”) + -graph (“write”).

meaning: solidly uniform; unchangeable; unyielding; N. monolith: large block of stone
etymology: From French monolithique. By surface analysis, monolith + -ic.

meaning: belief in one God
etymology: The term was coined by Henry More, ca. 1660, in explicit juxtaposition with both atheism and polytheism. It was redefined through etymological fallacy by Daniel Webster ca. 1828.

meaning: sameness leading to boredom; monotonousness; ADJ. monotonous; CF. monotone
etymology: From French monotonie, from Late Latin monotonia, from Ancient Greek μονοτονία (monotonía, “sameness of tone, monotony”).

meaning: massive; impressively large; built as a monument
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin monumentālis, from Latin monumentum; equivalent to monument + -al.

meaning: fits of depression or gloom; ADJ. moody: given to changeable moods; subject to periods of depression; gloomy CF. mood: state of mind or emotion
etymology: Either inherited from Middle English modinesse (“pride”), from Old English mōdiġnes, or formed anew from moody + -ness.

meaning: legal delay of payment or action; Ex. declare moratorium on the building of new houses
etymology: New Latin from Late Latin morātōrium, noun use of the neuter of morātōrius (“moratory, delaying”), from Latin moror (“to delay”), from mora (“delay”), from Proto-Indo-European *mere (“to delay, hinder”). See also moratory.

meaning: given to unwholesome or unhealthy thought; moody; characteristic of disease; Ex. morbid curiosity; N. morbidity; CF. disease
etymology: From Latin morbidus (“diseased”), from morbus (“sickness”), itself from the root of morī (“to die”) or directly from Proto-Indo-European *mer- (“to rub, pound, wear away”).

meaning: biting; sarcastic; stinging; (apprec.) incisive; cutting; Ex. mordant pen/wit
etymology: From French mordant, from Latin mordeō. Doublet of mordent.

meaning: conventions; moral standards; moral customs
etymology: From Latin mōrēs (“ways, character, morals”), the plural of mōs. Doublet of moeurs.

meaning: dying; at the point of death; CF. death
etymology: From Latin moribundus (“dying”).

meaning: ill-humored; sullen; sullenly melancholy
etymology: From French morose, from Latin mōrōsus (“particular, scrupulous, fastidious, self-willed, wayward, capricious, fretful, peevish”), from mōs (“way, custom, habit, self-will”). See moral.

meaning: undertaker; CF. death
etymology: From Latin mort- (“death”) + -ician.

meaning: funeral director; one whose business is to arrange burials
etymology: From undertake (verb) + -er.

meaning: humiliate by embarassing excessively; shame; punish the flesh; discipline (one'body) by self-denial; Ex. mortified by her blunder; Ex. mortify the flesh; CF. cause to die
etymology: From Anglo-Norman mortifier, Middle French mortifier, from Late Latin mortificō (“cause death”), from Latin mors (“death”) + -ficō (“-fy”).

meaning: picture made of small colorful inlaid tiles; ADJ.
etymology: From Middle French mosaïque, from Italian mosaico, from Medieval Latin musaicum, from Late Latin musivum (opus), from Latin museum, musaeum, probably from Ancient Greek Μουσεῖον (Mouseîon), shrine of the Muses (Μοῦσα (Moûsa)). Doublet of museum.

meaning: small speck (esp. of dust)
etymology: Compare West Frisian mot (“peat dust”), Dutch mot (“dust from turf; sawdust; grit”), Low German mut (“peat dust, grit”), Norwegian mutt (“speck; mote; splinter; chip”), Italian mota (“mud”), Spanish mota (“speck”).

meaning: small piece or mark; Ex. speck of dust in the eye
etymology: From Middle English spekke, from Old English specca (“small spot, stain”), from the same ultimate source as Proto-Germanic *sprakô (“spark”). Cognate with Low German spaken (“to spot with wet”).

meaning: theme; recurrent thematic element in a musical or literary work; single or repeated pattern; figure
etymology: From French motif (1848), with the meaning of "main idea or theme". Doublet of motive.

meaning: ability to move spontaneously; ADJ. motile: moving spontaneously
etymology: From motile + -ity.

meaning: multi-colored (as of a garment worn by a jester); mixed; heterogeneous; CF. jester: one who jests (as a paid fool at medieval courts)
etymology: From Middle English motle, from Anglo-Norman motteley (“parti-colored”), from Old English mot (“speck”). Doublet of mote. The English word can be analysed as mottle + -y.

meaning: brief statement used to express a principle
etymology: Borrowed from Italian motto (“a word, a saying”), from Latin muttum (“a mutter, a grunt”), late 16th c. Doublet of mot.

meaning: blotched in coloring; spotted; Ex. mottled face; V. mottle: mark with blotches of different colors
etymology: 1670-80 mottle + -ed.

meaning: spot; blot; CF. blot+botch
etymology: Uncertain. Perhaps a blend of blot + botch.

meaning: mar; spoil the beauty or perfection of; N: flaw or defect (that spoils perfection); Ex. blemishes in the crystal; CF. unblemished
etymology: From Middle English blemisshen, blemissen, from Old French blemiss-, stem of Old French blemir, blesmir (“make pale, injure, wound, bruise”) (French blêmir), from Old Frankish *blesmijan, *blasmijan (“to make pale”), from Old Frankish *blasmī (“pale”), from Proto-Germanic *blasaz (“white, pale”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to shine”). Cognate with Dutch bles (“white spot”), German blass (“pale”), Old English āblered (“bare, uncovered, bald, shaven”).

meaning: charlatan; boastful pretender
etymology: From archaic Italian montambanco (“quack who mounts a bench to hawk his wares”), contracted from monta-in-banco (“mount on bench”).

meaning: travel about selling (wares); CF. foot
etymology: Back-formation from pedlar. (Compare burgle from burglar.)

meaning: confuse; mix up confusedly; N: state of confusion
etymology: From Middle English modelen (attested in present participle modeland (“wallowing”)), from Middle Dutch moddelen (“to make muddy”), from modde, mod (“mud”) (Modern Dutch modder). By surface analysis, mud + -le. Compare German Kuddelmuddel.

meaning: (of weather) warm and damp
etymology: From dialectal English mug (“fog, mist; Scotch mist”) + -y, ultimately from Old Norse mugga (“drizzle, mist”); borrowed some time before 1390, when a derived verb, Middle English mugen (“of a fog: to drizzle”), is attested.

meaning: defraud a person of something; swindle; Ex. mulct the boy of his legacy
etymology: From Middle French mulcter (“to fine, punish”), from Latin mulcta (“penalty, fine”). Possibly a doublet of milk.

meaning: varied; greatly diversified; Ex. multifarious activities
etymology: From Latin multifārius.

meaning: having many forms
etymology: From multi- + form.

meaning: having many languages; fluent in several languages
etymology: From multi- + lingual.

meaning: state of being numerous or multiple; large number; Ex. multiplicity of details; ADJ. multiple: of more than one element
etymology: Derived from Latin multiplicitas.

meaning: worldly as opposed to spiritual; everyday; of the ordinary; Ex. mundane existence; CF. world
etymology: (ordinary): Compare typologically Russian несусве́тный (nesusvétnyj) (<~ не- (ne-) + (rare) сусве́тный (susvétnyj) < свет (svet)).

meaning: very generous in giving; Ex. munificent benefactor; N. munificience
etymology: Back-formation from munificence, from Latin mūnificentia.

meaning: wall painting
etymology: Borrowed from French mural, from Latin muralis, from murus (“wall”).

meaning: dark and gloomy; thick with fog; vague; Ex. murky night/fog; N. murk: partial or complete darkness; gloom
etymology: From Middle English mirky. Related to Old Norse myrkr, Russian мрак (mrak) and its Slavic cognates. By surface analysis, murk + -y.

meaning: ponder at length; N: source of inspiration (esp. of a poet)
etymology: From Middle French muse, from Latin Mūsa, from Ancient Greek Μοῦσα (Moûsa).

meaning: having the odor of musk; N. musk: odorous substance secreted by an Asian deer
etymology: From musk + -y.

meaning: gather; assemble (troops); Ex. muster up one'strength for the ordeal; N.
etymology: From Middle English musteren, borrowed from Anglo-Norman mostrer, Middle French monstrer, moustrer (whence the noun monstre, which gave the English noun), from Latin mōnstrō (“to show”), from moneō (“to admonish”). Cognate with French montrer (“to show”), Italian mostrare (“to show”), Spanish mostrar (“to show”). See also monster.

meaning: stale (in odor or taste); spoiled by age; CF. moist
etymology: * Spanish mustio (“wilted, withered; gloomy, sad”)

meaning: ability to change in form; fickleness; ADJ. mutable: able to change; fickle; CF. mutate; CF. mutant
etymology: From Middle English mutabilite, from Old French mutabilite, from Latin mutabilitas; equivalent to mutable + -ity.

meaning: silent; muffled; toned down; Ex. muted traffic noise
silent; without speech; not pronounced; unable to speak; N: one who is incapable of speech; V: soften the sound, color, shade of
etymology: From Middle English muet, from Anglo-Norman muet, moet, Middle French muet, from mu (“dumb, mute”) + -et, remodelled after Latin mūtus.

meaning: maim; injure lastingly; deprive of a limb or an essential part
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin mutilātus, the perfect passive participle of mutilō (“to mutilate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), itself from mutilus (“maimed”).

meaning: unruly; rebellious; Ex. mutinous teenagers; N. mutiny: open rebellion; CF. mutineer
nearsighted; lacking foresight; N. myopia
etymology: From myopia + -ic.

meaning: very large number; ADJ. CF. ten thousand
etymology: From French myriade, from Late Latin mȳriadem (accusative of mȳrias), from Ancient Greek μυριάς (muriás, “number of 10,000”), from μυρίος (muríos, “numberless, countless, infinite”). By surface analysis, myria- + -ad.

meaning: lowest point; point on the celestial sphere diametrically opposite the zenith
etymology: From Medieval Latin nadir, from Arabic نَظِير السَّمْت (naẓīr as-samt), composed of نَظِير (naẓīr, “counterpart, corresponding to”) and السَّمْت (as-samt, “the zenith”).

meaning: "quality of being unsophisticated; simplicity; artlessness; gullibility; ADJ. naive (na\""ive): ingenuous; lacking worldliness; simple; credulous"
conceited person; N. narcissism; CF. narcissus
etymology: From Narcissus (“a character in Greek mythology who became obsessed with his own reflection”) + -ist.

meaning: related to telling a story; N: narrated account; story; V. narrate: tell (a story); CF. narration
etymology: Borrowed from Middle Scots narrative, nerrative, from Middle French narratif, from Latin narrātīvus, from narrō (“to narrate”). By surface analysis, Latin narr- + -ate + -ive.

meaning: incipient; coming into being or existence; Ex. nascent ability in music
etymology: Borrowed from Latin nāscēns, nāscentis, present participle of nāscor (“to be born”). Doublet of naissant.

meaning: swimming
etymology: Borrowed from Latin natātiō.

meaning: neatly or smartly dressed; dapper; smart; Ex. natty dresser
etymology: Originally slang, perhaps related to natural.

meaning: intelligent; quick and energetic; fashionable; Ex. smart pace/restaurant; V: cause or feel a sharp pain; N: smarting pain
etymology: From Middle English smerten, from Old English *smeortan (“to smart”), from Proto-West Germanic *smertan, from Proto-Germanic *smertaną (“to hurt, ache”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)merd- (“to bite, sting”). Cognate with Scots smert, Dutch smarten, German schmerzen, Danish smerte, Swedish smärta.

meaning: cause to become sick; fill with disgust; fill nausea
etymology: From earlier nauseat, from Latin nauseātus (“nauseated”), perfect past participle of nauseō (“to feel sea sick, nauseate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix, of participial origin)), from nausea, from Ancient Greek ναυσία (nausía), from ναῦς (naûs), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)neh₂-. By surface analysis, nausea + -ate (verb-forming suffix).

meaning: feeling of sickness and desire to vomit; disgust; CF. seasickness
etymology: From Middle English nausea, a borrowing from Latin nausea, from Ancient Greek ναυσία (nausía, “sea-sickness”), from ναῦς (naûs, “ship”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)neh₂-. Displaced native Old English wlǣtta.

meaning: causing nausea; feeling nausea
etymology: From Latin nauseōsus (“causing nausea”), corresponding synchronically to nausea + -ous.

meaning: pertaining to ships or navigation
etymology: From Middle French nautique (“of or relating to sailors or navigation”) or its etymon, Classical Latin nauticus (“of or relating to ships, seafaring”), + -al (adjectival suffix). Nauticus is from Ancient Greek ναυτικός (nautikós), from ναύτης (naútēs, “sailor”) + -ικός (-ikós, adjecival suffix). Compare later nautic. With use as noun compare Classical Latin nauticus (“sailor”).

meaning: (of a body of water) wide and deep enough to allow ships to pass through; (of a ship or aircraft) able to be steered
etymology: From Middle French navigable, from Latin navigabilis.

meaning: vague; hazy; cloudy; of a nebula; Ex. nebulous proposal
etymology: * Old English nifol, neowol (“dark, gloomy, obscure, precipitous, prone”)

meaning: diffuse mass of interstellar dust or gas; galaxy
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin nebula (“little cloud, mist”). First attested in 1655. Akin to Ancient Greek νεφέλη (nephélē, “cloud”), German Nebel (“mist, nebula”), Old Norse nifl, Polish niebo (“sky, heaven”), Russian не́бо (nébo, “sky”).

meaning: black magic; sorcery; dealings with the dead; art that professes to communicate with the spirits of the dead so as to predict the future; CF. necromancer; CF. necro+divination; CF. necro-: death; Ex. necropolis
etymology: Circa 1300, from Middle English nigromancye, from Old French nigromancie, from Medieval Latin nigromantia, from Latin necromantia, from Ancient Greek νεκρομαντεία (nekromanteía), νεκρός (nekrós, “dead”) + μαντεία (manteía, “divination”). Medieval Latin spelling, incorporating niger (“black”), influenced by the notion of black art. Modern spelling adopted in mid-1500s. By surface analysis, necro- + -mancy.

meaning: very wicked
etymology: From Latin nefārius (“execrable, abominable”), from nefās (“something contrary to divine law, an impious deed, sin, crime”), from ne- (“not”) + fās (“the dictates of religion, divine law”), which is related to Latin for (“to speak, to say”) and cognate to Ancient Greek φημί (phēmí, “to say”).

meaning: cancel out; nullify; cause to have no effect; deny; N. negation
etymology: From Latin negātus, perfect passive participle of negō (“to deny, refuse, decline”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

meaning: neglect; failure to take reasonable care; ADJ. negligent: neglectful; lax; not taking enough care
etymology: From Middle English necligence, negligence, from Old French negligence, from Latin neglegentia.

meaning: so small, trifling, or unimportant as to be easily disregarded
etymology: From negligence/negligent + -ible, as if from New Latin *negligibilis, from Latin neglegō (“to neglect”) + -ibilis (“-ible”).

meaning: someone seeking revenge; source of downfall or ruin; CF. Nemesis
etymology: From the Greek goddess of retribution Nemesis (Ancient Greek Νέμεσις (Némesis)).

meaning: new or newly coined word or phrase
etymology: From French néologisme, from Ancient Greek νέος (néos, “new”) + λόγος (lógos, “word”) + -ism.

meaning: recent convert; new member of a religious group; beginner; CF. plant
etymology: Borrowed from Latin neophytus, from Ancient Greek νεόφυτος (neóphutos, “newly planted”), from νέος (néos, “new”) + φυτόν (phutón, “plant, child”). By surface analysis, neo- + -phyte.

meaning: favoritism (to a relative); CF. nephew
etymology: Borrowed from French népotisme, from Italian nepotismo, from Latin nepōs (“nephew”), a reference to the practice of popes appointing relatives (most often nephews) as cardinals (cardinal-nephew) during the Middle Ages and Renaissance.

meaning: display of partiality toward a favored person
etymology: From favorite + -ism.

meaning: lower; Ex. nether garments/regions
etymology: From Middle English nether, nethere, nithere, from Old English niþera (“lower, under, lowest”, adjective), from niþer, niþor (“below, beneath, down, downwards, lower, in an inferior position”, adverb), from Proto-West Germanic *niþer, from Proto-Germanic *niþer, *niþra (“down”), from Proto-Indo-European *ni-, *nei- (“in, down”). Cognates include Dutch neder, German nieder, Luxembourgish nidder, Danish, Norwegian and Swedish ned (“down”), Danish, Norwegian and Swedish nedre (“lower”), Faroese and Icelandic niður.

meaning: irritate; annoy; vex; ADJ. nettlesome
etymology: From Middle English netle, netel, from Old English netle, netele, netel, from Proto-West Germanic *natilā (cognate with Old Saxon netila, Middle Dutch netele (modern Dutch netel), German Nessel, Middle Danish nædlæ (“nettle”)), a diminutive of Proto-Germanic *natǭ (of unknown origin, perhaps from the same source as net).

meaning: connection
etymology: From Latin nexus (“connection, nexus; act of binding, tying or fastening together; something which binds, binding, bond, fastening, joint; legal obligation”), from nectō (“to attach, bind, connect, fasten, tie; to interweave; to relate; to unite; to bind by obligation, make liable, oblige; to compose, contrive, devise, produce”, supine stem nex-) + -tus (suffix forming verbal nouns).

meaning: beak (bill); pen point
etymology: From a variant of neb, perhaps due to association with nibble.

meaning: precision; accuracy; minute distinction or difference; Ex. to a nicety: exactly; precisely; Ex. distinguish between niceties
etymology: From Middle English nicetee, from Old French niceté (“simpleness, foolishness”), from nice (“simple, foolish”); equivalent to nice + -e- + -ty.

meaning: meanly stingy; parsimonious; N. niggard: stingy person
etymology: From niggard + -ly (adjectival suffix).

meaning: spend too much time on minor points (esp. when finding fault); find fault; Ex. niggle over details; ADJ. niggling
etymology: First attested in 1599. Origin uncertain, but likely borrowed from dialectal Norwegian nigla (“to be stingy, to busy oneself with trifles”), ultimately from Old Norse hnøggr (“stingy; miserly”), related to Old English hnēaw (“stingy; niggardly”). More at niggard.

meaning: one who considers traditional beliefs to be groundless and existence meaningless; absolute skeptic; revolutionary terrorist; CF. nihilism: belief that nothing has meaning or value; belief that destruction of existing political or social institutions is necessary for future improvement
etymology: From Latin nihil (“nothing”) + -ist.

meaning: snip off; stop something'growth or development; bite; make numb with cold; Ex. nip the plan; Ex. A guard dog nipped the postman; Ex. fingers nipped by the extreme chill
etymology: Related to Dutch nijpen, knijpen (“to pinch”), Danish nive (“pinch”); Swedish nypa (“pinch”); Low German knipen; German kneipen and kneifen (“to pinch, cut off, nip”), Old Norse hnippa (“to prod, poke”); Lithuanian knebti.

meaning: short quick cut with scissors; V: cut with scissors
etymology: From Dutch snippen (“to snip; shred”) or Low German snippen (“to snip; shred”), of imitative origin. Compare snap.

meaning: squeeze between the thumb and a finger, or other edges; Ex. I had to pinch myself to make sure I wasn't dreaming. N: amount that can be held between the thumb and a finger
etymology: From Middle English pinchen, from Old Northern French *pinchier (compare Old French pincier, pincer (“to pinch”)), a word of uncertain origin, possibly from Vulgar Latin *pinciāre (“to puncture, pinch”), from a merger of *punctiāre (“to puncture, sting”), from Latin punctiō (“a puncture, prick”) and *piccāre (“to strike, sting”), from Frankish *pikkōn, from Proto-Germanic *pikkōną (“to pick, peck, prick”). More at point, pick and pitch.

meaning: in Buddhist teachings, the ideal state in which the individual loses himself in the attainment of an impersonal beatitude
etymology: Borrowed from Sanskrit निर्वाण (nirvāṇa, “blown or put out, extinguished”), from निस् (nis, “out”) + वा (vā, “to blow”), the second part cognate with Russian ве́тер (véter, “wind”), weather, vent and wind.

meaning: not being a person; not showing personal feelings; Ex. impersonal force/manner/organization
etymology: From French impersonnel, from Latin impersōnālis, from im- (“not”) + persōnālis (“personal”), equivalent to im- + personal.

meaning: done or active at night; Ex. nocturnal animals/raids; CF. nocturne
etymology: From Middle French nocturnal, from Latin nocturnālis (“nocturnal”), from Latin nocturnus (“nocturnal”), from Latin nox (“night”), from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts (“night”). Cognates include Ancient Greek νύξ (núx), Sanskrit नक्ति (nákti), Old English niht (English night) and Proto-Slavic *noťь.

meaning: foul smelling; very unpleasant; unwholesome
etymology: From Middle English noysom; equivalent to noy + -some (short for annoy, from an(n)oien, enoien from Anglo-Norman anuier, from Old French enuier (French ennuyer), from Late Latin inodiare, from in- (intensive prefix) + odium (“hate”)).

meaning: wandering; N. nomad: tribe who migrates from place to place
etymology: From Ancient Greek νομαδικός (nomadikós), equivalent to nomad (“a member of a society or class of herdsmen”) + -ic (forming adjectives).

meaning: terminology (system of specialized words); system of names or naming things
etymology: Borrowed from Latin nōmenclātūra (“a calling by name, list of names”), from nōmen (“name”) + calāre (“call”). Doublet of nomenklatura.

meaning: in name only; of a name; trifling; (of a sum of money) very small; CF. nominate: propose as a candidate; appoint
etymology: From the Middle English nominalle (“of nouns”), borrowed from Latin nōminālis (“of names”), ultimately from oblique stem of Latin nōmen, nōminis (“name”) + -al.

meaning: indifference; lack of concern; composure; ADJ. nonchalant: unconcerned; cool; indifferent; Ex. nonchalant attitude to his debts
etymology: Borrowed from French nonchalance.

meaning: neutral; refusing commitment to a particular opinion; unpledged; undecided
etymology: From non- + committal.

meaning: undistinctive; ordinary; ordinary-looking; Ex. nondescript fellow in a crowd
etymology: From non- + descript (from Latin dēscrīptus, past participle of dēscrībō).

meaning: person of no importance; nonexistence
etymology: From non- + entity.

meaning: put at a loss; bring to a halt by confusion; perplex; CF. no more
etymology: The verb is derived from the noun.

meaning: homesickness; longing for the past; Ex. nostalgia for the clothes of 1920s; ADJ. nostalgic
etymology: Compare Italian nostalgia, Spanish nostalgia, Portuguese nostalgia and French nostalgie.

meaning: questionable medicine; quack medicine; CF. our (remedy)
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin nostrum (“ours”), nominative neuter of noster (“our, ours”).

meaning: conspicuous; worthy of note; remarkable; important; distinguished; noted
etymology: Inherited from Middle English notable (“worthy of note, profitable, useful”), in some senses from Anglo-Norman notable (“noteworthy”), from Latin notābilis (“noteworthy, extraordinary”), from notō (“to note, mark”); in some senses from Middle English note (“benefit, profit, use, advantage”), from Old English notu (“t-use, profit, advantage, employment”) + -able; equivalent to note + -able. Compare English noteful (“useful”).

meaning: disrepute; ill fame
etymology: Derived from Middle French notoriété, from Medieval Latin nōtōrietās, from nōtōrius, from nōtus (“known”), perfect passive participle of nōscō (“get to know”). By surface analysis, notorious + -ety.

meaning: star that suddenly becomes much brighter and then returns to its original brightness
etymology: Feminine nominative singular of Latin novus (“new”). The feminine is used since stella (“star”) is feminine; thus nova is a shortening of nova stella (“new star”), first used in this sense in 1573 by Tycho Brahe.

meaning: something new; newness; ADJ. novel: new; original
etymology: From Middle English novelte, from Old French novelté (Modern French nouveauté), from the adjective novel, ultimately from Latin novellus. By surface analysis, novel + -ty.

meaning: beginner
etymology: From Middle English novice, novys, from Anglo-Norman novice, Middle French novice, itself borrowed from Latin novīcius, later novitius (“new, newly arrived”) (in Late Latin as a noun, masculine novicius, feminine novicia (“one who has newly entered a monastery or a convent”)), from novus (“new”).

meaning: harmful; CF. obnoxious
etymology: From Latin noxius (“hurtful, injurious”), from noxa (“hurt, injury”), from nocere (“to hurt, injure”); see nocent.

meaning: shade of slight difference in meaning or color; subtle distinction
etymology: Compare typologically Italian sfumatura (< Latin fūmus).

meaning: slight difference in degree; nuance; degree of color; Ex. shades of meaning/grey
etymology: Inherited from Middle English schade, from Old English sċeadu, from Proto-West Germanic *skadu, from Proto-Germanic *skaduz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ḱh₃tús, from *(s)ḱeh₃-. Doublet of shadow. Cognate with Ancient Greek σκότος (skótos) (whence English scoto-) and σκιά (skiá) (whence English scia-, and uncertainly via σκίουρος (skíouros) English squirrel).

meaning: series of gradual stages; degree in such a progression
etymology: Borrowed from French gradation. By surface analysis, grade + -ation.

meaning: marriageable; of marriageable age; CF. connubial
etymology: From French nubile, from Latin nūbilis (“marriageable”), from nūbō (“marry, to take as husband”), from Proto-Indo-European *snewbʰ- (“to marry, to wed”). Possibly cognate with Ancient Greek νύμφη (númphē, “bride, young wife, nymph”) (English nymph), but this is disputed.

meaning: worthless; futile
etymology: Borrowed from Latin nūgātōrius, from nūgātor m (“jester”) + -ius (“suffix forming adjectives”).

meaning: make invalid; make null; invalidate
etymology: From null + -ify.

meaning: person who collects coins; N. numismatics: study or collection of money, coins, and medals
etymology: From numismatics + -ist.

meaning: nourish; feed; educate; rear; care for while it is growing or developing; foster; cultivate; N: something that nourishes; rearing
etymology: From Middle English norture, noriture, from Old French norriture, norreture, from Late Latin nutritura (“nourishment”), from Latin nutrire (“to nourish”).

meaning: nourishing substance; ADJ: providing nourishment
etymology: Borrowed from Latin nūtriēns, present participle of nūtriō (“to suckle, nourish, foster”).

meaning: process of nourishing or being nourished; CF. malnutrition
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French nutrition, from Old French nutricion, from Latin nutritio.

meaning: providing nourishment
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin nūtrītius, from nūtrītus, from nūtrīre.

meaning: provide with food necessary for life and growth
etymology: From Middle English norischen, from Old French nouriss-, stem of one of the conjugated forms of norrir, from Latin nutriō (“to suckle, feed, foster, nourish, cherish, preserve, support”).

meaning: something that nourishes; food
etymology: From Middle English norisshement, from Middle French, from Old French norissement, from norrir, equivalent to nourish + -ment.

meaning: stupid awkward person; CF. elf
etymology: Variant of awf, aufe, probably from Old Norse álfr (“elf”) (whence Norwegian Bokmål alv). Doublet of alf and elf.

meaning: stubborn; refusing to change one'belief
etymology: First attested in the 1450s, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English obdurat(e), borrowed from Latin obdūrātus (“hardened”), perfect passive participle of obdūrō (“to harden”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ob- (“against”) + dūrō (“to harden, render hard”), from dūrus (“hard”). Compare durable, endure.

meaning: bow (to show respect and obedience)
etymology: From Middle English obeisaunce (“obedience, obeisance”), from Old French obeïssance, derived from obeïssant (“obedient”), participle of obeïr (“to obey”), from Latin oboediō, obēdiō; ob- (“to, for”) + audiō (“to hear”). Cognate with obedience.

meaning: tall column tapering (becoming gradually narrower toward the end) and ending in a pyramid
etymology: From Middle French obelisque, from Latin obeliscus (“obelisk”), from Ancient Greek ὀβελίσκος (obelískos), diminutive of ὀβελός (obelós, “needle”). Compare obelus.

meaning: excessively fat; N. obesity
etymology: From Latin obēsus, derived from obedō (“to devour, eat away”), from ob (“away”) + edō (“to eat”).

meaning: confuse; muddle; cause confusion; make needlessly complex; make so confused as to be difficult to understand
etymology: The adjective is first attested in 1487, in Middle English, the verb in 1536; either borrowed from Middle French obfusquer, offusquer, from Old French offusquer, or directly from Late Latin obfuscātus, offuscātus, the perfect passive participle of obfuscō, offuscō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from Latin ob- + fuscō (“to darken”). Doublet of dusken (“to darken, make obscure”).

meaning: death notice (esp. in a newspaper); ADJ.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin obituārius (“obituary”) + English -ary (suffix denoting something relating to another thing or used in a place). Obituārius is derived from Latin obitus (“act of approaching or going toward, an approach; act of going down, setting; of the sun: sunset; death; destruction, downfall, ruin”) + -ārius (suffix forming adjectives and agent nouns); while obitus is a noun use of the perfect passive participle of obeō (“to go to meet, go towards; (figurative) to die, pass away, perish; (astronomy) to set”), from ob- (prefix meaning ‘toward’) + eō (“to go, move”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ey- (“to go”).

meaning: not influenced by emotions; fair; N: goal; aim
etymology: From Middle English obgectyf, from Middle French objectif and its etymon Medieval Latin obiectīvus. By surface analysis, object + -ive.

meaning: binding; required; compulsory; V. oblige: constrain; make grateful; do a favor; accommodate
etymology: From Middle English obligatorie, from Latin obligatōrius.

meaning: indirect; slanting (deviating from the perpendicular or from a straight line); Ex. oblique reference
etymology: From Middle French oblique, from Latin oblīquus (also spelled oblīcus) (“slanting, sideways, indirect, envious”).

meaning: destroy completely; wipe out; Ex. obliterate the village
etymology: * Spanish obliterar (“to destroy completely; to erase”)

meaning: obscurity; condition of being completely forgotten; forgetfulness
etymology: Inherited from Middle English oblivion, from Anglo-Norman oblivion, from Latin oblīviō (“forgetfulness”), from oblīvīscor (“to forget”).

meaning: inattentive or unmindful; unaware; wholly absorbed; forgetful (having the habit of forgetting)
etymology: From Middle English oblivious, from Latin oblīviōsus (“forgetful, oblivious”), formed from oblīvium (“forgetfulness, oblivion”) + -ōsus (“full of, overly, prone to”), from oblīvīscor (“to forget”).

meaning: slander; disgrace; infamy
etymology: From Middle English obloqui, obloquie, obloquy, from Middle French obloquie and its etymon Late Latin obloquium (“contradiction”), from Latin obloquor (“speak against, contradict”). By surface analysis, ob- + -loquy.

meaning: offensive; disagreeable; Ex. obnoxious smell
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin obnoxiōsus.

meaning: dark; vague; unclear; not well known; Ex. obscure meaning/village; V: darken; cover; make unclear; Ex. obscure the moon/meaning
etymology: From Middle English obscure, from Old French obscur, from Latin obscūrus (“dark, dusky, indistinct”), from ob- + *scūrus, from Proto-Italic *skoiros, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ḱeh₃-. Doublet of oscuro.

meaning: slavishly attentive; servile; full of servile compliance; sycophantic
etymology: From Middle English obsequyous, from Latin obsequiōsus (“complaisant, obsequious”), from obsequium (“compliance”), from obsequor (“comply with, yield to”), from ob (“in the direction of, towards”) + sequor (“follow”) (cf. sequel).

meaning: of or like a slave; servile; showing no originality; copied very closely; Ex. slavish devotion/copy of the original
etymology: From slave + -ish.

meaning: funeral ceremony
etymology: From Middle English obseque, from Old French obseque, osseque, from Latin obsequiī (“complaisant, yielding”), alteration of obsequia (“compliance”) (by confusion, in association with exsequia (“funeral rites”), from exsequī (“follow or accompany to the grave”)).

meaning: related to thinking about something constantly; of an obsession; preoccupying; N. obsession: compulsive preoccupation with a fixed idea; compulsive idea; V. obsess: preoccupy the mind of excessively
etymology: From obsess + -ive.

meaning: black volcanic rock
etymology: From Latin obsidianus; named after Obsidius, who was, according to Pliny, the Roman who discovered the stone in Aethiopia.

meaning: detached plant shoot used in grafting; descendant
etymology: From Middle English sion, sioun, syon, scion, cion, from Old French cion, ciun, cyon, sion, from Frankish *kīþō, *kīþ, from Proto-Germanic *kīþô, *kīþą, *kīþaz (“sprout”), from Proto-Indo-European *geye- (“to split open, sprout”), same source as Old English ċīþ (“a young shoot; sprout; germ; sprig”), Old Saxon kīth (“sprout; germ”), Old High German kīdi (“offshoot; sprout; germ”). See also French scion and Picard chion. Doublet of chit.

meaning: outmoded; no longer used
etymology: Borrowed from Latin obsolētus (“worn out, gone out of use”), past participle of obsolēscere (“to wear out, fall into disuse, grow old, decay”); see obsolesce.

meaning: physician specializing in delivery (assisting in giving birth) of babies; N. obstetrics; CF. midwife
etymology: From obstetrics + -ician.

meaning: stubborn; hard to control or treat; Ex. obstinate cough; N. obstinacy
etymology: Inherited from Middle English obstinat(e) (“obstinate, stubborn”), from Latin obstinātus, perfect passive participle of obstinō (“set one's mind firmly upon, resolve”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ob (“before”) + *stinare, from stare (“to stand”). Doublet of ostinato.

meaning: boisterous; noisy and uncontrollable
etymology: Borrowed from Latin obstreperus, first attested circa 17th c. Compare obstropulous.

meaning: push (oneself or one'ideas) forward or intrude; impose (oneself or one'ideas) on others; butt in; stick out or extrude; thrust out; Ex. obtrude A on B; ADJ. obtrusive; N. obtrusion; CF. unobtrusive
etymology: From Latin obtrūdō (“thrust off or against”), from ob- (“ob-”) + trūdō (“thrust”).

meaning: blunt; not sharp; stupid; slow in understanding
etymology: From Middle English obtuse, from Latin obtūsus (“blunt, dull; obtuse”), past participle of obtundere, from obtundō (“to batter, beat, strike; to blunt, dull”), from ob- (“against”) (see ob-) + tundō (“to beat, strike; to bruise, crush, pound”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewd-, from *(s)tew- (“to hit; to push”)). More at obtund.

meaning: make unnecessary; get rid of; Ex. obviate the need
etymology: First attested in 1567; borrowed from Latin obviātus, perfect passive participle of obviō (“to block, to hinder”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

meaning: the West
etymology: From Middle English occident, from Old French occident, from Latin occidentem (“western sky, part of the sky in which the sun sets”), from occido (“go down, set”).

meaning: shut; close; obstruct; Ex. A blood clot occluded an artery.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin occlūdere, from ob (“before”) and claudere (“to shut”).

meaning: mysterious; secret; supernatural; beyond human comprehension; CF. mysterious to human ?; OP. bare
etymology: Borrowed from Latin occultus (“hidden, secret”).

meaning: physician who specializes in treatment of the eyes
etymology: From French oculiste (“oculist”), from Latin oculus (“eye”).

meaning: arousing strong dislike; hateful (causing hatred); vile
etymology: From Middle English odious, from Old French odieus, from Latin odiōsus, from odium (“hate”).

meaning: detestation; quality of being odious; hatefulness; disrepute (resulting from hateful conduct)
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin odium, from Proto-Italic *odjom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ed-.

meaning: giving off an odor
etymology: From Latin. By surface analysis, odor + -i- (“bearing, carrying”) + -ferous.

meaning: having an odor
etymology: From Middle English odorous, from Medieval Latin odōrōsus, equivalent to odor + -ous.

meaning: long, eventful, adventurous journey
etymology: From Odyssey, from Ancient Greek Ὀδυσσεία (Odusseía, “the story of Odysseus”).

meaning: attacking; insulting; distasteful; V. offend: violate; hurt the feelings of; N. offense: offending; violating of a moral or social code; crime; attack; Ex. first offense
etymology: From Middle French offensif, from offendre + -if by analogy with défensif. Offendre is from Latin offendere (“to offend”); see offend.

meaning: casual; done without prior thought or preparation
etymology: From Middle English *ofhande, *ofhende, from Old English ofhende (“absent, lost”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *abahandijaz. Equivalent to (and re-formed as) off- + hand. Cognate with Icelandic afhendur. Compare onhand.

meaning: meddlesome; excessively pushy in offering one'services; overly eager in offering unwanted services or advices; Ex. officious bellboy
etymology: 15th century, from Middle English offycyous, from Latin officiōsus (“kindly”), from officium (“service”).

meaning: disagreeably aggressive
etymology: From push + -y.

meaning: look at amorously; make eyes at; Ex. old men ogling young girls
etymology: 17th century. Probably from Low German ögeln (“to ogle, to flirt with one's eyes”), from Middle Low German ö̂gelen, frequentative of Middle Low German ö̂gen, from Old Saxon ōgian, from Proto-West Germanic *augijan (“to show”). Alternatively from an equivalent Dutch *ogelen, but this seems unattested (only the simplex ogen). By surface analysis, eye + -le.

meaning: concerning the sense of smell
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin olfactōrius.

meaning: government by a privileged few
etymology: By surface analysis, oligo- (“few”) + -archy (“rule, command”).

meaning: threatening; of an evil omen
etymology: From Latin ōminōsus (“full of foreboding”), from ōmen (“forbidden fruit, omen”), from Old Latin osmen, of uncertain origin, with many origins proposed (see ōmen).

meaning: sign or warning (of coming danger); Ex. threat of rain; V: express a threat; give warning of (something bad); Ex. The cloud threatens rain.
etymology: From Middle English threte, thret, thrat, thræt, threat, from Old English þrēat (“crowd, swarm, troop, army, press; pressure, trouble, calamity, oppression, force, violence, threat”), from Proto-Germanic *þrautaz, closely tied to Proto-Germanic *þrautą (“displeasure, complaint, grievance, labour, toil”), from Proto-Indo-European *trewd- (“to squeeze, push, press”). Cognate with Scots thret, threte, threit (“threat”), Middle High German drōz (“annoyance, disgust, horror, terror, fright”), Middle Low German drōt (“threat, menace, danger”), Faroese treyt (“struggle, labour, distress”), Icelandic þraut (“struggle, labour, distress”), Belarusian, Bulgarian, Macedonian, Russian, and Ukrainian труд (trud, “work, labour”), Czech trud (“effot, hard work”), Polish trud (“hard work”), Serbo-Croatian trȗd (“effort, hard work”).

meaning: all-powerful; having unlimited power
etymology: Inherited from Middle English omnipotent(e), from Old French omnipotent, from Latin omnipotēns, omnipotentem.

meaning: universally present; ubiquitous
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin omnipraesēns, equivalent to omni- + present.

meaning: all-knowing
etymology: From Medieval Latin omnisciens (“all-knowing”), from Latin omnis (“all”) + sciens (“knowing”) (further analysable via scient).

meaning: eating both plant and animal food; devouring everything
etymology: From omni- + -vorous.

meaning: burdensome
etymology: Inherited from Middle English onerous, borrowed from Middle French onereux, from Old French onereus, a learned borrowing from Latin onerosus, from onus (“burden”) + -ōsus. Compare exonerate.

meaning: words formed in imitation of natural sounds
etymology: Borrowed from Latin onomatopoeïa, from Ancient Greek ὀνοματοποιία (onomatopoiía, “the coining of a word in imitation of a sound”), from ὀνοματοποιέω (onomatopoiéō, “to coin names”), from ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”) + ποιέω (poiéō, “to make, to do, to produce”). By surface analysis, onomato- + -poeia.

meaning: make slight sounds like silk moving or being rubbed together
etymology: From Middle English rustelen, russelen, of uncertain origin, but probably from Old English hrūxlian, hristlan, hrystlan, hristlian (“to make a noise”). Compare also Scots reesle (“to crackle; rattle; rustle”), West Frisian risselje, Dutch ritselen (“to rustle”), Afrikaans ritsel (“to rustle”), German rascheln (“to rustle”).

meaning: vicious assault; fierce attack; Ex. unexpected onslaught of the enemy
etymology: From on- + slaught. Formed after Middle Dutch aenslag, aenslach, equivalent to aen + slag, although slaught corresponds to Middle Dutch slacht; slag is cognate with the English weaving term sley. Compare Dutch aanslag and German Anschlag.

meaning: killing of animals for food; massacre; V: butcher (animals) for food; kill in large numbers
etymology: From Middle English slaughter, from Old Norse *slahtr, later sláttr, from Proto-Germanic *slahtrą, from Proto-Germanic *slahaną. Equivalent to slay + -ter (as in laughter). Eventually derived from Proto-Indo-European *slak- (“to hit, strike, throw”). Related with Dutch slachten, German schlachten, Finnish lahdata (all “to slaughter”).

meaning: burden; responsibility
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin onus (literally “burden”).

meaning: give; use; refrain from harming; save from experiencing; exempt; Ex. spare me 5 minutes; Ex. Take this money and spare my life; Ex. The emperor was spared the onus; ADJ: kept in reserve; free for other use; unoccupied; Ex. spare time
etymology: Compare Dutch spaar(zaam), German spar(sam) and spär(lich), Swedish spar(sam), Icelandic sparr (“sparing”); also Latin (pro)sperus (“lucky”), Old Church Slavonic споръ (sporŭ, “plentiful”), Albanian shperr (“earn money”), Persian سپار (sepâr, “entrust; deposit”), Ancient Greek σπαρνός (sparnós, “rare”), Sanskrit स्फिर (sphirá, “thick”).

meaning: iridescent; lustrous; like an opal; N. opalescence
etymology: From opal + -escent, after opalescence or French opalescent. First attested in 1814.

meaning: dark; not transparent; N. opacity
etymology: From Middle English opake, from Latin opacus (“shaded, shady, dark”) (of unknown origin), later reinforced from Middle French opaque. Doublet of ubac.

meaning: medicine to induce sleep or deaden pain; something that relieves emotions or causes inaction; sleep-producing drug containing opium
etymology: From Middle English opiate, from Medieval Latin opiātus.

meaning: timely; well-chosen
etymology: From Old French opportun, from Latin opportunus.

meaning: individual who sacrifices principles for expediency by taking advantage of circumstances; N. opportunism
etymology: From French opportuniste, equivalent to opportune + -ist.

meaning: infamy; disgrace arising from shameful conduct; vilification (slander); scorn; contempt; Ex. opprobrium hurled against him; ADJ. opprobrious: expressing contempt; shameful or infamous
etymology: * Spanish oprobrio (obsolete), oprobio

meaning: maker and seller of eyeglasses
etymology: Borrowed from French opticien.

meaning: person who looks on the bright side; N. optimism
etymology: Borrowed from French optimiste.

meaning: most favorable; optimal; N: most favorable condition
etymology: From New Latin, neuter of Latin optimus (“best, very good”), from the root in ops (“work”) or omnis (“all”).

meaning: not compulsory; left to one'choice; N. option: act of choosing; choice; freedom or power to choose; something available as a choice; Ex. have no option; Ex. two options
etymology: From option + -al.

meaning: one who fits glasses to remedy visual defects
etymology: From optometry + -ist.

meaning: extreme wealth; luxuriousness; abundance; ADJ. opulent: possessing great wealth; abundant
etymology: From French opulence, from Latin opulentia.

meaning: work (esp. musical composition); Ex. magnum opus: masterpiece; CF. opera
etymology: Borrowed from Latin opus.

meaning: of an oracle; prophetic; uttered as if with divine authority; mysterious or ambiguous; hard to understand; N. oracle: wiser person; prophecy made by an oracle
etymology: From Middle French oraculaire.

meaning: public speaker
etymology: From Middle English oratour, from Anglo-Norman oratour, from Latin ōrātor.

meaning: dramatic poem set to music; long musical work with singing but without acting; CF. cantata
etymology: Borrowed from Italian oratorio (“oratorical”), from Latin ōrātōrius. Doublet of oratory.

meaning: decree or command; grant holy orders; predestine; install as a minister, priest, or rabbi; N. ordainment; CF. ordination
etymology: From Middle English ordeynen, from Old French ordiner, from Latin ordinare (“to order”), from ordo (“order”). Doublet of ordinate.

meaning: severe trial or affliction; difficult experience; trial (test of patience or endurance); affliction
etymology: Cognate with Saterland Frisian Uurdeel (“judgement; verdict”), West Frisian oardiel (“judgement”), Dutch oordeel (“judgement, discretion”), Low German Oordeel (“judgement; verdict”), German Urteil (“judgement, verdict”).

meaning: decree; authoritative order
etymology: From Middle English ordinaunce (ca. 1300), from Old French ordenance (“decree, command”) (modern French ordonnance), from Medieval Latin ordinantia, from ordinans, the present participle of ordino (“put in order”) (whence ordain). Doublet of ordonnance.

meaning: ceremony conferring holy orders; ceremony of ordaining a priest
etymology: From Middle French ordination, from Old French ordinacion, from Latin ordinatio.

meaning: wild drunken revelry; unrestrained indulgence in an activity; Ex. orgy of shopping
etymology: Originally in plural from French orgies, from Latin orgia, from Ancient Greek ὄργια (órgia, “secret rites, mysteries”).

meaning: get one'bearings; adjust; make familiar with a situation; orientate
etymology: The adjective is derived from Middle English orient (“eastern; from Asia or the Orient; brilliant, shining (characteristic of jewels from the Orient)”), from Middle English orient (noun); see above.

meaning: act of finding oneself in society; orienting
etymology: From French orientation. By surface analysis, orient + -ation.

meaning: mouthlike opening; small opening (esp. to a cavern or passage of the body); CF. mouth
etymology: From Middle French, from Old French, from Late Latin ōrificium (“an opening, literally the making of a mouth”), compound of ōs (“mouth”) + faciō (“to make”).

meaning: excessively or elaborately decorated
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin ōrnātus, perfect passive participle of ōrnō (“to equip, adorn”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Doublet of orné.

meaning: scientific student of birds; N. ornithology: scientific study of birds
etymology: From ornithology + -ist.

meaning: traditional; (of someone) conservative in belief; adhering to an established doctrine
etymology: From Late Middle English orthodoxe, from Middle French orthodoxe and its etymon Late Latin orthodoxus, from Ancient Greek ὀρθόδοξος (orthódoxos), from ὀρθός (orthós, “straight”) + δόξα (dóxa, “opinion”). Displaced native Old English wuldorlīċ.

meaning: correct spelling; CF. ortho-: straight; correct; Ex. orthodontics
etymology: * Spanish ortografía

meaning: vibrate pendulumlike; waver
etymology: First attested in 1726; borrowed from Latin ōscillātus, perfect passive participle of Latin ōscillō (“to swing”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ōscillum (“a swing”), usually identified with ōscillum (“a little face or mask hung on a tree that sways with the wind”), diminutive of ōs (“mouth, face”). See also osculate.

meaning: made of bone; bony
etymology: Borrowed from Latin osseus (“bony, (attributive) bone”), from os (“bone”) + -eus.

meaning: change or harden into bone; become hard and unchanging in one'ideas
etymology: Back-formation from ossification, or modeled on French ossifier and formed from Latin os, ossis (“bone”) + -ify.

meaning: apparent; appearing as such; professed (pretended); pretended; Ex. ostensible purpose of the expedition
etymology: Borrowed from French ostensible, formed with the suffix -ible, from Latin ostensus, the past participle of ostendō (“show”), itself from obs- (“in front of”) (akin to ob- (“in the way”)) + tendō (“stretch”) (akin to Ancient Greek τείνω (teínō)). Cf. ostentatious.

meaning: evident; easily seen or understood; appearing as such; Ex. apparent improvement
etymology: From Middle English apparaunt, aparaunt, from Old French aparent, aparant, in turn from Latin appārēns, appārentis, present participle of appāreō.

meaning: showy; trying to attract attention; pretentious; N. ostentation: showy display
etymology: Originated 1590; from Latin ostentātus + -ious.

meaning: banish from a group; exclude from public favor; ban; Ex. His friends ostracized him. N. ostracism
etymology: From Ancient Greek ὀστρακίζω (ostrakízō, “to banish from a city by ostracism”), from ὄστρᾰκον (óstrăkon, “earthenware vessel; fragment of such a vessel, potsherd”) (from the fact that when voting was held to decide whether to banish people, their names were inscribed on potsherds) + -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō, suffix forming verbs)). The English word is cognate with French ostraciser.

meaning: vote against (an applicant); ostracize; N: negative vote
etymology: From black + ball.

meaning: expel; drive out; force out; N. ouster: ousting
etymology: From Anglo-Norman ouster, oustier, from Old French oster (modern French ôter), from post-classical Latin obstare (“to remove”), classical obstāre (“to obstruct, stand in the way of”). Not related to out.

meaning: bizzare; peculiar; unconventional
etymology: * Swedish utländsk (“foreign, non-domestic”)

meaning: no longer in fashion or use; no longer stylish; old-fashioned
fringes; outer borders (as of a city); Ex. outskirts of Boston
etymology: From out- + skirts.

meaning: candid; blunt
etymology: From outspeak, equivalent to out- + spoken.

meaning: having a dull edge; abrupt and frank in speech or manner; brusque; V: make or become blunt
etymology: Compare the Scandinavian-German munitons term blind (“non-live, dummy”), opposite of skarp (“live”, literally, “sharp”): Swedish and Danish blind patron (“dummy round”), Danish blindt skud, German blinder schuss (“dummy shot”), blinde granate (“dummy grenade”).

meaning: outrun; surpass; outdo
etymology: From out- (prefix forming verbs with the sense of exceeding or surpassing) + strip (“(obsolete) to move or pass by quickly”).

meaning: outsmart; defeat by behaving more cleverly
etymology: From out- + wit.

meaning: enthusiastic applause
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin ovātiōnem.

meaning: bossy; domineering and arrogant; decisively important; Ex. overbearing manner/importance; V. overbear: dominate
etymology: From overbear (“to bear down (on)”) + -ing.

meaning: open to view; public; not secret; CF. covert
etymology: From Middle English overt, uverte (“open, uncovered; unfastened; accessible, unobstructed; clear, manifest”), from Anglo-Norman overt, Middle French ouvert, Old French overt, ouvert, uvert (“opened”) (modern French ouvert), past participle of Anglo-Norman, Old French ovrir, ouvrir, uvrir (“to open”), from Late Latin operire, variant of Latin aperīre (“to open”), from aperiō (“to open, uncover”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epó (“away; from”) + *h₂wer- (“to cover, shut”). The English word is a doublet of apert and ouvert.

meaning: arrogant; presumptuous
etymology: From Middle English overweninge, equivalent to overween + -ing. Cognate with obsolete Dutch overwanig, overwaand (“presumptuous; cocky; conceited”).

meaning: nervous or excited; extremely agitated; hysterical; wrought-up; CF. wrought: made or done
etymology: Past participle of overwork; equivalent to over- + wrought.

meaning: excessive or uncontrollable excitement; N. hysteric: person suffering from hysteria; CF. hysterics: attack of hysteria
etymology: From New Latin hysteria, a back-formation from Latin hystericus, from Ancient Greek ὑστερικός (husterikós, “suffering in the uterus, hysterical”), from ὑστέρα (hustéra, “womb”). Compare French hystérie.

meaning: egg-shaped; CF. ovum; CF. ovulate
etymology: From Latin ōvum (“egg”) + -oid (“resembling”).

meaning: thick-skinned animal
etymology: Borrowed from French pachyderme, equivalent to pachy- (“thick”) + -derm (“skin”).

meaning: one opposed to force; antimilitarist; ADJ. N. pacifism: opposition to war as a means of resolving disputes
etymology: From French pacifiste, equivalent to pacific + -ist.

meaning: soothe; make calm or quiet; subdue; bring peace to
etymology: From Middle French pacifier, from Latin pāx (“peace”) + faciō (“to do, make”). Cognate with pay and peacify.

meaning: song of praise or joy; Ex. paeans celebrating the victory
etymology: Compare Middle French and French pæan (also French péan), Italian peana, Portuguese peã, péan.

meaning: taking pains; showing hard work; taking great care; very careful and through
etymology: From pains + taking; see take pains. The /ˈpeɪnˌsteɪkɪŋ/ pronunciation which dominates in the United States suggests a reanalysis of the word as pain + staking.

meaning: agreeable; pleasing to the taste
etymology: From palate + -able.

meaning: roof of the mouth; sense of the taste
etymology: From Middle English palate, from Latin palātum (“roof of the mouth, palate”), perhaps of Etruscan origin.

meaning: of or suitable for a palace; magnificent
etymology: Borrowed from French palatial, formed from the root of Latin palātium (“a palace”), from Palātium (“Palatine Hill”).

meaning: study of prehistoric life or fossils; CF. paleo-: ancient or prehistoric; Ex. paleography: study of ancient written documents
etymology: Attested since 1836 (as palæontology). From French paléontologie (attested since 1822). By surface analysis, paleo- (“ancient”) + onto- (“being”) + -logy (“study”).

meaning: board on which painter mixes pigments (coloring matters)
etymology: Borrowed from French palette. Doublet of pallet.

meaning: parchment or piece of writing material used for second time after original writing has been erased
etymology: From Latin palimpsēstus, from Ancient Greek παλίμψηστος (palímpsēstos, “scraped again”).

meaning: writing material made from the skin of a sheep or goat
etymology: From Middle English parchemyn, parchement, from Old French parchemin, via Latin pergamīna, from Ancient Greek Περγαμηνός (Pergamēnós, “of Pergamon”), which is named for the ancient city of Pergamon (modern Bergama) in Asia Minor, where it was invented as an expensive alternative for papyrus. Cognate with Danish pergament, Dutch perkament, French parchemin, German Pergament, Greek περγαμηνή (pergaminí), Italian pergamena, Norwegian pergament, Portuguese pergaminho, Galician pergameo, Romanian pergament, Russian пергамент (pergament), Spanish pergamino, and Swedish pergament.

meaning: become boring; grow tiresome
etymology: From Middle English pal, palle, from Old English pæl, pæll, from Old French paile and Latin pallium (“cloak; covering”) (and thus a doublet of pallium), probably from palla (“piece of cloth worn as apparel”) (possibly from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“to cover, wrap; hide, skin; cloth”)) + -ium (suffix forming abstract nouns).

meaning: small poor bed; Ex. straw pallet
etymology: From Middle English paillet, from Anglo-Norman paillete (“bundle of straw”), from Old French paille (“straw, chaff”), from Latin palea (“chaff”).

meaning: ease pain (without curing); make less severe or offensive (a crime or illness)
etymology: The verb was inherited from Middle English palliaten (“To palliate (a disease), relieve the symptoms of (a patient); to extenuate (an offense); to conceal, hide”), the adjective and participle from its participle palliat(e); further borrowed either from Middle French pallier or directly from Latin palliātus, perfect passive participle of palliō (“to cover with a cloak”)), from pallium (“a cloak”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

meaning: pale; wan; Ex. pallid complexion
etymology: From Latin pallidus. Doublet of pale.

meaning: tangible; (of something bad) easily perceptible; obvious; Ex. palpable blunder
etymology: From Middle French palpable and its source, Latin palpābilis, which is from palpō (“to touch softly”) + -bilis.

meaning: throb; beat rapidly; flutter; tremble; Ex. Her heart began to palpitate.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin palpitō, palpitātus (“throb, pulsate, palpitate”).

meaning: (of a heart or machine) beat rapidly or violently; N. Ex. hearthrob: heartbeat; sweetheart
etymology: From Middle English throbben; possibly of imitative origin. Cognate with Scots thrab (“to throb”). Compare also drub.

meaning: insignificant; petty; trifling; contemptible; Ex. paltry sum; CF. trash
etymology: Cognate with Low German palterig (“ragged, torn”), dialectal German palterig (“paltry”). Compare also Low German palte (“rag”), West Frisian palt (“rag”), Saterland Frisian Palte (“strip; band; tape”), dialectal German Palter (“rag”), Danish pjalt (“rag, tatter”), Swedish palta (“rag”). See also palterly and pelting.

meaning: criticize harshly
etymology: From Middle English Pan, from Latin Pān, from Ancient Greek Πάν (Pán).

meaning: cure-all; remedy for all diseases
etymology: From Latin panacēa, from Ancient Greek πανάκεια (panákeia), from πανακής (panakḗs, “all-healing”), from πᾶν (pân, “all”) (equivalent to English pan-) + ἄκος (ákos, “cure”).

meaning: flair; manner of doing things without any difficulty (causing admiration); flamboyance; bunch of feathers (on a helmet); Ex. with great panache; CF. ÀÜ ¾Æ·¡·Î ÃµÀ» »©³»´Â ¼Ø¾¾
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French panache, from Middle French pennache (“plume of feathers”), from Italian pennacchio, from Late Latin pinnāculum. Doublet of pinnacle.

meaning: widespread; affecting the majority of people; N: pandemic disease; CF. all people
etymology: From Ancient Greek πάνδημος (pándēmos, “of or belonging to all the people, public”) + English -ic (suffix forming adjectives from nouns with the sense ‘of or pertaining to’). πάνδημος is derived from παν- (pan-, prefix meaning ‘all, every’) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- (“to protect, shepherd”)) + δῆμος (dêmos, “the common people; free citizens, sovereign people”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *deh₂- (“to divide, share”)). Compare Late Latin pandēmus (“affecting all the people, general, public”).

meaning: wild tumult (commotion); wild noisy disorder; CF. Paradise Lost
etymology: Coined by John Milton in Paradise Lost as Pandæmonium, from Ancient Greek πᾶν (pân, “all”) (equivalent to pan-) + Late Latin daemonium (“evil spirit, demon”), from Ancient Greek δαιμόνιον (daimónion, “deity”).

meaning: cater to (the low desires of others)
etymology: From Middle English pandare, from Chaucer’s character Pandare (in Troilus and Criseyde; see also Shakespeare’s Troilus and Cressida), from Italian Pandaro (found in Boccaccio), from Latin Pandarus (found in Greek mythology), from Ancient Greek Πάνδαρος (Pándaros).

meaning: provide food and drink (for); cater to: try to satisfy (desires of a bad kind)
etymology: From Middle English catour (“acater, provisioner”), aphetic form of acatour (“acater”), from Old French acater (“to buy, to purchase”). Equivalent to cate + -er.

meaning: formal praise; encomium; Ex. I don't deserve such panegyrics.
etymology: From French panégyrique, from Ancient Greek πανηγυρικός (panēgurikós).

meaning: denoting an unobstructed and comprehensive view; N. panorama: unbroken view of a wide area
etymology: From panorama + -ic.

meaning: acting without dialogue; V.
etymology: First appears c. 1606, from Latin pantomīmus, from Ancient Greek παντόμιμος (pantómimos), from πᾶς (pâs, “each, all”) + μιμέομαι (miméomai, “to mimic”). The verbal form first appears c. 1768.

meaning: ancient paper made from stem of papyrus plant
etymology: From Middle English papirus, borrowed from Latin papȳrus, from Ancient Greek πάπυρος (pápuros), of unknown origin. Doublet of papyros.

meaning: short simple story teaching a moral
etymology: From Middle English parable, from Old French parable, parabole, from Late Latin parabola, from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ, “comparison”). Doublet of parabola, parole, and palaver.

meaning: model; example that serves as a model; pattern; list of all the inflectional forms of a word
etymology: From Middle English paradygme, from Late Latin paradīgma, from Ancient Greek παράδειγμα (parádeigma, “pattern”), from παραδείκνυμι (paradeíknumi, “I show [beside] or compare”) + -μα (-ma, suffix forming nouns concerning the results of actions). Doublet of paradigma.

meaning: something apparently contradictory in nature (that may nonetheless be true); statement that looks false but is actually correct
etymology: From Middle French paradoxe, from Latin paradoxum, from Ancient Greek παράδοξος (parádoxos, “unexpected, strange”).

meaning: model of perfection; Ex. paragon of virtue
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French paragon, paragone, from Old Italian paragone, from paragonare (“to test on a touchstone”), perhaps from Ancient Greek παρακονᾶν (parakonân, “to sharpen, whet”), from παρά- (pará-) + ἀκόνη (akónē, “whetstone, sharpening stone”), from ἀκή (akḗ, “point, edge”) (from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”)).

meaning: state of being parallel; similarity; analogy
etymology: From parallel + -ism and from Late Latin parallelismus.

meaning: similar; analogous; corresponding; N: parallel line; person or thing that is parallel (to another); similarity; Ex. know of no parallel to the case; Ex. without parallel; V: be similar to; make parallel; Ex. Your experience parallels mine; CF. unparalleled
etymology: From Middle French parallèle and its etymon Latin parallēlus, parallēlos. The verb is from the noun. See also para- and allo-.

meaning: limit; independent variable; Ex. parameters of the problem; Ex. within the parameters of the budget
etymology: From French paramètre, from New Latin parametrum (“parameter”), from Ancient Greek παρα- (para-, “beside”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”).

meaning: foremost in importance; supreme; CF. para-: beyond; above; Ex. paranormal
etymology: From Anglo-Norman paramont /paramount (“paramount, pre-eminent; above”), from Old French par /per (“by”) + amont /amunt (“upward”). Par is derived from Latin per (“by means of, through”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to go through; to carry forth, fare”); amont and amunt are from Latin ad montem (“to the mountain; upward”), from ad (“up to”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd (“at; to”)) + montem (the accusative singular of mōns (“mount, mountain”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to stand out, tower”)).

meaning: illicit lover
etymology: * Uses from the 17th century onwards are probably derived from the noun.

meaning: woman whom a man loves
etymology: Borrowed from Italian innamorata, the feminine form of innamorato (“lover, boyfriend”), from innamorare (“to make somebody fall in love”), from in- (“in”) + amore (“love”).

meaning: psychosis marked by delusions of grandeur or persecution; N: ADJ: paranoid, paranoiac
etymology: By surface analysis, para- (“abnormal, beyond”) + nous (“mind”) + -ia (“(medical) condition”).

meaning: equipment; odds and ends used in a particular activity; personal belongings; Ex. photographic paraphernalia; CF. married woman'property exclusive of her dowry
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin paraphernālia (“goods which a wife brings over and above her dowry”), use as noun (short for paraphernālia bona (“paraphernal goods”)) of neuter plural of paraphernālis, from Late Latin parapherna + Latin -ālis (suffix forming adjectives), from Ancient Greek παράφερνα (parápherna), a compound of παρά (pará, “beside”) + φερνή (phernḗ, “dowry”). In the propertied classes, a dowry was placed under the control of the husband, while the paraphernalia which she brought with her remained the wife’s property.

meaning: money or property brought by a bride to her husband at marriage
etymology: From Middle English dowarye, dowerie, from Anglo-Norman dowarie, douarie, from Old French douaire, from Medieval Latin dōtārium, from Latin dōs. Doublet of dower.

meaning: restate a passage in one'own words while retaining thought of author; N: restatement of a text in other words
etymology: From Middle French paraphrase, from Latin paraphrasis, from Ancient Greek παράφρασις (paráphrasis), equivalent to para- + phrase. Doublet of paraphrasis.

meaning: animal or plant living on another; toady; sycophant; CF. para-: beside
etymology: From Middle French parasite, from Latin parasitus, from Ancient Greek παράσιτος (parásitos, “person who eats at the table of another”), from noun use of adjective meaning "feeding beside", from παρά (pará, “beside”) + σῖτος (sîtos, “food”).

meaning: inhabit in numbers large enough to be harmful; Ex. Mice infested the house; Ex. shark-infested waters
etymology: From Middle English infesten, from Old French infester (“to infest”), from Latin īnfestō (“assail, molest”, verb), from īnfestus (“hostile”), of uncertain origin.

meaning: extremely dry; very thirsty; V. parch: make or become extremely dry (by exposure to heat)
social outcast; Ex. Mariah the pariah
etymology: Alternatively, derived from Sanskrit पर (para, “distant; outsider”).

meaning: one that has been excluded from a society; ADJ.
etymology: From Middle English outcasten, equivalent to out- + cast.

meaning: equality; close resemblance; CF. disparate
etymology: From Middle French parité, from Late Latin paritās, from Latin pār (“equal”). Equivalent to pari- + -ty.

meaning: language; manner of speaking; idiom; Ex. in legal/common parlance
etymology: From Middle English *parlaunce, from Anglo-Norman parlance, parlaunce, from parler (“to talk”) + -ance.

meaning: conference (between opponents); CF. speak
etymology: From Middle English parlai (“speech, parley”), from Old French parler (“to talk; to speak”), from Late Latin parabolō, from Latin parabola (“comparison”), from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ), from παρά (pará, “beside”) with βολή (bolḗ, “throwing”). Doublet of palaver.

meaning: narrow in scope or outlook; provincial; related to parishes
etymology: From Anglo-Norman parochial and its source Late Latin parochialis, an alteration of paroecialis (“of a church province”), from paroecia, from Hellenistic Greek παροικία (paroikía, “stay in a foreign land”), later “community, diocese”, from Ancient Greek πάροικος (pároikos, “neighbouring, neighbour”), from παρα- (para-) + οἶκος (oîkos, “house”).

meaning: area in the care of a single priest and served by one main church
etymology: From Middle English parisshe, from Old French paroisse (compare the obsolete variant paroch, from Anglo-Norman paroche, parosse), from Late Latin parochia, from Ancient Greek παροικία (paroikía, “a dwelling abroad”).

meaning: point of view; view from a particular place; expectation for the future; prospect; Ex. outlook on life; Ex. pleasing outlook; Ex. weather outlook
etymology: From out- + look.

meaning: humorous imitation; spoof; takeoff; travesty; V.
etymology: From Latin parōdia, from Ancient Greek παρῳδία (parōidía, “parody”), from παρά (pará, “besides”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”).

meaning: parody
etymology: Coined by English comedian Arthur Roberts in 1884 as the name of a card game involving deception and nonsense.

meaning: burlesque; act of leaving the ground
etymology: Deverbal from take off.

meaning: fit or attack of pain, laughter, rage; sudden outburst
etymology: From Late Middle English paroxism, paroxisme (“period of worsening of a disease, attack; sudden recurrent fever”), from Middle French paroxisme, paroxysme, and Old French peroxime (“period of worsening of a disease; bout of fever or illness”) (modern French paroxysme), and from their etymon Late Latin paroxismus, paroxysmus (“a fit; onset of a disease; violent impulse or sadness”), from Ancient Greek πᾰροξῠσμός (păroxŭsmós, “exasperation, irritation; severe fit of a disease”), from πᾰροξῡ́νω (păroxū́nō, “to irritate, provoke”) (from παρα- (para-, prefix meaning ‘parallel to but separate from or going beyond, beside’) + ὀξῡ́νω (oxū́nō, “to provoke; to sharpen”) (from ὀξῠ́ς (oxŭ́s, “sharp”), probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”))) + -μός (-mós, suffix forming abstract nouns). By surface analysis, para- + oxy- + -ism.

meaning: floor made of wood strips inlaid in a mosaic like matter; CF. strip: long narrow piece
etymology: Borrowed from French parquet.
