meaning: ward off a blow; deflect; Ex. He parried the unwelcome question very skillfully; N. CF. ¸·´Â´Ù´Â °³³äÀÌ ¾Æ´Ô
etymology: Alternative etymology derives the verb parry from French parez, the imperative form of parer (“to fend off”), ultimately from the Medieval Latin parāre. See above.

meaning: administrative division of a city; division in a hospital or prison; incompetent person placed under the protection of a guardian; V: guard; ward off: avert
etymology: From Middle English warde, from Old English weard (“keeper, watchman, guard, guardian, protector; lord, king; possessor”), from Proto-Germanic *warduz (“guard, keeper”), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to heed, defend”). Cognate with Dutch waard, German Wart.

meaning: stinginess; excessive frugality; ADJ. parsimonious
etymology: From Late Middle English parcimonie, parcimony (“economy, frugality, thrift”), borrowed from Latin parcimōnia, parsimōnia (“frugality, thrift, parsimony; moderation, restraint; stinginess”), from pars- (the past participial stem of parcō (“to economize, save up; etc.”)) + -mōnia (suffix forming abstract nouns). The further etymology of parcō is uncertain; it is possibly from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epó (“away; off”) + *h₂erk- (“to hold; to guard, protect; to lock”).

meaning: incomplete; favoring one side over another; having a liking for something
etymology: From Middle English partiall, parcial, from Old French parcial (“biased or particular”), from Late Latin partiālis (“of or pertaining to a part”), from Latin pars (“part”).

meaning: state of being partial; inclination; favorable bias; special fondness; preference
etymology: From Middle English parcialite, parcialtee, parcyalte, partialte, percialite, from Middle French partialité and its etymon Medieval Latin partiālitās. Doublet of partialitas.

meaning: one-sided; prejudiced; committed to a party (with dislike of any others); N: strong supporter of a party; guerrilla
etymology: The adjective in the military sense dates from the early 18th century.

meaning: upstart; newly rich person
etymology: See also parvenue f

meaning: divide into parts
etymology: Recorded c.1430, "division into shares, distinction," from Middle English particioun, from Old French particion (modern partition), from Latin partitio, partitionem (“division, portion”), from partitus, the past participle of partire (“to split (up), part(ition)”).

meaning: old-fashioned; past the prime
not active; acted upon; receiving an action without acting in return; accepting without resistance
etymology: From Middle English passyf, passyve, from Middle French, French passif, from Latin passivus (“serving to express the suffering of an action; in late Latin literally capable of suffering or feeling”), from passus, past participle of pati (“to suffer”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₁- (“to hurt”); compare patient.

meaning: imitation of another'style in musical composition or in writing; work of art openly imitating the works of other artists
etymology: Via French pastiche, from Italian pasticcio (“pie, something blended”), from Vulgar Latin *pastīcius, from Late Latin pasta (“dough, pastry cake, paste”), from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá, “barley porridge”), from παστός (pastós, “sprinkled with salt”). Doublet of pasticcio.

meaning: rural; of rural life; idyllic; of a pastor
etymology: From Middle French, Old French pastoral, from Latin pāstōrālis, from pāstor (“shepherd”), + adjective suffix -ālis.

meaning: obvious; easily seen; open for the public to read; of or protected by a patent; Ex. patent to everyone; N.
etymology: The verb is derived from the noun.

meaning: causing sadness, compassion, pity; touching
etymology: From Middle French pathétique, from Latin patheticus, from Ancient Greek παθητικός (pathētikós, “subject to feeling, capable of feeling, impassioned”), from παθητός (pathētós, “one who has suffered, subject to suffering”), from πάσχω (páskhō, “to suffer”). By surface analysis, path- + -etic.

meaning: causing a feeling of pity or sympathy; pathetic; V. touch: cause to feel pity or sympathy; ADJ. touched
etymology: From Middle English touchynge, equivalent to touch + -ing.

meaning: pertaining to disease; N. pathology: study of disease
etymology: From pathology + -ical.

meaning: tender sorrow; pity; quality in art or literature that produces these feelings; Ex. pathos that runs through the novel
etymology: From Ancient Greek πάθος (páthos, “suffering”).

meaning: green crust on old bronze works or copper; tone slowly taken by varnished painting
etymology: Borrowed from Italian patina, from Latin patina (“dish, pan”), itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek πατάνη (patánē), either from Proto-Indo-European *peth₂- (“to spread”) or from Pre-Greek. Doublet of paten, patena, patine, and (possibly) pan.

meaning: paint used to coat a surface with a glossy film; glossy coating produced by using this substance; Ex. nail varnish; V.
etymology: From Middle English vernisch, vernish, from Old French vernis, from Medieval Latin vernix, veronix, from Byzantine Greek Βερενίκη (Bereníkē, “Berenice”), a town in Cyrenaica, now called Benghazi.

meaning: local or provincial dialect
etymology: Borrowed from French patois (“regional dialect or language”), c. 1635.

meaning: father and ruler of a family or tribe
etymology: From Middle English patriark, patriarche, from Late Latin patriarcha; later reinforced by Old French patriarche, from Ancient Greek πατριάρχης (patriárkhēs, “the founder of the tribe/family”), from Ancient Greek πατριά (patriá, “generation, ancestry, descent, tribe, family”) + -ᾰ́ρχης (-ắrkhēs, “-arch”), with some senses likely influenced directly by Latin pāter (“father”) or Ancient Greek πᾰτήρ (pătḗr, “father”). Compare matriarch. By surface analysis, patri- + -arch.

meaning: noble; aristocratic; N: person of high rank; aristocrat; CF. member of the governing classes in ancient Rome; CF. plebian
etymology: May also have been derived from Latin patricius + -ian

meaning: support; act superior toward; treat in a condescending manner; be a customer of; N. patron: one that supports; regular customer; N. patronage; CF. boycott
etymology: From patron + -ize (verb ending); or from Old French patroniser, from Medieval Latin patronizāre (“to lead a galley as patron”). Piecewise doublet of patternize.

meaning: scarcity; dearth
etymology: From Middle English paucete, paucite, paucyte, partly from Middle French paucité and partly from its etymon, Latin paucitās (“a small number, fewness, scarcity”), from paucus (“few, little”). Related to few.

meaning: very poor person
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin pauper (“poor”). Originally a legal term. Doublet of poor.

meaning: slight offense or fault; CF. sin
etymology: From Spanish pecadillo, diminutive form of pecado (“sin”), from Latin peccatum (“sin, error, fault”), from peccō (“to sin, offend”).

meaning: hit with a sweeping motion; N.
etymology: From earlier swip (with a short vowel), from Middle English swippen, swype (“to move violently”), from Old English sweopian, swipian, swippan (“to scourge, strike, beat, lash”), from Proto-West Germanic *swippjan, *swipōn, *swipēn, from Proto-Germanic *swipōną, *swipjaną, *swipāną (“to move”), from Proto-Indo-European *sweyb- (“to bend, sway, swing, sweep, swerve, turn”). Cognate with German schwippen (“sway back and forth”), Danish svippe (“to smack; crack a whip”), Icelandic svipa (“riding crop, whip”). Related to sweep, swoop.

meaning: pertaining to money
etymology: From Latin pecūniārius, from pecūnia (“money”), itself from pecū (“cattle”) and thus related to fee.

meaning: teacher; CF. child leader
etymology: From Middle English pedagoge, from Middle French pedagogue, from Latin paedagōgus, from Ancient Greek παιδαγωγός (paidagōgós), from παῖς (paîs, “child”) + ἀγωγός (agōgós, “guide”) (from ἄγω (ágō, “lead”)). By surface analysis, ped- (“child”) + -agogue.

meaning: teaching; art of education
etymology: From Middle French pédagogie, from Ancient Greek παιδαγωγία (paidagōgía). By surface analysis, ped- (“child”) + -agogy.

meaning: scholar who overemphasizes book learning, trivial details of learning, or technicalities
etymology: From Middle French pedant, pedante, from Italian pedante (“a teacher, schoolmaster, pedant”), associated with unrelated Italian pedagogo (“teacher, pedagogue”). Compare French pédant.

meaning: bookish; showing off learning; marked by an excessive ostentatious concern for book learning; N. pedantry
etymology: From pedant + -ic.

meaning: fond of books and reading
etymology: From book + -ish.

meaning: given to diligent study
etymology: From Latin studiōsus. First recorded in English c. 1350.

meaning: ordinary; dull; unimaginative (lacking in imagination); going on foot; Ex. pedestrian prose; N.
etymology: From Latin pedester (oblique stem pedestri-) + English -an.

meaning: division of a city for election or police purposes; precincts: space that surrounds a building; Ex. precincts of the college
etymology: Cognate to Italian precingere (“to encircle”).

meaning: physician specializing in children'diseases; N. pediatrics
etymology: From pediatric + -ian.

meaning: having no equal; incomparable
etymology: From Middle English pereles, perles; equivalent to peer + -less.

meaning: one who has equal standing with another; nobleman; V: look intently; N. peerage; CF. peeress
etymology: The sense meaning "to be visible" is perhaps from a shortening of appear.

meaning: (of a word or phrase) suggesting that someone is of little value; negative in connotation; having a belittling effect; Ex. Many women now considers ``housewife'' a pejorative expression, because it patronized them.
etymology: From Late Latin peiōrātus (“worsened”, past participle of peiōrāre (“worsen”), from Latin peior (“worse”)) + -ive. Compare French péjoratif (“depreciative, disparaging”). By surface analysis, pejorate + -ive.

meaning: in confusion; disorderly; Ex. dash pell-mell
etymology: From French pêle-mêle, from Old French pesle-mesle, apparently a rhyme based on the stem of mesler (“to mix, meddle”). Compare meddle, melee.

meaning: transparent; limpid (crystal clear); clear in meaning; easy to understand
etymology: * Middle French pellucide (modern French pellucide (“pellucid”))

meaning: self-imposed punishment for sin; Ex. do penance for one'sins; CF. penitent
etymology: From Middle English penaunce, from Anglo-Norman, from Old French peneance, from Latin paenitentia (“repentance, penitence”). Doublet of penitence.

meaning: strong inclination; strong liking (esp. for something that is disapproved of by other people); Ex. penchant for fast cars
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French penchant, present participle of pencher (“to tilt, to lean”), from Middle French, from Old French pengier (“to tilt, be out of line”), from Vulgar Latin *pendicāre, a derivative of Latin pendere (“to hang”).

meaning: hanging down from something; pending; N: ornament (hanging from a necklace etc.)
not yet decided or settled; impending; Ex. pending decision; PREP. while awaiting; until; Ex. delay the decision pending his return
hanging; suspended
etymology: Borrowed from Latin pendulus (“pendant”), from pendeō (“to hang”).

meaning: cause to stop for a period; interrupt; hold in abeyance; defer; hang from above; exclude for a period from a position; Ex. suspended state; Ex. suspend judgment; Ex. suspended from the team; N. suspension
etymology: From Old French sospendre, from Latin suspendere.

meaning: state of being undecided; anxiety or apprehension resulting from uncertainty
etymology: From Middle English suspense, suspence, from Anglo-Norman suspens (as in en suspens) and Old French suspens, from Latin suspēnsus.

meaning: repentant; N.
etymology: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin paenitēns, poenitēns (“penitent”), present participle of paeniteō, poeniteō (“to cause to repent; to regret, repent”). Doublet of penitente.

meaning: dreamily or deeply thoughtful; sadly thoughtful; thoughtful with a hint of sadness; contemplative; CF. think over
etymology: From Middle English pensif, pensyfe, pencyve, from Old French pensif (“thoughtful”), from penser (“to think”) (from Latin pēnsō) + -if (English -ive).

meaning: partial shadow (in an eclipse); CF. almost shadow
etymology: From New Latin pēnumbra, from Latin paene (“almost”) + umbra (“shadow”).

meaning: extreme poverty; stinginess; ADJ. penurious: very poor; stingy
etymology: From Late Middle English penuri, penurie (“destitution, need, poverty; dearth, lack, scarcity”), borrowed from Latin pēnūria (“need, scarcity, want”) + Middle English -i, -ie (suffix forming abstract and collective nouns); further etymology uncertain, possibly related to paene (“almost, nearly; barely, hardly, scarcely”, adverb), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *peh₁- (“to hate; to hurt”).

meaning: landless agricultural worker; bond servant; menial worker; N. peonage
etymology: From a combination of Middle French pion, peon and Spanish peón, both from Late Latin pedōnem (“pedestrian”). Doublet of pawn.

meaning: insightful; showing a good ability at perceiving and understanding; aware; wise; of perception
etymology: From Latin perceptīvus.

meaning: striking one object against another sharply; Ex. percussion instrument; N: striking together of two bodies; sound caused by percussion
etymology: From Middle English percussioun, from Middle French, Old French percussion, from Latin percussiō (“striking”), from percutiō (“to strike”).

meaning: damnation; complete ruin; hell
etymology: From Middle English perdicioun, from Old French perdiciun, from Late Latin perditio, from Latin perdo (“to destroy, to lose”).

meaning: condemn; criticize severely; condemn to everlasting punishment; doom; bring to ruin; N. damnation
etymology: From Middle English dampnen, from Old French damner, from Latin damnāre (“to condemn, inflict loss upon”), from damnum (“loss”).

meaning: condemnation to a severe penalty; ruin; fate (esp. a tragic or ruinous one); V.
etymology: Compare Dutch doem (“condemnation, doom; judgement”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, and Swedish dom (“judgement”), Faroese and Icelandic dómur (“judgement”), Gothic 𐌳𐍉𐌼𐍃 (dōms, “insight, judgement”); also Ancient Greek θωμός (thōmós, “heap”), Bulgarian, Macedonian, Russian, and Ukrainian ду́ма (dúma, “thought”), Polish duma (“pride”). Doublet of duma. See also deem.

meaning: journey; V. peregrinate
etymology: From Late Middle English peregrinacioun, peregrinacion (“journey; pilgrimage; (figuratively) human journey through life”), from Anglo-Norman peregrinaciun (“human journey through life”), peregrination (“pilgrimage; overseas travel”), and Old French peregrinacion, peregrination (“pilgrimage; overseas travel”) (modern French pérégrination), and from their etymon Latin peregrīnātiō (“overseas sojourn or travel; (Late Latin) pilgrimage; sojourn; human journey through life”), from peregrīnātus (“living or travelling overseas”) + -iō (suffix forming abstract nouns). Peregrīnātus is the perfect passive participle of peregrīnor (“to live or travel overseas; to be overseas; to roam, rove; to be a stranger”), from peregrīnus (“alien, foreign; exotic”) (from peregrē̆ (“abroad; from abroad; heading abroad”) + -īnus (suffix forming adjectives meaning ‘of or pertaining to’)) + -or (suffix forming first-person singular present passive indicative verbs).

meaning: demanding and leaving no choice; imperative; Ex. peremptory decree/knock
etymology: From Anglo-Norman peremptorie, parentorie et al. (Modern French péremptoire), and its source, Latin peremptōrius (“deadly; precluding debate, decisive”), from perimō (“destroy, thwart”), from per- (“thorough”) + emō (“to obtain, buy”).

meaning: something long-lasting; perennial plant; ADJ: lasting through the year or many years; lasting for a long time; enduring
etymology: * Spanish perenne (“eternal; permanent; a perennial plant”)

meaning: treacherous; disloyal; N. perfidy: treachery
etymology: From Latin perfidiōsus (“treacherous”), from perfidia. By surface analysis, perfidy + -ous.

meaning: pierce; put a hole through
etymology: passive participle of perforō (“to bore or pierce through, to perforate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from per- (“through, thorough”) + forō (“to bore, pierce”). Participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.

meaning: done routinely and with little care; superficial; not thorough; lacking interest, care, or enthusiasm; Ex. perfunctory kiss
etymology: From Late Latin perfunctōrius (“careless, negligent”), from the past participial stem of perfungor, perfunct- (“perform, carry through”), from per- + fungor.

meaning: point of moon'orbit when it is nearest the earth; CF. apogee
etymology: From French périgée via Latin perigeum, perigaeum, ultimately from Ancient Greek περί (perí, “near”) + γῆ (gê, “Earth”).

meaning: outer boundary; length of the outer boundary; circumference
etymology: From Latin perimetros, Ancient Greek περίμετρος (perímetros). Equivalent to peri- + meter.

meaning: leap or spring; limit or confine; constitute the limit of; Ex. bounded by Canada; N: leap or jumping; boundary; ADJ: certain; having a duty to do something (legally or morally); confined by bonds; Ex. We are bound to be late; Ex. I am bound to say my opinion; CF. bounce, rebound
etymology: From Middle English bound, bund (preterite) and bounden, bunden, ibunden, ȝebunden (past participle), from Old English bund- and bunden, ġebunden respectively. See bind.

meaning: walking about from place to place (to work); moving; Ex. peripatetic school of philosophy
etymology: From French péripatétique, from Latin peripatēticus, from Ancient Greek περιπατητικός (peripatētikós, “given to walking around”), from περιπατέω (peripatéō, “to walk around”), from περί (perí, “around”) (English peri-)+ πατέω (patéō, “to walk”).

meaning: of a periphery; marginal; outer; of minor importance; not central; Ex. peripheral nerve/interest
etymology: From peripher(y) + -al.

meaning: outside edge especially of a round surface; perimeter; Ex. periphery of the town
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French peripherie. Compare Middle English periferie (“one of three layers of atmosphere (lower, middle, and upper) believed to surround the Earth”), from the same origin, although the Modern English term most likely does not descend from it.

meaning: false testimony while under oath; V. perjure oneself: testify falsely under oath
etymology: From Anglo-Norman perjurie, from Latin perjūrāre (“swear falsely”), from per- + jūrāre. Displaced native Old English mānāþ (literally “false oath”).

meaning: that can be permeated; penetrable; porous; allowing liquids or gas to pass through; V. permeate: spread or flow throughout; charge
etymology: From Middle English permeable, permiable, from Latin permeābilis.

meaning: very harmful; deadly; very destructive; Ex. pernicious effect/anemia
etymology: From Middle English, from Old French pernicios, from Latin perniciōsus (“destructive”), from perniciēs (“destruction”), from per (“through”) + nex (“slaughter, death”).

meaning: conclusion of an oration; perorating; V. perorate: conclude a speech; speak at great length
etymology: From Latin perōrō (“to speak at length, to conclude a speech”) (from per- (“very”) + ōrō (“to speak, to orate”) (English orate)) + -ation (“action (nominalizer)”) (from Latin -ātiō).

meaning: commit an offense; do (something wrong)
etymology: From Middle English perpetrat (“committed, perpetrated”), from Latin perpetrātus, past participle of perpetrāre (“to carry through”).

meaning: everlasting
etymology: From Middle English perpetuel, from Old French perpetuel, from Latin perpetuālis (“universal”), from perpetuus, from petō.

meaning: make perpetual; make something last for a long time; preserve from extinction; N. perpetuity
etymology: * Spanish perpetuar

meaning: any gain above stipulated salary; Ex. perquisites such as free meals and a car
attractive (in personality or appearance)
etymology: By surface analysis, person + -able (suffix meaning ‘relevant or suitable to’).

meaning: (of someone) having insight; penetrating; astute
etymology: First attested 1548, from Late Latin perspicācitās (“discernment”), from Latin perspicax (“sharp-sighted”), from perspiciō (“look through”), from per- (“through”) + speciō (“look at”). See also perspective.

meaning: clearness of expression; freedom from ambiguity
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin perspicuitās (“evidentness”, “self-evidency”, literally “transparency”, “clarity”, “lucidity”), from Latin perspicuus (“clear”, “transparent”; “evident”); compare perspicacity and the French perspicuité. By surface analysis, perspicuous + -ity.

meaning: (of something) plainly expressed; easy to understand; Ex. perspicuous comments
etymology: From Latin perspicuus, in turn from perspiciō (“see through”).

meaning: (esp. of a girl or young woman) impertinent; forward; trim; jaunty; Ex. pert young miss/hat
etymology: From Middle English pert, perte, aphetic form of apert.

meaning: presumptuous or bold
etymology: From Middle English foreward, from Old English foreweard (“forward, inclined to the front, fore, early, former”), from Proto-Germanic *fura- (“fore-”), *warþaz (“turned”), equivalent to fore + -ward. Cognate with Dutch voorwaarts (“forward”), German vorwärts (“forward”).

meaning: holding tenaciously to an action; stubborn; persistent
etymology: From pertinace + -ious, from Old French pertinace, from Latin pertinax, from per- (“very”) + tenax (“tenacious”).

meaning: suitable; to the point; relevant
etymology: Inherited from Middle English pertinent, borrowed from Old French pertinent and Latin pertinēns, pertinentem.

meaning: disturb greatly
etymology: From Late Middle English perturben (“to disturb (someone) mentally, disquiet; to cause disorder to (something), confuse; to hinder (something)”), from Old French perturber, and from its etymon Latin perturbāre, the present active infinitive of perturbō (“to confuse; to alarm, disturb, trouble, perturb”), from per- (intensifying prefix) + turbō (“to agitate, disturb, unsettle, perturb; to upset”) (from turba (“disorder, disturbance, turmoil”) (possibly from Ancient Greek τῠ́ρβη (tŭ́rbē, “confusion, disorder, tumult”), either from Pre-Greek, or Proto-Indo-European *(s)twerH- (“to agitate, stir up; to urge on, propel”)) + -ō (suffix forming infinitives of regular first-conjugation verbs)).

meaning: read through with care; N. perusal
etymology: From either Medieval Latin perūtor, perūsitō (“wear out”) or Anglo-Norman peruser (“use up”), originally leading to two concurrent meanings, but only those derived from "to examine" survive today. By surface analysis, per- + use.

meaning: spread throughout; V. pervade: (of smells, ideas, feelings) spread throughout; charge; permeate
etymology: From Latin pervāsus, from pervādō (“spread through, pervade”), from per (“through”) + vādō (“go, walk”).

meaning: purposely continuing to do something wrong; stubbornly wrongheaded; perverted; directed away from what is right; wicked and unacceptable; Ex. perverse satisfaction; Ex. Hannibal Lecter in a perverse mood; N. perversity
etymology: From Middle English perverse, pervers, from Old French pervers, from Latin perversum (“thoroughly turned”), past participle of pervertere, from per- (“thoroughly”) + vertere (“to turn”).

meaning: corruption; turning from right to wrong
etymology: Inherited from Middle English perversion.

meaning: corrupt; turn from right to wrong; misuse; Ex. perverted sexual desire/scientific knowledge; N: person whose sexual behavior is not natural
etymology: From Old French pervertir, itself from the Latin pervertō.

meaning: stubbornly wrong
etymology: From wrong + headed.

meaning: belief that life is basically bad or evil; gloominess; tendency to take the gloomiest possible view of a situation; ADJ. pessimistic
etymology: As a doctrine, from German Pessimismus as used by the German philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer in 1819.

meaning: causing plague; tending to cause death; baneful; N. pestilence: fatal epidemic disease (esp. bubonic plague)
tool for mashing or grinding substances in a hard bowl or mortar
etymology: From Middle English pestel, pestell, from Old French pestel, from Latin pistillum, from pīnsō (“pound, beat”). Doublet of pistil and pistillum.

meaning: vessel in which substances are crushed with a pestle
etymology: From Middle English morter, from Old French mortier, from Latin mortārium. Doublet of mortarium.

meaning: crush into mash; convert into mash; N: mixture of ground grain and nutrients fed to livestock and fowl
etymology: From Middle English mash, from Old English mǣsċ, māsċ, māx, from Proto-Germanic *maiskaz, *maiskō (“mixture, mash”), from Proto-Indo-European *meyǵ-, *meyḱ- (“to mix”). Akin to German Meisch, Maische (“mash”), (compare meischen, maischen (“to mash, wash”)), Swedish mäsk (“mash”), and to Old English miscian (“to mix”). See mix.

meaning: turn to stone; cause to become stonelike; stun or paralyze
etymology: From Middle French pétrifier, from Medieval Latin petrificāre, from Latin petra (“rock”), from Ancient Greek πέτρα (pétra, “rock”) + -ficāre, from facere (“do, make”), equivalent to petro- + -ify.

meaning: trivial; unimportant; very small; small-minded; petty-minded
etymology: The noun is derived from the adjective.

meaning: touchy; peevish; ill-tempered
etymology: From Middle French, from Latin petulāns, akin to petō (“to ask for”).

meaning: formation of infantry carrying overlapping shields and long spears; group of men packed together (for attack or defense)
etymology: Borrowed from Latin phalanx or Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx, “battle order; array”). Doublet of phalange, planch, plancha, planche, and plank.

meaning: pertaining to the Pharisees, who paid scrupulous attention to tradition; self-righteous; hypocritical
etymology: From Late Latin Pharisaicus + -al.

meaning: Pharisee: member of an ancient Jewish group that emphasized strict observance of the Mosaic law (considering themselves very holy); hypocritical self-righteous person
etymology: From Latin Pharisaeus, from Ancient Greek Φαρισαῖος (Pharisaîos), a transliteration of Aramaic פְּרִישַׁיָּא (pərîšayyâ’), emphatic plural of פְּרִישׁ (pərîš, “separatist”, literally “separated”), related to Hebrew פרוש (parush), qal passive participle of the verb פָּרַשׁ (pāraš), meaning one who is separated for a life of purity.

meaning: sure of one'own righteousness; moralistic
etymology: From self- + righteous.

meaning: observable facts; subjects of scientific investigation; SG. phenomenon: observable fact; very unusual person, thing, or event; marvel; wonder; CF. phenomenons; ADJ. phenomenal: very unusual; extraordinary; of a phenomenon; Ex. phenomenal strength
etymology: The plural form of phenomenon, formed according to the Ancient Greek -ον (-on) → -α (-a) pluralisation pattern.

meaning: faithless lover; flirt
etymology: From philander (“lover”) + -er, from Ancient Greek φίλανδρος (phílandros), from φίλος (phílos, “love”) + ἀνήρ (anḗr, “man”).

meaning: lover of mankind; doer of good; N. philanthropy
etymology: From philanthropy + -ist; compare French philanthrope.

meaning: stamp-collector; N. philately: stamp collecting
etymology: From philately + -ist.

meaning: narrow-minded person, uncultured and exclusively interested in material gain; uncultured person who is indifferent to artistic and cultural values; member of an ancient people in Palestine; OP. aesthete
etymology: The adjective is derived from the noun. For the etymology of the "ignorant person" sense, see philistine.

meaning: study of language or words
etymology: Inherited from Middle English Philologie, from Latin philologia, from Ancient Greek φιλολογίᾱ (philologíā, “love of argument or reasoning, love of learning and literature”).

meaning: calm and unexcitable; not easily disturbed; CF. phlegm: sticky mucus produced in the respiratory tract
etymology: From Middle English fleumatik, flewmatik, flematik, fleumatyke, flewmatyk, from Old French fleumatique, from Latin phlegmaticus, from Ancient Greek φλεγματικός (phlegmatikós), from φλέγμα (phlégma), referring to the humour which ancient Hippocratic and later Galenic medicine associated with mildness, coldness, sluggishness, and indifference. Spelling later altered to resemble the word's Latin and Greek roots, with modern pronunciation following this new spelling.

meaning: morbid fear
etymology: First attested in c. 1790, from words ending in -phobia, ultimately from Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”). Compare ism, from -ism, itis, from -itis, and ana, from -ana.

meaning: symbol of immortality or rebirth; Ex. phoenix rising from its ashes
etymology: From Old English and Old French fenix, from Medieval Latin phenix, from Latin phoenīx, from Ancient Greek φοῖνιξ (phoînix), from Egyptian b-n:nw*w-G31 (bnw, “grey heron”). Doublet of Bennu. The grey heron was venerated at Heliopolis and associated in Egypt with the cyclical renewal of life because the bird rises in flight at dawn and migrates back every year in the flood season to inhabit the Nile waters.

meaning: major classification, second to kingdom, of plants and animals; category ranking below a kingdom and above a class; division
etymology: From Latin phylum, from Ancient Greek φῦλον (phûlon, “tribe, race”).

meaning: face (as showing the character and the mind); art of judging human character from facial features
etymology: Inherited from Middle English phisonomie, from Anglo-Norman phisenomie, Middle French phisonomie et al., ultimately from Late Latin physiognomia, from Ancient Greek φυσιογνωμία (phusiognōmía, “physiology”), from φύσις (phúsis, “physique, appearance”) + γνώμη (gnṓmē, “means of knowing”). Middle English phisonomie would regularly develop into *physnomy /ˈfɪznəmi/ (forms of this type are common in Early Modern English, such as fisnomie in All's Well that Ends Well); the modern spelling and pronunciation are due to learned influence.

meaning: pertaining to the science of the function of living organisms; N. physiology
etymology: Either from physio- + -logical (equivalent to physiology + -ical) or Latin physiologicus + -al.

meaning: of different colors; mottled; spotted in different colors (esp. in black and white); Ex. piebald horse; CF. pie+bald
etymology: Compare typologically Polish srokaty < sroka.

meaning: one part at a time; gradually; in stages; Ex. read a novel piecemeal
etymology: From Middle English pecemele, from pece (“piece”) + mele (from Old English mǣlum (“at a time”), dative plural form of mǣl (“time, measure”), taking the place of Old English styċċemǣlum (“in pieces, bit by bit, piecemeal; to pieces, to bits; here and there, in different places; little by little, by degrees, gradually”); equivalent to piece + -meal.

meaning: piebald; variegated (many-colored); multicolored
etymology: Compare typologically Polish srokaty < sroka.

meaning: devoutness; reverence for God; ADJ. pious
etymology: From Middle English piete, borrowed from Middle French pieté, from Latin pietās. See also the doublets pietà and pity. By surface analysis, pious + -ety.

meaning: coloring matter (usually powder to be mixed with water or oil)
etymology: From Middle English pigment, from Latin pigmentum (“pigment”), itself from pingō (“to paint”) + -mentum; variants of this word may have been known in Old English (e.g. 12th century pyhmentum). Doublet of pimiento, pimento, and piment.

meaning: plunder
etymology: From Old French pillage, from piller (“plunder”), from an unattested meaning of Late Latin piliō, probably a figurative use of Latin pilō (“to remove (hair)”), from pilus (“hair”).

meaning: punish by placing in a wooden frame or pillory; subject or expose to criticism and ridicule; N.
etymology: From Middle English pilory, pillorie, from Old French pilori, pellori, which is either from Old Occitan espilori or Latin pīla (“pillar”).

meaning: long for; yearn; languish from longing or grief; decline
etymology: From Middle English pyne, from Old English *pīne, from Proto-West Germanic *pīnā, from Latin pīnus, see there for more. Doublet of pinus. Possibly related to fat.

meaning: restrain or immobilize by binding the wings or legs; N: bird'wing
etymology: From Middle English pynyon, from Old French pignon, from Latin penna (“feather”).

meaning: peak; highest point; acme; Ex. pinnacle of fame
etymology: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French pinacle, pinnacle, from Late Latin pinnāculum (“a peak, pinnacle”), from Latin pinna (“a pinnacle”); see pin. Doublet of panache.

meaning: devout; religious; N. piety
etymology: Borrowed from Latin pīus (“pious, dutiful, blessed, kind, devout”), from Proto-Indo-European *pewH- (“pure”). Cognate with Old English fǣle (“faithful, trusty, good; dear, beloved”). More at feal.

meaning: pleasantly tart-tasting; spicy; pleasantly stimulating; Ex. piquant situation when my old enemy asked for my help
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French piquant (“pricking, stimulating, irritating”), present participle of piquer, possibly from Old French pikier (“to prick, sting, nettle”). Doublet of picong. Related to pike.

meaning: sharp to the taste; acid-tasting; caustic; sarcastic; Ex. tart apple/reply
etymology: From Middle English tart, from Old English teart (“sharp, rough, severe”), from Proto-West Germanic *tart, from Proto-Germanic *tartaz (“rough, sharp, tearing”), from Proto-Germanic *teraną (“to tear”), from Proto-Indo-European *der- (“to flay, split, cleave”). Related to Scots tairt (“tart; tartness”), Dutch tarten (“to defy, challenge, mock”), German trotzen (“to defy, brave, mock”), perhaps Albanian thartë (“sour, acid, sharp”).

meaning: having a sharp or acid taste; acid; tart; bad-tempered; V.
etymology: Old Church Slavonic сꙑръ (syrŭ, “moist, cheese”).

meaning: irritation; resentment from wounded pride (eg. loss in a contest); V: provoke; arouse; annoy; cause to feel resentment; Ex. pique her curiosity
etymology: The noun is borrowed from Middle French pique (“a quarrel; resentment”) (modern French pique), from piquer, picquer (verb); see above.

meaning: pertaining to fishing; CF. Pisces
etymology: From Latin piscātor (“fisherman”), from piscis (“fish”).

meaning: hidden danger; concealed trap
etymology: First recorded use in the 14th century from pit + fall in the sense of "pit trap, pit snare", from Old English fealle (“trap, snare”), from Proto-Germanic *fallą, *fallaz (“a fall, trap”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pōl-. Cognate with German Falle (“trap, snare”).

meaning: be cautious (of)
etymology: From Middle English bewar, be war, be ware, forms of Middle English ben ware (“to be on one's guard, be vigilant”, literally “be ware”), equivalent to be + ware or be + aware. Compare Old English bewarian.

meaning: core or marrow; spongelike substance in the center of stems; essence; substance
etymology: * West Frisian piid (“pulp, kernel”)

meaning: soft fatty tissue that fills most bone cavities and is the source of blood cells
etymology: From Middle English mary, marow, marwe, marowȝ, from Old English mearg, from Proto-West Germanic *maʀg, from Proto-Germanic *mazgą, *mazgaz, from Proto-Indo-European *mosgʰos. Compare West Frisian moarch, Dutch merg, German Mark, Swedish märg, Icelandic mergur, and also Russian мозг (mozg, “brain”), Polish mózg (“brain”), Ashkun amōźã, Kamkata-viri muč, muj, Waigali muj, Persian مغز (maġz, “brain”), Sanskrit मज्जन् (majján). Doublet of maghaz.

meaning: concise and meaningful; substantial; meaty
etymology: From Middle English pithy, pythy, equivalent to pith + -y.

meaning: small amount (of money); small allowance or wage
etymology: From Middle English pitaunce, from Old French pitance, pitence, from Medieval Latin *pietāntia, from Latin pietās (“piety”).

meaning: of a pivot; central; critical; crucial
etymology: From pivot + -al.

meaning: pacify; bring peace to; conciliate; appease
etymology: First attested in the late 17ᵗʰ century; borrowed from Latin plācātus, perfect passive participle of plācō (“appease, placate”, literally “smooth, smoothen”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more), ultimately thought to be from Proto-Indo-European *plāk- (“smooth, flat”), from *pele- (“broad, flat, plain”). Related to Latin placeō (“appease”), Old English flōh (“flat stone, chip”). More at please.

meaning: harmless substance prescribed as a dummy pill
etymology: Inherited from Middle English placebo, borrowed from Latin placēbō (“I will please”), the first-person singular future active indicative of placeō (“to please”).

meaning: small round piece of medicine; flat piece of stone or metal bearing an inscription; Ex. stone tablet on the wall
etymology: From Middle English tablet, from Old French tablete (Modern French tablette), diminutive of table (“table”). Compare English table, -et.

meaning: peaceful; calm; Ex. placid child/lake
etymology: Borrowed from French placide, from Latin placidus (“peaceful, calm, placid”), from placeō (“please, satisfy”).

meaning: steal another'ideas or writings and pass them off as one'own; Ex. ideas plagiarized from my article; N. plagiarism; CF. kidnap
etymology: From plagiary + -ize, ultimately from Latin plagiare (“to kidnap, to abduct”).

meaning: expressing sorrow; mournful; Ex. plaintive song
etymology: From Middle English pleintif, plentyff, from Old French pleintif (“aggrieved, lamenting”) (whence modern French plaintif), from plainte (“lament, complaint”); see plaint. Doublet of plaintiff.

meaning: braid; interwine; interweave strands or lengths of; make by weaving strands together; Ex. plaited hair; N: braided length as of hair o fabric; CF. pigtail, ponytail
etymology: From Middle English pleit, from Anglo-Norman pleit (compare Old French ploit), from Latin plectō, which is akin to Old Norse flétta (Danish flette), Russian плести́ (plestí) and also to Old English fleohtan, which it displaced. Doublet of plight (“plait, fold”) and pleat.

meaning: ability to be molded; ADJ. plastic: capable of being shaped or molded; Ex. plastic material such as clay
etymology: From plastic + -ity.

meaning: trite remark; commonplace statement; ADJ. platitudinous
etymology: Borrowed from French platitude, from plat (“flat”).

meaning: ordinary; N: something ordinary or common; trite remark
etymology: A calque of Latin locus commūnis, referring to a generally applicable literary passage, itself a calque of Ancient Greek κοινὸς τόπος (koinòs tópos).

meaning: nation governed by the people; republic; people of a nation
etymology: Also from the 1520s treated as a synonym or loan-translation of res publica (republic) (Rollison 2017:67f).

meaning: purely spiritual; theoretical; without sensual desire
etymology: From Latin Platōnicus. By surface analysis, Platon (“Plato”) + -ic (“relating to”).

meaning: praise; enthusiastic approval; round (succession or series) of applause; ADJ. plauditory; CF. applaud
etymology: For earlier plaudite, borrowed from Latin plaudite, second-person plural imperative of plaudere (“to applaud”).

meaning: conceivably true; having a show of truth but open to doubt; specious
etymology: From Latin plausibilis (“deserving applause, praiseworthy, acceptable, pleasing”), from the participle stem of plaudere (“to applaud”).

meaning: common; vulgar; pertaining to the common people; N: common people in ancient Rome; CF. patrician
etymology: From Latin plēbēius (“a commoner; common”) + -an (adjective-forming suffix), from Latin plēbēs + -ius (adjective-forming suffix), possibly under the influence of Middle French plebeyen, plebein, plebien (“a commoner”) and plebeien (“concerning the common people”). Cf. Medieval Latin plēbēiānus (“a commoner”), from plēbēius + -ānus.

meaning: direct vote by the entire electorate (on an important issue)
etymology: * Spanish plebiscito, plebisçito (obsolete)

meaning: direct vote by all the people
etymology: From Latin referendum (“that which ought to be announced”), from refero (“to announce”).

meaning: (of power) complete; full; fully attended by all qualified members; Ex. plenary power
etymology: From Middle English plenarie, plenarye, from Late Latin plēnārius, from Latin plēnus (“full”).

meaning: abundance; plenty; great amount; completeness; fullness; CF. plenary, plenty
etymology: From Middle English plenitude, that borrowed from Anglo-Norman plenitude, Middle French plenitude, and their source, Latin plēnitūdō.

meaning: excess; overabundance; Ex. a plethora of excuses
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin plēthōra, from Ancient Greek πληθώρα (plēthṓra, “fullness, satiety”), from πλήθω (plḗthō, “to be full”) + -η (-ē, nominal suffix).

meaning: flexible; easily influenced; yielding; adaptable
etymology: From Middle French, from Old French ploiable, from ploiier (“to fold”). By surface analysis, ply + -able. Compare pliant.

meaning: flexible; easily influenced
etymology: From Middle English pliaunt, from Old French ploiant, present participle of ploiier (“to fold”).

meaning: difficult condition; condition or state (esp. a bad state or condition); predicament
etymology: From Middle English plit (“fold, wrinkle, bad situation”), conflation of Middle English pliht, plight (“risky promise, peril”) (from Old English pliht "danger, risk"; see Etymology 2) and Anglo-Norman plit, plyte (“fold, condition”), from Old French pleit (“condition, manner of folding”) (from Vulgar Latin *plictum, from Latin plicitum (“fold”)).

meaning: courage; V: pull off or out; pull out the hair or feathers of; ADJ. plucky: courageous; brave
etymology: The noun sense of "heart, liver, and lights of an animal" comes from it being plucked out of the carcass after the animal is killed; the sense of "fortitude, boldness" derives from this meaning, originally being a boxing slang denoting a prize-ring, with semantic development from "heart", the symbol of courage, to "fortitude, boldness".

meaning: feathers of a bird;
etymology: From Late Middle English plumage, plummage (“bird’s feathers collectively, plumage; (falconry) feathers fed to a hawk to cause it to regurgitate, casting”), from Middle French plumage, plomage (“bird’s feathers collectively; person’s (showy) clothing”), from Old French plumage (“bird’s feathers collectively”) (modern French plumage), from plume (“feather, plume”) + -age (suffix forming nouns denoting a state of being). Plume is derived from Latin plūma (“feather, plume”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *plewk- (“to flow; to fly; to run; etc.”), from Proto-Indo-European *plew- (“to flow; to fly; to run”). By surface analysis, plume + -age (suffix forming nouns with a sense of appurtenance or collection).

meaning: feather, esp. large or showy one; something that rises into the air (like the shape of a feather); Ex. plume of smoke: ¹ö¼¸ ±¸¸§
etymology: From Late Middle English plum, plume (“feather; plumage”), from Anglo-Norman plum, plume, from Old French plume, plome (“feather, plumage”), from Latin plūma (“feather, plumage”) (compare Late Latin plūma (“pen, quill”)), from Proto-Italic *plouksmā, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *plewk- (“to fly”). Doublet of pluma.

meaning: exactly vertical; N: weight on the end of a line; V: examine very carefully or critically in order to understand; measure depth (by sounding); Ex. plumb the depth of
etymology: From Middle English plumbe, plumme, from Old French *plombe, from Latin plumba, plural of plumbum.

meaning: one who installs and repairs pipes and plumbing (pipes)
etymology: The verb sense “to botch” is perhaps from the negative stereotype of the occupation.

meaning: fall sharply; fall straight down; Ex. Stock prices plummeted.
etymology: From Middle English plommet (“ball of lead, plumb of a bob-line”), recorded since 1382, from Old French plommet or plomet, the diminutive of plom, plum (“lead, sounding lead”), from Latin plumbum (“lead”). The verb is first recorded in 1626, originally meaning “to fathom, take soundings", from the noun.

meaning: society ruled by the wealthy
etymology: From Ancient Greek πλουτοκρατία (ploutokratía, “rule of the wealthy”), from πλουτοκρατέω (ploutokratéō, “I rule through wealth”), from πλοῦτος (ploûtos, “wealth”) + κρατέω (kratéō, “I rule”) (from κράτος (krátos, “power”, “might”)).

meaning: doctor who treats ailments of the feet; chiropodist; N. podiatrics
etymology: From podiatry + -ist.

meaning: pedestal; raised platform
etymology: Borrowed from Latin podium, from Ancient Greek πόδιον (pódion, “base”), a diminutive of πούς (poús, “foot”). Doublet of pew.

meaning: support or base as for a pillar or statue
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French piédestal, itself borrowed from Italian piedistallo (literally “foot stand”). Spelling influenced by Latin pēs, pedem.

meaning: quality of being deeply moving; keenness of emotion; ADJ. poignant: touching; deeply moving; (of sorrow, grief, etc.) painful; keenly distressing to the mind; Ex. poignant memory/anxiety; CF. prick
split into opposite extremes or camps
etymology: From French polariser, equivalent to polar + -ize.

meaning: state of having two opposite qualities
of a pole; characterized by opposite extremes; Ex. polar opposites
etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin polāris. By surface analysis, pole + -ar.

meaning: group sharing a common cause or opinion
etymology: The verb is from Middle English campen, from Old English campian, compian (“to fight, war against”), from Proto-West Germanic *kampōn (“to fight, do battle”), from *kamp (“field, battlefield, battle”), see above. Cognate with Dutch kampen, German kämpfen (“to struggle”), Danish kæmpe, Swedish kämpa.

meaning: attack or defense of an opinion; controversy or refutation; argument in support of point of view; N. polemics: art of debate or controversy
etymology: From French polémique, from Ancient Greek πολεμικός (polemikós, “of war”), from πόλεμος (pólemos, “war”). By surface analysis, polem- + -ic.

meaning: aggressive in verbal attack; disputatious (rather than simply expressing opinions)
prudent; judicious; well judged; expedient; well devised
etymology: From Middle French politique, from Latin polīticus, from Ancient Greek πολιτικός (politikós), from πολίτης (polítēs, “citizen”). Cognate with German politisch (“political”). Doublet of politico.

meaning: (particular form of) political organization; form of government of nation or state; Ex. student polity
etymology: From Middle French politie, from Latin polītīa, from Ancient Greek πολιτεία (politeía, “polity, policy, the state”). Doublet of police, policy, and polis (“police”).

meaning: one who has more than one spouse at a time; CF. bigamy; CF. polyandry
etymology: From polygamy + -ist.

meaning: speaking several languages; multilingual; Ex. polyglot person/society; N.
etymology: Noun sense 1 (“publication in several languages”) is probably derived from Late Latin polyglottus, from Attic Greek πολύγλωττος (polúglōttos): see above.

meaning: self-important behavior; acting like a stuffed shirt (pompous person); ADJ. pompous: self-important
etymology: From Middle English pomposite (“solemnity”), from Latin pompōsitās. By surface analysis, pomp + -osity.

meaning: having great weight; weighty; unwieldy; lacking lightness; dull; Ex. ponderous body/style of writing
etymology: Ultimately from Latin ponderōsus (“weighty”).

meaning: pertaining to a bishop or pope; pompous or pretentious; CF. pontiff: pope; bishop
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin pontificālis.

meaning: study industriously; ponder; scrutinize; Ex. pore over the book; N.
etymology: From Middle English pore, from Old French pore, from Latin porus, from Ancient Greek πόρος (póros, “passage”). Displaced native English sweat hole from Middle English swet hole, which might have been a reformation of Old English swātþȳrel (literally “sweat hole”), which competed with līcþēote (literally “body pipe”).

meaning: full of pores; like a sieve
etymology: From Old French poros, from Latin porus (“an opening”). By surface analysis, pore + -ous.

meaning: narrow space between things
etymology: From late Middle English interstice, from Old French interstice or directly from Latin interstitium (“a space between, gap, interval”), ultimately from intersistere (“to stand in between, to stop in the middle”), from inter- + sistere (“to stand, to stop”).

meaning: foretell; presage; be a sign or warning of; N. portent: sign; omen; forewarning
etymology: Borrowed from Latin portendere (“to foretell”), from por- (“forward”) + tendere (“to stretch”).

meaning: one who foretells the future
etymology: From Middle English sothsaier, zothziggere, by surface analysis, sooth (“truth”) + sayer.

meaning: stout; corpulent
etymology: From an archaic sense of port (“manner in which a person carries himself; bearing; deportment; carriage”) + -ly.

meaning: rather fat; strong in body; sturdy; resolute; determined; strong in determination; Ex. stout stick/supporter
etymology: The noun "strong, dark-brown beer" is first recorded 1677, from the adjective.

meaning: person who pretends to be sophisticated, elegant, etc., to impress others; person who poses; CF. pose
etymology: Borrowed from French poseur.

meaning: assume a particular posture; put forward; present; affect a particular attitude (to impress others); Ex. pose a threat; N.
etymology: From Middle English pose, from Old English ġeposu pl (“cold in the head; catarrh”, literally “(the) sneezes; (the) snorts”), from Old English pos, ġepos (“sneeze, snort”), from Proto-West Germanic *pos, from Proto-Germanic *pusą (“sneeze, snort”), from Proto-Germanic *pusōną, *pusjaną (“to snort, blow”), from *pus- (“to blow, breathe hard”), from Proto-Indo-European *bew- (“to blow, swell”). Compare Low German pusten (“to blow, puff”), German dialectal pfausen (“to sneeze, snort”), Norwegian dialectal pysa (“to blow”).

meaning: descendants; future generations; Ex. go down to posterity; CF. posterior, anterior
etymology: Late 14th century, from Middle French posterité, from Latin posteritas, from posterus (“following, coming after”), from post (“after”) (English post-).

meaning: after death (as of child born after father'death or book published after author'death); coming or occurring after one'death; Ex. posthumous fame/novel
etymology: From Latin posthumus, a variant spelling of postumus, superlative form of posterus (“coming after”), the ⟨h⟩ added by association with humus (“ground, earth”) referring to burial.

meaning: autopsy; ADJ: occurring after death; of a postmortem
self-evident truth; something assumed without proof; V: assume the truth of (as a basis of an argument)
etymology: Borrowed from Latin postulātum, a neuter nominalization of postulātus, perfect passive participle of postulō, possibly from poscō. See -ate (noun-forming suffix) for more. Cognate with French postulat.

meaning: assume an affected pose; act artificially; N: pose; attitude
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French posture, from Italian postura, from Latin positūra (“position, situation”). Doublet of positura.

meaning: suitable for drinking; drinkable
etymology: The noun is derived from the adjective.

meaning: powerful; convincing; persuasive; greatly influential
etymology: From Middle English potent, borrowed from Latin potens, potentis (“powerful, strong, potent”), present participle of posse (“to be able”), from potis (“able, powerful, originally a lord, master”).

meaning: monarch; sovereign
etymology: From Middle English potentat, from Old French, from Late Latin potentātus (“rule, political power”), from Latin potēns (“powerful, strong”), the active present participle of possum (“to be able”).

meaning: expressing possibility; latent; N: capacity for growth
etymology: From Late Latin potentialis, from Latin potentia (“power”), from potens (“powerful”). By surface analysis, potent + -ial.

meaning: dose (of liquids); liquid dose
etymology: From Middle English pocioun, borrowed from Old French pocion, from Latin pōtiō (“a drinking”), pōtiōnis, from pōtāre (“to drink”). Displaced native Old English drenċ whence Modern English drench. Doublet of poison.

meaning: heterogeneous mixture; medley; mixture of dried flower petals a pot (to give a pleasant smell to a room)
etymology: From French pot-pourri (“stew, potpourri”), a calque of Spanish olla podrida (“stew”, literally “rotten pot”). Doublet of olla podrida.

meaning: soothing application applied to sore and inflamed portions of the body
etymology: From Middle English pultes, from Latin pultes, plural of puls. The phonological development from Middle English is regular; compare poultry.

meaning: feasible
etymology: Borrowed from Latin prācticābilis, partly modelled on Middle French praticable. By surface analysis, practice (verb) + -able.

meaning: based on experience; of or acquired through practice (rather than theory); useful; Ex. practical man
etymology: From Middle English practical, practicale, praktycall, from Medieval Latin practicālis.

meaning: practical (as opposed to idealistic); concerned with practical worth or impact of something; Ex. pragmatic test of the skill
etymology: From Middle French pragmatique, from Late Latin pragmaticus (“relating to civil affair; in Latin, as a noun, a person versed in the law who furnished arguments and points to advocates and orators, a kind of attorney”), from Ancient Greek πραγματικός (pragmatikós, “active, versed in affairs”), from πρᾶγμα (prâgma, “a thing done, a fact”), in plural πράγματα (prágmata, “affairs, state affairs, public business, etc.”), from πράσσω (prássō, “to do”) (whence English practical).

meaning: practical person; N. pragmatism: pragmatic way of dealing with things
etymology: From Ancient Greek πρᾶγμα (prâgma, “thing”).

meaning: move about in a spirited manner (proudly and confidently)
etymology: From Middle English prancen, prauncen (“to prance”, literally “to show off”), variant of Middle English pranken (“to prank”), thus probably from the same ultimate root as prank. Cognate with Bavarian prangezen, prangssen (“to put on airs”), Alemannic German pranzen (“to strut”).

meaning: talk idly; speak foolishly; boast idly
etymology: Related to Dutch praten (“to talk, chat”), Low German praten, dated German pfrassen, Danish prate, Swedish prata (“to talk, prate”), Faroese práta (“to talk, gossip”), Icelandic prata;; also cognate with Polish bredzić (“to rave, jabber”), Latvian bradāt (“to talk nonsense”).

meaning: talk idly; babble; N. CF. prate
etymology: From prate + -le (early modern English frequentative suffix). Compare Dutch pruttelen and Dutch preutelen (“to mutter”).

meaning: not working; not employed or busy; lazy; without purpose; useless; lacking substance; baseless; not based on truth; Ex. idle worker; Ex. talk idly; V.
etymology: From Middle English idel, ydel, from Old English īdel, from Proto-West Germanic *īdl, from Proto-Germanic *īdlaz. Cognate with Dutch ijdel (“vain, meaningless”), ijl (“rareified, skinny”), iel (“thin, slender”); German Low German iedel (“vain, idle”); German eitel (“vain, conceited”); and possibly Old Norse illr ("bad"; > English ill).

meaning: introductory statement
etymology: From Middle English preamble, from Old French preambule (French préambule), from Medieval Latin praeambulum, from praeambulō (“to walk before”).

meaning: unsafe; lacking in stability; uncertain; risky; Ex. precarious living
etymology: From Latin precārius (“begged for, obtained by entreaty”), from prex, precis (“prayer”). Compare French précaire, Portuguese precário, and Spanish and Italian precario.

meaning: something preceding in time which may be used as an authority or guide for future action; V. precede; CF. unprecedented
etymology: From Middle French, from Old French, from Latin praecēdēns, present participle of praecēdere (“to precede”); See precede.

meaning: practical rule guiding conduct; Ex. mother'precept
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin praeceptum, form of praecipiō (“to teach”), from Latin prae (“pre-”) + capiō (“take”).

meaning: cliff; dangerous position; Ex. on the edge of the precipice
etymology: Distantly related to precept through Latin praecipiō (“to teach”), from prae + capiō (“take”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap-, *keh₂p- (“to hold; to seize”).

meaning: edge (at the top of a cliff); Ex. on the brink of the Grand Canyon
etymology: From Middle English brinke, brenke, from Old Norse *brenka, brekka, from Proto-Germanic *brinkǭ, *brinkaz (“hill, edge (of land)”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰren- (“to project”). Cognate with Dutch brink (“grassland”), regional German Brink, Icelandic brekka (“slope”); also Tocharian B prenke (“island”), Irish braine (“prow”).

meaning: something that causes a substance in a chemical solution to separate out in solid form; Ä§ÀüÁ¦; OP. solvent
etymology: The adverb and noun are derived from the adjective.

meaning: hurl downward; throw headlong; hasten; cause to happen sooner; condense and fall as rain or snow; cause (a solid substance) to be separated from a solution; ADJ. hasty; rash; premature; sudden
etymology: From Latin praecipitātus, perfect passive participle of praecipitō (“throw down, hurl down, throw headlong”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more), from praeceps (“head foremost, headlong”) (praecipit- in its oblique stem), from prae (“before”) + -ceps (“headed”).

meaning: steep; overhasty; precipitate
etymology: From obsolete French précipiteux, from Vulgar Latin *praecipitōsus, from praeceps, praecipit- (“ precipice”) + -ōsus (“-ful, -ous”), from prae- (“before”) + caput (“head”). Equivalent to precipice (“steep cliff, brink”) + -ous.

meaning: abstract; concise summing up of main points; concise summary of a text
exact
etymology: From Middle French précis, from Latin praecīsus, perfect passive participle of praecīdere, from prae- (“before, in front”) + caedere (“cut; strike”), cognate with hit. Related to incise. Doublet of précis.

meaning: make impossible; prevent; exclude; eliminate
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin praeclūdere.

meaning: advanced in development; N. precocity
etymology: From Latin praecox (“premature, precocious, ripe before time, early ripe”), from praecoquō (“to ripen beforehand, ripen fully, also boil beforehand”), from prae (“before”) + coquō (“to cook, boil, ripen”). Doublet of apricot.

meaning: forerunner; predecessor
etymology: Inherited from Middle English precursour, from Middle French precurseur or its etymon Latin praecursor (“forerunner”). By surface analysis, precurse + -or.

meaning: predatory animal or bird; predatory person; creature that seizes and devours another animal; person who robs or exploits others; ADJ. predatory: living by preying on other organisms; plundering; N. predation
etymology: Borrowed from Latin praedātor, from praedor (“loot, pillage”), from praeda (“booty, spoils, prey”).

meaning: former occupant of a post
etymology: From Middle English predecessour, from Old French predecesseor (“forebear”), from Late Latin praedēcessor, from Latin prae- (“pre-”) + Latin dēcessor (“retiring officer”), from Latin dēcēdō (“to retire, to die”) (English decease).

meaning: determine in advance; predestine; settle or decide beforehand; influence markedly
etymology: From Latin praedēterminō; equivalent to pre- + determine.

meaning: difficult situation; tricky or dangerous situation; dilemma
etymology: From Middle English predicament, from Old French predicament, from Late Latin praedicāmentum (“that which is predicated, a predicament, category”).

meaning: preference; partiality
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin praedīlēctiō.

meaning: give an inclination toward (in advance); make susceptible to; Ex. predispose people to certain cancer; N. predisposition
etymology: Either a back-formation from predisposition or borrowed from Middle French predisposer.

meaning: outstanding; superior
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French preeminent and its source, Latin praeēminēns, present participle of praeēmineō (“to stand out, excel”), from prae- (“pre-”) + ēmineō.

meaning: prevent in advance; head off (forestall); forestall by acting first; appropriate for oneself before others; supplant; take the place of; displace; Ex. preempt any attempts; ADJ. preemptive
etymology: Back-formation from preemption.

meaning: make oneself tidy in appearance; feel self-satisfaction or pride; (of a bird) smooth or clean (feathers) with the beak; Ex. preen oneself on; CF. prune
etymology: The verb is from Middle English prenen, from pren (“a preen”), akin to German pfriemen.

meaning: introductory; of a preface
etymology: Note that this is borrowed from Latin, not derived in English from preface, as in occasional misspelling *prefecatory.

meaning: capable of grasping or holding (esp. by wrapping around); Ex. prehensile tails
etymology: Borrowed from French préhensile, from Latin perfect passive participle prehēnsus, from prehendō (“grasp, seize”) + adjective suffix -ile, from Latin -ilis.

meaning: church dignitary; priest of high position in the church (esp. bishop)
etymology: From Old French prelat (French prélat), from Medieval Latin praelātus, perfect passive participle of praeferō (“to carry before, prefer, exceed”), see -ate (noun-forming suffix). Doublet of prefer. See also infer, relate and refer, delate and defer, as well as collate and confer among others.

meaning: introduction; introductory performance or event; forerunner
etymology: From Middle French prélude (“singing to test a musical instrument”), from Medieval Latin preludium, from Latin praelūdere.

meaning: plan in advance; Ex. premeditated murder
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin praemeditātus, past participle of praemeditor (“to premeditate”). By surface analysis, pre- + meditate.

meaning: assumption; postulate; proposition upon which an argument is based
etymology: Sense 4, a piece of real estate arose from the misinterpretation of the word by property owners while reading title deeds where the word was used with the legal sense.

meaning: forewarning; presentiment; foreboding
etymology: First use appears c. 1533. From Anglo-Norman premunition, from Ecclesiastical Latin praemonitiōnem (“a forewarning”), form of praemonitiō, from Latin praemonitus, past participle of praemoneō, from prae (“before”) (English pre-) + moneō (“to warn”) (from which English monitor). Compare Germanic forewarning.

meaning: serving to warn
etymology: Borrowed from Latin praemonitōrius.

meaning: superiority of power, quantity, etc.; V. preponderate: be greater in power, weight, or importance; ADJ. preponderant
etymology: From preponderant + -ance.

meaning: absurd; completely unreasonable; ridiculous
etymology: From Latin praeposterus (“with the hinder part before, reversed, inverted, perverted”), from prae (“before”) + posterus (“coming after”).

meaning: privilege; unquestionable right; CF. ask before
etymology: From Anglo-Norman prerogative (noun), from Latin praerogātīva (“previous verdict; claim, privilege”), noun use of the feminine singular of praerogātīvus (“having first vote; privileged”).

meaning: foretell; be a warning or sign of; N: presentiment; foreboding; omen
etymology: From Middle English presage, from Latin praesāgium.

meaning: ability to foretell the future; knowledge of actions before they occur; ADJ. prescient
etymology: Inherited from Middle English prescience, from Old French prescience, from Latin praescientia.

meaning: premonition; foreboding; feeling something will happen; anticipatory fear
etymology: From French pressentiment, from Middle French, equivalent to pre- + sentiment.

meaning: respect or admiration; impression produced by achievements or reputation; ADJ: causing admiration; ADJ. prestigious: having prestige
etymology: From French prestige (“illusion, fascination, enchantment, prestige”), from Latin praestīgium (“a delusion, an illusion”). Despite the phonetic similarities and the old meaning of “delusion, illusion, trick”, the word has a different root than prestidigitator (“conjurer”) and prestidigitation.

meaning: going beyond what is right; excessively forward; arrogant; taking liberties
etymology: From Middle English presumptuous, borrowed from Old French presumpcieus, presumptieus, presumptuos and its etymon Medieval Latin praesūmptuōsus.

meaning: take for granted; assume; act overconfidently; take liberties; presume on/upon: take unfair advantage of (someone'kindness or connection); N. presumption
etymology: From Middle English presumen, from Anglo-Norman presumer and its source, Latin praesūmere (“to take beforehand, anticipate”), from prae- + sūmere (“to take”).

meaning: ostentatious; showy; pompous; making unjustified claims; overambitious; Ex. pretentious films that claim to be art
etymology: Note that pretentious is spelled with a ‘t’, unlike related pretense, pretension. This is due to the French spelling: *-sious does not occur as an English suffix, though -sion and -tion both do.

meaning: feign; pretend to: claim to possess; make pretensions to; Ex. I don't pretend to much expertise; N. pretense
etymology: From Anglo-Norman pretendre, Middle French pretendre (French prétendre (“to claim, demand”)), from Latin praetendere (“to put forward, hold out, pretend”), from prae- (“pre-”) + tendō (“stretch”); see tend.

meaning: pretentiousness; claim (without foundation); Ex. I make no pretensions to skill as an artist.
etymology: From Middle English pretencioun, pretensioun, from Medieval Latin prētēnsiō.

meaning: beyond what is normal in nature; supernatural; Ex. preternatural strength/forces
etymology: From preter- + natural, after Latin prēternātūrālis/praeternātūrālis, from praeter nātūram, from praeter (“beyond”) + nātūra (“nature”); compare supernatural.

meaning: excuse
etymology: From Latin praetextum (“an ornament, etc., wrought in front, a pretense”), neuter of praetextus, past participle of praetexere (“to weave before, fringe or border, allege”).

meaning: be widespread; triumph over; gain victory; prevail on: persuade; induce; Ex. Justice has prevailed; Ex. prevail on someone to do something
etymology: From Middle English prevailen, from Old French prevaler, from Latin praevaleō (“be very able or more able, be superior, prevail”), from prae (“before”) + valeō (“be able or powerful”). Displaced native Old English rīcsian.

meaning: widespread; generally accepted
etymology: From Latin praevalēns. By surface analysis, pre- + -valent.

meaning: lie; hide the truth (by equivocating)
etymology: Borrowed from Latin praevāricātus, perfect active participle of praevāricor (“to walk crookedly; to play a false or double part”), from prae- + vāricō (“to stand with feet apart, straddle”), from vāricus (“with feet spread apart”); see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

meaning: target of a hunt; victim; V: hunt and eat as prey; victimize; Ex. Cats prey on mice.
etymology: From Middle English preye, prei, preyȝe, borrowed from Anglo-Norman and Old French preie, one of the variants of proie, from Latin praeda. Compare predator. Doublet of prede.

meaning: proper to the point of affectation; very precise and formal; exceedingly proper
etymology: Oxford English Dictionary proposed a relation with primp and prink. Chiefly Scottish and U.S.

meaning: seniority by birth; state of being the first-born child; right of the eldest child (to inherit the entire property of one or both parents)
etymology: From French, from Late Latin primogenitura, from Latin primus (“first”) + genitura (“birth”) (from genitus, past participle of gignere).

meaning: existing at the beginning (of time); rudimentary
etymology: From the Latin prīmōrdiālis (“of the beginning”). Compare primordium and -al.

meaning: groom oneself with care; adorn oneself
etymology: 16th century, a variant of prim.

meaning: unspoiled; remaining in a pure state; characteristic of earlier times; primitive; Ex. an old book in pristine condition
etymology: From Middle French pristin, borrowed from Latin prīstinus.

meaning: lack of the basic necessities or comforts of life; hardship; want; CF. deprive
etymology: Inherited from Middle English privacioun, from Middle French privation, privacion, from Old French privacion, from Latin prīvātiō; compare French privation. See private.

meaning: secret; hidden; not public; made a participant in something secret; Ex. privy chamber government; Ex. be privy to a discussion; CF. private
etymology: From Middle English pryvy, prive, from Old French privé (“private”), from Latin prīvātus (“deprived”), perfect passive participle of prīvō (“to bereave, deprive; to free, release”). Doublet of private.

meaning: explore with a probe or tools; investigate; N: slender instrument used to explore a wound or body cavity; device designed to investigate an unknown region; thorough investigation; Ex. space probe
etymology: For noun: borrowed from Late Latin proba (“a proof”), from probare (“to test, examine, prove”); Doublet of proof. Compare Spanish tienta (“a surgeon's probe”), from tentar (“try, test”); see tempt.

meaning: uprightness; honesty; incorruptibility
etymology: From Middle French probité, from Latin probitās (“uprightness, honesty”), from probus (“good, excellent, honest”); see probe, prove.

meaning: embezzle
etymology: First attested in the 1530s, in the sense “to lop off”; borrowed from Medieval Latin dēfalcātus, perfect passive participle of dēfalcō (“to cut or lop off”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin dē (“off”) + falx (“sickle, scythe, pruning hook”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).

meaning: causing a problem; open to doubt; doubtful; unsettled; questionable; Ex. Whether the arena will ever be completed is problematic.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French problématique, from Late Latin problematicus, from Ancient Greek προβληματικός (problēmatikós), from πρόβλημα (próblēma, “outjutting, barrier, problem”), from προβάλλω (probállō, “I throw, place before”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + βάλλω (bállō, “I throw, place”). By surface analysis, problem + -atic.

meaning: inclination; natural tendency (esp. towards something bad)
etymology: From Latin prōclīvitās, from prōclīvis (“prone to”).

meaning: postpone; delay or put off
etymology: First attested in 1548; from Latin prōcrastinātus, perfect passive participle of prōcrastinō (“defer, put off till tomorrow”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from prō- (“in favor of”) + crāstinus (“of or belonging to tomorrow”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix), from crās (“tomorrow”).

meaning: obtaining; V. procure: obtain by effort; obtain (a prostitute) for another
etymology: Inherited from Middle English procurement, from Old French procurement, from procurer.

meaning: poke (with a pointed object); stir up; urge; goad to action; N: pointed object used to prod; prodding
etymology: Alteration of earlier brod (perhaps through influence of poke; compare prog), from Middle English brodden (“to goad, incite, urge; to sprout”), from brod (“goad, nail; shoot, sprout”), from Old Norse broddr (“shaft, spike, thorn”), from Proto-Germanic *bruzdaz. Cognate with Icelandic broddur, Danish brod. Doublet of brad. Or, from or influenced by sound symbolism.

meaning: wasteful; reckless with money; profuse; Ex. a mind prodigal of ideas; N. prodigality
etymology: The senses of "abandoning a person or cause" and "returning after abandonment" are by allusion to the New Testament story commonly called "The Parable of the Prodigal Son", Luke 15:11–32. See prodigal son.

meaning: enormous; marvelous; extraordinary; Ex. prodigious amount/memory
etymology: * Spanish prodigioso

meaning: highly gifted child; person with exceptional talents; marvel; wonder
etymology: From Middle English prodige (“portent”), from Latin prōdigium (“omen, portent, prophetic sign”).

meaning: violate; desecrate (something holy); treat unworthily; be profane for; ADJ: secular; nonreligious; irreverent for holy things
etymology: From Middle English prophane, from Middle French profane, prophaine, prophane and its etymon Classical Latin profānus (“not religious, unclean”) (also Late Latin prophānus), from pro- (“instead of”) + fānum (“temple”).

meaning: wasteful (of money); dissipated; wildly immoral; dissolute; N: profligate person; N. profligacy
etymology: The adjective is first attested in 1535, the verb in 1542; borrowed from Latin prōflīgātus, perfect passive participle of prōflīgō (“to strike down, cast down”) (see -ate (etymology 1, 2 an 3) and pro-), from prō- (“forward”) + flīgō (“to strike, dash”) + -ō (1st conjugation compound verb-forming suffix). Common participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.

meaning: deep; not superficial; complete; Ex. profound thinker/remark/silence/deafness; N. profundity
etymology: From Middle English profound, profounde, from Anglo-Norman profound, from Old French profont, profonde, from Latin profundus (“deep, profound”), from prō + fundus (“bottom; foundation”).

meaning: great amount; plenty; overabundance; excess; lavish expenditure; Ex. profusion of choices; ADJ. profuse: plentiful; copious; giving or given abundantly; extravagant
etymology: From Middle French profusion, from Late Latin profusio.

meaning: ancestor
etymology: From Middle English progenitour, from Anglo-Norman progenitour, Middle French progeniteur (Modern French progéniteur), and their etymon Latin prōgenitor, from prōgenitus, perfect participle of prōgignere (“to beget”), itself from prō- (“forth”) + gignere (“to beget”). By surface analysis, pro- (“prior, fore-”) + genitor.

meaning: children; offspring; descendants
etymology: From Middle English progenie, from Old French progenie, from Latin prōgeniēs, from prōgignō (“beget”).

meaning: forecasted course of a disease; prediction; CF. prognostic
etymology: * Sanskrit प्रज्ञा (prajñā, “intelligence, wisdom; judgment; knowledge”)

meaning: predict (according to present indications)
etymology: From Medieval Latin prognosticare; see prognostic for more.

meaning: so high as to prohibit purchase or use; tending to prevent the purchase or use of something; prohibiting; inclined to prevent or forbid; Ex. prohibitive tax
etymology: From Middle English prohibitif, prohibityve, from Medieval Latin prohibitīvus, from prohibit-, past-participle stem of Latin prohibēre. By surface analysis, prohibit + -ive.

meaning: missile; fired or thrown object (such as stone or bullet)
etymology: From Medieval Latin prōiectilis (“projectile”), from Latin prōiectus, perfect passive participle of prōiciō (“throw forth; extend; expel”).

meaning: member of the working class; blue collar guy; N. proletariat: working class (who have to work for wages)
etymology: From Latin proletarius (“a man whose only wealth is his offspring, or whose sole service to the state is as father”), from proles (“offspring, posterity”).

meaning: grow rapidly (in numbers); spread; multiply; N. proliferation
etymology: Back-formation from proliferation.

meaning: producing offspring or fruit in abundance; fertile; fecund; abundantly fruitful; producing abundant works; Ex. prolific writer
etymology: First use appears c. 1635. From French prolifique and its etymon Latin prōlificus, from prōlēs (“offspring”) + -ficus (“making”).

meaning: tedious wordiness; verbosity; ADJ. prolix: wordy; verbose; diffuse
etymology: From Old French prolixite, from Latin prolixitas. By surface analysis, prolix + -ity.

meaning: introduction (to a poem or play)
etymology: From Middle English prologue, prologe, from Old French prologue, from Latin prologus, from Ancient Greek πρόλογος (prólogos). Equivalent to pro- + -logue.

meaning: bitter prolonged quarrel (usually between two peoples or families); V. CF. Romeo and Juliet; CF. feudal, feudalism
etymology: Cognate to Old English fǣhþ, fǣhþu, fǣhþo (“hostility, enmity, violence, revenge, vendetta”), German Fehde, and Dutch vete (“feud”) (directly inherited from Proto-West Germanic) alongside Danish fejde (“feud, enmity, hostility, war”) and Swedish fejd (“feud, controversy, quarrel, strife”) (borrowed from Middle Low German).

meaning: lengthen; extend; draw out
etymology: Either a back-formation from prolongation, or from Old French prolonguer or porloignier, from Latin prōlongō, from prō + longō. Doublet of purloin.

meaning: protruding (sticking out); conspicuous; notable; eminent
etymology: From obsolete French prominent (compare proéminent), from Latin prōminēns, present active participle of prōmineō (“jut out, to project”), from prō (“before, forward”) + mineō (in compounds, “jut, project”).

meaning: mixed indiscriminately; indiscriminate; not choosing carefully; indiscriminate in the choice of sexual partners; irregular, particularly sexually; Ex. promiscuous life/girl; N. promiscuity
etymology: From Latin prōmiscuus (“mixed, not separated”), from prō (“forth”) + misceō (“mix”).

meaning: headland
etymology: From Medieval Latin prōmontōrium, from prōmineō, from prō- + *mineō (“to project or jut”, from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to stand out”)) + -tōrium (“place”).

meaning: advance in rank; advance; help to flourish; advocate; help actively in forming; publicize or popularize; Ex. Milk promotes health; Ex. promote a match/bill; Ex. promote a new product
etymology: From Latin prōmōtus, perfect passive participle of prōmoveō (“move forward, advance”).

meaning: cause; urge; provoke; provide a cue (for an actor); ADJ: done without delay; done at the right time; punctual; on time; N: reminder or cue
etymology: The verb is from Middle English prompen, apparently from the adjective. The noun is from the verb.

meaning: word or signal (as in a play to prompt another actor'speech or entrance); reminder or hint; V: give a cue to
etymology: From Middle English cu (used for half a farthing, from q as an abbreviation for Latin quadrāns (“quarter of an as”)), from Latin cū, kū. Compare French ku.

meaning: announce; proclaim a doctrine or law; make known by official publication
etymology: Inherited from Middle English promulgaten, from Latin prōmulgātus, perfect passive participle of prōmulgō (“to make known, publish”), either from provulgō (“to make known, publish”), from pro (“forth”) + vulgō (“to publish”), or from mulgeō (“to bring forth”, literally “to milk”); see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Doublet of promulge.

meaning: inclined to; likely to (suffer); prostrate; lying with the front downward; Ex. prone to disease/make mistakes; Ex. accident-prone
etymology: From Middle English prone, proone, proon, from Latin prōnus (“turned forward, bent or inclined”), from prō (“forward”).

meaning: increase in number by producing young; multiply; spread; Ex. Most plants propagate by seed; Ex. newspaper propagating their ideas
etymology: First attested in 1535; from Latin prōpāgātus, perfect passive participle of prōpāgō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Participial usage up until Early Modern English.

meaning: substance which propels or drives forward (such as an explosive charge or a rocket fuel)
natural inclination
etymology: Learned borrowing from New Latin prōpensitās. By surface analysis, propense (“inclined, disposed”) + -ity.

meaning: of a prophet or prophecy; having to do with predicting the future; N. prophecy; V. prophesy; N. prophet
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French prophétique, from Latin prophēticus, from Ancient Greek προφητικός (prophētikós), equivalent to prophet + -ic.

meaning: used to prevent disease; N: something prophylactic; condom; N. prophylaxis: prevention of disease
etymology: From Latin prophylacticus, from Ancient Greek προφυλακτικός (prophulaktikós, “prophylactic”).

meaning: nearness (in space or relationship); proximity; kinship
