etymology: From Middle English wyndwen, from Old English windwian (“to winnow, fan, ventilate”), from Proto-West Germanic *windwōn, from Proto-Germanic *windwōną, *winþijaną (“to throw about, winnow”), from Proto-Indo-European *wē- (“to winnow, thresh”). Cognate with West Frisian wynje (“to winnow”), dialectal Dutch winden, winnen (“to winnow”), Middle High German winden (“to winnow”), Icelandic vinsa (“to pick out, weed”), Latin vannus (“a winnowing basket”). See fan, van.

meaning: put through a sieve to separate fine from coarse particles; sort or examine carefully
etymology: From Middle English syften, from Old English siftan, from Proto-West Germanic *siftijan.

meaning: charming (in a childlike way); agreeable; gracious; engaging
etymology: Inherited from Middle English wynsom, winsom, winsome, winsum, wunsum (“beautiful; agreeable, gracious, pleasant; generous; of situations: favourable, propitious”), from Old English wynsum (“joyful, merry, pleasant; winsome”), from Proto-West Germanic *wunnjusam (“joyful”). By surface analysis, winne (“delight, joy, pleasure”) + -some.

meaning: thin; slight; barely discernible
etymology: From wisp + -y.

meaning: small bunch (of hair); faint streak (of smoke)
etymology: From Middle English wispe, wyspe, wips, wipse, perhaps from an unrecorded Old English *wisp, *wips. Cognate with West Frisian wisp, Dutch wisp (“bundle of hay or straw”), Norwegian bokmål/Swedish/Bornholm Danish visp (“handful or bundle of grass, hay, etc.”). Akin also to Middle Dutch/Middle Low German wispel (“measure of grain”).

meaning: sadly thoughtful (because of desires or memories); sadly pensive; vaguely longing
etymology: Presumably from *whistful, from whist (“silent”) + -ful, based on older wistly. It is implausible that it derives from wishful, the required sound change being wishful → *wisful → wistful, which could not occur in Modern English, particularly not with wishful continuing in use. However, the sense of “longing” appears to be influenced by wishful, making wistful an ambiguous poetic word.

meaning: introverted; retiring; remote
distant in manner; aloof
etymology: From Middle English remote, from Old French remot, masculine, remote, feminine, from Latin remotus, past participle of removere (“to remove”), from re- + movere (“to move”).

meaning: (of a plant) dry up from loss of moisture; lose freshness; shrivel; decay
etymology: More at weather.

meaning: make or become shrunken and wrinkled (often by drying)
etymology: First recorded as shriveled (“shrivelled”), probably of North Germanic origin related to dialectal Swedish skryvla (“to wrinkle, shrivel”); perhaps ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *skrinkwaną (“to shrivel, shrink”) or *skrimpaną (“to shrink”).

meaning: refuse to give; hold back; Ex. withholding tax
etymology: From Middle English withholden. Equivalent to with- + hold.

meaning: stand up against; resist successfully
etymology: From Middle English withstanden, from Old English wiþstandan, from Proto-West Germanic *wiþistandan (“to withstand, resist”), equivalent to with- (“against”) + stand. Cognate with Old Frisian withstanda (“to resist”). Compare also Dutch weerstaan (“to withstand, repel”), German widerstehen (“to withstand, resist, defy”), Russian противостоять (protivostojatʹ, “to withstand”).

meaning: lacking intelligence or wit; foolish; idiotic
etymology: From Middle English witles, from Old English witlēas (“senseless; witless”), from Proto-Germanic *witjalausaz (“witless”), equivalent to wit + -less. Cognate with Swedish vettlös (“senseless; witless; wild”), Icelandic vitlaus (“senseless; witless; foolish; mad”).

meaning: witty saying; wisecrack (clever joking remark)
etymology: From witty + -icism; coined in the 1670s by John Dryden, by analogy to criticism.

meaning: sorcery; magic
etymology: From wizard + -ry.

meaning: shriveled; withered; Ex. wizened apple/old lady
etymology: Inherited from Middle English wisenen, from Old English wisnian, weosnian, from Proto-Germanic *wisnōjaną. Cognate with Icelandic visna.

meaning: great sorrow; deep inconsolable grief; affliction; suffering; Ex. financial woes
etymology: Cognate with Scots wae (“woe”), Cimbrian bèa (“woe!”), Dutch wee (“nauseating”), German Weh, Wehe (“misery, woe; pain”), Yiddish וויי (vey, “pain; woe”), Danish, Norwegian Nynorsk, Norwegian Bokmål, and Swedish ve (“woe”), Icelandic væl (“cry, wail”), væla (“to cry, wail; to complain”), Gothic 𐍅𐌰𐌹 (wai, “woe!”); also Cornish gew, go (“woe!”), Welsh gwae (“misery, woe”), Catalan, Italian, and Portuguese guai (“woe!”), Ladino guay, גואי (“woe”), Latin vae (“woe”), Romanian vai (“woe”), Spanish guay (“way”), Ancient Greek οὐαί (ouaí, “woe!”), Albanian vaj (“woe!”), Latvian vai (“oh!”), Bulgarian уви́ (uví, “alas”), Russian увы́ (uvý, “alas!”), Serbo-Croatian авај, avaj (“alas!”), Armenian վայ (vay, “sorrow, woe”), Persian وای (vây, “woe”).

meaning: sad; (of something bad) deplorable; deplorably bad; Ex. woeful housing conditions
etymology: From Middle English woful, waful, equivalent to woe + -ful. Compare Old English wālīċ (“woeful”), Old English tēonful (“woeful”).

meaning: (the stated person's) habit or custom; habitual procedure; ADJ. wonted: customary
etymology: Compare German Low German Gewohnte (“custom, habit”), Dutch gewoonte, Swedish van. Likely related to wone, wonder, wean, and win.

meaning: engrossed in matters of this earth; not spiritual; of the material world
etymology: From Middle English worldly, worldlich, wordly (adjective), from Old English woruldlīċ, worldlīċ, weoroldlīċ (“worldly; earthly; temporal; mundane; secular”), from Proto-Germanic *weraldilīkaz, equivalent to world + -ly. Cognate with Dutch wereldlijk (“worldly; secular”), German Low German weltlik (“worldly”), German weltlich (“worldly”), Danish verdslig (“worldly”), Swedish världslig (“worldly”), Icelandic veraldlegur (“worldly; secular”).

meaning: quarrel noisily; obtain through arguing; herd cattle; N.
etymology: * German rangeln (“to wrestle”)

meaning: group of animals; crowd; one who looks after a herd; Ex. shepherd/goatherd; Ex. herd instinct; Ex. herdsman; V: come together in a herd; look after a herd; Ex. herd cattle
etymology: From Middle English herde, heerde, heorde, from Old English hierd, heord (“herd, flock; keeping, care, custody”), from Proto-West Germanic *herdu, from Proto-Germanic *herdō (“herd”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerdʰ- (“file, row, herd”). Cognate with German Herde, Danish hjord, Swedish hjord. Non-Germanic cognates include Albanian herdhe (“nest”) and Serbo-Croatian krdo.

meaning: anger; fury
etymology: The verb is derived from Middle English wratthen (“to be or become angry, to rage; to quarrel; to cause wrath, offend; to become troubled or vexed; to cause grief or harm, grieve, vex”) [and other forms], from wratthe, wretthe (noun) (see above) + -en (suffix forming the infinitive of verbs).

meaning: inflict; Ex. wreak one'vengeance on
etymology: From Middle English wreken, from Old English wrecan, from Proto-West Germanic *wrekan, from Proto-Germanic *wrekaną, from Proto-Indo-European *wreg- (“push, shove, drive, track down”). Cognate via Proto-Germanic with Dutch wreken, German rächen, Swedish vräka; cognate via PIE with Latin urgēre (English urge), and distantly cognate with English wreck.

meaning: twist; pull; strain; Ex. He wrenched the gun out of her hands.
etymology: From Middle English wrench, from Old English wrenċ, from Proto-Germanic *wrankiz, from Proto-Indo-European *wreng- (“to turn”). Compare German Rank (“plot, intrigue”).

meaning: obtain by pulling violently; pull away; take by violence; Ex. wrest victory from their grasp
etymology: The noun is derived from the verb.

meaning: written command issued by a court (telling someone to do or not to do something)
etymology: From Middle English writ, from Old English writ and ġewrit (“writing”), from Proto-Germanic *writą (“fissure, writing”), from Proto-Indo-European *wrey-, *wrī- (“to scratch, carve, ingrave”). Cognate with Scots writ (“writ, writing, handwriting”), Icelandic rit (“writing, writ, literary work, publication”).

meaning: twist in coils; contort in pain
etymology: From Middle English writhen, from Old English wrīþan, from Proto-West Germanic *wrīþan, from Proto-Germanic *wrīþaną (“to weave, twist, turn”), from Proto-Indo-European *wreyt- (“to twist, writhe”). Cognate with Middle Dutch writen (“to turn, twist”), dialectal German reiden (“to turn, twist, lace”), Danish vride (“to twist”), Swedish vrida (“to turn, twist, wind”), French rider (“to wrinkle, furrow, ruffle”, (< Germanic)). Compare also Lithuanian riēsti (“to unbend, wind, roll”).

meaning: (esp. of an expression of the face) twisted; with a humorous twist (expressing displeasure)
etymology: From Middle English wrien, from Old English wrīġian (“to go, turn, twist, bend, strive, struggle, press forward, endeavor, venture”), from Proto-Germanic *wrigōną (“to wriggle”), from Proto-Indo-European *wreyḱ- (“to turn, wrap, tie”), from *wer- (“to turn, bend”). Compare awry, wriggle.

meaning: fear or hatred of foreigners; N. xenophobe
etymology: From xeno- + -phobia.

meaning: strong desire; longing; urge; Ex. yen for travel
etymology: From Medhurst and Hepburn’s romanizations, under the influence of earlier Portuguese romanizations, of Japanese 圓(えん) (en, “round; a round object”) as ye or yen, now 円(えん) (en), from Chinese 銀圓 /银圆 (yínyuán, “round silver object(s), especially a piece of eight”): 銀 /银 (yín, “silver”) + 圓 /圆 (yuán, “circular, round; yuan, yen, dollar”). Cognate with Chinese 元 (yuán, “monetary unit, especially RMB”) and Korean 원 (won, “North or South Korean won”). Doublet of won and yuan.

meaning: man or farmer owning small estate; middle-class farmer
etymology: * A contraction of yong man; compare dialectal yeomath (“aftermath”) for a possible parallel.

meaning: amount produced; crop; income on investment; profit obtained from an investment; V: produce; give in; surrender
etymology: The noun is cognate with West Frisian jild (“money”), Dutch geld (“money”), Low German and German Geld (“money”), Danish gæld (“debt”), Faroese and Icelandic gjald (“fee, payment”), Norn gild (“payment”), Norwegian gjeld (“debt”), and Swedish gäld (“debt”). See also geld.

meaning: join together; unite; N: crossbar used to joining two draft animals
etymology: Cognate with Saterland Frisian Juk (“yoke”), Cimbrian jòch (“yoke”), Dutch juk (“yoke; burden”), German Joch (“yoke”), Luxembourgish Jach (“yoke”), Danish åg (“yoke”), Faroese, Icelandic, and Swedish ok (“yoke”), Norwegian Bokmål and Norwegian Nynorsk åk (“yoke”), Gothic 𐌾𐌿𐌺 (juk, “yoked pair of animals”); also Breton yev (“yoke”), Irish and Scottish Gaelic cuing (“yoke; bond, tie”), Manx quing (“yoke”), Welsh iau (“yoke”), Latin iugum, jugum (“yoke”), Greek ζυγός (zygós, “even; twin”), Latvian jūgs (“yoke; bondage; cart”), Lithuanian jungas (“yoke”), Bulgarian и́го (ígo), юго (jugo, “yoke”), Czech jho (“yoke”), Kashubian jigò, jugò (“yoke”), Macedonian иго (igo, “yoke”), Polabian jaiďü (“yoke”), Russian и́го (ígo, “yoke”), Serbo-Croatian и́го, ígo (“yoke”), Slovene igo (“yoke”), Ukrainian і́го (ího, “yoke”), Armenian լուծ (luc, “harness, yoke”), Persian یوغ (yuġ, “yoke”), Hittite 𒄿𒌑𒃷 (yukan, “yoke”), Tocharian A yokäm (“door”), Sanskrit युग (yuga, “yoke; brace; couple, pair”).

meaning: rustic; country bumpkin; ÃÌ³ð
etymology: First use appears c. 1812, possibly from dialectal German Jokel, diminutive of Jakob, cf. Yankee (“little John”) and jacquerie (“a peasant uprising”). Alternatively, from dialectal English yokel, yuckle (“a European green woodpecker”), itself probably a variant of hickwall.

meaning: time long past; Ex. in the days of yore
etymology: From Middle English yore, yoare, yare, ȝore, ȝare, ȝeare, from Old English ġeāra (“long ago”), of unclear origin but probably from Proto-Germanic *jērǫ̂ (literally “of years”), the genitive plural of Proto-Germanic *jērą (“year”). More at year.

meaning: comic; crazy; N: clown; comical person (given to outlandish behavior)
etymology: From Middle French zani, zanni, from Italian zanni (“a kind of masked clown character”), from Zanni, a Venetian form of Giovanni. Doublet of Zanni, John, and Giovanni.

meaning: eager enthusiasm (to a cause or ideal); ADJ. zealous
etymology: From Middle English zele, from Old French zel, from Late Latin zēlus, from Ancient Greek ζῆλος (zêlos, “zeal, jealousy”), from Proto-Indo-European *yeh₂- (“to search”). Related to jealous.

meaning: one who is zealous; fanatic; person who shows excessive zeal
etymology: Initially only found as Middle English zelote, an epithet of Simon the Zealot, acquiring its current senses in the 16th and 17th centuries. The Middle English derives from Latin zēlōtēs, from Ancient Greek ζηλωτής (zēlōtḗs, “emulator, zealous admirer, follower”), from ζηλόω (zēlóō, “to emulate, to be jealous”), from ζῆλος (zêlos, “zeal, jealousy”).

meaning: point directly overhead in the sky; summit; acme; highest point
etymology: From Middle English cenyth, from Medieval Latin cenit, from Arabic سَمْت (samt, “direction, path”), from the fuller form سَمْت اَلرَّأْس (samt ar-raʔs, “direction of the head”). The -ni- for -m- is sometimes thought to be due to a misreading of the three strokes, which is plausible, though it could be a mere phonetic approximation.

meaning: gentle breeze; west wind
etymology: From Latin zephyrus (“west wind”), from Ancient Greek Ζέφυρος (Zéphuros). Doublet of zefir, zéphire, Zephyr, and Zephyrus. The confectionery sense is a semantic loan from Russian зефи́р (zefír).

meaning: Womanlike
To melt away, disappear as if by melting
(Linguistics) a minimum unit of meaning
etymology: From semantic + -eme.

meaning: Use of more words than necessary for clear expression (ex: burning fire). Some pleonastic phrases are idiomatic. A form of tautology
etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin pleonasmus, from Ancient Greek πλεονασμός (pleonasmós), from πλεονάζω (pleonázō, “to be superfluous”), from πλείων (pleíōn, “more”).

meaning: beveled edge connecting two surfaces
etymology: Back-formation from chamfering, from Middle French chanfrain, from Middle French, Old French chanfraindre, possibly a compound of chant (“corner”), from Latin canthus (of either Celtic or Latin origin) + fraindre (“to break”), from frangō (“to break”).

meaning: In Latin grammar, an adverbial phrase syntactically independent from the rest of the sentence and containing a noun or pronoun plus an adjunct, usually a participle or adjective, with both elements in the ablative case.
etymology: Calque of Latin ablativus absolutus.

meaning: removal of material from the surface of an object by an erosive process
etymology: From Late Middle English ablacioun (“removal”), from Late Latin ablātiō (“a taking away”), from auferō (“to take away, carry off, withdraw, remove”) + -tiō (“-tion”, nominal suffix). Doublet of ablatio. Compare French ablation. By surface analysis, ablat(e) + -ion.

meaning: A vowel change, characteristic of Indo-European languages, that accompanies a change in grammatical function; for example, i, a, u in sing, sang, sung. Also called gradation.
etymology: Borrowed from German Ablaut (“sound gradation”), which is from ab- or ab (“down, off”), + Laut (“sound”). Ab is used here in the sense of “deviating, varying” as in Abgott (“god other than the true God”), Abart (“different sort, variety, anomality”).

meaning: Loss or impairment of the ability to make decisions or act independently.
etymology: From New Latin abūlia, from Ancient Greek ἀβουλία (aboulía, “irresolution”), from ἀ- (a-, “without”) + βουλή (boulḗ, “will”).

meaning: having no leader. Biology: headless or lacking a clearly defined head "Acephalous worms"
etymology: From French acéphale, from Ancient Greek ἀκέφαλος (aképhalos, “headless”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”). By surface analysis, a- + -cephalous.

meaning: An almost horizontal entrance to a mine.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin aditus (“entrance, access”), from ad (“to, up to”) + itus (“going, departure”).

meaning: 1. To give a sketchy outline of. 2. To prefigure indistinctly; foreshadow. 3. To disclose partially or guardedly. 4. To overshadow; shadow or obscure.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin adumbrātus (“represented in outline”), from adumbrāre (“cast a shadow on”), from umbra (“shadow”).

meaning: The sayings of Jesus not written in the canonical Gospels but known from other ancient sources.

1. Dependent on chance, luck, or an uncertain outcome: "an aleatory contract between an oil prospector and a landowner." 2. Of or characterized by gambling: "aleatory contests." 3. also Aleatoric: Music Using or consisting of sounds to be chosen by the performer or left to chance; indeterminate: "An object placed inside the piano added an aleatory element to the piece."
etymology: From Latin āleātōrius, from āleātor (“dice-player”), from ālea (“a die”).

meaning: adv: In the fresh air; outdoors: "dining alfresco." adj: Taking place outdoors; outdoor: "an alfresco conference."
etymology: From Italian al fresco. Compare Spanish al fresco.

meaning: Sexual gratification derived from inflicting or experiencing pain. From greek lagneia (lust) other forms: algolagnic, algolagnist
etymology: From German Algolagnie, from Ancient Greek ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”) + λαγνεία (lagneía, “lust”). Equivalent to algo- + -lagnia.

meaning: Growing at high altitudes; alpine or subalpine.
etymology: Latin Alpestris.

meaning: (noun) A person with severely deficient intellectual capacity.
etymology: From Latin āmentum (“thong, string”).

meaning: A steroid hormone excreted in urine that reinforces masculine characteristics.
1. A devotional composition sung responsively as part of a liturgy. 2. A response; a reply: "It would be truer . . . to see conservation as an antiphon to the modernization of the 1950s and 1960s"
etymology: From French antiphone or Medieval Latin antiphōna, from Ancient Greek ἀντίφωνα (antíphōna, “responses, musical accords”), neuter plural substantive of ἀντίφωνος (antíphōnos, “concordant”) from ἀντί (antí, “in return”) + φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound”). Doublet of anthem.

meaning: A direct or diametrical opposite: "We just sit and listen to the fullness of the quiet, as an antipode to focused busyness"
etymology: Back-formation from antipodes.

meaning: anecdotes considered as a group
etymology: From anecdote + -age.

meaning: 1. A discerning perception; an insight: "Her schmoozy but magisterial aperçus inspired widespread emulation among the young" 2. A short outline or summary; a synopsis.
inability or refusal to swallow
etymology: Coined based on Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “without”) + φάγος (phágos, “glutton”) + -ία (-ía).

meaning: 1. having no light 2. Of or relating to the (deep) region of a body of water that is not reached by sunlight and in which photosynthesis is unable to occur.
etymology: From a- (prefix meaning ‘not; without; opposite of’) + photic.

meaning: Having carpels that are free from one another. Used of a single flower with two or more separate pistils, as in roses.
etymology: From apo- + -carpous.

meaning: An embellishing note, usually one step above or below the note it precedes and indicated by a small note or special sign.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian appoggiatura, derived from appoggiare (“to lean”).

meaning: A strong clear Scandinavian liquor distilled from potato or grain mash and flavored with caraway seed.
etymology: From Swedish and Danish akvavit and Norwegian akevitt, from Medieval Latin aqua vitae (“water of life”). Doublet of aqua vitae and akvavit. Compare eau de vie, whisky, whiskey, and water of life from the same source.

meaning: flying buttress
A unit of length formerly used in Russia and Turkey, equal to about 71 centimeters (28 inches).
Having the form of a bow; curved. other forms: arcuated, arcuately
etymology: From Latin arcuātus.

meaning: 1. The complete equipment of a physician or medical institution, including books, supplies, and instruments. 2. The complete range of materials available or used for a task.
etymology: From Latin armāmentārium (“arsenal”), from armāmenta (“tools, equipment, rigging”) + -ārium. By surface analysis, armament + -arium.

meaning: 1. A medieval royal proclamation by which vassals were summoned to military service. 2. the vassals summoned.
The sharp edge or ridge formed by two surfaces meeting at an angle, as in a molding. A chamfer is when the arris is cut away to make a bevel.
etymology: From Old French areste, from Latin arista (“beard (of grain), fishbone”). Doublet of arista.

meaning: An abnormal accumulation of serous fluid in the abdominal cavity.
etymology: From Latin ascītēs, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀσκίτης (askítēs), from ἀσκός (askós, “wineskin”).

meaning: A medieval instrument, now replaced by the sextant, that was once used to determine the altitude of the sun or other celestial bodies.
etymology: From Middle English astrelabie et al., from Middle French astrolabe, Old French astrelabe, from Ancient Greek ἀστρολάβος (astrolábos, “star-taking”), from ἄστρον (ástron, “star”) + λαμβάνω (lambánō, “I take”).

meaning: 1. lack of normal muscle tone 2. lack of accent or stress
etymology: Borrowed from New Latin atonia, from Ancient Greek ἀτονία (atonía, “languor”), from ἄτονος (átonos, “languid”), from ἀ- (a-, “privative”) + τόνος (tónos, “accent”), from τείνω (teínō, “to stretch”).

meaning: adj. Varying slightly from sphericity and having only slight aberration, as a lens.
etymology: From a- + spheric.

meaning: To examine by auscultation. (listening to the internal sounds of the body, usually using a stethoscope)
etymology: Back-formation from auscultation.

meaning: The destruction of tissues or cells of an organism by the action of substances, such as enzymes, that are produced within the organism. Also called self-digestion.
etymology: From auto- (“self”) + -lysis (“breakdown”).

meaning: 1. Occurring singly; not one of a pair, as a vein or muscle. 2. odd, unpaired.
etymology: From a- + -zygous.

meaning: 1. A platform lining a trench or parapet wall on which soldiers may stand when firing. 2. also ban·kit (bngkt) KEY Southern Louisiana & East Texas A raised sidewalk: "The flower of loafers . . . was found stretched on the banquette on Tuesday night" (New Orleans Daily Picayune). See Regional Note at beignet. 3. A long upholstered bench placed against or built into a wall. 4. A ledge or shelf, as on a buffet.
etymology: Borrowed from French banquette, the diminutive form of banc; by surface analysis, bank + -ette.

meaning: A free-diving deep-sea vessel consisting of a large flotation hull with a crewed observation capsule attached to its underside, usually capable of reaching full ocean depths.
etymology: Borrowed from French bathyscaphe. Analyzable as bathy- + Ancient Greek σκάφη (skáphē, “little boat, skiff”).

meaning: 1. The collection of organisms living on or in sea or lake bottoms. 2. The bottom of a sea or lake.
etymology: From Ancient Greek βένθος (bénthos, “the depths”).

meaning: 1. A narrow forked flag or streamer attached to a staff or lance or flown from a ship's masthead. 2. A representation of a ribbon or scroll bearing an inscription.
Custom-made. Said especially of clothes.
etymology: In sense “custom-made”, 1755, from earlier bespoken (c. 1600), form of bespeak, in sense “arrange beforehand” (1580s), a prefixed variant of speak; compare order, made-to-order.

meaning: A flat, round baked roll topped with onion flakes.
etymology: From Yiddish ביאַלי (byali), from the Polish name of the city of Białystok.

meaning: 1. Given to or marked by the consumption of alcoholic drink: a bibulous fellow; a bibulous evening. 2. Very absorbent, as paper or soil.
etymology: From Latin bibulus from bibō (“drink”) + -ulus from Proto-Italic *pibō, from Proto-Indo-European *píph₃eti, from root *peh₃- (“drink”); whence also imbibe and beverage via Old French beivre.

meaning: 1. a. A rich, creamy soup made from meat, fish, or shellfish. b. A thick cream soup made of puréed vegetables. 2. Ice cream mixed with crushed macaroons or nuts.
etymology: Borrowed from French bisque, possibly from Biscaye.

meaning: Weight loss, wasting of muscle, loss of appetite, and general debility that can occur during a chronic disease.
etymology: From Late Latin cachexia or French cachexie, from Ancient Greek καχεξία (kakhexía), from κακός (kakós, “bad; injurious”) + ἕξῐς (héxĭs, “act of having; habit or state of body”) (ultimately from ἔχω (ékhō, “to have”)) + -ῐᾰ (-ĭă, suffix added to adjectives to form abstract nouns).

meaning: The junction of the sagittal and coronal sutures at the top of the skull.
etymology: Borrowed from Ancient Greek βρέγμα (brégma, “top of the head”).

meaning: To laugh hard, loudly, or convulsively; guffaw.
etymology: From Latin cachinnō (“laugh aloud”), of onomatopoeic origin.

meaning: A pastille used to sweeten the breath. (a breath mint)
etymology: From French cachou, from Portuguese cachu, from Malay kacu (“type of acacia”).

meaning: 1. A watertight structure within which construction work is carried on under water. 2. See camel. 3. A large box open at the top and one side, designed to fit against the side of a ship and used to repair damaged hulls under water. 4. A floating structure used to close off the entrance to a dock or canal lock. 5. a. A horse-drawn vehicle, usually two-wheeled, used to carry artillery ammunition and coffins at military funerals. b. A large box used to hold ammunition.
etymology: Borrowed from French caisson. Doublet of cassone and cajón.

meaning: A tropical fever once believed to be caused by the heat.
etymology: From Middle French calenture, from Spanish calentura.

meaning: 1. An ornamental covering for a horse or for its saddle or harness; trappings. 2. Richly ornamented clothing; finery.
etymology: From Middle French caparasson (Modern French caparaçon), from Old Spanish caparazón, from Old Occitan capairon.

meaning: Feeding on fruit; fruit-eating.
etymology: From carpo- + -phagous, from Ancient Greek.

meaning: 1. A Eurasian currant (Ribes nigrum) bearing black berries. 2. A cordial made from the berries of this plant.
etymology: Borrowed from French cassis (“black currant”), probably from Latin cassia, from Hebrew קציעה (qetzi'ah).

meaning: 1. The misapplication of a word or phrase, as the use of blatant to mean "flagrant." 2. The use of a strained figure of speech, such as a mixed metaphor.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin catachrēsis, borrowed from Ancient Greek κατάχρησις (katákhrēsis, “misuse (of a word)”).

meaning: Blatant refers to anything that is offensive, notorious, or shocking, especially in an obvious or conspicuous way. Something that is blatant is often obtrusive in a crass manner - and blatant can be used of persons and things. Flagrant refers to anything that is evil or wrong, a willful or glaring violation of a promise or flouting of law or morality. A flagrant offense or error is so bad that it cannot escape notice. Flagrant is definitely the stronger term. Blatant was purportedly created by the English poet Spenser; flagrant derives from an Aryan word meaning 'to blaze' and its original meaning was 'blazing, burning, flaming'. Examples are: He blatantly lied about having permission to leave the school. / It was a flagrant violation of human rights.

adj: Of or being a group of primates including the Old World monkeys, apes, and humans, characterized by nostrils that are close together and directed frontward or downward. noun: A catarrhine primate, such as a gorilla.
1. The intensified part of the action directly preceding the catastrophe in classical tragedy. 2. The climax of a drama.
etymology: From Ancient Greek κατάστασις (katástasis, “settling, appointment”).

meaning: A saclike cavity with only one opening.
1. Furnished with turrets and battlements in the style of a castle. 2. Having a castle.
etymology: From Medieval Latin castellātus (“fortified, castellate”) + -ed (forming past participles). Equivalent to the past participle of castellate but attested earlier than other uses of the verb.

meaning: A company of badgers
The master of a castle; a castellan.
etymology: From Middle English chateleyn, from Middle French chatelaine, from Old French chastelein and castelain (“castellan”), from chastel and castel (“castle”) + -ain (“-an: forming adj.”), from Medieval Latin castellum, from Latin castrum (“fort”) + -ellum (“-elle: forming diminutives”). Doublet of Castilian, castellano, castellanus, and castellan.

meaning: ADJECTIVE: Having a changeable luster. NOUN: A chatoyant stone or gemstone, such as the cat's-eye.
etymology: From French chatoyant, present participle of chatoyer (“to iridesce, like a cat's eye”), from chat (“cat”, because of the reflective qualities of a cat's eye).

meaning: Of or relating to the underworld.
etymology: From Ancient Greek χθών (khthṓn, “ground, soil”) + -ic.

meaning: 1. A tropical Asian grass (Cymbopogon nardus) having bluish-green, lemon-scented leaves and an essential oil. 2. A pale yellow to brownish aromatic oil obtained from this plant, used chiefly in perfumery and also in some insect repellents and commercial flavorings.
etymology: Borrowed from French citronnelle.

meaning: 1. Separable into parts or having removable sections: a clastic anatomical model. 2. (Geology) Made up of fragments of preexisting rock; fragmental.
etymology: From Ancient Greek κλαστός (klastós, “broken in pieces”), from κλάω (kláō, “to break”) + -ic.

meaning: Having one end thickened; club-shaped: "clavate antennae."
etymology: First attested in 1661; borrowed from New Latin clāvātus, from Latin clāva (“club”) + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix). By surface analysis, clav(a) + -ate.

meaning: ADJECTIVE: Glittering with gold or tinsel. NOUN: Imitation gold leaf; tinsel; glitter.
etymology: From French clinquant, from clinquer (“to clink”).

meaning: The fiber obtained from the husk of a coconut, used chiefly in making rope and matting.
etymology: Borrowed from Tamil கயிறு (kayiṟu), Malayalam കയർ (kayaṟ).

meaning: Of, relating to, or being a surface characterized by smooth, shell-like convexities and concavities, as on fractured obsidian.
etymology: From conchoid + -al.

meaning: the act of condoning, especially the implied forgiveness of an offense by ignoring it.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin condōnātiō, condōnātiōnem. Equivalent to condone + -ation.

meaning: 1. A folk dance performed in two lines with the partners facing each other. 2. The music for a contredanse.
1. Labor exacted by a local authority for little or no pay or instead of taxes and used especially in the maintenance of roads. 2. A day of unpaid work required of a vassal by a feudal lord.
etymology: From French corvée, from Late Latin conrogāta, derived from Latin conrogāre (“call together by entreaty”).

meaning: Of, resembling, or characteristic of crows.
etymology: From Latin corvīnus.

meaning: 1. The leader of a Greek chorus. 2. A leader or spokesperson.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin coryphaeus, from Ancient Greek κορυφαῖος (koruphaîos, “leader of the chorus in an Ancient Greek drama”), from κορυφή (koruphḗ, “top of the head, crown”) (possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂- (“head, top; horn”)) + -ῐος (-ĭos, suffix forming adjectives meaning ‘belonging to, pertaining to’).

meaning: A practice in certain cultures in which the husband of a woman in labor takes to his bed as though he were bearing the child.
etymology: From French couvade (“brooding”).

meaning: 1. A conceited dandy; a fop. 2. Obsolete A jester's cap; a cockscomb.
etymology: From Middle English cokke’s comb.

meaning: a type of contraction in which two vowels or diphthongs merge into one new vowel or diphthong — making one word out of two. seen in Portugese, Arabic, and Ancient Greek. French examples: de le → du de les → des à le → au en les → ès
etymology: From Ancient Greek κρᾶσις (krâsis, “mixture”).

meaning: Procrastination; delay.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin cūnctātiō (“a delaying, tarrying”), from cūnctor (“linger, hesitate”).

meaning: The removal of tissue or growths from a body cavity, such as the uterus, by scraping with a curette. Also called curettement.
etymology: Borrowed from French curettage.

meaning: 1. To march from a narrow or confined area into the open. 2. To emerge; issue: "His companions still lay in the bed of the ravine, through which the smaller stream debouched" (James Fenimore Cooper).
etymology: From French déboucher (de + bouche (“mouth”)), modelled on Italian sboccare.

meaning: NOUN: 1. The process of transferring pictures or designs printed on specially prepared paper to materials such as glass or metal. 2. A decal.
etymology: Borrowed from French décalcomanie.

meaning: To make a crackling sound when roasted.
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin dēcrepitātus, perfect passive participle of dēcrepitō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin dē- + crepitō.

meaning: To withhold (something) by force from the rightful owner.
etymology: From Old French.

meaning: NOUN: 1. Delight. 2. Enjoyment; pleasure.
etymology: Attested from the mid 14th century, from Old French delectation (“enjoyment”), from Latin dēlectātiōnem, accusative singular of dēlectātiō, from the verb Latin dēlectō (“to delight, charm, please”), frequentative of dēliciō, from de- (“away”) + laciō (“to lure, to deceive”), from Proto-Italic *lakjō (“to draw, pull”), of unknown ultimate origin. By surface analysis, delect + -ation or delectate + -ion. Related to delight and delicious.

meaning: NOUN: 1. A style of glazed earthenware, usually blue and white. 2. Pottery made in this style.
etymology: After the Dutch city of Delft.

meaning: noun: Aberration of mind; delirium. Deliration or alienation of the understanding.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dēlīrātio.

meaning: noun: (Medicine) the sudden disappearance of a lesion or of the signs and symptoms of a disease
etymology: See delitescent.

meaning: ADJECTIVE: Serving to soothe or soften. NOUN: A soothing, usually mucilaginous or oily substance, such as glycerin or lanolin, used especially to relieve pain in inflamed or irritated mucous membranes.
etymology: From Latin dēmulcēns, present active participle of dēmulceō (“to stroke caressingly; to soften, soothe, allure”), from dē- (“from; of”) + mulceō (“to move or touch gently or lightly, to stroke; to make pleasant or sweet; to soften, soothe, alleviate, relieve”).

meaning: noun: 1. A discussion or discourse on a theme. 2. Music: An ornamental melody or counterpoint sung or played above a theme. verb: To comment at length; discourse: "He used to descant critically on the dishes which had been at table" (James Boswell).
etymology: From Anglo-Norman descaunt, from Medieval Latin discantus. Doublet of discant.

meaning: To wish to have or see happen.
etymology: From Latin, from the participle stem of the verb dēsīderāre (“to desire”). The verb is a doublet of desire.

meaning: A grammatical ending; an inflection. (an inflectional suffix, ex: the 's' in 'girls')
etymology: Borrowed from French désinence, from Latin dēsinentia, present participle of dēsinō (“to stop, end, close, make an end”).

meaning: A state of disuse or inactivity.
etymology: From Late Middle English desuetude, dissuetude (“discontinuance of a practice, disuse”), from Middle French désuétude (“obsolescence”) (modern French désuétude), from Latin dēsuētūdo (“discontinuance of a practice or a habit, disuse”), from dēsuētus + -tūdō (“suffix forming abstract nouns indicating conditions or states”). Dēsuētus is the perfect passive participle of dēsuēscō (“to make unaccustomed”), from de- (prefix having a reversing or undoing effect) + suēscō (“to become accustomed or used to; (Late Latin) to accustom, habituate, train”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swé (“self”) + *dʰeh₁- (“to do; to place, put”), in the sense “to set as one’s own”).

meaning: One of the 6,000 citizens chosen each year in ancient Athens to sit in the law courts, with functions resembling those of a judge and juror.
etymology: From Ancient Greek δικαστής (dikastḗs, “judge”).

meaning: ADJECTIVE: 1. Having digits or fingerlike projections. 2. Botany Having distinct parts arising from a common point or center; palmate.
etymology: The adjective is first attested in 1661, the verb in 1657; the adjective was borrowed from Latin digitātus (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), the verb from digitātus, perfect passive participle of digitō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)).

meaning: 1. (math) Formed by or having two plane faces; two-sided. 2. Relating to, having, or forming a dihedral angle.
etymology: From di- + -hedral.

meaning: A unit of refractive power that is equal to the reciprocal of the focal length (in meters) of a given lens.
etymology: From Latin dioptra, from Ancient Greek διόπτρα (dióptra).

meaning: An instrument used for measuring ocular refraction.
etymology: From di- + opto- + -meter.

meaning: adj: 1. nullifying 2. (Christianity / Ecclesiastical Terms) (of an impediment to marriage in canon law) totally invalidating
etymology: From Latin dirimēns (“separating”).

meaning: (botany) Arranged in two vertical rows on opposite sides of an axis: distichous leaves.
etymology: From distich + -ous.

meaning: intr. verb: To diverge at a wide angle; spread apart. adj: 1. (Biology) Branching or spreading widely from a point or axis, as branches or on an insect's wings; diverging. 2. Relating to a separation of two bones normally adjacent or attached but not located in a joint; distatic.
etymology: The verb is first attested in 1623, the adjective in 1788; borrowed from Latin dīvāricātus, perfect passive participle of dīvāricō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from dis- + vāricō (“to straddle, to stretch (the legs) apart”), from vāricus (“straddling”).

meaning: "adj. 1. (of a word) Polysyllabic; long: ""sesquipedalian surnames"". 2. Characterized by long words; long-winded."
etymology: From sesquipedal + -ian (adjective- and noun-forming suffix), root from Latin sēsquipedālis (literally “a foot and a half long”), from Latin sēsqui (“one and a half times”) + Latin pedālis (“measuring a foot, foot (relational)”) (an adjective from pēs (“foot”)).

meaning: 1. Pathology An excessive accumulation of serous fluid in tissue spaces or a body cavity. 2. Botany Extended swelling in plant organs caused primarily by an excessive accumulation of water.
etymology: From New Latin oedēma, from Ancient Greek οἴδημα (oídēma, “swelling”), from οἰδέω (oidéō, “I swell”).

meaning: In Arthurian legend, a woman who died of unrequited love of Lancelot.
etymology: From Old French Elaine, a variant of Elene, cognate to Helen, ultimately from Ancient Greek Ἑλένη (Helénē). A Celtic origin has also been suggested since the name appears in Arthurian legend. Doublet of Helen.

meaning: 1. Enthusiastic vigor and liveliness. 2. Distinctive style or flair.
Ejected matter, as that from an erupting volcano.
etymology: Neuter plural of Latin ējectus.

meaning: 1. Eager or ambitious to equal or surpass another. 2. Characterized or prompted by a spirit of rivalry. 3. Obsolete Covetous of power or honor; envious.
etymology: From Middle English emulous, from Latin aemulus (“striving to equal or excel, rivaling; in a bad sense, envious, jealous”) + -ous, from Ancient Greek ἁμιλλάομαι (hamilláomai, “strive, contend”), akin to Latin imitari (“to imitate”); see imitate.

meaning: A place where goods are stored or deposited and from which they are distributed.
1. To explain; elucidate. 2. (Biology) To remove the nucleus of. [adj: lacking a nucleus)
etymology: Borrowed from Latin ēnucleātus, from ēnucleō (“to remove the kernel from”), from ē- + nucleus (“kernel”).

meaning: 1. Epic poetry, especially as a literary genre. 2. An epic poem.
etymology: Borrowed from French épopée.

meaning: to belch
etymology: From Latin ēructō.

meaning: The act or an instance of belching.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin ērūctātiōnem, accusative of ērūctātiō (“a belching forth, burp”), from ērūctāre (“to belch, burp”). Compare Middle English eructuacioun (“belching, burp”), borrowed from the same root.

meaning: A long, narrow ridge of coarse gravel deposited by a stream flowing in or under a decaying glacial ice sheet.
etymology: From Irish eiscir (“esker, glacial ridge”).

meaning: 1. A tree or shrub that is trained to grow in a flat plane against a wall, often in a symmetrical pattern. 2. A trellis or other framework on which an espalier is grown.
etymology: Borrowed from French espalier, from Italian spalliera, from spalla (“shoulder”).

meaning: In English law, estovers is wood that a tenant is allowed to take, for life or a period of years, from the land he holds for the repair of his house, the implements of husbandry, hedges and fences, and for firewood.
Hungry; greedy.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin ēsurient, ēsurientem, from ēsuriēns (“hungering”), present participle of ēsuriō (“to be hungry, to hunger for something”), a desiderative verb from edō (“to eat”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁édti (“to eat”)) + -turiō (suffix indicating a desire for an action).

meaning: 1. a. To cause to appear pale and sickly: a face that was etiolated from years in prison. b. To make weak by stunting the growth or development of 2. (Botany) To cause (a plant) to develop without chlorophyll by preventing exposure to sunlight.
etymology: French étioler, from Norman French étieuler, ultimately from Old French estuble (“stubble”), from Latin stupla, from stipula (“straw, stubble”) (English stubble).

meaning: A theory attributing the origin of the gods to the deification of historical heroes.
etymology: From Euhemerus + -ism, ultimately from Latin Euhēmerus, from Ancient Greek Εὐήμερος (Euḗmeros), an ancient Greek Sicilian Skeptic who proposed most or all mythology derived from historical figures and natural events which received supernatural characteristics only through retelling.

meaning: A space on the reverse of a coin or medal, usually below the central design and often giving the date and place of engraving.
etymology: Borrowed from French exergue.

meaning: full of foul or impure matter, fecal.
etymology: From Middle French feculent, from Latin faeculentus, from faex.

meaning: An insoluble white protein that is the essential component of raw silk and spider-web filaments.
1. a. Capable of being molded; plastic. b. Formed of a moldable substance, such as clay or earth. 2. Of or relating to earthenware or pottery.
etymology: Latin fictilus, from fictus (from fingere (“to shape, form, devise”)) + -ilis

meaning: adj: 1. a. Of or relating to a holding of something in trust for another: a fiduciary heir; a fiduciary contract. b. Of or being a trustee or trusteeship. c. Held in trust. 2.Of or consisting of fiat money. Noun: One, such as an agent of a principal or a company director, that stands in a special relation of trust, confidence, or responsibility in certain obligations to others.
etymology: From Latin fīdūciārius (“held in trust”), from fīdūcia (“trust”).

meaning: The treasury of a kingdom or state.
etymology: Partly from Middle French fisc and partly from its etymon, Latin fiscus (“basket, money-bag, public treasury”); see fiscal.

meaning: The passage from the back of the mouth to the pharynx, bounded by the soft palate, the base of the tongue, and the palatine arches.
etymology: Borrowing from Latin faucēs (“the upper part of a throat”).

meaning: "1. Characterized by extremely brutal or cruel crimes; vicious. 2. Infamous; scandalous: ""That remorseless government persisted in its flagitious project"" (Robert Southey)."
etymology: From Old French flagitieux or Latin flāgitiōsus, both ultimately from flāgitium (“shameful crime”), related to flagrum (“whip”).

meaning: To strip the blubber or skin from (a whale, for example).
etymology: Borrowed from Danish flense (now spelled flænse).

meaning: 1. A salted and cured side of bacon. 2. A longitudinal cut from the trunk of a tree.
etymology: From Middle English flicche, from Old English fliċċe (“side of an animal, flitch”), from Proto-Germanic *flikkiją (“side, flitch”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁ḱ- (“to tear, peel off”). Cognate with Low German flikke, French flèche, Icelandic flikki (“flitch”), Middle Low German vlicke.

meaning: "medical term for a sensation that resembles that of insects crawling (tactile hallucination) on (or under) the skin. It is one specific form of a set of sensations known as paresthesia, which also include the more common prickling, tingling sensation of ""pins and needles""."
etymology: Circa 1700, from Latin formīca (“ant”) + -tion.

meaning: "sensation of tickling, tingling, burning, pricking, or numbness of a person's skin with no apparent long-term physical effect. It is more generally known as the feeling of ""pins and needles"" or of a limb ""falling asleep""."
etymology: From Ancient Greek παραίσθησις (paraísthēsis). By surface analysis, para- + -esthesia.

meaning: Adapted for or used in burrowing or digging: the fossorial forefeet of a mole
etymology: From Latin fossōrius (“adapted for digging or delving”), from fodiō (“dig”).

meaning: A jumble; a hodgepodge.
etymology: From French galimafrée, from Old French calimafree (“stew of various kinds of meats”); further etymology uncertain, but possibly from a combination of Old French galer (“to have fun, to enjoy oneself”) and Old Northern French (Picard) mafrer (“to eat gluttonously”).

meaning: Something that garnishes; an embellishment.
etymology: From Middle English garnetture, from Anglo-Norman garniture, gerneiture, from Old French garneture (“accessory for a saddle”), from Old French garnir, guarnir, from Frankish *warnijan (“to prevent, deny”).

meaning: Introduction of nutritive material into the stomach by means of a tube.
etymology: Borrowed from French gavage, from gaver (“to stuff or cram”).

meaning: One that rules or manages.
etymology: From Latin gerēns, present participle of gerō.

meaning: Flashing like lightning; dazzlingly bright.
A style of black letter formerly used in German manuscripts and printing. So-called because the script's form is angular and broken up, compared to a smoothly curved typeface.
etymology: First appears c. 1886 as fractur, and c. 1904 as fraktur, from German Fraktur, from Latin frāctūra (“breaking”, noun), from frangere (“to break”), past participle fractus. Compare English fracture, fraction. Doublet of fracture.

meaning: A woolen cap that is creased lengthwise and often has short ribbons at the back. (After the valley in central Scotland)
etymology: From Glengarry, a valley in northern Scotland, from Scottish Gaelic Gleann Garaidh (“valley of the River Garry”).

meaning: Intuitive apprehension of spiritual truths, an esoteric form of knowledge sought by the Gnostics.
etymology: Derived from Ancient Greek γνῶσῐς (gnôsĭs, “knowledge”).

meaning: The doctrines of certain pre-Christian pagan, Jewish, and early Christian sects that valued the revealed knowledge of God and of the origin and end of the human race as a means to attain redemption for the spiritual element in humans and that distinguished the Demiurge from the unknowable Divine Being.
etymology: From Gnostic + -ism.

meaning: 1. A powerful creative force or personality. 2. A public magistrate in some ancient Greek states. 3. Demiurge A deity in Gnosticism, Manichaeism, and other religions who creates the material world and is often viewed as the originator of evil. 4. Demiurge A Platonic deity who orders or fashions the material world out of chaos.
etymology: No relation with English demi- (as in demigod).

meaning: feeding on grasses
etymology: From oblique stem of Latin grāmen, grāminis (“grass, turf, herb, plant”) + -i- + -vorous.

meaning: Carrying developing young or eggs: a gravid uterus; a gravid female.
etymology: From Latin gravidus (“laden, pregnant”), from gravis (“heavy”).

meaning: adj: 1. Having or resembling drops. 2. Spotted as if by drops.
etymology: Partly borrowed from Latin guttātus, partly from gutta + -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

meaning: Government by people considered to be holy, such as priests or saints. Also called hagiocracy.
etymology: From hagio- + -archy.

meaning: A large piece of cotton, silk, or wool cloth worn as an outer garment in Morocco.
etymology: From Arabic حَيْك (ḥayk).

meaning: A cloth covering for a cap, having a flap to cover and protect the back of the neck.
etymology: From Havelock, after Sir Henry Havelock.

meaning: The presence of blood in the urine.
etymology: From hemat- + -uria.

meaning: The surgical grafting of tissue obtained from one individual or species to another.
etymology: From hetero- + -plasty.

meaning: The bristling of the body hair, as from fear or cold; goose bumps.
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin horripilatio, horripilationem.

meaning: farsightedness antonym: myopia
etymology: From hyper- + -opia.

meaning: "adj. 1. Inducing sleep; soporific. 2. Of, relating to, or occurring in the state of intermediate consciousness preceding sleep: ""hypnagogic hallucinations."""
1. A name of endearment; a pet name. 2. The use of such names.
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin hypocorisma, a loan from Ancient Greek ὑποκόρισμα (hupokórisma), ὑποκορισμός (hupokorismós, “pet name”), from ὑποκορίζεσθαι (hupokorízesthai), ὑποκορίζομαι (hupokorízomai, “to use a pet name; to act in a childish manner”), from ῠ̔πο- (hŭpo-, prefix indicating a small degree) + κορίζομαι (korízomai, “to caress”) (from κόρος (kóros, “boy; youth”), κόρη (kórē, “girl; young woman”)).

meaning: of or pertaining to a physician or physicians.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἰατρικός (iatrikós, “medical”).

meaning: noun. 1. The act of inferring or drawing conclusions. 2. A conclusion drawn; a deduction. Also called illative.
etymology: From Latin illātiō (“logical inference, deduction, conclusion”), from illātus, perfect passive participle of inferō (“carry or bring into somewhere; conclude”), from in + ferō (“bear, carry; suffer”).

meaning: adj: Having regularly arranged, overlapping edges, as roof tiles or fish scales. verb: To overlap in a regular pattern, to be arranged with regular overlapping edges (as in roofing tiles)
etymology: Borrowed from Latin imbricātus (“tiled”).

meaning: "adj: 1. Having no opening; not perforated. 2. Not separated by rows of perforations: imperforate sheets of stamps. 3. (Medicine) Lacking a normal opening: ""an imperforate anus."""
etymology: From im- + perforate.

meaning: 1. Exhaustion, as from lack of nourishment or vitality. 2. The condition or quality of being empty.
etymology: From Middle English inanicioun, borrowed from Old French inanition, itself borrowed from Late Latin inānītio, from inānīre (“to make empty”), from inānis (“empty, vain”); see inane.

meaning: "verb 1. To make hard; harden: soil that had been indurated by extremes of climate. 2. To inure, as to hardship or ridicule. 3. To make callous or obdurate: ""It is the curse of revolutionary calamities to indurate the heart"" (Helen Maria Williams). adj: Hardened; obstinate; unfeeling."
Difficult or impossible to eradicate or destroy.
etymology: From in- + extirpable.

meaning: The administration of the Eucharist by dipping the host into the wine and thus offering both simultaneously to the communicant.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin intinctiō, from intingere (“to dip in”).

meaning: To take within, as in telescoping one part of the intestine into another; invaginate.
A cosmetic preparation, such as powdered antimony sulfide, used especially in the Middle East to darken the rims of the eyelids.
etymology: From the German surname, from Kohl (“cabbage”). Compare Koehl, Cole, Coll, Kail, Kale.

meaning: 1. Having a fringe; fringed. 2. Shaped or formed like a fringe, as a ligament. 3. Slashed into narrow pointed lobes: a laciniate leaf.
1. (Greek Mythology) A monster represented as a serpent with the head and breasts of a woman that ate children and sucked the blood from men. 2. A female vampire.
etymology: From Latin lamia, from Ancient Greek Λάμια (Lámia).

meaning: 1. A four-wheeled carriage with front and back passenger seats that face each other and a roof in two sections that can be lowered or detached. 2. A style of automobile with a similar roof.
etymology: Named after the German city of Landau, where such carriages were first made. Compare German Landauer.

meaning: The inheritor of a legacy.
etymology: From legate + -ee.

meaning: A person with a slender, thin, or frail body.
etymology: From lepto- (“thin”) + -some (“body”).

meaning: A philosophy asserting the primacy of observation in assessing the truth of statements of fact and holding that metaphysical and subjective arguments not based on observable data are meaningless. Also called logical empiricism.
An abnormal forward curvature of the spine in the lumbar region. From Greek 'lordos': 'bent backward'
etymology: From Ancient Greek λορδός (lordós, “bent backward”) + English -osis.

meaning: To write in a scholarly fashion; produce scholarship.
etymology: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin lūcubrātus, perfect passive participle of lūcubrō (“to work by candlelight”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from lūx (“light”).

meaning: To put out of joint; dislocate.
etymology: From Latin luxātus (“dislocated”) perfect passive participle of lū̆xō (“to dislocate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more.

meaning: adj: 1. Of or containing a mixture of vernacular words with Latin words or with vernacular words given Latinate endings: macaronic verse. 2. Of or involving a mixture of two or more languages.
etymology: From New Latin, 1517 coinage, macaronicus, from Italian (Neapolitan dialect) maccarone (“coarse dumpling”).

meaning: "Of or relating to the aspect of the Socratic method that induces a respondent to formulate latent concepts through a dialectic or logical sequence of questions. Noun: Maieutics A pedagogical method based on the idea that the truth is latent in the mind of every human being due to innate reason but has to be ""given birth"" by answering intelligently proposed questions (or problems)."
etymology: From Ancient Greek μαιευτικός (maieutikós, “obstetric”). The rhetorical sense comes from a passage in Plato's Theaetetus where Socrates likens his procedure to that of a midwife.

meaning: having nipples
Gentleness of manner; mildness.
etymology: Via Middle French mansuetude or directly from Latin mansuētūdō, from mansuētus, perfect passive participle of mansuēscō (“to tame”), from manus (“hand”) + suēscō (“become accustomed”).

meaning: Of, relating to, or having the power of divination; prophetic.
etymology: Borrowed from Ancient Greek μαντικός (mantikós), from μάντις (mántis, “seer, soothsayer”), from μαίνομαι (maínomai, “I am mad, raving”).

meaning: Withering but not falling off, as a blossom that persists on a twig after flowering.
etymology: From Latin marcescens, present participle of marcescere.

meaning: A navigable body of water, such as a sea, that is under the jurisdiction of one nation and closed to all others.
etymology: From Latin mare clausum (“closed sea”).

meaning: A large mountain mass or compact group of connected mountains forming an independent portion of a range.
etymology: Borrowed from French massif, from Middle French massif, ultimately from Latin massa, from Ancient Greek μᾶζα (mâza, “barley-cake, lump (of dough)”).

meaning: (irish) 'My Darling'
etymology: Hiberno-English, from Irish mo mhuirnín (“my darling”) (diminutive of muirn (“affection”)).

meaning: A body opening or passage, such as the opening of the ear or the urethral canal.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin meātus (“a going, passing; a way, path, passage”).

meaning: A dealer in textiles, especially silks.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman marcer, mercer (“merchant, textile merchant”), from merz (“commodity”) (from Latin merx).

meaning: An individual with a robust, muscular body build caused by the predominance of structures developed from the embryonic mesodermal layer.
etymology: Derived from mesoderm + -morph by William Herbert Sheldon. Equivalent to meso- + -morph.

meaning: The intersection of vertical lines through the center of buoyancy of a floating body when it is at equilibrium and when it is floating at an angle. The location of the metacenter is an indication of the stability of a floating body.

The regular alternation of forms or of mode of reproduction in the life cycle of an organism, such as the alternation between diploid and haploid phases, or between sexual and asexual reproductive cycles.
etymology: From meta- + -genesis.

meaning: 1. a. Relaxation of monastic rules, as a dispensation from fasting. b. The room in a monastery used by monks who have been granted such a dispensation. 2. A narrow dagger used in medieval times to deliver the death stroke to a seriously wounded knight.
etymology: From 1200–1250, from Middle English misericorde (“an act of clemency”) from Old French, from Latin misericordia (“pity”). Doublet of misericordia.

meaning: : 1. Exemption from a rule or usual requirement. 2. Permission to be exempted from the laws or observances of a church.
etymology: From Middle English dispensacioun, from Old French despensacion, from Latin dispensātiō. By surface analysis, dispens(e) + -ation.

meaning: Hatred of reason, argument, or enlightenment.
etymology: From Ancient Greek μισολογία (misología), from μισόλογος (misólogos), from μισέω (miséō, “I hate”) + λόγος (lógos, “account, reason”).

meaning: Hatred or fear of change or innovation.
etymology: From Italian misoneismo (after Cesare Lombroso). Equivalent to miso- + neo- + -ism.

meaning: Having a wavy or rippled surface pattern. Used of fabric.
etymology: Borrowed from French moiré (“watered, clouded”).

meaning: 1. A dull or boring person. 2. (Chiefly British) A donkey.
etymology: Unknown. In the sense of a variety performer, comes from "The Lively Moke" (or "Musical Moke"), an 1860s blackface song, dance and multi-instrumental routine popularized by Johnny Thompson, William J. "Billy" Ashcroft and others.

meaning: "adj. Conveying an admonition or a warning: ""a monitory glance."""
etymology: From Latin monitorius.

meaning: 1. An ode for one voice or actor, as in Greek drama. 2. A poem in which the poet or speaker mourns another's death.
etymology: From Latin monodia, from Ancient Greek μονῳδία (monōidía).

meaning: Complete paralysis of a single limb, muscle, or muscle group.
etymology: From mono- + -plegia.

meaning: Of or being a legal marriage between a person of royal or noble birth and a partner of lower rank, in which it is agreed that no titles or estates of the royal or noble partner are to be shared by the partner of inferior rank nor by any of the offspring of the marriage.
etymology: From New Latin morganāticus, from the Medieval Latin phrase mātrimōnium ad morganāticum, from Proto-Germanic *murgnagebō (“morning gift”) (whence Old English morgenġiefu).

meaning: A woman who has given birth two or more times.
A sheet of water flowing over a dam or similar structure.
etymology: From French nappe. Doublet of map, mop, and nape.

meaning: hookah
etymology: From French narghilé, from Turkish nargile, from Persian نارگیله (nârgile) from نارگیل (nârgil, “a coconut”), which was formerly used to construct the bowl, likely ultimately from Sanskrit नारिकेल (nārikela, “a coconut”), from a Dravidian language.

meaning: An essential oil distilled from orange flowers and used in perfumery.
etymology: Borrowed from French néroli (“neroli”), from Nerola, a town and comune in the Metropolitan City of Rome, Lazio, Italy. Marie Anne de La Trémoille, princesse des Ursins (1642–1722), Princess of Nerola but originally from France, is thought to have made neroli popular as a fragrance in her country of birth around 1670. The word is cognate with Italian (obsolete) nerola, neroli.

meaning: A congenital growth or mark on the skin, such as a mole or birthmark.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin naevus.

meaning: noun. A cowardly person; a wretch.
etymology: A variant of nithing, resulting from the letter eth (ð) in Early Middle English niðing in the writings of the English historian William of Malmesbury (c. 1095 – c. 1143) being mistaken for a d followed by a mark of suspension representing a letter that had been omitted as an abbreviation. This led to niðing being wrongly spelled as nidering in early printed versions of his works. The word was later popularized by the Scottish novelist and poet Sir Walter Scott (1771–1832).

meaning: Any of a class of dyes, varying from blue to black, used in the manufacture of inks and for dyeing wood and textiles.
etymology: Latin niger (“black”), + -ine.

meaning: A man who investigates complaints and mediates fair settlements, especially between aggrieved parties such as consumers or students and an institution or organization.
etymology: Borrowed from Swedish ombudsman (equivalent to ombud (“representative, proxy”) + man), from Old Norse umboðsmaðr.

meaning: adj. Of, relating to, or resembling snakes.
etymology: From Latin ophidia (from Ancient Greek ὄφις (óphis, “snake”)) + -ian.

meaning: The study of mountains.
etymology: From oro- + -logy.

meaning: A mechanical model of the solar system.
etymology: Named after Charles Boyle, 4th Earl of Orrery (1676–1731), for whom such a device was made. The placename is from Irish Orbhraighe, originally the name of a tribe (Orbh-raighe (“Orb's people”)), and then of a territory and a barony.

meaning: 1. A small scrap or leaving of food after a meal is completed. Often used in the plural. 2. A scrap; a bit.
etymology: From Middle English orte, from Old English *oreta (“that which is left after eating”, literally “out-eat”); for more, see Old English or-, English eat. Cognate with Middle Low German orte (“refuse of food”), Middle Dutch ooraete, ooreete, Low German ort (“ort”), Middle High German urez, German Uräß and also German Ort (“quarter (of a thaler, etc)”). As the term for a coin, probably borrowed from the central European languages which used it: German Ort (“quarter (of a thaler)”), Polish ort (“coin”), etc.

meaning: 1. The study of the pronunciation of words. 2. The customary pronunciation of words.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ὀρθοέπεια (orthoépeia), possibly via Latin orthoepia, from Ancient Greek ὀρθός (orthós, “correct”) + ἔπος (épos, “word”) + -ία (-ía, “-y”).

meaning: noun. 1. The act of yawning. 2. The state of being drowsy or inattentive; dullness.
etymology: From Latin oscitans + -cy, present participle of ōscitō (“to yawn, gape, open the mouth”), from Latin os (“the mouth”).

meaning: adj. Of, relating to, or characteristic of sheep; sheeplike.
etymology: The noun is derived from the adjective.

meaning: adj. 1. About to bring forth young; being in labor. 2. Of or relating to giving birth. 3. About to produce or come forth with something, such as an idea or a discovery
etymology: Borrowed from Latin parturiēns, present participle of parturiō (“to be in labour”).

meaning: adj. 1. Sinful; guilty. 2. Violating a rule or an accepted practice; erring.
etymology: The noun is derived from the adjective.

meaning: Wealth or riches, especially when dishonestly acquired.
etymology: From Late Middle English pelf, pelfe (“stolen goods, booty, spoil; forfeited property; money, riches; property; valuable object”), possibly from Anglo-Norman pelf (a variant of pelfre (“booty, loot”)) and Old French peufre (“frippery; rubbish”); further etymology uncertain, possibly a metathesis of Old French felpe, ferpe, frepe (“a rag”). The English word is perhaps related to Late Latin pelfa, pelfra, pelfrum (“forfeited or stolen goods”), Middle French peuffe and French peufe, peuffe (“old clothes; rubbish”) (Normandy), and pilfer.

meaning: A thin skin or film, such as an organic membrane or liquid film.
etymology: From Latin pellicula, from pellis (“skin”). Doublet of pellicule.

meaning: marked by arbitrary often ruthless disregard of individual differences or special circumstances (Greek mythology) Procrustes was a rogue smith that invited travelers to spend the night, sleeping on an iron bed. Procustes would use his smith's hammer to make the unwitting guest 'fit' the iron bed.
etymology: From Procrustes + -an.

meaning: The fruit of any of various related plants, such as the cantaloupe, watermelon, cucumber, squash, pumpkin, and melon, having a hard or leathery rind, fleshy pulp, and numerous flattened seeds.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin pepō, from Ancient Greek πέπων (pépōn, “large melon”), from πέπων (pépōn, “ripe”), from πέπτω (péptō, “ripen”). Doublet of pumpion; compare pumpkin.

meaning: An arbor or a passageway of columns supporting a roof of trelliswork on which climbing plants are trained to grow.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian pergola, from Latin pergula.

meaning: 1. Situated around the ear. 2. Of or relating to the bones immediately around the inner ear.
etymology: From peri- + otic.

meaning: A sudden change of events or reversal of circumstances, especially in a literary work.
etymology: From Late Latin peripetia, and its source Ancient Greek περιπέτεια (peripéteia), from περιπίπτω (peripíptō, “to change suddenly”), from περί (perí, “round, around, about”) + the stem of πίπτω (píptō, “to fall”).

meaning: 1. The use of circumlocution. 2. A circumlocution.
etymology: From Ancient Greek περίφρασις (períphrasis).

meaning: adj. 1. Having the nature of or characterized by periphrasis. 2. (Grammar) Constructed by using an auxiliary word rather than an inflected form; for example, of father is the periphrastic possessive case of father but father's is the inflected possessive case, and did say is the periphrastic past tense of say but said is the inflected past tense.
etymology: Borrowed from Ancient Greek περιφραστικός (periphrastikós), from περίφρασις (períphrasis, “periphrasis”).

meaning: Having a single row of columns on all sides.
A measure of the ability of a material to resist the formation of an electric field within it. Also called dielectric constant, relative permittivity.
etymology: From permittive + -ity.

meaning: A carving or line drawing on rock, especially one made by prehistoric people.
etymology: From French pétroglyphe, from Ancient Greek πέτρα (pétra, “rock”) + γλυφή (gluphḗ, “carved work”). By surface analysis, petro- + glyph.

meaning: The process of printing from an intaglio plate, etched according to a photographic image.
etymology: From photo- + gravure.

meaning: 1. (Judaism) Either of two small leather boxes, each containing strips of parchment inscribed with quotations from the Hebrew Scriptures, one of which is strapped to the forehead and the other to the left arm; traditionally worn by Jewish men during morning worship, except on the Sabbath and holidays. 2. An amulet or A reminder.
etymology: The modern use of "phylactery" as a term for a lich's artifact originates from Dungeons and Dragons.

meaning: A movement in which a horse trots in place with high action of the legs.
etymology: Borrowed from French piaffer.

meaning: Covered with fine soft hair.
etymology: From Latin pilōsus, from pilus (“hair”).

meaning: Noun: 1. An alloy of zinc and copper used as imitation gold. 2. A cheap imitation. adj: 1. Made of pinchbeck. 2. Imitation; spurious.
etymology: Named after Christopher Pinchbeck, an 18th century London watchmaker who developed the alloy.

meaning: The process of erosion and deposition in which a nearly level surface is produced, as by streams, wind, or ocean currents.
etymology: From plane + -ation.

meaning: 1. To plait or interlace (branches or vines, for example), especially in making a hedge or an arbor. 2. To shade or border with interlaced branches or vines.
etymology: The noun is derived from the verb.

meaning: 1. A secluded garden or landscaped area. 2. Pleasure or a source of pleasure.
etymology: From Middle English plaisaunce, plesaunce, from Old French plaisance. By surface analysis, please + -ance.

meaning: "1. Excessive in quantity; superabundant: ""this successful industry of England, with its plethoric wealth"" (Thomas Carlyle). 2. Excessive in style; turgid: plethoric prose."
etymology: From Late Latin plethoricus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek πληθωρικός (plēthōrikós), from πληθώρα (plēthṓra, “plethora”). By surface analysis, plethora + -ic.

meaning: 1. The act or process of folding, The state of being folded. 2. A fold.
etymology: From Middle French plicacion, and its source, Latin plicatio.

meaning: A rubber-soled cloth shoe; a sneaker.
etymology: From Samuel Plimsoll, a Bristol merchant who created a system of marks and symbols for the waterline of ships. The shoe was possibly named because the line of its sole resembled the Plimsoll line of ship.

meaning: 1. A puckered finish given to fabric by treating it with a caustic soda. 2. Fabric having such a finish.
etymology: Borrowed from French plissé.

meaning: An area of low-lying land, especially in the Netherlands, that has been reclaimed from a body of water and is protected by dikes.
etymology: Borrowed from Dutch polder, from Middle Dutch polre, from Old Dutch polra, of uncertain origin.

meaning: A problem that severely tests the ability of an inexperienced person.
etymology: From New Latin pons asinorum, from Latin pōns (“bridge”) + genitive plural of asinus (“donkey”). Literally, “bridge of donkeys”.

meaning: A stipend drawn from the endowment or revenues of an Anglican cathedral or church by a presiding member of the clergy; a cathedral or church benefice.
etymology: From Middle French prebende, from Medieval Latin prebenda, from Late Latin praebenda, from Latin praebendus, verbal adjective of praebere. Doublet of provender.

meaning: 1. The act of advancing to a higher position or office; promotion. 2. A position, appointment, or rank giving advancement, as of profit or prestige. 3. The act of preferring or the state of being preferred.
etymology: From Middle English preferment, preferrement, prefferment; equivalent to prefer + -ment.

meaning: 1. The act of passing by, disregarding, or omitting. 2. (Law) Neglect of a testator to mention a legal heir in his or her will. 3. (Christianity) The Calvinist doctrine that God neglected to designate those who would be damned, positively determining only the elect.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin praeteritiō, from praetereō (“to omit”).

meaning: 1. A. To turn or rotate (the hand or forearm) so that the palm faces down or back. B. To turn or rotate (the foot) by abduction and eversion so that the inner edge of the sole bears the body's weight. 2. To place in a prone position.
etymology: From Latin prōnatus, past participle of prōnare (“to bend forward”). See prone.

meaning: "Forward displacement of an organ, especially an eyeball. (""Eye-popping"")"
A figure of speech in which an absent or imaginary person is represented as speaking.

1. television graphics that occupy the lower area of the screen (may not actually occupy the entire lower third as the name suggests) 2. Any predominantly text-based video graphic as used mainly by television news broadcasts Other common terms include captions, superbars (or simply supers), name straps and astons.
etymology: Genericization of the trademark Chyron, from Chiron (“centaur of Greek mythology”).

meaning: To walk about.
etymology: First attested in 1614; borrowed from Latin obambulātus, perfect passive participle of obambulō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

meaning: adj.: bent or curved backward
noun: Any of various straight muscles, as of the abdomen, eye, neck, and thigh.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin rēctus (“straight, upright”), clipping of mūsculus rēctus (“straight muscle”).

meaning: verb.: To break out anew or come into renewed activity, as after a period of quiescence. antonym: quiescence
"Tending to irritate; repellent: ""He became rebarbative, prickly, spiteful"" (Robert Craft)."
etymology: From French rébarbatif, rébarbative (“repellent, disagreeable”), from Middle French rebarber (“to oppose”), ultimately from Latin barba (“beard”), literally “to stand beard to beard against”.

meaning: adj.: Having numerous small branches.
etymology: From Latin ramulosus, from ramulus, diminutive of ramus (“branch”).

meaning: A traditional melodic type in Hindu music, consisting of a theme that expresses an aspect of religious feeling and sets forth a tonal system on which variations are improvised within a prescribed framework of typical progressions, melodic formulas, and rhythmic patterns.
etymology: Borrowed from Sanskrit राग (rāga, “dye, colour”).

meaning: "adj.: That once was; former: ""the quondam drunkard, now perfectly sober"" (Bret Harte)."
etymology: Borrowed from Latin quondam. Compare whilom.

meaning: adj.: Arranged in groups of five: quinate leaflets.
etymology: First attested in 1760. From the post-Classical Latin quīnātus, from the distributive numeral quīnī (“five each”, “five at a time”); compare binate, ternate, and quaternate, as well as the French quiné.

meaning: adj.: Feeding on decaying organic matter.
etymology: From sapro- (“putrid, rotten matter”) + -phagous (“eating, feeding on”).

meaning: 1. Compassion or pity for another. 2. Sorrow or misery about one's own misdeeds or flaws.
etymology: From Middle English ruthe, reuthe, reuþe, reowthe, rewthe (“compassion, pity, sympathy; mercy; grief, sorrow; cause or event of pity or sorrow; lamentation; calamity, trouble; distress; regret, remorse; cruelty, ill treatment”), from reu, reuen (“to feel compassion or pity; to regret, rue; etc.”) + -th, -the (suffix denoting a condition, quality, state of being, etc.), possibly influenced by an early Scandinavian language (compare Old Norse hrygð, hryggð (“affliction, grief, sorrow, ruth”), from the Proto-Germanic word indicated below). Reuen is derived from Old English hrēowan (“to grieve; to regret, rue; to repent”), from Proto-West Germanic *hreuwan (“to cause pain; to regret”), from Proto-Germanic *hrewwaną (“to cause regret, rue; to feel sorrow, grieve”); further etymology uncertain, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *krew(H)-, possibly related to Proto-Indo-European *krewh₂- (“blood”) and *krows- (“to fall, beat, break, bruise”). By surface analysis, rue (“to regret; etc.”) + -th (suffix forming abstract nouns from verbs).

meaning: Containing or yielding salt.
a. The formal proposal of a law in ancient Rome by a tribune or consul to the people for acceptance or rejection. b. A law proposed in this manner.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin rogātiō, from rogō (“request”). By surface analysis, Latin rog- + -ate + -ion.

meaning: 1. A facing, as of masonry, used to support an embankment. 2. A barricade against explosives.
etymology: From French revêtement, from Old French revestiment, from revestir (French revêtir), from Late Latin revestire (“to clothe again”), from Latin re- + vestire (“to clothe”).

meaning: An anatomical mesh or network, as of veins, arteries, or nerves.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin rete.

meaning: 1.A net or mesh foundation for lace. 2. (Astronomy) A reference grid of fine lines forming uniform squares on a photographic plate or print, used to aid in measurement. 3. A mosaic screen of fine lines of three colors, used in color photography.
noun: 1. An action to recover personal property said or claimed to be unlawfully taken. 2. The writ or procedure of such an action.
etymology: Anglo-Norman, from Old French replevir (“recover”), from re- + plevir (apparently from a Germanic word which was also the source of English pledge).

meaning: 1. A small mark or sketch engraved in the margin of a plate to indicate its stage of development prior to completion. 2. A print or proof from a plate carrying such a mark.
etymology: Borrowed from French remarque.

meaning: Gradual recession of water in a sea, lake, or stream, leaving permanently dry land.
1. Ecology An organism or species of an earlier time surviving in an environment that has undergone considerable change. 2. Something that has survived; a remnant. 3. A widow.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English relicte (“widow”), from Middle French relicte (“widow”), from Late Latin relicta (“widow”), from Latin relictus, past participle of relinquō (“to abandon, to relinquish, to leave (behind)”), from re- + linquō (“to leave, quit, forsake, depart from”). Doublet of relic, derelict, and relinquish.

meaning: A dissenter; a nonconformist.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin recūsans, recūsāntis, from recūsō (“to refuse, decline; to object to; to protest”). See recuse.

meaning: 1. A plain square block higher than a plinth, serving as a pedestal for sculpture, a vase, or a column. 2. A plain plinth supporting a wall.
etymology: From French socle, from Italian zoccolo (“wooden shoe”), from Latin socculus, diminutive of soccus (“sock”). Doublet of zoccolo.

meaning: The quantitative study of interpersonal relationships in populations, especially the study and measurement of preferences.
etymology: From socio- + -metry.

meaning: To produce a high, shrill, wailing tone. Used of bagpipes.
etymology: Originally from Scots and Northern English dialects (as a verb), probably of Old Norse origin; ultimately imitative.

meaning: 1. One of a number of women regarded as oracles or prophets by the ancient Greeks and Romans. 2. A woman prophet.
etymology: From Latin Sibylla, from Ancient Greek Σίβυλλα (Síbulla).

meaning: To utter or pronounce with a hissing sound.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin sībilātus, past participle of sībilō. Doublet of siffle.

meaning: 1. A piece of paper money issued privately and devalued by inadequate security or by inflation. 2. A piece of paper money of small denomination issued by the government, especially one issued by the U.S. government from 1862 to 1878.
etymology: Probably coined during the American War of Independence (1775–1783). Named for its resemblance to, and suitability for makeshift use as, a bandage for dressing the shin.

meaning: adj.: Containing, secreting, or resembling serum.
etymology: From French séreux, from Latin serosus, from serum.

meaning: 1. The presence of pathogenic organisms or their toxins in the blood or tissues. 2. The poisoned condition resulting from the presence of pathogens or their toxins, as in septicemia.
etymology: From Ancient Greek σῆψις (sêpsis, “putrefaction”), from σήπω (sḗpō, “to make rotten”), from σήψ (sḗps, “a kind of lizard; also a kind of serpent whose bite was alleged to cause putrefaction”).

meaning: 1. An explanatory note or commentary, as on a Greek or Latin text. 2. A note amplifying a proof or course of reasoning, as in mathematics.
etymology: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek σχόλιον (skhólion, “comment”), from σχολή (skholḗ, “discussion”).

meaning: Thin, membranous, and dry: scarious bracts; a scarious tongue.
etymology: French scarieux. Compare scary.

meaning: 1. Having or covered with scales or small projections and rough to the touch. 2. Difficult to handle; knotty: a scabrous situation. 3. Dealing with scandalous or salacious material: a scabrous novel.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin scaber (“scabrous, rough; scabby, mangy, itchy”) (from scabō (“to scratch, scrape, abrade”), from Proto-Indo-European *skabʰ- (“to scratch”)) + English -ous; compare French scabreux, Late Latin scabrōsus.

meaning: 1. Saturnalia The ancient Roman seven-day festival of Saturn, which began on December 17. 2. (used with a sing. verb) A celebration marked by unrestrained revelry and often licentiousness; an orgy.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin Sāturnālia.
