meaning: A protective box made in the form of a book, for holding such items as botanical specimens, maps, and color plates.
etymology: From D. C. Solander, Swedish botanist.

meaning: A feeling for language; an ear for the idiomatically correct or appropriate.
1. A flexible piece of wood, hard rubber, or metal used in drawing curves. 2. A wooden or metal strip; a slat.
etymology: Mid-1700s East Anglian dialect. Origin uncertain but perhaps from Old Danish splind or North Frisian splinj and ultimately related to the root of splinter.

meaning: 1. Shining or lustrous; brilliant. 2. Admired by many; illustrious.
etymology: From Middle English splendaunt, from Old French splendiant, present participle of esplendiier, and esplendent, and Latin splendēns, splendentis, present participle of splendēre (“to shine”).

meaning: 1. A. A saucy, coquettish, intriguing maidservant in comedies or comic opera. B. An actress or a singer taking such a part. 2. A young woman regarded as flirtatious or frivolous.
etymology: Borrowed from French soubrette, from Occitan soubreta (“coy”) (feminine of soubret), from soubra (Provençal sobrar), from Latin superare (“be above”).

meaning: 1.The act or process of shaking violently, especially as a method of diagnosis to detect the presence of fluid and air in a body cavity. 2. The condition of being shaken violently.
etymology: From Latin succussio, from succutere.

meaning: To produce a shrill grating, chirping, or hissing sound by rubbing body parts together, as certain insects do.
etymology: Back-formation from stridulation. (From earlier term stridulous; from Latin strīdulus (“giving a shrill sound, creaking”), from strīdō (“utter a shrill or harsh sound; creak, shriek, grate, hiss”))

meaning: 1. An instrument used to level off grain or other material in a measure. 2. A foundry tool used to shape a mold in sand or loam. 3. A tool for sharpening scythes
etymology: From Middle English strikile, strikelle, strikyll, from Old English stricel, equivalent to strick + -le (diminutive suffix). Compare Middle Dutch strijkel, streekel, strekel.

meaning: 1. (Ecclesiastical) A basin or font for holy water at the entrance of a church. 2. A drinking vessel, such as a cup or tankard.
etymology: From Old Norse staup, from Proto-Germanic *staupo- (whence Old English stēap). See stoop (“a vessel”). More at stop.

meaning: 1. Of, relating to, or characterized by conjecture; conjectural. 2. (Statistics) A. Involving or containing a random variable or variables: stochastic calculus. B. Involving chance or probability: a stochastic stimulation.
etymology: From Ancient Greek στοχαστικός (stokhastikós), from στοχάζομαι (stokházomai, “aim at a target, guess”), from στόχος (stókhos, “an aim, a guess”).

meaning: An extreme accumulation of fat on the buttocks.
etymology: From steato- + pygo- + -ia.

meaning: Belonging to or designating a class of verbs that express a state or condition.
etymology: From Latin stativus.

meaning: To overlap and even (chamfered or beveled plank edges) so that they form a flush surface.
etymology: Unknown.

meaning: 1. The master or director of a symposium, especially one in ancient Greece. 2. A toastmaster.
etymology: From Ancient Greek συμποσίαρχος (sumposíarkhos). By surface analysis, symposium + -arch.

meaning: A slim, graceful woman or girl.
etymology: More at Wikipedia.

meaning: ADJ.: Floating on the surface.
etymology: From super- + natant.

meaning: 1. Regulating or limiting personal expenditures. 2. A. Regulating commercial or real-estate activities: sumptuary laws discouraging construction of large houses on small plots of land. B. Regulating personal behavior on moral or religious grounds: sumptuary laws forbidding gambling.
etymology: * Spanish suntuario

meaning: ADJ.: Relating to or resembling a sylph.
etymology: From French sylphide. By surface analysis, sylph + -id.

meaning: Causing or increasing sweat.
etymology: From New Latin sudorificus, from sūdor (“sweat”) (from Proto-Indo-European *sweyd- (“sweat; to sweat”)) + -ificus (from Proto-Italic *-fakos (suffix forming adjectives that denote bringing or making), ultimately related to Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to do, put, place”)).

meaning: A painfully urgent but ineffectual attempt to urinate or defecate.
etymology: Borrowing from Medieval Latin tēnesmus, from Ancient Greek τεινεσμός (teinesmós, “vain endeavor to evacuate”), from τείνω (teínō, “to stretch, to pull tight”) + -εσμός (-esmós, nominal suffix).

meaning: A hypocrite, especially one who affects religious piety.
etymology: From French tartuffe, from the protagonist Tartuffe (from Italian tartufo (“truffle”)) in the play of the same name by Molière. Doublet of tartufo.

meaning: A king who for his crimes was condemned in Hades to stand in water that receded when he tried to drink, and with fruit hanging above him that receded when he reached for it.
etymology: From Latin Tantalus, from Ancient Greek Τάνταλος (Tántalos, “Tantalus”), a Phrygian king in Greek mythology who was condemned to stand in a pool of water which receded every time he tried to drink, and with overhanging branches of fruit which pulled back whenever he tried to eat. Doublet of Tantalus.

meaning: A punishment identical to the offense, as the death penalty for murder.
etymology: From Middle French talion, from Latin talis (“such”).

meaning: A small hand drum of northern India.
etymology: From Hindustani طبلہ / तबला (tablā), from Arabic طَبْلَة (ṭabla). Cognate of Catalan, Spanish, Portuguese tambor.

meaning: Progressive bodily wasting or emaciation.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin tābēs.

meaning: 1. Something that cannot be classified into either of two groups considered exhaustive; an intermediate thing or factor. 2. A third person or thing of indeterminate character.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin tertium quid (“third thing”).

meaning: A male hawk used in falconry.
The belief that the soul is inherited from the parents along with the body.
etymology: From traducian + -ism.

meaning: Having horizontal beams or lintels rather than arches.
etymology: From Latin trabs (“beam”).

meaning: 1. An investment plan in which participants buy shares in a common fund and receive an annuity that increases every time a participant dies, with the entire fund going to the final survivor or to those who survive after a specified time. 2. Each member's share of a tontine. 3. The subscribers to a tontine.
etymology: From French tontine, named after Lorenzo de Tonti, who introduced the scheme into France in around 1653. Thus, from Tonti + -ine.

meaning: To sting or whip with or as if with nettles. To produce a stinging or itching sensation.
etymology: From or formed like (post-Classical?) Latin urticatus, from Latin urtīca (“nettle”).

meaning: adj: Causing itching or stinging. noun: A substance that causes itching or stinging.
Of a wife; regarded as befitting a wife.
etymology: From Latin uxōrius (“of or pertaining to a wife; overly fond of one’s wife”) + English -al (suffix forming adjectives). Uxōrius is derived from uxor (“wife”) + -ius (suffix forming adjectives).

meaning: 1. A crowd of attendants or menials. 2. A disorderly crowd; a rabble.
etymology: Compare Old French valeterie (“young unmarried nobles”).

meaning: 1. The killing of a wife by her husband. 2. A man who kills his wife.
etymology: Borrowed from French uxoricide or Latin uxor + English -icide.

meaning: Of or relating to the sole of the foot or the palm of the hand.
etymology: From Latin vola.

meaning: 1. Flying or capable of flying. 2. Moving quickly or nimbly; agile.
etymology: From Middle French volant, present participle of voler (“to fly”), from Latin volāre.

meaning: Giving birth to living offspring that develop within the mother's body. Most mammals and some other animals are viviparous.
etymology: From Latin vīviparus, from vīvus (“alive, life, living”) + pariō (“give birth, produce, bring forth”).

meaning: A woman who accompanies troops to sell them food, supplies, and liquor.
ADJ: 1. Of, relating to, or associated with the yolk of an egg. 2. Having the yellow hue of an egg yolk; dull yellow. NOUN: The yolk of an egg.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin vitellīnus.

meaning: "By word of mouth: ""a report submitted viva voce; a viva voce examination."""
etymology: From Latin vīvā (“living”) and vōce (“voice”) (ablative of vōx).

meaning: The presence of male secondary sexual characteristics in a female.
etymology: From virile + -ism.

meaning: A bond or tie.
etymology: From Latin vinculum (“bond, link”), from vinciō (“bind, fetter, tie”) + -ulum.

meaning: 1. Having a variety of colors; variegated. 2. Changing in color; iridescent.
1. The slope of a side of a mountain or mountain range. 2. The general slope of a region.
etymology: Borrowed from French versant, present participle (used as a noun) of verser, from Latin versō, frequentative of vertō (“to turn”).

meaning: An Anglo-Saxon advisory council to the king, composed of about 100 nobles, prelates, and other officials, convened at intervals to discuss administrative and judicial affairs.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Old English witena ġemōt (literally “assembly of the wise”).

meaning: 1. A person who is fervently devoted, as to a leader or ideal; a faithful follower. 2. A person who is filled with enthusiasm, as for a pursuit or hobby; an enthusiast
etymology: From Latin votus, past participle of vovere (“to vow, to devote”).

meaning: 1. a. a word or saying used by adherents of a party, sect, or belief and usually regarded by others as empty of real meaning b. a widely held belief, truism, platitude. 2.a use of language regarded as distinctive of a particular group
etymology: Learned borrowing from Biblical Hebrew שִׁבֹּלֶת /שיבולת (šibbṓleṯ, “ear [of wheat] or stream, torrent”). Doublet of sebboleth and Middle English sebolech, both from Late Latin sebboleth in the Vulgate.

meaning: "unique Latin - ""of its own kind/genus"", ""unique in characteristics"""
etymology: Borrowed from Latin suī generis (literally “of its own kind/class”).

meaning: "contrary to fact [history] - form of historiography exploring ""what if""'s [psychology] counterfactual thinking - tendency for people to imagine alternatives to reality - ""what if?"" [grammar] counterfactual conditional - conditional statement - what would be the case if an antecedent were true"
etymology: From counter- + factual.

meaning: very stubborn from latin pervicax (stubborn)
etymology: From Latin pervicāx + -ious.

meaning: a person or thing without an equal
lively, active, vigorous from latin 'vegere' (to enliven)
etymology: Borrowed from Latin vegetus.

meaning: adjective: 1. Cautious. 2. Crafty.
etymology: From Middle French cauteleux.

meaning: 1.the action of disputing : verbal controversy 2. an academic exercise in oral defense of a thesis by formal logic
etymology: English dispute + -ation, from Old French disputation, from Latin disputatio.

meaning: noun: Warm friendliness; comfortableness; coziness. (guh-myoot-lish-KYT, -likh-, -MOOT-)
noun: 1. A child prodigy. 2. A person who achieves great success early in the career.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from German Wunderkind, from Wunder (“wonder”) + Kind (“child”). Compare native wonderchild.

meaning: adj. In a state of excitement, anxiety, or confusion, often in expectation of something.
etymology: From a- + dither.

meaning: "an obssessive impulse to write also known as ""scribomania"""
etymology: From grapho- + -mania.

meaning: 1 : biography of saints or venerated persons 2 : idealizing or idolizing biography
etymology: From hagiography + -ic.

meaning: noun. The branch of zoology concerned with the study of mites and ticks.
etymology: From acaro- + -logy, based on Ancient Greek ἄκαρι (ákari, “cheese mite, tick”) + -λογία (-logía).

meaning: "1. Becoming rigid and unresponsive; losing the ability to adapt: ""sclerotic management"". 2. Having sclerosis"
etymology: From scler(a) + -otic.

meaning: (kool-TOOR-kahmpf) noun: A cultural conflict, especially one religious in nature. The original Kulturkampf took place in the 1880s between the German government and the Roman Catholic Church over control of education, laws related to marriage, etc.
etymology: Borrowed from German Kulturkampf (“culture conflict”).

meaning: (KAH-fee-klach) noun: An informal social gathering for coffee and conversation.
etymology: Borrowed from German Kaffeeklatsch, 1877.

meaning: adj. 1. Given to speaking at length, esp. in a boring or ill-tempered manner; expressed vociferously or at length. 2. Of sound, esp. music: extremely loud; grating, dissonant.
adjective: Inflexibly just or severe. In Greek mythology, Rhadamanthus was the son of Zeus and Europa. He was a judge of the underworld and known for his strict justice.
etymology: From Rhadamanthus + -ine, after Rhadamanthus, a king in Greek myths.

meaning: noun: A careless, indifferent, or nonchalant person. adj.: Careless, indifferent, nonchalant. etymology: probably via the name of Seigneur Pococurante, a fictional apathetic Venetian senator in Voltaire's Candide (1759)
etymology: Borrowed from French pococurante, itself - from Pococurante, a nonchalant Venetian senator in Candide, coined by Voltaire based on Italian poco (“little”) + curante (“caring”).

meaning: noun: The developing of immunity to a poison by taking gradually increasing doses of it. After Mithridates VI, king of Pontus (now in Turkey) 120-63 BCE, who is said to have acquired immunity to poison by ingesting gradually larger doses of it
etymology: From Mithridates (referring to Mithridates VI of Pontus) + -ism.

meaning: 1. An impossibility. 2. Rhetoric. A figure of speech by which an impossible (or highly unlikely) situation is used for emphasis; an instance of this.
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin adynaton (“impossibility; adynaton”), or directly from its etymon Ancient Greek ἀδύνατον (adúnaton, “an impossibility; impracticality”), substantivized neuter singular of ἀδύνατος (adúnatos, “unable; that cannot be done, impossible”) + -ον (-on, suffix forming nouns). The word ἀδύνατος is derived from ἀ- (a-, the alpha privative, a prefix forming words having a sense opposite to the word or stem to which it is attached) + δῠνᾰτός (dŭnătós, “mighty, strong; possible, practical”) (from δῠ́νᾰμαι (dŭ́nămai, “to be able, capable; it can be, it is possible”) (from Proto-Indo-European *dewh₂- (“to fit”)) + -τος (-tos, suffix forming verbal adjectives of possibility)).

meaning: (Art): An image of a person at prayer with arms outstretched. Also attrib.: designating such a figure or posture.
etymology: Derived from Latin orans (“praying”). Doublet of orant.

meaning: 1. A message sent by radio. Now disused. 2. a. A telegram conveyed on part of its journey by aeroplane. rare (now disused). b. A letter sent by air mail
etymology: From aero- + -gram.

meaning: adjective: Of or relating to an over-ambitious attempt that ends in ruin.

"noun: A sense of shame or embarrassment; bashfulness, modesty, or reticence S. Rushdie, ""Ground beneath her Feet"" (2000) xiv. 435 Their band,..the supposed shock troops of the new wave, fizzled in the face of American pudeur and ended up fatally shooting each other."
etymology: From French pudeur, from Latin pudor. Doublet of pudor.

meaning: adjective: Northern. From Latin septentriones, literally the seven ploughing oxen, a name for the seven stars of the Great Bear constellation that appears in the northern sky. From Latin septem (seven) + triones (ploughing oxen).
etymology: Borrowed from Latin septentriōnālis, from septentriōnēs (“seven plow oxen”), a name for the constellations now known as Ursa Major and Ursa Minor, which appear in the northern sky.

meaning: The action of providing or seeking assistance for a woman in labour.

noun: 1. A shifting scene made up of many elements. 2. A sequence of fantastic imagery, illusions, etc. From French fantasmagorie, from fantasme (phantasm), perhaps combined with Greek agora (assembly). Earliest documented use: 1802. In the late 18th and 19th century, use of a magic lantern (an early form of slide projector) to display fantastic images was popular. It was known as a phantasmagoria and was first exhibited in London in 1802.
etymology: Borrowed from French phantasmagorie, from Ancient Greek φάντασμα (phántasma, “ghost”) + possibly either ἀγορά (agorá, “assembly, gathering”) + the suffix -ia or ἀγορεύω (agoreúō, “to speak publicly”).

meaning: n. A person who entertains people with antics and buffoonery; a clown; a mountebank's assistant. adj. That is or resembles a merry-andrew; characteristic of a merry-andrew; foolish. probably from the performances of a particular entertainer whose persona was that of a fool
adjective: Relating to or inducing tears.
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin lachrymālis, from lachryma (“a tear”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix). Doublet of lacrimal.

meaning: "noun: A harmonious arrangement of various parts ""There was a moment of inner peace in which belief and doubt merged into a strangely comforting concinnity."""
A fragment scraped off, a shaving. Formerly also: a tiny particle, an atom.
etymology: From Latin ramentum (“a scraping”).

meaning: A. n. 1. A person who returns from the dead; a reanimated corpse; a ghost. 2. A person who returns to a place. B. adj.2 That has returned from, or as if from, the dead; resembling or reminiscent of a ghost.
etymology: 19th century. From French revenant, the present participle of revenir (“to return”). Compare revenue.

meaning: adjective: Shaped like a pouch or a sac. From Latin bursa (bag, pouch), from Greek byrsa (skin, hide). Earliest documented use: 1835.
etymology: From New Latin bursiformis, from Latin bursa (“purse”).

meaning: adj. 1. Esp. of a clause in a charter: that contains, includes, or represents the date. s usually of significance indicating a new die design. 2. Of, relating to, or according to date; chronological.

A. n. 1. a. A person who obstinately adheres to old ways in spite of clear evidence that they are wrong; an ignorant and bigoted opponent of reform. b. (derogatory) An old person. 2. A traditional custom or notion obstinately adhered to, however unreasonable it is shown to be; stubborn archaism, esp. in speech or language. B. adj. Obstinately conservative. Obs.
etymology: Malapropism of Latin sumpsimus, form of sūmō (“to take”), from a story of an old monk who misrecited the Eucharist with quod in ōre mumpsimus instead of quod in ōre sumpsimus “which we have taken into the mouth”, and stubbornly continued using the incorrect form even after being corrected. Attested 1530 in The Practice of Prelates by William Tyndale, variously attributed to Richard Pace (1517) or Desiderius Erasmus.

meaning: a term often used in conferences to define the portions of the conference when all members of all groups are invited to attend.
etymology: From plenarius (“full, entire”).

meaning: noun: The senior member of a group, profession, etc. From French doyen (most senior member), from Latin decanus (chief of ten), from decem (ten).
etymology: Borrowed from French doyen, from Late Latin decānus, from Latin decem. Compare the doublet dean.

meaning: A type of Italian dessert made in a similar way to ice cream, but which is not fully frozen and has a lighter, aerated texture; a serving of this. Also occas. more broadly: any of various other desserts made with cream and eggs and served chilled but not frozen.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian semifreddo.

meaning: noun: 1. A group of seven. 2. A period of seven days; a week.
etymology: From Late Latin hebdomada (“number seven; group of seven; seven days”), hebdomas (“number seven; seven days; seventh day”), from Ancient Greek ἑβδομάς (hebdomás, “group of seven, especially seven days or seven years”), from ἕβδομος (hébdomos, “seventh”) + -ᾰ́ς (-ắs, suffix forming abstract nouns of number from numerals). The word is cognate with French hebdomadaire, hebdo (“weekly periodical”), hebdomadairement (“weekly”), Portuguese hebdomadário (“weekly periodical”), Spanish hebdomadario (“weekly; weekly periodical; hebdomadary”).

meaning: noun: A conceited person; a coxcomb. Also princock.
The branch of statistical theory concerned with the analysis of economic phenomena, in particular the application of statistical methods to economic data.
etymology: An adaptation of the French économétrie. Coined by Norwegian economist Ragnar Frisch in 1926. Compare the earlier German Oekonometrie (now generally spelt Ökonometrie), first used (in a different sense) by Polish economist Paweł Ciompa in 1910.

meaning: An imaginary monster, esp. one invoked to frighten children; a hobgoblin. Also in extended use. Etymology: ancient Greek μορμώ a hideous female monster (also as proper noun, and as an exclamation to frighten children)
etymology: From Ancient Greek Μορμώ (Mormṓ, “a hideous she-monster, a bugbear”).

meaning: Power, authority, or prestige; spec. (in Polynesian and Melanesian religions) an impersonal supernatural power which can be associated with people or with objects and which can be transmitted or inherited.
etymology: The use of "mana" for "magical energy" in role-playing games originated from Larry Niven, when he wrote the short story, "Not Long Before the End", in 1969. It was later popularised by his The Magic Goes Away setting.

meaning: Talk, esp. when foolish, inconsequential, or insolent; prattle, gossip. Also in to set up one's gash: to talk, esp. insolently. (british colloquial)
etymology: Alteration of older garsh, from Middle English garsen, from Old French garser, jarsier (Modern French gercer), from Vulgar Latin *charaxāre, from Ancient Greek χαρακτήρ (kharaktḗr, “engraver”).

meaning: A person empowered to act on behalf of others
etymology: From Latin adiūtāre + -or.

meaning: noun: A person regarded as unimportant and presumptuous, especially someone young. Perhaps an alteration of whipsnapper, representing noise and uselessness, or an alteration of snippersnapper, similar in sense. Earliest documented use: 1674.
etymology: Extension of *whip-snapper (“a cracker of whips”), or perhaps from snipper-snapper. Compare also whipperginnie (“term of abuse for a woman”), late 16th c.

meaning: a pompous-sounding title; (also) a person assuming such a title; a pretender to elevated dignity, viewed as an object of derision. an imaginary Turkish title (invented by Molière in Le Bourgeois Gentilhomme (1670) iv. iii, where it is pretended to have been conferred by the Sultan upon M. Jourdain)
A period of four years.
etymology: From Late Latin quadrennium, from Latin quadriennium, from quadriennis (“4-year”) + -ium (suffix forming abstract nouns).

meaning: "adjective: Wakeful; alert. ""If you're still wakerife let me suggest another, possibly chastening, exercise in memory."""
The office or function of a president, presidency; the fact of being a president; (also) the period during which a president holds office.
etymology: From president + -ship.

meaning: 1. A perfume distilled from flowers of different kinds 2. A pattern of flowers and leaves used in tapestry, on porcelain, or in other decorative items.
adj. Feminine, womanly.
A plant adapted to growing in a very dry or desert environment.
etymology: From xero- (“dry”) + -phyte (“plant”).

meaning: noun: A formal gathering for conversation, especially on arts, literature, etc.
etymology: From Italian conversazione (“conversation”). Doublet of conversation.

meaning: adj. 1. (of the voice or phrasing) Full, round, and imposing 2. (of writing, style, or expression) Pompous; pretentious.
etymology: The noun is derived from the adjective.

meaning: A theory or science of faith.
etymology: From Ancient Greek πίστις (pístis, “faith”) + -ology.

meaning: In Anglo-Saxon England: a man who rules over a large area or a shire, usually subject to the king. Also used as a title placed immediately before (and in Old English also immediately after) a name.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Old English ealdormann. See alderman (from Old English aldormann).

meaning: Originally referred to a superior abbot whom a bishop appointed to supervise several 'ordinary' abbots (each styled hegumenos) and monasteries, or to the abbot of some especially great and important monastery. The title is also used as one purely of honour, with no connection to any actual monastery, and is bestowed on clergy as a mark of respect or gratitude for service to the Church.

n. Discharge of the emotional energy associated with a psychic trauma that has been forgotten or repressed; the process of bringing such a trauma back to consciousness, esp. as a psychotherapeutic technique; an instance of this.
etymology: Partial calque of German Abreagierung, from ab (“away from”) + Reagierung (“reaction”).

meaning: v. 1. To speak boastfully or bombastically about; to brag of; to extol. 2. To speak boastfully or bombastically; to indulge in gasconade.
etymology: From French gasconnade, from Gascon (“native of Gascony”) + -ade, equivalent to Gascon (“native of Gascony”) + -ade, literally "to talk like a Gascon". See French gasconnade.

meaning: adjective: Of or relating to the day before yesterday.
etymology: From Latin nū̆diū̆stertiānus (“taking place the day before yesterday”), from nudius tertius. Coined by Nathaniel Ward (1578–1652) in The Simple Cobler of Aggawam in America (1647).

meaning: n. A New Year's gift; a Christmas box, gift.

noun (phrase): An instance of the writing of ‘mene mene tekel upharsin’; (allusively) a sign or warning of impending disaster, an obscure omen. (similar to 'the writing on the wall'). etymology: The phrase is an elaborate piece of wordplay, relying on the fact that each word can also denote a different coin. The words written by a bodiless hand on the wall at Belshazzar's feast (as recounted in the biblical Book of Daniel)
etymology: A transliteration of Aramaic מְנֵא מְנֵא תְּקֵל וּפַרְסִין (mənē mənē təqēl ūp̄arsīn, “a mina, a mina, a shekel, and half-shekels”) from Daniel 5:25.

meaning: gift or tip
etymology: Borrowed from Hokkien 感謝 /感谢 (kám-siā, “thank you”).

meaning: dreadful, loathsome
etymology: From Middle English ugsom, equivalent to ug + -some.

meaning: n. A body of poetry, tales, etc., preserved through oral transmission as part of a particular culture, esp. a preliterate one
etymology: Blend of oral + literature, said to have been coined by the Ugandan linguist and literary theorist Pio Zirimu (died 1977): see the 1972 quotation.

meaning: n. A person who loves or is fond of woods or forests
etymology: From Ancient Greek νέμος (némos) + -philist.

meaning: "n. 1.) Practice, as opposed to the theory. 2.) Accepted praxis or custom 3.) A set of practice exercises. ""The contradiction between the declared intent and the actual praxis causes a clash."" "
etymology: Partly from Latin prāxis and partly from its etymon Ancient Greek πρᾶξις (prâxis, “action, activity, practice”).

word: "Sine qua non"
meaning: """without which not"" something absolutely indispensable or essential "

An obsessive womanizer. After Don Juan, a legendary 14th century Spanish nobleman, who devoted his life to seducing women. The story of Don Juan has been portrayed by many authors, including Moliere, Mozart, Byron, and Shaw. Earliest documented use: 1848.
etymology: After the legendary 14th-century Spanish nobleman Don Juan.

meaning: adj. Foolish, stupid; mentally confused or disordered. Also: perverse, obstinate, intractable; awry.
money (UK slang)
adj. of or relating to Saint Peter
etymology: From Latin Petrus + -ine, perhaps after Pauline. Compare Ancient Greek πέτρινος (pétrinos, “stony, rocky”) and Late Latin petrinus (“of stone”).

meaning: noun. a pounding with a pestle
etymology: From Latin pistillum + English -ation.

meaning: noun. A nagging, ill-tempered woman After the wife of Socrates,

noun: A man notorious for his many love affairs; a seducer. After Giacomo Casanova (1725-1798), Italian adventurer, known for womanizing, whose memoirs describe his promiscuous affairs. Earliest documented use: 1888.
etymology: Named after Venetian writer and adventurer Giacomo Casanova (1725–1798).

meaning: noun. ice beer (ice bock) A type of strong lager chilled to sub-zero temperatures after fermentation so that ice crystals may be strained off, thereby concentrating the flavour and alcohol content
etymology: Borrowed from German.

meaning: noun. 1.) a donkey, an ass 2.) a stupid person, a fool
etymology: From Ned + -y, Ned being a diminutive of Edward.

meaning: 1.) hypochondria 2.) Psychol. The biological drive towards self-preservation; love of life; (now chiefly Psychoanal.) this drive an indicator of normal and healthy emotional and social development; opposed to necrophilia. 3.) A love of or empathy with the natural world, esp. when seen as a human instinct.
etymology: From bio- + -philia.

meaning: intr. To move, stir, make a slight noise; to start, flinch.
etymology: Compare Saterland Frisian kwinkje (“to blink, wink with the eyes”), Middle Dutch quincken, quinken ("to shake, quiver"; whence modern Dutch kwinken, kwinkeleren (“to warble”)), German Low German quinken (“to blink, wink”).

meaning: A state of limited competition, in which a market is dominated by a small number of producers or sellers.
etymology: From oligo- (prefix meaning ‘few; several’) + -poly (suffix meaning ‘pertaining to the number of sellers in a market’), by analogy with monopoly.

meaning: An instrument or device used to measure the specific gravity or fat content of milk
etymology: From galacto- + -meter.

meaning: adjective: 1.) Sluggish; lacking energy. 2.) Of or relating to lymph. From Latin lympha (lymph, water). Formerly it was believed that an excess of lymph in the system resulted in sluggishness. Earliest documented use: 1649.
etymology: From lymph + -atic.

meaning: noun. Whispering; a whispering noise.
ear wax
etymology: From Medieval Latin caerūmen, from cera + -men. The appearance of the u is unexplained, but may have been influenced by words like albūmen and bitūmen.

meaning: adj. Mincing, affected; without force, drive, or spirit
noun: A member of a religious order living in a monastic community. (Also see eremite and anchorite.)
etymology: From Old French cenobite or Ecclesiastical Latin coenobīta, from coenobium, from Ancient Greek κοινόβιον (koinóbion, “community life, convent”), from κοινός (koinós, “common”) + βίος (bíos, “life”).

meaning: noun. A mythical conductor or guide of souls to the place of the dead (Charon, Hermes, Anubis) Also in extended use. In analytical psychology: (Jung's term for) the anima or animus, regarded as the link between the ego and the unconscious.
etymology: From Latin psȳchopompus, from Ancient Greek ψῡχοπομπός (psūkhopompós), from ψῡχή (psūkhḗ, “soul”) + πομπός (pompós, “conductor”).

meaning: 1.) a scar resulting from formation and contraction of fibrous tissue in a wound 2.) a mark resembling a scar especially when caused by the previous attachment of an organ or part (as a leaf)
etymology: Borrowed from Latin cicatrix.

meaning: adj. Of or belonging to the dawn From Latin aurora (dawn, goddess of the dawn). Earliest documented use: 1820.
etymology: Either the Latin aurōre(us) + the English -an or formed from the two English elements auror(a) + -ean.

meaning: noun. A flexible and informal style of organization and management, characterized by a lack of bureaucracy. Also (depreciative): bureaucracy characterized by inconsistency and lack of planning.
etymology: From ad hoc + -cracy, by analogy with bureaucracy; coined by American organizational consultant Warren Bennis (1925–2014) and American sociologist Philip Slater (1927–2013) in The Temporary Society (1964), and popularized by American futurist Alvin Toffler (1928–2016) in his book Future Shock (1970).

meaning: adjective: 1.) Having a common boundary. 2.) Confined within one common boundary. 3.) Having the same scope, in time, meaning, etc
etymology: Borrowed from Latin conterminus.

meaning: noun. The countryside; a district, esp. one frequented by tramps. Hence: the way of life of a tramp (British)
etymology: From monk + -ery.

meaning: "Adjective 1.) Overcome with anger; extremely indignant. 2.) Relating to or denoting apoplexy (stroke): ""an apoplectic attack"". "
etymology: From French apoplectique, from Late Latin apoplēcticus, from Ancient Greek ἀποπληκτικός (apoplēktikós), from ἀπόπληκτος (apóplēktos), from ἀποπλήσσω (apoplḗssō), from ἀπό (apó, “of, from”) + πλήσσω (plḗssō, “I strike”).

meaning: " let the buyer beware a principle in commerce: without a warranty the buyer takes the risk (from caveat, ""may he beware"", the subjunctive of cavere, ""to beware"" + emptor, ""buyer"") "
etymology: Latin for “buyer beware”; from Latin caveat (“may he / she / subject-noun beware”), the third-person subjunctive of caveō (“to beware”) + ēmptor (“buyer”).

meaning: adj: Hanging by a thread.
etymology: From, for respective components, Latin filum (“thread”) and pendulus (“hanging”).

meaning: noun. 1.) A container for storing books, a bookcase; 2.) (occas.) a room where books or other documents are stored, a library, an archive. 3.)Formerly also: †a repository or compendium of knowledge, such as a chronicle or commentary (obs.). Now hist. (chiefly in the form almery) and rare.
noun: The day after tomorrow. adjective: Of or relating to the day after tomorrow.
etymology: * Middle Low German övermorgen

meaning: noun. A letter of thanks for entertainment or hospitality, sent by a departed guest; a ‘bread-and-butter’ letter etymology: the name of a character, William Collins, in Jane Austen's Pride & Prejudice (ch. xxii)
etymology: * As a Slovene surname, Americanized from Kolenc, from koleno (“knee”) and the obsolete kolenc (“nipplewort”).

meaning: noun. Someone who gathers offal. often used disparagingly
The wavelike muscular contractions of the alimentary canal or other tubular structures by which contents are forced onward toward the opening. (is in the digestive system)
1.) A primeval god, offspring of Chaos. 2.) A part of the underworld where the wicked suffered punishment for their misdeeds. 3.) The underworld below the realm of Hades
etymology: From Latin Tartarus, from Ancient Greek Τάρταρος (Tártaros).

meaning: noun. Marriage late in life.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ὀψέ (opsé, “late”) + -gamy.

meaning: noun. 1. A tyrannical ruler; a tyrant. 2. A great or skilful hunter (freq. ironic); any person who likes to hunt. Also fig. 3. N. Amer. slang. A stupid or contemptible person; an idiot. Etymology:
etymology: Another possibility is that there was a (possibly unattested) dialectal or slang term for an idiot similar to Australian English ning nong (also compare nincom, ninny and nitwit; in fact, nincom – or even nimnod, conventionally considered a variant of nimrod – might exactly be the slang term in question), and that it became conflated with the more respectable term, perhaps as a euphemism.

meaning: noun: The study of proper names or of terms used in a specialized field.
etymology: First attested in 1936, from the adjective onomastic (“of or belonging to naming”) (1716) with a suffix -s, from French onomastique, from Ancient Greek ὀνομαστικός (onomastikós), from ὀνομαστός (onomastós, “named”), form of ὀνομάζω (onomázō, “I name”), from ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥ (“name”) (whence English name).

meaning: A. meaning: "In law, a per curiam decision (or opinion) is a ruling issued by an appellate court of multiple judges in which the decision rendered is made by the court (or at least, a majority of the court) acting collectively and anonymously. In contrast to regular opinions, a per curiam does not list the individual judge responsible for authoring the decision, but minority dissenting and concurring decisions are signed. Per curiams are not the only type of decision that can reflect the opinion of the court. Other types of decisions can also reflect the opinion of the entire court, such as unanimous decisions, in which the opinion of the court is expressed with an author listed. The Latin term per curiam literally means ""by the court""."

"The term pro forma, Latin for ""as a matter of form"" or ""for the sake of form"", is a term applied to practices or documents that are done as a pure formality, perfunctorily, or seek to satisfy the minimum requirements or to conform to a convention or doctrine In law, pro forma court rulings are intended merely to facilitate the legal process (to move matters along).Pro forma audiences are used to obey a formal demand. For example, one pro forma audience may be heard for a judge to order the production of a certain proof or to schedule another date. "

"The calends (Latin: kalendae, ""the called"") were the first days of each month of the Roman calendar. The Romans assigned these calends to the first day of the month, signifying the start of the new moon cycle. According to some ancient or modern proposed etymologies of the word, it was derived from the phrase kalo Iuno Covella or kalo Iuno Novella, meaning respectively ""hollow Juno I call you"" and ""new Juno I call you"", an announcement about the Nones or in proclaiming the new moon that marked the Kalends which the pontiffs made every first day of the month on the Capitoline Hill in the Announcement Hall. "
The Nones was eight days before the Ides, and fell on the 5th or 7th day of the month, depending on the position of the Ides. Thought to have originally been the day of the half moon.
Idus, Ides—thought to have originally been the day of the full moon, was the 13th day of the months with 29 days, but the 15th day of March, May, July, and October (the months with 31 days).

meaning: "1. plural but sing or plural in constr : the study of the methodological principles of interpretation (as of the Bible) 2 : a method or principle of interpretation The term hermeneutics , a Latinized version of the Greek hermeneutice , has been part of common language from the beginning of the 17 th century. Nevertheless, its history stretches back to ancient philosophy. Addressing the understanding of religious intuitions, Plato used this term in a number of dialogues, contrasting hermeneutic knowledge to that of sophia . Religious knowledge is a knowledge of what has been revealed or said and does not, like sophia , involve knowledge of the truth-value of the utterance. Aristotle carried this use of the term a step further, naming his work on logic and semantics Peri hermeneias , which was later rendered as De interpretatione "
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἑρμηνευτῐκός (hermēneutĭkós, “of or for interpreting”), from ἑρμηνεύω (hermēneúō, “translate, interpret”), from ἑρμηνεύς (hermēneús, “translator, interpreter”); sometimes ascribed as a Carian loanword. By surface analysis, hermeneutic + -s. Folk etymology suggests a connection with Hermes. The term was introduced c. 360 BCE by Aristotle in his text Perì Hermeneías (On Interpretation).
